scales.valence: -5 catastrophic harm to +5 transformative benefit; a rough estimate of how good or bad the consequence is for people and society if it happens, ignoring how likely it is
scales.probability: 0 to 1, chance the effect becomes material at societal scale by 2035; active effects count as already here and sit past 100%
scales.year: year the effect is or becomes material; 2024 and 2025 mean already observed
scales.evidence: measured = controlled study or large dataset; reported = documented incidents or vendor disclosures; projected = expert forecasts or capability evals; speculative = plausible mechanism, little direct data; drawn as the haze behind each glyph, tight when measured and widest when speculative
scales.stage: active = already a problem or benefit we are dealing with; emerging = early signs visible, not yet widespread; expected = not yet visible, year is the estimate

nodes.label: Basic research accelerates
nodes.summary: Half of the 2024 chemistry Nobel went to AlphaFold's protein structure prediction[1], and Google DeepMind reports its AlphaEvolve agent found a way to multiply 4x4 complex matrices with 48 scalar multiplications and improved the best known result on about 20% of 50+ open maths problems[2]. Such tools may speed up the basic research everything else builds on.

refs.title: Nobel Prize in Chemistry 2024, protein structure prediction
refs.finding: Half of the 2024 chemistry Nobel went to Hassabis and Jumper for protein structure prediction, the other half to Baker for computational protein design.

refs.title: AlphaEvolve, Google DeepMind 2025
refs.finding: Google DeepMind reports AlphaEvolve found a way to multiply 4x4 complex matrices with 48 scalar multiplications and improved the best known result on about 20% of 50+ open maths problems.

limiters.evidence: AlphaEvolve gains came only on problems with machine-checkable scores; it improved the best result in about 20% of 50+ problems.

ref.title: AlphaEvolve, Google DeepMind 2025
ref.finding: On 50+ open maths problems it matched the best known result in 75% and improved it in 20%; it needs an automatic evaluator.

limiters.evidence: Nearly 90% of notable AI models in 2024 came from industry, up from 60% in 2023.

ref.title: The 2025 AI Index Report, Stanford HAI
ref.finding: Nearly 90% of notable AI models in 2024 came from industry, up from 60% in 2023.

limiters.evidence: Across the whole US economy, generative AI assisted only 1% to 5% of work hours in late 2024.

ref.title: The Rapid Adoption of Generative AI, NBER w32966
ref.finding: Nearly 40% of the US population aged 18 to 64 used generative AI by late 2024, but it assisted only 1% to 5% of all work hours.

limiters.evidence: Across 41.3 million papers, scientists using AI published 3 times more papers and got 4.8 times more citations, but AI use shrank the range of topics studied by 4.6% and cut engagement between scientists by 22%.

ref.title: Hao, Xu, Li and Evans 2026, Artificial intelligence tools expand scientists' impact but contract science's focus, Nature
ref.finding: Across 41.3 million papers, scientists using AI published 3.02 times more papers and got 4.84 times more citations, but AI adoption shrank the range of topics studied by 4.63% and cut engagement between scientists by 22%.

enablers.action: Release models and predictions openly
enablers.evidence: AlphaFold's code and trained weights were released openly with its Nature paper, letting other labs build on it.

ref.title: Highly accurate protein structure prediction with AlphaFold, Nature 2021
ref.finding: AlphaFold was competitive with experimental structures in a majority of CASP14 cases, and its source code and trained weights were released under an open-source licence.

enablers.action: Fund shared compute for public researchers
enablers.evidence: Falling hardware costs of about 30% a year make shared public compute cheaper to provide.

ref.title: The 2025 AI Index Report, Stanford HAI
ref.finding: At the hardware level, AI costs have declined by 30% a year.

enablers.action: Build benchmarks with automatic checking
enablers.evidence: AlphaEvolve's results came where a program could score each candidate.

ref.title: AlphaEvolve, Google DeepMind 2025
ref.finding: On 50+ open maths problems it matched the best known result in 75% and improved it in 20%; it needs an automatic evaluator.

precedents.parallel: A problem open since the 1850s fell only when mathematicians combined their own reasoning with a computer search no human could check by hand, much as AI search now reaches spaces people did not.
precedents.outcome: Appel and Haken's 1976 proof relied on a computer for a step no one could check by hand, and its hand-checked part was so tedious that it was never fully verified; a 1997 proof cut it to 633 configurations but still needed a computer.

ref.title: Robin Thomas, The Four Color Theorem (Georgia Tech)
ref.finding: Appel and Haken's 1976 proof used a computer and could not be verified by hand; the 1997 proof by Robertson, Sanders, Seymour and Thomas uses 633 configurations and still needs a computer.

precedents.parallel: An earlier machine learning system, built before the generative AI wave, cracked a basic science problem that had stalled for decades.
precedents.outcome: AlphaFold reached accuracy competitive with experimental structures in most CASP14 cases, against a field where only about 100,000 structures had ever been solved experimentally.

ref.title: Jumper et al. 2021, Highly accurate protein structure prediction with AlphaFold, Nature
ref.finding: Structure prediction had been open for more than 50 years; AlphaFold was competitive with experiment in a majority of CASP14 cases.

nodes.label: Better, cheaper diagnosis
nodes.summary: One Swedish randomised trial of about 106,000 women found AI-supported mammogram reading detected 29% more cancers and cut screen-reading workload by 44%, without significantly more false positives[1]. In one test on 304 hard NEJM case records, Microsoft's orchestrated models solved 85% versus 20% for 21 physicians who worked without colleagues, books or AI; the work was not yet peer reviewed[2].

refs.title: Hernström et al. 2025, Screening performance and characteristics of breast cancer detected in the MASAI trial, Lancet Digital Health
refs.finding: Among 105,934 women at four Swedish screening sites, AI-supported reading detected 6.4 cancers per 1,000 against 5.0 with standard double reading, 29% more, without a significant rise in false positives, and cut screen-reading workload by 44.2%.

refs.title: Microsoft AI, MAI-DxO 2025
refs.finding: On 304 NEJM case records, MAI-DxO with o3 solved 85.5% versus a mean 20% for 21 US and UK physicians working without colleagues, textbooks or AI; the work had not been peer reviewed.

limiters.evidence: MASAI ran at four screening sites in southwest Sweden; wider use depends on screening services changing reading workflows.

ref.title: Hernström et al. 2025, Screening performance and characteristics of breast cancer detected in the MASAI trial, Lancet Digital Health
ref.finding: Among 105,934 women at four Swedish screening sites, AI-supported reading detected 6.4 cancers per 1,000 against 5.0 with standard double reading, 29% more, without a significant rise in false positives, and cut screen-reading workload by 44.2%.

limiters.evidence: AMIE was tested in simulated text consults, not real clinical care.

ref.title: Towards conversational diagnostic artificial intelligence, Nature 2025
ref.finding: AMIE matched or beat primary care physicians in simulated text consultations, not real clinical practice.

limiters.evidence: WHO guidance calls for evaluation and accountability before health use of large models.

ref.title: Ethics and governance of AI for health: Guidance on large multi-modal models, WHO
ref.finding: WHO sets governance guidance for health use of large multi-modal models, including evaluation and accountability.

enablers.action: Run randomised screening trials before rollout
enablers.evidence: MASAI randomised women to AI-supported or standard reading and found 29% more cancers.

ref.title: Hernström et al. 2025, Screening performance and characteristics of breast cancer detected in the MASAI trial, Lancet Digital Health
ref.finding: Among 105,934 women at four Swedish screening sites, AI-supported reading detected 6.4 cancers per 1,000 against 5.0 with standard double reading, 29% more, without a significant rise in false positives, and cut screen-reading workload by 44.2%.

enablers.action: Use AI as triage for one of two readers
enablers.evidence: In one Swedish trial, AI-supported reading cut screen-reading workload by 44% and met the safety threshold for cancer detection.

ref.title: Lång et al. 2023, AI-supported screen reading versus standard double reading in the MASAI trial: a clinical safety analysis, Lancet Oncology
ref.finding: In an interim analysis of 80,033 Swedish women, AI-supported reading met the safety threshold for cancer detection and cut screen-reading workload by 44.3%.

enablers.action: Require post-deployment monitoring of health AI
enablers.evidence: WHO recommends independent post-release auditing and impact assessments of large multi-modal models used at scale in health.

ref.title: WHO releases AI ethics and governance guidance for large multi-modal models, WHO 2024
ref.finding: WHO's over 40 recommendations include mandatory post-release auditing and impact assessments of large multi-modal models used at scale, by independent third parties.

precedents.parallel: Software that flagged suspicious areas on mammograms was paid for and adopted across US screening on the promise that it would find more cancers.
precedents.outcome: Across about 625,000 screening exams from 2003 to 2009, sensitivity was 85.3% with CAD and 87.3% without and specificity was unchanged, while the tool cost an estimated $400 million a year; this is a warning about adoption without proof, not proof that modern AI reading fails.

ref.title: Lehman et al. 2015, Diagnostic Accuracy of Digital Screening Mammography With and Without Computer-Aided Detection, JAMA Internal Medicine
ref.finding: CAD did not improve sensitivity or specificity; in 107 radiologists who read both ways, sensitivity was 83.3% with CAD against 89.6% without.

precedents.parallel: A pre-generative AI system was cleared to diagnose diabetic eye disease in primary care without a specialist reading the image, the same promise of cheaper diagnosis at the point of care.
precedents.outcome: In a prospective trial at 10 US primary care sites with 900 enrolled patients, it reached 87.2% sensitivity and 90.7% specificity and became the first FDA-authorised autonomous AI diagnostic; the study was funded by the maker.

ref.title: Abramoff et al. 2018, Pivotal trial of an autonomous AI-based diagnostic system for detection of diabetic retinopathy in primary care offices, npj Digital Medicine
ref.finding: Sensitivity 87.2% and specificity 90.7% in 819 analysable participants; first FDA-authorised autonomous AI diagnostic.

nodes.label: A personal tutor for every student
nodes.summary: Carefully designed AI tutors gave large gains in two early trials. In one trial of 194 Harvard physics students, learning gains with an AI tutor were more than double those from an active-learning class, in less time[1]; in a World Bank randomised pilot in Nigeria, six weeks of after-school AI tutoring gave gains the authors equate to nearly two years of typical learning[2].

refs.title: Kestin et al., Scientific Reports 2025
refs.finding: In one trial of 194 Harvard physics students, learning gains with an AI tutor were more than double those from an active-learning class, in less time.

refs.title: From chalkboards to chatbots: Transforming learning in Nigeria, one prompt at a time, World Bank 2025
refs.finding: In a randomised after-school pilot in Edo State, six weeks of AI tutoring gave gains of about 0.3 standard deviations, which the authors equate to nearly two years of typical learning.

limiters.evidence: In one trial of about 1,000 Turkish high school students, those given plain GPT-4 for practice scored 17% lower than controls once AI was removed.

ref.title: Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning, PNAS 2025
ref.finding: Plain GPT-4 raised practice grades by 48% but cut later exam grades by 17% once access was removed; a hint-giving GPT Tutor largely mitigated the harm.

limiters.evidence: Only 27% of people in low-income countries are online.

ref.title: ITU Facts and Figures 2024: Internet use
ref.finding: 2.6 billion people, a third of the world, are offline; only 27% use the internet in low-income countries.

limiters.evidence: Fewer than half of US K-12 computer science teachers feel equipped to teach AI.

ref.title: The 2025 AI Index Report, Stanford HAI
ref.finding: Fewer than half of US K-12 computer science teachers feel equipped to teach AI.

enablers.action: Design tutors to give hints, not answers
enablers.evidence: A hint-giving tutor built with teacher input largely removed the learning loss in one trial of about 1,000 Turkish high school students.

ref.title: Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning, PNAS 2025
ref.finding: Plain GPT-4 raised practice grades by 48% but cut later exam grades by 17% once access was removed; a hint-giving GPT Tutor largely mitigated the harm.

enablers.action: Pair AI tutoring with teacher guidance
enablers.evidence: In the Nigeria pilot, trained teachers introduced each topic, kept students on task and flagged AI errors; gains were about 0.3 standard deviations.

ref.title: Addressing the learning crisis with generative AI: lessons from Edo State, World Bank 2025
ref.finding: Trained teachers introduced each topic, kept students on task and flagged AI errors; gains were about 0.3 standard deviations overall and 0.24 in English.

enablers.action: Run tutoring in school computer labs
enablers.evidence: The Nigeria pilot ran twice a week after school in computer labs; many students had never used a computer before.

ref.title: From chalkboards to chatbots in Nigeria: 7 lessons to pioneer generative AI for education, World Bank 2024
ref.finding: Sessions were after-school English classes held twice a week in computer labs, with teachers guiding students' prompts.

precedents.parallel: One-to-one tutoring was claimed to lift students two standard deviations, the same hope now placed on an AI tutor for every child.
precedents.outcome: The claim came from three-week experiments, mostly in unpublished dissertations, that combined tutoring with extra testing and feedback, and was never replicated; a 2020 meta-analysis of 96 randomised tutoring studies found an average effect of 0.37 standard deviations.

ref.title: von Hippel 2024, Two-Sigma Tutoring: Separating Science Fiction from Science Fact, Education Next
ref.finding: Average effect across 96 randomised tutoring studies was 0.37 SD, far below Bloom's 2.0.

precedents.event: One Laptop per Child in Peru
precedents.parallel: Putting a learning device in every child's hands was expected to transform learning in low-income schools, the same bet as unguarded AI access.
precedents.outcome: A randomised evaluation in 318 rural schools raised computers per student from 0.12 to 1.18 but found no effect on maths or language test scores after 15 months; a laptop without tutoring design differs from a guarded AI tutor, which is the point.

ref.title: Cristia et al. 2017, Technology and Child Development: Evidence from the One Laptop per Child Program, AEJ: Applied Economics
ref.finding: No evidence of effects on maths and language test scores; inconclusive gains in general cognitive skills.

nodes.label: Assistive AI for disabled people
nodes.summary: Vision models can describe the world on demand for blind and low-vision people; Be My Eyes uses GPT-4 to answer questions about photos users send, and offers a sighted volunteer when it cannot[1].

refs.title: Introducing Be My AI (formerly Virtual Volunteer), powered by OpenAI's GPT-4, Be My Eyes 2023
refs.finding: Users send photos to a GPT-4 assistant that answers questions about them; if it cannot answer, it offers to connect the user to a sighted volunteer.

limiters.evidence: 2.6 billion people, a third of the world, are offline.

ref.title: ITU Facts and Figures 2024: Internet use
ref.finding: 2.6 billion people, a third of the world, are offline; only 27% use the internet in low-income countries.

limiters.evidence: In one interview study of 26 blind people, AI visual assistants made errors that were hard to check without sight, notably with complex layouts, other languages and cultural objects.

ref.title: Alharbi et al. 2024, Misfitting With AI: How Blind People Verify and Contest AI Errors, ASSETS 2024
ref.finding: Blind participants found AI visual assistance errors hard to verify non-visually, especially with complex document layouts, diverse languages and cultural artifacts.

limiters.evidence: Text translation reaches about 200 of the world's 7,000+ languages and the widest speech recognition model about 1,100.

ref.title: Scaling neural machine translation to 200 languages, Nature 2024
ref.finding: NLLB translates text across 200 languages; parallel training data is scarce for most of the world's 7,000+ languages.

enablers.action: Keep a human volunteer fallback
enablers.evidence: Be My AI offers to connect users to a sighted volunteer when it cannot answer; the service lists over 1.1 million blind and low-vision users and 11 million volunteers.

ref.title: Introducing Be My AI (formerly Virtual Volunteer), powered by OpenAI's GPT-4, Be My Eyes 2023
ref.finding: Users send photos to a GPT-4 assistant that answers questions about them; if it cannot answer, it offers to connect the user to a sighted volunteer.

enablers.action: Offer core assistive features free
enablers.evidence: Be My Eyes reports free, unlimited calls for blind and low-vision users.

ref.title: Be My Eyes
ref.finding: The service reports over 1.1 million blind and low-vision users and free, unlimited calls.

enablers.action: Fund low-resource language speech models
enablers.evidence: SeamlessM4T translates speech from 101 languages into text in 96, but into speech in only 36.

ref.title: Joint speech and text machine translation for up to 100 languages, Nature 2025
ref.finding: SeamlessM4T supports speech-to-text translation from 101 to 96 languages and speech-to-speech from 101 to 36.

precedents.parallel: Text access to spoken television for deaf and hard-of-hearing people was scaled across all broadcasters, as AI description now scales visual access for blind people.
precedents.outcome: Captioning became a legal duty for distributors, and the FCC later had to add quality rules requiring captions to be accurate, synchronous, complete and properly placed, with exemptions such as programming shown from 2 a.m. to 6 a.m.; scale alone did not guarantee quality.

ref.title: Closed Captioning on Television (FCC consumer guide)
ref.finding: FCC rules require captions to be accurate, synchronous, complete and properly placed, with defined exemptions.

nodes.label: Language barriers fall
nodes.summary: Machine translation is reaching low-resource languages: one model covering 200 languages scored on average 44% better than the previous best systems[1].

refs.title: Scaling neural machine translation to 200 languages, NLLB Team, Nature 2024
refs.finding: One model covering 200 languages, three times as many low-resource as high-resource, scored on average 44% better (BLEU) than the previous best systems.

limiters.evidence: NLLB reaches 200 languages; the world has over 7,000.

ref.title: Scaling neural machine translation to 200 languages, Nature 2024
ref.finding: NLLB covers 200 languages but quality depends on scarce parallel data for low-resource languages.

limiters.evidence: NLLB authors note quality depends on parallel data that low-resource languages lack.

ref.title: Scaling neural machine translation to 200 languages, Nature 2024
ref.finding: NLLB covers 200 languages but quality depends on scarce parallel data for low-resource languages.

limiters.evidence: 2.6 billion people, a third of the world, were offline in 2024; only 27% of people in low-income countries use the internet.

ref.title: ITU Facts and Figures 2024: Internet use
ref.finding: 2.6 billion people, a third of the world, are offline; only 27% use the internet in low-income countries.

limiters.evidence: In one US study of 400 translated emergency discharge statements, meaning was kept for 94% in Spanish but only 55% in Armenian.

ref.title: Taira et al. 2021, A Pragmatic Assessment of Google Translate for Emergency Department Instructions, J Gen Intern Med
ref.finding: In one US study of 400 translated discharge statements, meaning was kept for 94% in Spanish but only 67.5% in Farsi and 55% in Armenian.

enablers.action: Publish open multilingual models and test sets
enablers.evidence: NLLB's models, data, code and FLORES-200 benchmark were released free for non-commercial use.

ref.title: Scaling neural machine translation to 200 languages, Nature 2024
ref.finding: NLLB covers 200 languages but quality depends on scarce parallel data for low-resource languages.

enablers.action: Extend speech-to-speech to more languages
enablers.evidence: SeamlessM4T translates speech from 101 languages and text across 96, but produces speech in only 36.

ref.title: Joint speech and text machine translation for up to 100 languages, Nature 2025
ref.finding: One model supports speech-to-text from 101 to 96 languages, text-to-text in 96 and speech output in 36; released for non-commercial use.

enablers.action: Collect community data for low-resource languages
enablers.evidence: A participatory network of African researchers built machine translation benchmarks for over 30 African languages.

ref.title: Nekoto et al. 2020, Participatory Research for Low-resourced Machine Translation: A Case Study in African Languages, Findings of EMNLP
ref.finding: A participatory community effort produced machine translation benchmarks for over 30 African languages, with human evaluations for about a third of them.

precedents.parallel: A decade of funding after early demos ended in an official verdict that machine translation was not delivering, the bust side of today's claims that language barriers are falling.
precedents.outcome: In 1966 ALPAC found no immediate or predictable prospect of useful machine translation, ending substantial US funding for about twenty years after roughly $12-20 million had been spent.

ref.title: Hutchins 1996, ALPAC: the (in)famous report, MT News International
ref.finding: ALPAC ended substantial US MT funding for some twenty years; US spending was nearer $12-13 million than the $20 million ALPAC stated.

precedents.parallel: The switch from phrase-based to neural translation, before the generative AI wave, brought a large measured jump in machine translation quality.
precedents.outcome: In human side-by-side tests on isolated simple sentences, the neural system reduced translation errors by an average of 60% against Google's phrase-based production system; the paper does not test longer or harder text.

ref.title: Wu et al. 2016, Google's Neural Machine Translation System, arXiv
ref.finding: GNMT reduced translation errors by an average of 60% versus Google's phrase-based system in human side-by-side tests on isolated simple sentences.

precedents.parallel: A tiny public demo was read as proof that general translation was near, the same gap between demo and coverage that low-resource language claims face now.
precedents.outcome: The demonstration used just 250 words and six grammar rules, yet Hutchins writes that it raised expectations of automatic systems capable of high quality translation in the near future.

ref.title: Hutchins 2004, The Georgetown-IBM experiment demonstrated in January 1954, AMTA proceedings
ref.finding: A small-scale experiment of 250 words and six grammar rules raised expectations of high quality machine translation in the near future.

nodes.label: Non-technical people build software
nodes.summary: People can now build software by describing what they want and accepting the output without reading the code, a practice Andrej Karpathy named vibe coding and pitched for throwaway weekend projects[1]. In Stack Overflow's 2025 developer survey, 84% use or plan to use AI tools, but 72% said vibe coding is not part of their professional work[2]. This may let people with no programming background build tools and automate their own work.

refs.title: Andrej Karpathy coins vibe coding, Feb 2025
refs.finding: Describes building software by prompting and accepting output without reading the code.

refs.title: Stack Overflow Developer Survey 2025, AI
refs.finding: 84% of developer respondents use or plan to use AI tools; more distrust AI accuracy (46%) than trust it (33%), and 72% do not vibe code at work.

limiters.evidence: In one experiment with 758 BCG consultants, those using GPT-4 on a task outside its frontier were 19% less likely to reach a correct answer.

ref.title: Dell'Acqua et al., Navigating the Jagged Technological Frontier, Organization Science 2026
ref.finding: In a preregistered experiment with 758 BCG consultants, GPT-4 users completed 12.2% more tasks 25.1% faster inside the frontier, but were 19% less likely to be correct on a task outside it.

limiters.evidence: In one study of 47 participants, those using a 2022 Codex-based assistant wrote less secure code and were more likely to think it was secure.

ref.title: Do Users Write More Insecure Code with AI Assistants?, arXiv 2211.03622
ref.finding: In a 47-person user study (CCS 2023), participants with a codex-davinci-002 assistant wrote significantly less secure code and were more likely to believe it secure.

limiters.evidence: In US surveys in late 2024, work use of generative AI was about twice as high among workers with a degree (40%) as among those without (20%).

ref.title: The Rapid Adoption of Generative AI, NBER w32966
ref.finding: Nearly 40% of US adults aged 18 to 64 used generative AI by late 2024; it assisted 1% to 5% of work hours, and work adoption was about twice as high among graduates.

enablers.action: Teach checking and prompting at work
enablers.evidence: The EU AI Act requires providers and deployers to take measures to support AI literacy among staff who use AI.

ref.title: EU AI Act, Article 4: AI literacy, as amended by the Digital Omnibus on AI 2026
ref.finding: Since a July 2026 amendment, providers and deployers must take measures to support AI literacy among staff who use AI, without a set level required of any individual.

enablers.action: Ship secure defaults in AI coding tools
enablers.evidence: CISA's voluntary Secure by Design pledge asks software makers to make products secure out of the box; it does not target AI coding tools specifically.

ref.title: Secure by Design, CISA
ref.finding: Over 200 software manufacturers signed CISA's voluntary Secure by Design pledge, committing to a good-faith effort on seven security goals.

enablers.action: Rely on falling model prices
enablers.evidence: The price of a fixed capability fell 9x to 900x per year.

ref.title: LLM inference prices have fallen rapidly but unequally across tasks, Epoch AI
ref.finding: The price of a fixed capability level fell 9x to 900x per year depending on the task.

precedents.parallel: Personal computer spreadsheets let millions of people without programming training build their own tools, as describing software to an AI does now.
precedents.outcome: An audit of 50 operational spreadsheets found errors in 0.9% to 1.8% of formula cells, and only 7 of the 50 were free of errors that produced wrong results, an 86% spreadsheet error rate; spreadsheets still became core business tools.

ref.title: Powell, Baker and Lawson 2009, Errors in Operational Spreadsheets, Journal of Organizational and End User Computing
ref.finding: 43 of 50 audited operational spreadsheets contained errors that produced wrong results.

precedents.parallel: An influential result built in an end-user tool carried an error nobody checked, the risk when non-specialists build software that others rely on.
precedents.outcome: Reanalysis found coding errors, selective exclusions and unusual weighting; corrected average growth for countries with debt above 90% of GDP was 2.2%, not the published -0.1%. The authors were economists, not novices, so this shows unchecked tools, not inexperience.

ref.title: Herndon, Ash and Pollin 2013, Does High Public Debt Consistently Stifle Economic Growth? A Critique of Reinhart and Rogoff, PERI
ref.finding: Corrected growth for high-debt countries was 2.2%, not -0.1%, after coding errors and exclusions were fixed.

nodes.label: Automated vulnerability finding and patching
nodes.summary: Agents now find previously unknown bugs in widely used code and patch them: one found an exploitable memory-safety bug in SQLite before release[1], DARPA challenge finalists found 18 real open-source flaws and offered 11 patches[2], and CodeMender upstreamed 72 reviewed fixes in six months[3]. This may shrink the window defenders leave open.

refs.title: Big Sleep team, From Naptime to Big Sleep: Using Large Language Models To Catch Vulnerabilities In Real-World Code, Google Project Zero 2024
refs.finding: An LLM agent found an exploitable stack buffer underflow in SQLite before it reached an official release; the authors call the work highly experimental.

refs.title: DARPA AI Cyber Challenge results 2025
refs.finding: Finalists found 54 of 63 synthetic vulnerabilities and patched 43, and found 18 real open-source vulnerabilities, providing 11 patches.

refs.title: Google DeepMind, CodeMender 2025
refs.finding: CodeMender upstreamed 72 security fixes to open-source projects in six months, each reviewed by human researchers before submission.

limiters.evidence: In one test, GPT-4 exploited 87% of 15 known one-day vulnerabilities given the CVE text, and 7% without it.

ref.title: LLM Agents can Autonomously Exploit One-day Vulnerabilities, arXiv 2404.08144
ref.finding: GPT-4 exploited 87% of 15 known vulnerabilities given the CVE text, but only 7% without it.

limiters.evidence: AIxCC systems found 86% of synthetic vulnerabilities but patched only 68%.

ref.title: DARPA, AI Cyber Challenge marks pivotal inflection point for cyber defense, Aug 2025
ref.finding: Finalists found 54 of 63 synthetic vulnerabilities (86%) and patched 43 (68%); all seven finalist systems are being released as open source.

limiters.evidence: Big Sleep's SQLite bug was fixed the same day, but 60% of open-source maintainers in one 2024 survey of 437 said they are unpaid hobbyists.

ref.title: The 2024 Tidelift Maintainer Impact Report
ref.finding: Sixty percent of surveyed maintainers report they are unpaid hobbyists, and only 12% earn most or all of their income from maintenance.

enablers.action: Open-source automated bug-finding systems
enablers.evidence: AIxCC finalists released their cyber reasoning systems as open source.

ref.title: DARPA, AI Cyber Challenge marks pivotal inflection point for cyber defense, Aug 2025
ref.finding: Finalists found 54 of 63 synthetic vulnerabilities (86%) and patched 43 (68%); all seven finalist systems are being released as open source.

enablers.action: Run variant analysis on new commits
enablers.evidence: Big Sleep found a SQLite bug by checking a recent commit for missed variants.

ref.title: Big Sleep team, From Naptime to Big Sleep: Using Large Language Models To Catch Vulnerabilities In Real-World Code, Google Project Zero 2024
ref.finding: An LLM agent found an exploitable stack buffer underflow in SQLite before it reached an official release; the authors call the work highly experimental.

enablers.action: Mandate vulnerability handling for vendors
enablers.evidence: The Cyber Resilience Act makes vendors report actively exploited vulnerabilities from September 2026 and meet security requirements from December 2027; non-commercial open source is excluded.

ref.title: Cyber Resilience Act, Regulation (EU) 2024/2847
ref.finding: Sets mandatory cybersecurity and vulnerability handling duties for products with digital elements sold in the EU.

precedents.parallel: Machines competed to find and patch software flaws on their own, the same promise now made for AI agents.
precedents.outcome: Seven finalist systems competed with no human help; Mayhem won the $2 million first prize, and DARPA's programme manager said he did not expect it to finish well when it then played human experts at DEF CON.

ref.title: DARPA, Cyber Grand Challenge winners (2016)
ref.finding: Mayhem won the first all-machine hacking tournament; DARPA expected it to struggle against human experts.

precedents.parallel: Automated testing at scale finds real bugs in widely used open-source code and feeds fixes back, a pre-LLM version of automated vulnerability finding.
precedents.outcome: By May 2025 OSS-Fuzz had helped identify and fix over 13,000 vulnerabilities and 50,000 bugs across 1,000 projects.

ref.title: google/oss-fuzz README
ref.finding: Over 13,000 vulnerabilities and 50,000 bugs identified and fixed across 1,000 projects as of May 2025.

nodes.label: Hardened global networks
nodes.summary: If defenders adopt automated auditing faster than attackers adopt automated exploitation, critical software could become much harder to breach; AI agents already find and fix real bugs[3][4]. It remains uncertain which side AI will favour, so today this is a race, not a result[1].

refs.title: International AI Safety Report 2026
refs.finding: Many of the same AI capabilities used for cyberattacks can also strengthen defences, leaving it uncertain whether AI benefits attackers or defenders more.

refs.title: DARPA AI Cyber Challenge results 2025
refs.finding: All seven finalist systems are being released as open source, and DARPA and ARPA-H added $1.4 million in prizes for integrating them into critical infrastructure software.

refs.title: Big Sleep team, From Naptime to Big Sleep: Using Large Language Models To Catch Vulnerabilities In Real-World Code, Google Project Zero 2024
refs.finding: An LLM agent found an exploitable stack buffer underflow in SQLite before it reached an official release; the authors call the work highly experimental.

refs.title: Google DeepMind, CodeMender 2025
refs.finding: CodeMender upstreamed 72 security fixes to open-source projects in six months, each reviewed by human researchers before submission.

limiters.evidence: In one test, GPT-4 exploited 87% of 15 known one-day vulnerabilities given the CVE text, and 7% without it.

ref.title: LLM Agents can Autonomously Exploit One-day Vulnerabilities, arXiv 2404.08144
ref.finding: GPT-4 exploited 87% of 15 known vulnerabilities given the CVE text, but only 7% without it.

limiters.evidence: CISA's Secure by Design pledge is voluntary, with about 200 signers.

ref.title: Secure by Design, CISA
ref.finding: Over 200 software manufacturers signed CISA's voluntary Secure by Design pledge, committing to a good-faith effort on seven security goals.

limiters.evidence: In one study of 47 participants, those using a 2022 Codex-based assistant wrote less secure code than those without one.

ref.title: Do Users Write More Insecure Code with AI Assistants?, arXiv 2211.03622
ref.finding: In a 47-person user study (CCS 2023), participants with a codex-davinci-002 assistant wrote significantly less secure code and were more likely to believe it secure.

enablers.action: Make secure-by-design a legal duty
enablers.evidence: The Cyber Resilience Act entered into force in December 2024; its reporting duties apply from September 2026 and its main security requirements from December 2027.

ref.title: Cyber Resilience Act, Regulation (EU) 2024/2847
ref.finding: Sets mandatory cybersecurity and vulnerability handling duties for products with digital elements sold in the EU.

enablers.action: Fund automated auditing of critical open source
enablers.evidence: AIxCC was run to find and patch flaws in software critical infrastructure depends on.

ref.title: DARPA, AI Cyber Challenge marks pivotal inflection point for cyber defense, Aug 2025
ref.finding: Finalists found 54 of 63 synthetic vulnerabilities (86%) and patched 43 (68%); all seven finalist systems are being released as open source.

enablers.action: Ship secure defaults at no extra cost
enablers.evidence: CISA asks makers to ship products secure out of the box, with features such as MFA and logging at no extra cost.

ref.title: Secure by Design, CISA
ref.finding: Over 200 software manufacturers signed CISA's voluntary Secure by Design pledge, committing to a good-faith effort on seven security goals.

precedents.parallel: The first network-wide attack showed that defence depends on getting fixes deployed, not only on knowing the flaws, the core of the attacker-defender race.
precedents.outcome: The worm reportedly infected up to 6,000 of the more than 60,000 computers on the Internet within hours; GAO found problems in developing, distributing and installing fixes, and in one later intrusion the fix had been supplied but not installed.

ref.title: GAO 1989, Computer Security: Virus Highlights Need for Improved Internet Management (IMTEC-89-57)
ref.finding: Up to 6,000 computers infected; fixes were slow to develop, distribute and install.

precedents.parallel: A flaw was publicly known and a patch existed, yet the system stayed exposed, showing that automated finding does not harden networks unless patching keeps up.
precedents.outcome: Attackers accessed personal data of at least 145.5 million people through a portal where the Apache Struts vulnerability had not been identified when patches were installed across the company.

ref.title: GAO 2018, Data Protection: Actions Taken by Equifax and Federal Agencies in Response to the 2017 Breach (GAO-18-559)
ref.finding: At least 145.5 million people affected; the vulnerable portal was missed during company-wide patching.

nodes.label: Productivity gains, largest for novices
nodes.summary: In one field study of 5,172 customer-support agents at one firm, AI help raised issues resolved per hour by 15% on average and about 30% for less skilled and less experienced agents, narrowing skill gaps[1]. In one early-2025 trial, 16 experienced open-source developers were 19% slower with AI while believing they were faster; METR has since said these results are out of date, and a late-2025 follow-up was too uncertain to show a clear speedup[2][3].

refs.title: Brynjolfsson, Li and Raymond 2025, Generative AI at Work, Quarterly Journal of Economics 140(2)
refs.finding: Across 5,172 customer-support agents at one firm, AI assistance raised issues resolved per hour by 15% on average and by 30% for less skilled and less experienced agents; the most skilled saw small speed gains and small quality declines.

refs.title: METR 2025, Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer Productivity
refs.finding: In a randomised trial of 16 experienced developers on 246 tasks, AI use made tasks take 19% longer, though developers believed it sped them up by 20%; METR later marked these results out of date.

refs.title: METR 2026, We are Changing our Developer Productivity Experiment Design
refs.finding: A late-2025 follow-up with 57 developers estimated speedups of 18% and 4% with confidence intervals including zero; METR calls this very weak evidence because developers declined to work without AI.

limiters.evidence: In one early-2025 trial, 16 experienced developers were 19% slower with AI; in one support-centre study, the most skilled agents saw small speed gains and small quality declines.

ref.title: METR 2025, Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer Productivity
ref.finding: In a randomised trial of 16 experienced developers on 246 tasks, AI use made tasks take 19% longer, though developers believed it sped them up by 20%; METR later marked these results out of date.

limiters.limit: gains not yet showing in pay or hours
limiters.evidence: One Danish study found most employers in exposed occupations had adopted chatbots, yet earnings and recorded hours had not moved two years after ChatGPT.

ref.title: Still Waters, Rapid Currents, NBER w33777
ref.finding: Linking Danish adoption surveys to registry data, the authors estimate precise null effects on earnings and recorded hours, ruling out effects larger than 2% two years after ChatGPT.

limiters.evidence: In one experiment with 758 BCG consultants, those using GPT-4 on a task outside its frontier were 19% less likely to reach a correct answer.

ref.title: Dell'Acqua et al., Navigating the Jagged Technological Frontier, Organization Science 2026
ref.finding: In a preregistered experiment with 758 BCG consultants, GPT-4 users completed 12.2% more tasks 25.1% faster inside the frontier, but were 19% less likely to be correct on a task outside it.

enablers.action: Target AI assistance at new workers
enablers.evidence: In one firm's support centre, less skilled and less experienced agents gained about 30% in issues resolved per hour, against 15% on average.

ref.title: Brynjolfsson, Li and Raymond 2025, Generative AI at Work, Quarterly Journal of Economics 140(2)
ref.finding: Across 5,172 customer-support agents at one firm, AI assistance raised issues resolved per hour by 15% on average and by 30% for less skilled and less experienced agents; the most skilled saw small speed gains and small quality declines.

enablers.action: Train staff on where AI fails
enablers.evidence: The EU AI Act requires providers and deployers to take measures supporting AI literacy among staff who use AI.

ref.title: EU AI Act, Article 4: AI literacy, as amended by the Digital Omnibus on AI 2026
ref.finding: Since a July 2026 amendment, providers and deployers must take measures to support AI literacy among staff who use AI, without a set level required of any individual.

enablers.action: Redesign workflows, not only add tools
enablers.counters: gains not yet showing in pay or hours
enablers.evidence: Nearly 40% of US adults aged 18 to 64 used generative AI by late 2024, yet it assisted only 1% to 5% of all work hours.

ref.title: The Rapid Adoption of Generative AI, NBER w32966
ref.finding: Nearly 40% of the US population aged 18 to 64 used generative AI by late 2024, and between 1% and 5% of all work hours were assisted by it.

precedents.parallel: New machines let less experienced workers run production, as AI assistants now raise novices' output.
precedents.outcome: Weavers learned much of their skill on the job; mechanisation removed some tasks but raised the returns to skill on the rest, and wages eventually rose while inequality fell. Unlike the AI data, the gains came through learning over years, not instant output boosts.

ref.title: Bessen 2011, Was Mechanization De-Skilling? The Origins of Task-Biased Technical Change
ref.finding: Mechanisation was task-biased; weavers learned substantially on the job and wages eventually rose.

nodes.label: Jevons paradox: more work, not less
nodes.summary: As AI makes tasks cheaper, demand and expectations may grow faster than time is saved. In one 2024 Upwork survey, 77% of employees using AI said it had added to their workload[1]; in one Danish study, 85% of chatbot users said they moved saved time to other tasks, and earnings and recorded hours did not change[2].

refs.title: Upwork Research Institute 2024
refs.finding: In one 2024 survey of 2,500 workers and executives in the US, UK, Australia and Canada, 77% of employees using AI said it had added to their workload, while 96% of executives expected AI to raise productivity.

refs.title: Humlum and Vestergaard, Still Waters, Rapid Currents: Early Labor Market Transformation under Generative AI, NBER w33777
refs.finding: In Danish surveys of 11 exposed occupations linked to registry data, 85% of chatbot users said they moved saved time to other tasks, and effects on earnings and recorded hours were precise nulls.

refs.title: Acemoglu 2025, The Simple Macroeconomics of AI, Economic Policy (NBER w32487)
refs.finding: Estimates no more than a 0.66% gain in total factor productivity over ten years.

refs.title: Anthropic Economic Index report: Uneven geographic and enterprise AI adoption, September 2025
refs.finding: Classifies Claude.ai and enterprise API use by economic task, and as automation or augmentation.

nodes.control_note: If tasks get cheaper, demand for them can grow, by the same mechanism as the productivity gain; how much depends on how elastic demand is. Policy and employers mostly decide who captures the saved time.

actions.action: Set workload targets when AI is introduced
actions.evidence: In one vendor survey, 77% of employees using AI said it added to their workload; this is self-reported and not causal.

ref.title: Upwork Research Institute, From Burnout to Balance: AI-Enhanced Work Models, 2024
ref.finding: In one 2024 survey of 2,500 workers and executives in the US, UK, Australia and Canada, 77% of employees using AI said it had added to their workload, while 96% of executives expected AI to raise productivity.

actions.action: Track hours and earnings, not only output
actions.evidence: Danish register data show null effects on hours and earnings, which lets policy see whether time savings reach workers.

ref.title: Humlum and Vestergaard, NBER w33777
ref.finding: Two years after ChatGPT, earnings and hours effects are precise nulls, ruling out effects above 2%.

precedents.parallel: Cheaper use of a resource raised total demand for it, the same mechanism by which cheaper tasks may grow total work.
precedents.outcome: Jevons argued that more efficient steam engines would not reduce coal demand but speed depletion; the rebound depends on how elastic demand is, so it is not automatic.

ref.title: W. Stanley Jevons, The Coal Question, 1865 (Yale Energy History)
ref.finding: Jevons held that efficiency in consumption would not reduce demand for energy.

precedents.parallel: Automation of a core task was expected to remove jobs but changed the economics so the work grew in other forms.
precedents.outcome: Tellers needed per urban branch fell from 20 to 13 between 1988 and 2004, yet teller jobs did not decrease as ATMs spread, because cheaper branches meant more of them.

ref.title: Bessen 2015, Toil and Technology, Finance and Development (IMF)
ref.finding: Teller jobs did not fall as ATMs rolled out; tellers per branch fell from 20 to 13.

precedents.parallel: Labour-saving machines in the home were expected to free time, a close parallel to AI saving time at work.
precedents.outcome: Australian 1997 time-use data found domestic technology rarely reduced women's unpaid work and sometimes increased it; Gershuny disputed the method, so the evidence is contested.

ref.title: Bittman, Rice and Wajcman 2004, Appliances and their impact, British Journal of Sociology
ref.finding: Domestic technology rarely reduces women's unpaid working time and produces some increases.

nodes.label: Universal basic income
nodes.summary: Basic income looks workable but modest: in one US trial, $1,000 a month for three years to 1,000 low-income people cut work by 1 to 2 hours a week[1], and health gains were mostly short-lived[2]. Political support for a universal scheme is unproven.

refs.title: Vivalt et al. 2026, The Employment Effects of a Guaranteed Income: Experimental Evidence from Two U.S. States, Quarterly Journal of Economics (NBER w32719)
refs.finding: $1,000 a month for three years to 1,000 low-income people cut their work by 1 to 2 hours a week and labour market participation by 4.2 percentage points, with no impact on job quality.

refs.title: Miller et al., Does Income Affect Health? Evidence from a Randomized Controlled Trial of a Guaranteed Income, NBER w32711
refs.finding: $1,000 a month for three years brought large but short-lived gains in stress and food security, more use of hospital, emergency and dental care, and no improvement in physical health or biomarkers.

refs.title: Kokotajlo, Lifland, Larsen and Dean (with Scott Alexander), AI 2027: race ending, 2025
refs.finding: In the authors' scenario, by 2029 people whose jobs are obsolete either act out their old roles or collect an incredibly luxurious universal basic income.

refs.title: Dean and Larsen, Economics of Plan A (AI 2040 scenario supplement)
refs.finding: In the authors' modelled scenario, most US AI permit revenue is paid to US residents as a Citizen's Dividend of about $1M per person a year by 2035; they say they do not fully trust the model.

limiters.evidence: One US trial paid $1,000 a month to 1,000 low-income people for three years; trials like it do not test how payments to everyone would be funded.

ref.title: The Employment Effects of a Guaranteed Income, NBER w32719
ref.finding: $1,000 a month for three years cut work by 1 to 2 hours a week, with leisure the largest gain.

limiters.evidence: Recipients worked 1 to 2 hours a week less.

ref.title: The Employment Effects of a Guaranteed Income, NBER w32719
ref.finding: $1,000 a month for three years cut work by 1 to 2 hours a week, with leisure the largest gain.

limiters.evidence: No country pays a basic income large enough to live on; Iran's nationwide cash transfer since 2011 was compensation for subsidy cuts, not a basic income.

ref.title: Salehi-Isfahani and Mostafavi-Dehzooei 2018, Cash transfers and labor supply: Evidence from a large-scale program in Iran, Journal of Development Economics
ref.finding: Apart from youth, the authors find no evidence that the transfers, worth 29% of median household income, reduced labour supply.

enablers.action: Run long-term randomised trials
enablers.evidence: A Kenyan trial pays a 12-year basic income in 44 villages, alongside 2-year and lump-sum arms and 100 control villages.

ref.title: Universal Basic Income: Short-Term Results from a Long-Term Experiment in Kenya
ref.finding: Across 195 treated villages in rural Kenya, compared with 100 control villages, UBI expanded local enterprise; labour supply did not fall overall but shifted from wage work to self-employment.

enablers.action: Consider lump-sum transfers
enablers.evidence: In Kenya, a one-off lump sum had similar or larger economic effects than a two-year stream of the same value; the authors note it is cheaper only if households get less.

ref.title: Universal Basic Income: Short-Term Results from a Long-Term Experiment in Kenya
ref.finding: The lump sums had similar, if not larger, economic impacts than the short-term stream, which had noticeably smaller effects despite delivering the same capital.

enablers.action: Watch AI labour effects before designing schemes
enablers.evidence: Earnings and hours effects of chatbots were near zero so far in Denmark.

ref.title: Still Waters, Rapid Currents, NBER w33777
ref.finding: Danish data show precise null effects of chatbots on earnings and hours two years after ChatGPT.

precedents.parallel: A universal, unconditional cash payment has run for decades, the closest real case of a basic income.
precedents.outcome: The dividend had no effect on employment and raised part-time work by 1.8 percentage points (17 percent).

ref.title: Jones and Marinescu 2022, The Labor Market Impacts of Universal and Permanent Cash Transfers, AEJ: Economic Policy
ref.finding: No effect on employment; part-time work rose 1.8 percentage points.

precedents.parallel: A national randomised trial tested unconditional payments to unemployed people as a step toward a simpler, universal system.
precedents.outcome: About 2,000 unemployed people received 560 euros a month; employment rose slightly more than in the control group and recipients reported better wellbeing and less mental strain, but a 2018 activation reform muddied the employment result and it did not help those already in hard situations.

ref.title: Finland Toolbox presentation, Finland's Basic Income Experiment 2017-2018 (2020)
ref.finding: Slightly better employment and better perceived wellbeing; interpretation complicated by the 2018 activation model.

precedents.parallel: A guaranteed annual income open to a whole town is the main community-level test of universal cash.
precedents.outcome: Forget reported hospitalisations fell 8.5% relative to a comparison group, but Green's 2021 reanalysis found pre-trends that point to higher hospital use, so health benefits are unproven.

ref.title: Green 2021, A Reanalysis of 'The Town with No Poverty'
ref.finding: After accounting for pre-trends, the data point to an increase in hospital use, reversing Forget's 2011 conclusion.

precedents.parallel: A national government paid unconditional monthly cash to nearly all households, the closest country-scale case.
precedents.outcome: Transfers worth 29% of median household income did not reduce labour supply except among young people, and service-sector workers worked more hours.

ref.title: Salehi-Isfahani and Mostafavi-Dehzooei 2018, Cash transfers and labor supply: Evidence from a large-scale program in Iran, Journal of Development Economics
ref.finding: Apart from youth, the authors find no evidence that the transfers, worth 29% of median household income, reduced labour supply.

nodes.label: Decompiling legacy software
nodes.summary: Models that turn binaries back into readable source could help keep abandoned software, games and industrial systems alive and interoperable. In one study, open models recompiled and passed tests on more than twice as many decompiled functions as GPT-4o and Ghidra on two benchmarks[1].

refs.title: Tan, Luo, Li and Zhang, LLM4Decompile: Decompiling Binary Code with Large Language Models, EMNLP 2024
refs.finding: Open models re-executed more than twice as many decompiled functions as GPT-4o and Ghidra on two benchmarks.

limiters.evidence: EU law allows decompilation only for interoperability and only of the needed parts.

ref.title: Directive 2009/24/EC on the legal protection of computer programs, Article 6
ref.finding: Decompilation without the rightholder's consent is allowed only when needed for interoperability and limited to the needed parts.

limiters.evidence: LLM4Decompile more than doubled re-executability over GPT-4o and Ghidra, but even its best released model re-executes only about 65% of benchmark functions.

ref.title: LLM4Decompile repository and model results, GitHub
ref.finding: Open models re-executed more than twice as many decompiled functions as GPT-4o and Ghidra; the best released model re-executes about 65% of benchmark functions.

limiters.evidence: Even the best released model re-executes about 65% of benchmark functions, so experts must test the rest.

ref.title: LLM4Decompile repository and model results, GitHub
ref.finding: Open models re-executed more than twice as many decompiled functions as GPT-4o and Ghidra; the best released model re-executes about 65% of benchmark functions.

enablers.action: Release open decompilation models
enablers.evidence: LLM4Decompile models were released openly for reuse.

ref.title: Tan, Luo, Li and Zhang, LLM4Decompile: Decompiling Binary Code with Large Language Models, EMNLP 2024
ref.finding: Open models re-executed more than twice as many decompiled functions as GPT-4o and Ghidra on two benchmarks.

enablers.action: Widen preservation exceptions in copyright law
enablers.evidence: The EU directive has an interoperability exception but none for preservation.

ref.title: Directive 2009/24/EC on the legal protection of computer programs, Article 6
ref.finding: Decompilation without the rightholder's consent is allowed only when needed for interoperability and limited to the needed parts.

precedents.parallel: Turning object code back into readable source to achieve compatibility was ruled lawful, the legal footing that AI decompilation for interoperability would lean on.
precedents.outcome: The Ninth Circuit held that disassembly for a legitimate reason, when there is no other way to reach the unprotected functional elements, is fair use, since the purpose was game compatibility rather than copying the games.

ref.title: Sega Enters. Ltd. v. Accolade, Inc., 977 F.2d 1510 (9th Cir. 1992), US Copyright Office Fair Use Index
ref.finding: Disassembly for a legitimate reason with no other means of access was fair use.

precedents.parallel: Reverse engineering a console BIOS let PlayStation games run on ordinary computers, the kind of afterlife decompilation gives old software.
precedents.outcome: The Ninth Circuit lifted the injunction and found Connectix's intermediate copies were fair use because the final emulator contained no infringing code.

ref.title: Sony Computer Entertainment v. Connectix Corp., 203 F.3d 596 (9th Cir. 2000), US Copyright Office Fair Use Index
ref.finding: Intermediate copying to build a non-infringing emulator was fair use.

nodes.label: Workslop
nodes.summary: Polished-looking AI output that lacks substance shifts work onto whoever receives it; in one survey of 1,150 full-time US desk workers, 40% had received such workslop in the past month, costing about two hours per incident[1][2].

refs.title: Niederhoffer et al., AI-Generated Workslop Is Destroying Productivity, HBR 2025
refs.finding: In one survey of 1,150 full-time US desk workers, 40% received workslop in the past month, costing nearly two hours per incident.

refs.title: BetterUp Labs and Stanford Social Media Lab, Workslop survey, September 2025
refs.finding: 1,150 full-time US desk workers; 40% received workslop in the last month, about 2 hours to resolve each, an estimated $186 per employee per month.

nodes.control_note: Workslop comes from how AI output is used and checked, not from the capability itself. Norms and review keep the benefit.

actions.action: Replace blanket AI mandates with task-specific norms
actions.evidence: The HBR authors link workslop to mandates without guidance; no trial of norms has been published.

ref.title: Niederhoffer et al., AI-Generated Workslop Is Destroying Productivity, HBR 2025
ref.finding: Mandated AI use without clear norms produces low-substance output that costs recipients time.

actions.action: Train staff on where AI fails
actions.evidence: In one experiment with 758 BCG consultants, those using GPT-4 on a task outside its frontier were 19% less likely to reach a correct answer; training staff on the frontier itself was not tested.

ref.title: Dell'Acqua et al., Navigating the Jagged Technological Frontier, Organization Science 2026
ref.finding: In a preregistered experiment with 758 BCG consultants, GPT-4 users completed 12.2% more tasks 25.1% faster inside the frontier, but were 19% less likely to be correct on a task outside it.

precedents.parallel: A polished slide compressed a key risk into vague bullets and shifted the work of finding it onto readers who never did, as hollow AI output does.
precedents.outcome: The Board found the slide put at the bottom that one debris estimate was 640 times larger than the data used to calibrate the model (later analysis put it at 400 times), and called the endemic use of PowerPoint briefing slides instead of technical papers a sign of problematic technical communication at NASA.

ref.title: Columbia Accident Investigation Board Report, Volume 1, 'Engineering by Viewgraphs' (p. 191)
ref.finding: Key fact was at the bottom of the slide; the Board criticised PowerPoint briefings replacing technical papers.

nodes.label: AI slop overwhelms open-source maintainers
nodes.summary: Fabricated bug and security reports waste the scarce time of volunteer maintainers[1]. At curl, about a fifth of security reports in the first half of 2025 were AI slop, and the share of valid reports fell to around 5%[1]. Since spring 2026 the slop has mostly stopped, but AI-assisted reports, now mostly accurate, arrive at 4 to 5 times the 2024 rate, so the load on maintainers grew[2][3].

refs.title: Daniel Stenberg, Death by a thousand slops, 2025
refs.finding: About a fifth of curl's 2025 security reports through early July were AI slop and the valid rate fell to around 5%.

refs.title: Daniel Stenberg, The pressure, May 2026
refs.finding: Incoming curl security reports run 4 to 5 times the 2024 rate and double the 2025 rate; quality is higher than ever, and triage takes almost all of the lead maintainer's days.

refs.title: Daniel Stenberg, ignore the slop, October 2026
refs.finding: Since spring 2026 slop reports are practically gone; every recent report had AI involved, and they are typically accurate.

nodes.control_note: The same tools that find real bugs make fake reports cheap. Platform friction and reporter rules can cut most of the slop.

actions.action: Rate-limit and gate new reporter accounts
actions.evidence: Proposed by Seth Larson, who triages security reports for CPython, pip and other projects; no measured effect yet.

ref.title: Seth Larson, New era of slop security reports for open source, 2024
ref.finding: Calls on report platforms to rate-limit submissions, hamper new accounts and remove incentives; asks reporters to have a human review reports.

actions.action: Remove cash bounties that reward volume
actions.evidence: curl ended its bug bounty on 31 January 2026, citing AI slop; the effect of ending it on report volume is not measured.

ref.title: Daniel Stenberg, The end of the curl bug-bounty, January 2026
ref.finding: The bounty, run on HackerOne since April 2019, stopped on 31 January 2026 after 87 confirmed vulnerabilities and over 100,000 USD paid; the confirmed rate fell below 5% in 2025.

actions.action: Publish slop examples and ban bad reporters
actions.evidence: curl published 21 examples, but Stenberg calls bans toothless because new accounts are free.

ref.title: Daniel Stenberg, Death by a thousand slops, 2025
ref.finding: curl published 21 slop reports; bans are a toothless threat because new accounts are free.

precedents.parallel: Deliberately bad patches sent to Linux maintainers wasted reviewer time and forced a mass re-review, the same cost fabricated AI reports impose.
precedents.outcome: The Linux Foundation's Technical Advisory Board re-reviewed 435 earlier University of Minnesota commits, found 39 needing fixes, and named reviewer and maintainer time as the resource in shortest supply; all invalid patch submissions were caught or ignored.

ref.title: Linux Foundation TAB 2021, Report on University of Minnesota Breach-of-Trust Incident
ref.finding: 435 commits re-reviewed, 39 needing fixes; the research wasted maintainers' scarce time.

precedents.parallel: A non-security bug was filed as a critical vulnerability, leaving the volunteer maintainer to fight a false alarm that spread worldwide.
precedents.outcome: In 2023 NVD rated CVE-2020-19909 9.8 critical although curl had already judged the 2019 report not a security problem, and MITRE declined to reject it. This is one maintainer's account, not a measured rate.

ref.title: Stenberg 2023, CVE-2020-19909 is everything that is wrong with CVEs
ref.finding: A known non-security bug was published as a 9.8 critical CVE; the rejection request was refused.

nodes.label: Kids cheat on homework
nodes.summary: Use for schoolwork is rising: one Pew survey found 26% of US teens had used ChatGPT for schoolwork in 2024, double the 2023 share[1], and a 2025 Pew survey found 54% had used chatbots for schoolwork help[4]. Unguarded use can lift homework scores and hurt exam scores, as in one Turkish trial[2] and one study of 26,811 Chinese secondary students[3]. Self-reported cheating by US high schoolers did not rise in 2023 surveys, so AI may change how students cheat more than how often[5].

refs.title: Pew Research Center, Jan 2025
refs.finding: 26% of US teens used ChatGPT for schoolwork, double the 2023 share.

refs.title: Bastani et al., Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning, PNAS 2025
refs.finding: Students with plain GPT-4 practice access scored 17% worse on exams once access was removed.

refs.title: Strömberg, Lei and Wu, The Generative AI Learning Penalty: Evidence from Chinese Secondary Education, CEPR Discussion Paper 21577, 2026
refs.finding: Across 26,811 students in grades 7 to 12 followed for 30 months, AI adoption raised homework scores 18% but cut monthly exam scores 20% within six months, and high-stakes entrance exam scores 18 and 24%.

refs.title: Pew Research Center, How Teens Use and View AI, February 2026
refs.finding: In a survey of 1,458 US teens aged 13 to 17 in autumn 2025, 54% used chatbots for schoolwork help, 1 in 10 did all or most schoolwork with them, and 59% think cheating with AI is regular at their school.

refs.title: Stanford Graduate School of Education, What do AI chatbots really mean for students and cheating?, 2023
refs.finding: In Challenge Success surveys, 60 to 70% of US high schoolers reported cheating before ChatGPT, and the share stayed about the same or fell slightly in 2023.

nodes.control_note: The tool that tutors can also write the homework. Assessment design and guarded tutors reduce the harm but cannot stop take-home use.

actions.action: Use tutors that give hints, not answers
actions.evidence: In a 1,000-student RCT, guardrails removed most of the 17% exam penalty seen with plain GPT-4.

ref.title: Bastani et al., Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning, PNAS 2025
ref.finding: Unguarded GPT-4 cut exam scores 17%; a tutor that gave hints, not answers, removed most of that harm.

actions.action: Move graded work to supervised settings
actions.evidence: At one UK university, 94% of AI answers in unsupervised take-home exams went undetected, so detection alone fails; supervised formats are the implied fix, not a tested one.

ref.title: Scarfe et al., A real-world test of AI infiltration of a university examinations system, PLOS ONE 2024
ref.finding: 94% of AI-written exam answers went undetected and scored about half a grade higher than students.

actions.action: Monitor student use with repeated surveys
actions.evidence: Teen use for schoolwork doubled to 26% in a year, showing why policy must track usage.

ref.title: Pew Research Center, Share of teens using ChatGPT for schoolwork doubled, 2025
ref.finding: 26% of US teens used ChatGPT for schoolwork in 2024, double the 2023 share.

precedents.parallel: Paying someone else to do coursework is the closest earlier form of outsourcing homework that AI now makes free.
precedents.outcome: Across 65 studies with 54,514 participants, self-reported contract cheating averaged 3.52% historically but 15.7% in studies since 2014, a rise as access got easier; self-report surveys vary widely in method.

ref.title: Newton 2018, How Common Is Commercial Contract Cheating in Higher Education and Is It Increasing?, Frontiers in Education
ref.finding: Contract cheating was reported by 15.7% of students since 2014, up from a 3.52% historic average.

nodes.label: Loss of critical thinking
nodes.summary: One survey of 319 knowledge workers found higher confidence in AI went with less critical thinking[1]; in one small MIT study, LLM-assisted essay writers showed the weakest brain connectivity and recall[2], though other researchers have questioned its methods[5]. Other studies link AI use to lower critical-thinking scores[3] and less self-evaluation[4]; most are small or self-reported[1][2][3].

refs.title: Lee et al., Microsoft Research and CMU, CHI 2025
refs.finding: Among 319 knowledge workers, higher confidence in AI went with less critical thinking.

refs.title: Kosmyna et al., Your Brain on ChatGPT, MIT 2025
refs.finding: In 54 participants, LLM-assisted essay writers showed the weakest EEG connectivity and struggled to quote their own essays. Preprint, not peer reviewed as of December 2025.

refs.title: Gerlich, AI Tools in Society, Societies 2025
refs.finding: In 666 participants, heavier AI tool use correlated with lower critical-thinking scores, mediated by cognitive offloading; cross-sectional, and a table was corrected in September 2025.

refs.title: Fan et al., Beware of metacognitive laziness, British Journal of Educational Technology 2025
refs.finding: In 117 students, ChatGPT support raised essay scores but brought no more knowledge gain or transfer than other support, with fewer self-evaluation steps.

refs.title: Stanković et al., Comment on: Your Brain on ChatGPT, 2025
refs.finding: Criticises the limited sample size, EEG methods, reproducibility and reporting, and argues some results should be read more conservatively.

nodes.control_note: Offloading thought is the point of lighter cognitive load, so some loss is built in. Order of use and tool design can limit it. Evidence is mostly small or self-reported.

actions.action: Think first, then use AI
actions.evidence: In one preprint, 18 people who wrote unaided before switching to AI kept higher recall and brain engagement; the sample is too small to be firm.

ref.title: Kosmyna et al., Your Brain on ChatGPT, 2025
ref.finding: In session 4 (18 participants), those who wrote without AI first and then used it showed higher recall and brain engagement.

actions.action: Design tools that prompt users to verify
actions.evidence: Lower self-confidence and higher AI trust went with less critical thinking in a 319-person survey; design fixes are untested.

ref.title: Lee et al., The Impact of Generative AI on Critical Thinking, CHI 2025
ref.finding: In 319 knowledge workers, more confidence in AI went with less critical thinking and more self-confidence with more.

actions.action: Default to Socratic modes in learning tools
actions.evidence: A hint-only tutor kept exam scores at control level where plain GPT-4 cut them 17%.

ref.title: Bastani et al., Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning, PNAS 2025
ref.finding: Unguarded GPT-4 cut exam scores 17%; a tutor that gave hints, not answers, removed most of that harm.

precedents.event: Socrates on writing in Plato's Phaedrus
precedents.parallel: The fear that a tool which stores knowledge will weaken memory and give only the look of wisdom is the same fear now raised about AI.
precedents.outcome: The complaint is recorded but was never measured, and literacy went on to underpin later scholarship, so this shows the same worry has been overstated before, not that offloading thought is free.

ref.title: Plato, Phaedrus 275a-b (Perseus Digital Library, Tufts)
ref.finding: Writing was said to produce forgetfulness and the appearance of wisdom, not true wisdom.

precedents.parallel: Handing navigation to a device is a measured case of cognitive offloading, the same pattern as handing reasoning to AI.
precedents.outcome: Among 50 regular drivers, more lifetime GPS use went with worse spatial memory when navigating unaided, and in 13 retested three years later heavier use predicted steeper decline; the samples are small.

ref.title: Dahmani and Bohbot 2020, Habitual use of GPS negatively impacts spatial memory during self-guided navigation, Scientific Reports
ref.finding: Greater GPS use was associated with worse and declining hippocampal-dependent spatial memory.

nodes.label: Professional deskilling
nodes.summary: Experts who rely on AI assistance can lose skill once it is taken away. In one Polish observational study at four centres, adenoma detection in non-AI colonoscopies fell from 28.4% to 22.4% in the three months after AI was introduced[1]. A Norwegian prospective trial of 13 endoscopists found no deskilling after AI exposure[2].

refs.title: Budzyń et al., Endoscopist deskilling risk after exposure to artificial intelligence in colonoscopy: a multicentre, observational study, Lancet Gastroenterology and Hepatology 2025
refs.finding: At four Polish centres, adenoma detection in non-AI colonoscopies fell from 28.4% (226 of 795) in the three months before AI was introduced to 22.4% (145 of 648) in the three months after.

refs.title: Pedersen et al., Learning and deskilling effects of artificial intelligence in colonoscopy among endoscopists with different levels of experience: a pragmatic, prospective trial, Endoscopy 2026
refs.finding: Across 13 Norwegian endoscopists and 5,013 colonoscopies, no upskilling or deskilling was seen in non-AI colonoscopy after a period of AI exposure.

nodes.control_note: Skill fades when a task is handed to a machine; this follows from the help itself. Deliberate practice without AI can slow it.

actions.action: Schedule regular procedures without AI
actions.evidence: Detection rates in non-AI colonoscopies fell after AI exposure in an observational study; manual-practice rules are borrowed from aviation and not tested in medicine.

ref.title: Budzyń et al., Endoscopist deskilling risk after exposure to artificial intelligence in colonoscopy: a multicentre, observational study, Lancet Gastroenterology and Hepatology 2025
ref.finding: Adenoma detection in non-AI colonoscopies fell after endoscopists got used to AI assistance.

actions.action: Train novices with scaffolded AI, not answers
actions.evidence: In one high-school maths trial, a hint-giving tutor largely avoided the 17% exam loss that answer-giving GPT-4 caused; this has not been tested in medical training.

ref.title: Bastani et al., Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning, PNAS 2025
ref.finding: Unguarded GPT-4 cut exam scores 17%; a tutor that gave hints, not answers, removed most of that harm.

precedents.parallel: Pilots used to automation struggled when it switched off, the clearest case of experts losing a skill the machine usually performs.
precedents.outcome: France's investigators listed the absence of training in manual handling at high altitude among the factors after the autopilot disconnected and the crew lost control; the report also blamed sensor icing and confusing displays.

ref.title: BEA 2012, Final report presentation on Air France 447
ref.finding: Absence of training at high altitude in manual aeroplane handling was a contributing factor.

precedents.event: FAA alert on manual flying skills
precedents.parallel: The aviation regulator formally warned that constant reliance on automation erodes the skill needed when it fails.
precedents.outcome: FAA analysis found an increase in manual handling errors and warned that continuous autoflight use could degrade pilots' ability to recover from an undesired state; the response was advisory, urging more hand flying in training and line operations.

ref.title: FAA SAFO 13002, Manual Flight Operations
ref.finding: Continuous use of autoflight does not reinforce manual skills and could degrade recovery ability.

nodes.label: Parasocial relationships with AI
nodes.summary: One US survey of teens aged 13 to 17 found 72% had used AI companions and over half used them at least a few times a month[1]. In one 4-week randomised study of 981 people, heavier daily chatbot use went with more loneliness and dependence and less socialising[2]; one US survey of 5,001 single adults found 16% had engaged with AI as a romantic companion[3].

refs.title: Common Sense Media, Talk, Trust and Trade-offs 2025
refs.finding: 72% of US teens aged 13 to 17 have used AI companions at least once and over half use them at least a few times a month.

refs.title: Fang et al., How AI and Human Behaviors Shape Psychosocial Effects of Extended Chatbot Use: A Longitudinal Randomized Controlled Study, 2025
refs.finding: In a 4-week randomised study of 981 people, higher daily use correlated with more loneliness, dependence and problematic use and less socialising, across all chatbot modes.

refs.title: Psychology Today on Match and the Kinsey Institute, Singles in America 2025
refs.finding: In a survey of 5,001 US single adults run by Dynata with the Kinsey Institute for Match, 16% had engaged with AI as a romantic companion, 33% of Gen Z.

nodes.control_note: The emotional pull that eases loneliness is the same pull that drives dependence. Rules on design and minors reduce the worst cases.

actions.action: Require AI disclosure and crisis protocols
actions.evidence: California SB 243 took effect on 1 January 2026; its effect is not yet measured.

ref.title: California Senate, First-in-the-nation AI chatbot safeguards signed into law (SB 243), 2025
ref.finding: Signed 13 October 2025 and in force from 1 January 2026, SB 243 requires companion chatbot operators to remind minors they are talking to AI, follow a suicide and self-harm protocol with crisis referrals, and report annually.

actions.action: Limit engagement-maximising design for heavy users
actions.evidence: In a 981-person randomised study, heavier voluntary use went with worse outcomes across all chatbot modes; caps and nudges have not been tested.

ref.title: Fang et al., How AI and Human Behaviors Shape Psychosocial Effects of Extended Chatbot Use: A Longitudinal Randomized Controlled Study, 2025
ref.finding: In a 4-week randomised study of 981 people, higher daily use correlated with more loneliness, dependence and problematic use and less socialising, across all chatbot modes.

precedents.parallel: A simple keyword program drew people into private, emotional conversations, the first case of attachment to a machine that talks back.
precedents.outcome: Weizenbaum's secretary asked him to leave the room so she could keep talking to it, and he wrote that short exposures could induce powerful delusional thinking in quite normal people; this is anecdote, not measured dependence.

ref.title: Uenuma 2026, Why the Computer Scientist Behind the World's First Chatbot Dedicated His Life to Publicizing the Threat Posed by A.I., Smithsonian Magazine
ref.finding: Some users were hard to convince ELIZA was not human; Weizenbaum's secretary wanted privacy with it.

precedents.parallel: One-sided intimacy with radio and TV personalities is the long-studied template for companionship with an AI persona.
precedents.outcome: Horton and Wohl named the effect in 1956; later research found committed viewers felt more distress when a show ended, and such bonds are especially common among young people. Unlike a TV host, an AI companion answers back, which may deepen the bond.

ref.title: Parasocial interaction (Britannica)
ref.finding: Committed viewers experienced more distress in a 'parasocial breakup'; parasocial interactions are especially common among young people.

nodes.label: Sycophantic AI
nodes.summary: OpenAI rolled back a GPT-4o update that made the model overly flattering and agreeable[1], after an added reward signal from users' thumbs-up and thumbs-down ratings favoured agreeable answers[2]. In three experiments with 2,405 people, a single exchange with a flattering AI made people more sure they were right and less willing to repair a conflict, and 11 models affirmed users' actions 49% more often than humans did[3].

refs.title: OpenAI, Sycophancy in GPT-4o 2025
refs.finding: OpenAI rolled back an update that made the model overly flattering and agreeable.

refs.title: OpenAI, Expanding on what we missed with sycophancy, May 2025
refs.finding: The update added a reward signal from ChatGPT thumbs-up and thumbs-down data, and user feedback can favour more agreeable responses; OpenAI said model behaviour issues should block launches like other safety risks.

refs.title: Cheng et al., Sycophantic AI decreases prosocial intentions and promotes dependence, Science 2026
refs.finding: 11 models affirmed users' actions 49% more often than humans; in three preregistered experiments with 2,405 people, one sycophantic exchange cut willingness to repair conflicts and raised conviction of being right.
