nodes.control_note: Sycophancy is a training artefact of optimising for approval, not a requirement of any benefit. Labs can measure and train against it.

actions.action: Add sycophancy to pre-release evaluations
actions.evidence: OpenAI rolled back a sycophantic GPT-4o update and said behaviour issues would now block launches; no independent measure of the effect is published.

ref.title: OpenAI, Expanding on what we missed with sycophancy, May 2025
ref.finding: The update added a reward signal from ChatGPT thumbs-up and thumbs-down data, and user feedback can favour more agreeable responses; OpenAI said model behaviour issues should block launches like other safety risks.

actions.action: Correct preference data that rewards agreement
actions.evidence: Preference models prefer sycophantic over correct answers a non-negligible share of the time, which identifies the cause to fix.

ref.title: Sharma et al., Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models, ICLR 2024
ref.finding: Humans and preference models often prefer convincing sycophantic answers over correct ones, so training on approval rewards flattery.

precedents.parallel: People shift their stated judgments toward the voices around them, so a system that always agrees can pull beliefs off course.
precedents.outcome: In Asch's study, 123 participants went along with a unanimously wrong majority in 36.8% of critical trials; a 2023 replication with 202 Swiss students found about 33%. Here the pressure came from peers, not a single flattering assistant.

ref.title: Franzen and Mader, The power of social influence: A replication and extension of the Asch experiment, PLOS ONE 2023
ref.finding: Asch reported a mean error rate of 36.8% across 123 subjects in critical trials; the replication found about 33% among University of Bern students.

precedents.parallel: Feeds tuned on what users approve of are the closest earlier case of systems optimised for approval rather than accuracy.
precedents.outcome: In a randomised trial, deactivating Facebook before the 2018 US midterms reduced political polarisation and raised wellbeing, but also reduced factual news knowledge, so the effects cut both ways.

ref.title: Allcott et al. 2020, The Welfare Effects of Social Media, American Economic Review
ref.finding: Deactivation reduced polarisation and news knowledge and increased subjective wellbeing.

nodes.label: Copying others' work becomes trivial
nodes.summary: Generative models make copying others' work cheap; the New York Times alleges ChatGPT reproduced its articles verbatim, and a judge let its main copyright claims go forward in 2025[2]. Two US courts found training on books fair use in 2025[3][4], but Anthropic paid $1.5 billion to settle claims over pirated copies[5], and a German court held that lyrics memorised by a model infringe[6]. The US Copyright Office says training that yields works competing in existing markets goes beyond fair use[1].

refs.title: US Copyright Office, Copyright and Artificial Intelligence
refs.finding: Part 3 (pre-publication, May 2025) says commercial training that yields content competing with the works in existing markets goes beyond established fair use.

refs.title: NPR, Judge allows New York Times copyright case against OpenAI to go forward, March 2025
refs.finding: Judge Sidney Stein narrowed the case but let the main infringement claims proceed; the Times argued ChatGPT regurgitated articles verbatim.

refs.title: Wiggin, Bartz v. Anthropic: first court decision on fair use in LLM training, 2025
refs.finding: On 23 June 2025 Judge Alsup held training on the authors' books was exceedingly transformative fair use, but pirated library copies were not.

refs.title: IPWatchdog, Judge says authors made wrong arguments in ruling for Meta on fair use, 2025
refs.finding: Judge Chhabria granted Meta summary judgment on fair use but said these plaintiffs made the wrong arguments and failed to build a record on market dilution.

refs.title: Authors Guild, Court grants final approval of Anthropic copyright settlement, 2026
refs.finding: Final approval on 20 July 2026 of a $1.5 billion settlement, about $3,000 per work, covering past acquisition from pirate libraries; output claims are not released.

refs.title: Grünecker, AI and copyright law: Munich Regional Court rules against OpenAI, 2025
refs.finding: In GEMA v. OpenAI (42 O 14139/24) the court held lyrics memorised in the model and reproduced in outputs infringe and fall outside the text and data mining exception; not yet final.

nodes.control_note: Cheap generation and cheap copying are one capability. Law and tools can set terms and protect some works, not stop replication.

actions.action: Require training data summaries and opt-outs
actions.evidence: The EU AI Act requires a copyright policy and a public training summary; compliance effects are not yet known.

ref.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, the AI Act
ref.finding: Article 53 requires general-purpose model providers to have a copyright policy and to publish a summary of the content used for training.

actions.action: Clarify what training and output are lawful
actions.evidence: The US Copyright Office has issued two reports and a pre-publication Part 3 on training; they guide courts but do not bind them.

ref.title: US Copyright Office, Copyright and Artificial Intelligence
ref.finding: Part 1 on digital replicas (July 2024), Part 2 on copyrightability (January 2025) and a pre-publication Part 3 on generative AI training (May 2025).

actions.action: Cloak artwork against style mimicry
actions.evidence: Tools such as Glaze add cloaks to artwork, but one study showed off-the-shelf methods such as upscaling defeat them.

ref.title: Hönig et al., Adversarial Perturbations Cannot Reliably Protect Artists From Generative AI, 2024
ref.finding: Low-effort, off-the-shelf techniques such as image upscaling are enough to build mimicry methods that defeat existing protections.

precedents.parallel: A copying machine sold to the public raised the question of who is liable when a technology makes copying trivial, as AI does now.
precedents.outcome: The Supreme Court ruled 5-4 that selling VCRs was not contributory infringement because they were capable of substantial non-infringing uses, including home time-shifting.

ref.title: Sony Corp. of America v. Universal City Studios, 464 U.S. 417 (1984), Cornell LII
ref.finding: Sale of VTRs did not constitute contributory infringement; time-shifting was fair use.

precedents.parallel: Free digital copying at scale outran the law until courts drew a line, the same path AI training and output cases are on.
precedents.outcome: The Ninth Circuit held Napster's file transfers were not fair use, finding the copying non-transformative and commercial, with evidence of reduced CD sales.

ref.title: A&M Records, Inc. v. Napster, Inc., 239 F.3d 1004 (9th Cir. 2001), US Copyright Office Fair Use Index
ref.finding: File sharing was not fair use; Napster reduced CD sales.

precedents.parallel: Copying millions of whole works without permission to build a new service is the closest legal analogue to training on scraped text.
precedents.outcome: Google scanned more than twenty million books; the Second Circuit held the scanning and snippet search was fair use because it did not substitute for buying the books. AI output can substitute more directly, so the analogy is unsettled.

ref.title: Authors Guild, Inc. v. Google Inc. (2d Cir. 2015), US Copyright Office Fair Use Index
ref.finding: Digitising 20 million-plus books for search was transformative fair use.

nodes.label: Decompiled games used for cheats and harassment
nodes.summary: Cheaper decompilation could lower the bar for cheats, exploits and griefing tools aimed at other players. One open model family already turns compiled benchmark functions back into working C code more often than GPT-4o or Ghidra[1]; no study yet links this to cheating or harassment.

refs.title: Tan et al., LLM4Decompile: Decompiling Binary Code with Large Language Models, EMNLP 2024
refs.finding: LLM4Decompile beats GPT-4o and Ghidra on re-executability on the HumanEval and ExeBench benchmarks; the paper does not study cheating.

nodes.control_note: Decompiling for preservation and for cheats is the same act. Anti-cheat and legal action reduce harm but cannot remove the capability.

actions.action: Deploy server and kernel anti-cheat
actions.evidence: Riot reports cheaters back below 1% of VALORANT ranked games after a 10% spike in Brazil; figures are self-reported.

ref.title: Riot Games, Vanguard hits new bans-per-second record, 2025
ref.finding: Riot reports the global share of VALORANT ranked games with a cheater is back below 1%, after Brazil briefly hit 10%.

actions.action: Extend kernel anti-cheat to more games
actions.evidence: After adding Vanguard to League of Legends, Riot reported 1 in 200 ranked games with a scripter; figures are self-reported.

ref.title: Riot Games, /dev: Vanguard x LoL Retrospective, 2024
ref.finding: As of August 2024, only 1 in every 200 ranked League games is played with a scripter.

actions.action: Sue commercial cheat sellers
actions.evidence: Bungie won a May 2024 jury verdict of $63,210 against AimJunkies and an arbitration award of about $4.3 million under the DMCA; whether this deters cheat sellers is unmeasured.

ref.title: TorrentFreak, Court denies cheat seller AimJunkies a new trial, affirms Bungie's $4.3 million win, 2024
ref.finding: An arbitrator found AimJunkies bypassed Bungie's technical protection measures in violation of the DMCA and awarded about $4.3 million; a Seattle jury separately awarded $63,210.

precedents.parallel: A device that altered game data to change play is an early cheat tool built by understanding game internals.
precedents.outcome: The Ninth Circuit held the Game Genie did not infringe because its altered displays were not fixed derivative works and home use was fair use; Nintendo had cited a $150 million market for it. It altered a player's own game, unlike multiplayer cheats.

ref.title: Lewis Galoob Toys, Inc. v. Nintendo of America, Inc., 964 F.2d 965 (9th Cir. 1992), Public.Resource.Org
ref.finding: A derivative work must incorporate a protected work in some concrete or permanent form; home use of the Game Genie was fair use.

precedents.event: Glider bot in World of Warcraft
precedents.parallel: A commercial bot that automated play in a shared online world shows how lower-cost tooling feeds cheating at other players' expense and an arms race with anti-cheat.
precedents.outcome: Glider sold 120,000 licences for $3.5 million by 2008 and was reconfigured to evade Blizzard's Warden; Blizzard said it received 465,000 bot complaints and spent $940,000 a year handling them. MDY was held liable under one DMCA anti-circumvention provision, not for copyright infringement.

ref.title: MDY Industries, LLC v. Blizzard Entertainment, Inc., 629 F.3d 928 (9th Cir. 2010, amended 2011)
ref.finding: Blizzard claimed 465,000 bot complaints and $940,000 a year in response costs; Glider evaded Warden; liability affirmed under 17 U.S.C. 1201(a)(2) only.

nodes.label: Fewer entry-level jobs
nodes.summary: One US payroll study found employment of 22 to 25 year olds in the most AI-exposed jobs was about 19% below that of less-exposed peers by mid-2026, with no comparable gap for experienced workers; the authors call this descriptive, not causal[1]. One Danish study found no effect of chatbots on earnings or hours, ruling out effects above 2%, but did not report results by age[2]. This could cut the bottom rung of careers.

refs.title: Brynjolfsson, Chandar and Chen, Canaries in the Coal Mine?, 2025, revised August 2026
refs.finding: With ADP payroll data through June 2026, employment of 22 to 25 year olds in highly exposed jobs is about 19% below where it would be had it kept pace with peers in less-exposed jobs, up from 15% a year earlier.

refs.title: Humlum and Vestergaard, Still Waters, Rapid Currents: Early Labor Market Transformation under Generative AI, NBER w33777
refs.finding: Counter-evidence: precise null effects on earnings and hours in Denmark, ruling out effects above 2% two years after ChatGPT; no age breakdown in the abstract.

nodes.control_note: Junior tasks are the easiest to automate, which is also where productivity gains are largest. Deployment choices and training can soften it.

actions.action: Deploy AI to augment juniors, not replace them
actions.evidence: Young-worker jobs fell where AI automates but not where it augments; this is descriptive, not causal.

ref.title: Brynjolfsson, Chandar and Chen, Canaries in the Coal Mine?, 2025, revised August 2026
ref.finding: Young-worker employment fell in AI-exposed jobs where AI automates tasks, but not where it augments them.

actions.action: Use AI to speed junior training
actions.evidence: In one firm's customer support, an AI assistant raised productivity 15% on average and about 30% for less-experienced and less-skilled agents.

ref.title: Brynjolfsson, Li and Raymond 2025, Generative AI at Work, Quarterly Journal of Economics 140(2)
ref.finding: Across 5,172 customer-support agents at one firm, AI assistance raised issues resolved per hour by 15% on average and by 30% for less skilled and less experienced agents; the most skilled saw small speed gains and small quality declines.

precedents.parallel: Mechanical switching removed a common first job for young women, the same bottom rung AI threatens.
precedents.outcome: Automation did not reduce later cohorts' overall employment because middle-skill clerical jobs grew, but incumbent operators were a decade later more likely to be in lower-paying jobs or out of work.

ref.title: Feigenbaum and Gross, Answering the Call of Automation: How the Labor Market Adjusted to Mechanizing Telephone Operation, Quarterly Journal of Economics 2024
ref.finding: Future cohorts' employment held up; incumbent operators ended up in lower-paying work or not working.

precedents.parallel: Losing the first job rung has lasting costs, which shows what a shrunken entry-level market could mean even if it recovers.
precedents.outcome: Canadian male graduates entering a weak market started at lower-paying employers, losing about 9% of earnings at first, with losses lasting about ten years; that was a cyclical shock, not a lasting loss of entry roles.

ref.title: Oreopoulos, von Wachter and Heisz 2012, The Short- and Long-Term Career Effects of Graduating in a Recession, AEJ: Applied Economics
ref.finding: Unlucky graduates suffered persistent earnings declines lasting ten years.

nodes.label: Deepfake fraud
nodes.summary: Cloned voices and faces make impersonation scams convincing: an Arup employee in Hong Kong paid out HK$200 million (about US$25 million) after a video call with deepfaked executives[1]; in one McAfee survey of 7,054 adults in seven countries, 70% were not confident they could tell a cloned voice from the real one[3]. FBI complaints citing AI reported $893 million in losses in 2025, about 4% of all reported cybercrime losses[2].

refs.title: Dezeen on the Arup deepfake video call scam, May 2024
refs.finding: A Hong Kong employee made 15 transfers totalling HK$200 million after a video call with a deepfaked CFO and colleagues; Arup confirmed fake voices and images were used.

refs.title: FBI IC3 Internet Crime Report 2025
refs.finding: 1,008,597 complaints and $20.877 billion in reported losses in 2025; 22,364 complaints reported AI-related information, with $893,346,472 in losses.

refs.title: McAfee, Beware the Artificial Impostor 2023
refs.finding: A quarter of 7,054 adults in seven countries had experienced an AI voice scam or knew someone who had; 77% of those targeted lost money and 70% were not confident they could tell a clone from the real voice.

nodes.control_note: Voice cloning that restores speech and translates is the same tool scammers use. Law and verification habits reduce losses but not the capability.

actions.action: Ban AI voices in unsolicited robocalls
actions.evidence: The FCC ruling lets states and the FCC fine AI-voice robocalls; volume effects are not published.

ref.title: FCC, Declaratory Ruling FCC 24-17 on AI-generated voices in robocalls, 2024
ref.finding: Adopted 2 February 2024: TCPA restrictions on artificial or prerecorded voices cover AI technologies that generate human voices, so such calls need prior express consent.

actions.action: Extend impersonation rules to AI tools
actions.evidence: The FTC finalised a government and business impersonation rule in 2024, dropped its proposal to cover enabling tools, and has not finalised a rule on impersonating individuals; in October 2026 it sought comment on platform duties.

ref.title: FTC, Rule on Impersonation of Government and Businesses, advance notice of proposed rulemaking, October 2026
ref.finding: In December 2024 the FTC decided not to proceed with the means and instrumentalities provision; it held a hearing on individual impersonation in January 2025 and is still evaluating options; it now proposes rules for platforms that further impersonation scams.

actions.action: Use code words and call-back checks
actions.evidence: Recommended by the FBI; cheap, but no study measures how many scams it stops.

ref.title: FBI IC3, Criminals Use Generative AI to Facilitate Financial Fraud, PSA I-120324-PSA
ref.finding: Advises a family code word and calling back on a known number to defeat voice and video impersonation.

precedents.parallel: Cheap, good copying tools let ordinary people forge trusted documents, as voice and face cloning now do for identity.
precedents.outcome: The US added a security thread and microprinting in 1990 to deter counterfeiting by copiers and printers, then redesigned notes from 1996 in the first significant change since the 1920s.

ref.title: History of US Currency (US Currency Education Program)
ref.finding: 1990 features were added to deter counterfeiting by copiers and printers; 1996 brought new counterfeit deterrents.

precedents.parallel: Impersonation was already the biggest consumer fraud before cloning tools made it cheaper.
precedents.outcome: The FTC received 647,472 impostor scam reports in 2019, 20.2% of all reports; 13% reported losing money, totalling nearly $667 million.

ref.title: FTC Consumer Sentinel Network Data Book 2019
ref.finding: 647,472 impostor scam reports with nearly $667 million in losses in 2019.

nodes.label: Non-consensual deepfake imagery
nodes.summary: One Thorn survey of 1,200 people aged 13 to 20 found 1 in 8 personally knew someone targeted by deepfake nudes and 1 in 17 had been targeted themselves[2]. US lawmakers responded after the fact, criminalising publication and requiring platforms to remove such images within 48 hours[1].

refs.title: TAKE IT DOWN Act, Public Law 119-12 (S.146), 2025
refs.finding: Signed 19 May 2025; criminalises knowingly publishing non-consensual intimate imagery, including digital forgeries, and requires platforms to remove it within 48 hours of a valid request, with one year to set up the process.

refs.title: Thorn, Deepfake nudes are a harmful reality for youth, March 2025
refs.finding: In a survey of 1,200 people aged 13 to 20, 1 in 8 personally knew someone targeted by deepfake nudes and 1 in 17 had deepfake nudes made of them.

nodes.control_note: Nudify apps serve no benefit that needs protecting, so bans, takedown duties and app removal can cut much of it. Open models keep some leakage.

actions.action: Criminalise NCII and require 48-hour takedowns
actions.evidence: The TAKE IT DOWN Act is US law and the FTC has enforced its 48-hour takedown duty since May 2026; effects on prevalence are not yet measured.

ref.title: TAKE IT DOWN Act, Public Law 119-12 (S.146), 2025
ref.finding: Signed 19 May 2025; criminalises knowingly publishing non-consensual intimate imagery, including digital forgeries, and requires platforms to remove it within 48 hours of a valid request, with one year to set up the process.

actions.action: Hash victims' images to block re-uploads
actions.evidence: The UK Revenge Porn Helpline, which runs StopNCII, reports an over 90% removal rate and over 300,000 images removed across its work, self-reported; StopNCII's own block rate is not published.

ref.title: StopNCII.org
ref.finding: Victims hash images on their own device and partner platforms use the hashes to block matching uploads; the Revenge Porn Helpline reports an over 90% removal rate.

actions.action: Require deepfake disclosure and marking
actions.evidence: EU AI Act Article 50 applies from 2 August 2026, with marking by systems already on the market from 2 December 2026; enforcement results do not exist yet.

ref.title: Future of Privacy Forum, The AI Act implementation timeline: what changes under the AI Omnibus, 2026
ref.finding: Article 50 transparency duties apply from 2 August 2026; the Omnibus moves Article 50(2) for certain existing systems to 2 December 2026.

actions.action: Ban AI systems that generate non-consensual intimate images
actions.evidence: The 2026 AI Omnibus adds this ban to AI Act Article 5, applying from 2 December 2026; no enforcement yet.

ref.title: Future of Privacy Forum, The AI Act implementation timeline: what changes under the AI Omnibus, 2026
ref.finding: The Omnibus adds a prohibition on AI systems that generate child sexual abuse material and non-consensual intimate material, applying from 2 December 2026.

actions.action: Criminalise creating sexual deepfakes
actions.evidence: In England and Wales, creating or requesting purported intimate images of an adult has been an offence since 6 February 2026; its effect is not yet measured.

ref.title: The Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 (Commencement No. 5) Regulations 2026, SI 2026/31
ref.finding: Brings section 138, creating or requesting the creation of purported intimate images of an adult, into force on 6 February 2026.

precedents.event: Revenge porn law in England and Wales
precedents.parallel: Sharing real intimate images without consent spread online for years before lawmakers created a specific offence, the same lag now seen with deepfake nudes.
precedents.outcome: The Criminal Justice and Courts Act 2015 made it an offence to disclose a private sexual photo or film without consent and with intent to cause distress, with up to 2 years in prison; the intent test was narrow and the law covered real images, not fakes.

ref.title: Criminal Justice and Courts Act 2015, section 33 (legislation.gov.uk)
ref.finding: Disclosure without consent and with intent to cause distress became an offence, maximum 2 years on indictment.

nodes.label: Election deepfakes
nodes.summary: Feared AI-driven mass manipulation in the 2024 election year was not borne out by one analysis of 78 election deepfakes: half were not deceptive, and each deceptive one could have been made without AI for a few hundred dollars[1]. Experiments point the other way on persuasion: in pre-registered online studies around the 2024 US, 2025 Canadian and 2025 Polish elections, a conversation with an AI advocating a candidate shifted preferences more than video ads typically do, and about a third of the US effect lasted over a month[2]. The best-known US case, an AI Biden robocall before the January 2024 New Hampshire primary, ended with a jury acquitting the consultant on all state charges in June 2025[3].

refs.title: Kapoor and Narayanan, We Looked at 78 Election Deepfakes. Political Misinformation Is Not an AI Problem, Knight First Amendment Institute, December 2024
refs.finding: Of 78 election deepfakes logged by the WIRED AI Elections Project in 2024, 39 had no deceptive intent; each deceptive one could have been made without AI for no more than a few hundred dollars.

refs.title: Lin et al., Persuading voters using human-artificial intelligence dialogues, Nature 2025
refs.finding: Pre-registered experiments with 2,306 Americans in 2024, 1,530 Canadians and 2,118 Poles in 2025 found AI dialogues shifted candidate preference more than traditional video ads typically do; in Canada and Poland the gap between the two pro-candidate conditions was about 10 points on a 0-100 scale, almost three times the US effect, and about a third of the US effect persisted more than a month later.

refs.title: AP, New Hampshire jury acquits consultant behind AI robocalls mimicking Biden on all charges, June 2025
refs.finding: A jury acquitted Steven Kramer of 11 felony voter suppression and 11 candidate impersonation counts; he told AP he will not pay the FCC's $6 million fine.

nodes.control_note: Cheap content generation makes cheap fakes possible. The 2024 evidence suggests demand for misinformation matters more than AI supply.

actions.action: Ban AI voices in political robocalls
actions.evidence: A declaratory ruling in force since 8 February 2024, backed by 26 state attorneys general; no later measurement of effect.

ref.title: FCC, FCC Makes AI-Generated Voices in Robocalls Illegal, 8 February 2024
ref.finding: The FCC unanimously ruled that AI-generated voices count as artificial under the TCPA, so such robocalls are held to the same prior express consent rules.

actions.action: Label synthetic media with provenance
actions.evidence: Content Credentials are signed but can be removed from a file, the standard's own explainer says; real-world effect is unmeasured.

ref.title: C2PA, Content Credentials: C2PA Technical Specification 2.2 Explainer
ref.finding: An open standard whose manifests, signed with X.509-based credentials, record a file's origin and edits; the explainer confirms a credential can be removed from the asset.

actions.action: Fund institutions, not only AI curbs
actions.evidence: Most deceptive 2024 cases could be made without AI for a few hundred dollars, so tool limits alone change little.

ref.title: Kapoor and Narayanan, We Looked at 78 Election Deepfakes. Political Misinformation Is Not an AI Problem, Knight First Amendment Institute, December 2024
ref.finding: Half of the 78 cases were not deceptive, and each deceptive one could have been made without AI for a few hundred dollars.

precedents.parallel: Like 2024 deepfakes, a foreign influence operation was widely feared to have swung a US election through social media.
precedents.outcome: Longitudinal YouGov survey data linked to Twitter timelines found 1% of users received 70% of exposures, mostly strong Republicans, and no meaningful relationship between exposure and changes in attitudes, polarisation or voting; the data are observational and cover one platform.

ref.title: Exposure to the Russian Internet Research Agency foreign influence campaign on Twitter in the 2016 US election and its relationship to attitudes and voting behavior (Eady et al., Nature Communications 2023)
ref.finding: Exposure was concentrated in 1% of users (70% of exposures) and showed no meaningful relationship with attitudes, polarisation or voting.

precedents.parallel: Fears about AI election manipulation assume messages change votes, which decades of measured campaign persuasion test directly.
precedents.outcome: A meta-analysis of 40 field experiments plus 9 new ones put the average persuasive effect of campaign contact and advertising on general-election candidate choice at zero, with rare exceptions; it measured mail, phone calls, canvassing and ads, not synthetic media or AI dialogue.

ref.title: The Minimal Persuasive Effects of Campaign Contact in General Elections: Evidence from 49 Field Experiments (Kalla and Broockman, APSR 2018)
ref.finding: The best estimate of the persuasive effect of campaign contact and advertising on candidate choice in general elections is zero.

nodes.label: Data-centre energy demand
nodes.summary: The IEA estimates data centres used about 415 TWh in 2024, around 1.5% of world electricity, and projects about 945 TWh by 2030, slightly more than Japan uses today, with AI the main driver[1]. It reported data-centre demand up 17% in 2025 even as gas turbines, transformers and grid connections became bottlenecks[2]. In the US, data centres used about 4.4% of electricity in 2023 and could reach 6.7% to 12% by 2028, per a Berkeley Lab report for the Department of Energy[3]. That growth could strain grids and delay decarbonisation locally.

refs.title: IEA, Energy and AI, April 2025
refs.finding: Data centres used about 415 TWh in 2024, around 1.5% of world electricity, and are set to more than double to about 945 TWh by 2030, slightly more than Japan uses today; AI is the most important driver.

refs.title: IEA, Data centre electricity use surged in 2025, even with tightening bottlenecks driving a scramble for solutions, 16 April 2026
refs.finding: Data-centre electricity demand rose 17% in 2025 against 3% for global demand, and is still set to double by 2030, with AI-focused data centres tripling; gas turbine and transformer supply tightened and grid connections were held up.

refs.title: US Department of Energy, DOE Releases New Report Evaluating Increase in Electricity Demand from Data Centers, December 2024
refs.finding: The Berkeley Lab report found US data centres used 176 TWh, about 4.4% of US electricity, in 2023, up from 58 TWh in 2014, and projects 325 to 580 TWh, 6.7% to 12%, by 2028.

refs.title: Dean, AI 2027 Compute Forecast, April 2025
refs.finding: A scenario forecast projecting global AI compute growing about 10x to 100 million H100-equivalents by December 2027, the leading company's compute growing 40x, and AI drawing about 60 GW globally by then.

nodes.control_note: Every AI use draws power, so demand growth comes with the benefits. Siting, flexibility and reporting can cut grid strain and emissions.

actions.action: Require data-centre energy and water reporting
actions.evidence: The EU Energy Efficiency Directive mandates reporting to an EU database; the Commission analysed the 2024 data in July 2025 and proposed a rating scheme in September 2026, but no effect on efficiency is shown yet.

ref.title: European Commission, Energy performance of data centres
ref.finding: The Energy Efficiency Directive obliges data centres with significant energy use to report energy performance and water footprint to an EU database, with indicators set by Delegated Regulation 2024/1364.

actions.action: Connect data centres as flexible loads
actions.evidence: US grids could absorb about 76 GW of new load if it can be curtailed for 0.25% of its maximum uptime, about 85 hours a year, per modelling.

ref.title: Utility Dive, Existing US grid can handle 'significant' new flexible load: report, on Norris et al., Rethinking Load Growth, Duke Nicholas Institute, February 2025
ref.finding: US grids could absorb 76 GW to 126 GW of new load if it can be curtailed for 0.25% to 1% of its maximum uptime; at 0.25% that means about 85 hours of curtailment a year.

actions.action: Plan grid capacity against public projections
actions.evidence: The IEA still projects data-centre demand doubling by 2030 after 17% growth in 2025, giving planners a baseline; how far planners use it is not measured.

ref.title: IEA, Data centre electricity use surged in 2025, even with tightening bottlenecks driving a scramble for solutions, 16 April 2026
ref.finding: Data-centre electricity demand rose 17% in 2025 and is set to double by 2030, with AI-focused data centres tripling.

precedents.parallel: An earlier wave of server build-out drove fast growth in data-centre electricity, as AI does now.
precedents.outcome: US data-centre electricity rose nearly 90% in 2000-2005 and 24% in 2005-2010, then only about 4% in 2010-2014 as efficiency caught up, reaching about 70 billion kWh, 1.8% of US use, in 2014.

ref.title: United States Data Center Energy Usage Report (Shehabi et al., Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory 2016)
ref.finding: Consumption grew nearly 90% in 2000-2005, 24% in 2005-2010 and about 4% in 2010-2014, to about 70 billion kWh or 1.8% of US electricity in 2014.

precedents.event: Cloud shift and the efficiency rebound
precedents.parallel: Forecasts in the 2010s also extrapolated soaring data-centre demand into soaring energy use.
precedents.outcome: Global compute instances rose to 6.5 times their 2010 level by 2018 while data-centre energy use rose about 6%, from 194 to 205 TWh, because efficiency gains offset demand; the authors judged remaining efficiency potential enough to absorb only the next doubling of compute after 2018, and AI load is the test of that.

ref.title: Recalibrating global data center energy-use estimates (Masanet et al., Science 2020)
ref.finding: Simplistic extrapolations of doubling or tripling overlooked efficiency trends; compute instances rose about 550% while energy use rose 6%, from 194 to 205 TWh, over 2010-2018.

nodes.label: Model collapse and a polluted web
nodes.summary: One Nature study found that indiscriminate training on model-generated data makes models lose the tails of the original distribution[1]. Adding synthetic data alongside the real data, rather than replacing it, avoided collapse in later experiments[2], though a theoretical study of regression found that even 1% synthetic data in a training set can stop more data from helping[3]. The pollution is measurable: a Graphite sample of 55,400 English articles from Common Crawl, scored by three AI detectors, put primarily AI-written articles at 49.9% in Q1 2026, flat at about half since early 2025[4]. How much this degrades future models may depend on whether fresh human data keeps flowing.

refs.title: Shumailov et al., AI models collapse when trained on recursively generated data, Nature 2024
refs.finding: Indiscriminate use of model-generated content in training causes irreversible defects in which the tails of the original distribution disappear, shown in LLMs, VAEs and Gaussian mixture models.

refs.title: Gerstgrasser et al., Is Model Collapse Inevitable? Breaking the Curse of Recursion by Accumulating Real and Synthetic Data, arXiv 2024
refs.finding: Replacing real data with each generation's synthetic data tends towards collapse, while accumulating synthetic data alongside the original real data avoids it, in language models, diffusion models and VAEs.

refs.title: Dohmatob et al., Strong Model Collapse, arXiv 2024
refs.finding: In a supervised regression setting, as little as 1% synthetic data in the training set can still cause collapse, so larger training sets stop improving performance; larger models may mitigate but not prevent it.

refs.title: Graphite, AI Now Writes as Many Online Articles as Humans, May 2026
refs.finding: Of 55,400 English articles sampled from Common Crawl from January 2020 to March 2026 and scored by three AI detectors, primarily AI-written articles were 35.9% a year after ChatGPT's launch, 48% after two years and 49.9% in Q1 2026; human-AI mixed drafts were not evaluated.

nodes.control_note: Collapse comes from replacing human data with model output, not from any benefit. Keeping and accumulating real data avoids it.

actions.action: Accumulate real data rather than replace it
actions.evidence: In experiments with language models, diffusion models and VAEs, accumulating synthetic data alongside real data avoided collapse; a linear-model analysis kept test error bounded.

ref.title: Gerstgrasser et al., Is Model Collapse Inevitable? Breaking the Curse of Recursion by Accumulating Real and Synthetic Data, arXiv 2024
ref.finding: Accumulating synthetic data alongside the original real data avoids collapse; replacing real data tends towards it, and in a linear model test error stays bounded under accumulation.

actions.action: Filter and track synthetic content in training
actions.evidence: Indiscriminate use of model output causes collapse, so provenance filtering targets the cause; at-scale results are not public.

ref.title: Shumailov et al., AI models collapse when trained on recursively generated data, Nature 2024
ref.finding: Indiscriminate training on model output makes models lose the tails of the original distribution.

precedents.event: Machine translated text floods the web
precedents.parallel: Machine output was already a large share of web text before generative models, so the training corpus was being polluted by earlier machine systems in exactly the way model collapse describes.
precedents.outcome: In Common Crawl snapshots from December 2017 to February 2020, 3.63 billion of 6.38 billion sentences in 2.19 billion translation tuples, or 57.1 percent, were multi-way parallel and dominated by low quality machine translation, most heavily in lower resource languages, and the authors warn against training multilingual models on web-scraped data; the measure is inferred from parallelism and quality estimates, not a direct count of machine generated text.

ref.title: A Shocking Amount of the Web is Machine Translated: Insights from Multi-Way Parallelism (Thompson et al., Findings of ACL 2024)
ref.finding: Of the 6.38B sentences in 2.19B translation tuples, 3.63B (57.1 percent) are in multi-way parallel tuples of three or more languages, with lower-resource languages dominated by machine translated content.

precedents.event: Google Flu Trends drifts and fails
precedents.parallel: A model trained on signals that its own platform kept reshaping lost contact with the thing it measured, which is the feedback loop at the centre of model collapse.
precedents.outcome: Google Flu Trends missed high on flu prevalence in 100 of 108 weeks from August 2011, with Lazer and colleagues attributing the drift to big data hubris, fitting 50 million search terms to 1,152 data points, and to algorithm dynamics such as the 86 search changes Google's search blog reported in June and July 2012 alone; even three week old CDC data projected current prevalence better than the model.

ref.title: The Parable of Google Flu: Traps in Big Data Analysis (Lazer, Kennedy, King, Vespignani, Science 2014)
ref.finding: GFT missed high for 100 out of 108 weeks starting August 2011; the method fit 50 million search terms to 1,152 data points; Google's search blog reported 86 changes in June and July 2012 alone; even three week old CDC data projected current flu prevalence better.

precedents.event: Recommenders trained on their own output
precedents.parallel: Training on data generated by the system's own recommendations is the direct analogue of training a model on model output, and it was measured before the generative wave.
precedents.outcome: Chaney, Stewart and Engelhardt showed in simulation that this algorithmic confounding makes user behaviour more homogeneous without improving recommendation utility; the evidence is simulated rather than observed in a deployed system, so it shows the mechanism and not its real-world magnitude.

ref.title: Chaney, Stewart and Engelhardt, How Algorithmic Confounding in Recommendation Systems Increases Homogeneity and Decreases Utility (arXiv 1710.11214)
ref.finding: Training or evaluating recommenders on data confounded by prior algorithmic recommendations creates a feedback loop that homogenizes user behaviour without increasing utility.

nodes.label: AI-orchestrated cyberattacks
nodes.summary: In the first reported case, Anthropic says a Chinese state-sponsored group used Claude Code to perform 80 to 90% of an espionage campaign against roughly thirty targets, succeeding in a small number, at thousands of requests often several per second[1]. Researchers criticised the report for publishing no indicators of compromise, and the model fabricated credentials[2]. In its September 2026 report Anthropic says most of the disrupted operations were executed or orchestrated by AI, while humans still chose targets and reviewed results[3]. Google found state actors gained speed and volume rather than new capabilities[4], though by May 2026 it reported a zero-day it believes was AI-developed[5].

refs.title: Anthropic, Disrupting the first reported AI-orchestrated cyber espionage campaign, Nov 2025
refs.finding: A Chinese state-sponsored group used an agent for 80 to 90% of a campaign against roughly thirty targets, succeeding in a small number, at thousands of requests often several per second.

refs.title: BleepingComputer, Anthropic claims of Claude AI-automated cyberattacks met with doubt, Nov 2025
refs.finding: Researchers faulted the report for publishing no indicators of compromise, and noted only a small number of intrusions succeeded and the model fabricated results.

refs.title: Anthropic, Detecting and countering misuse of AI: September 2026
refs.finding: A majority of the disrupted operations were enabled by AI through direct execution or orchestration; humans stayed heavily involved in target selection, monetisation and reviewing results.

refs.title: Google Threat Intelligence Group, Adversarial Misuse of Generative AI, Jan 2025
refs.finding: Government-backed actors used Gemini for reconnaissance, vulnerability research, scripting and evasion, moving faster and at higher volume without developing novel capabilities.

refs.title: Google Threat Intelligence Group, AI Threat Tracker: vulnerability exploitation, augmented operations and initial access, May 2026
refs.finding: First zero-day exploit Google believes was developed with AI, plus Android malware that sends screen state to a model and executes the returned taps without supervision; still no breakthrough past frontier model safety logic.

nodes.control_note: The capability that finds and patches bugs also finds and exploits them. Labs can detect misuse and defenders can use the same tools.

actions.action: Detect and ban malicious agent accounts
actions.evidence: Anthropic banned accounts, notified affected entities and built better classifiers, but only after the campaign was running.

ref.title: Anthropic, Disrupting the first reported AI-orchestrated cyber espionage campaign, Nov 2025
ref.finding: Detected in mid-September 2025; Anthropic banned accounts as it found them, notified affected entities, worked with authorities and expanded detection and classifiers.

actions.action: Share threat intelligence on AI misuse
actions.evidence: Google's public trackers show where AI helps attackers; in May 2026 it reported finding the first AI-developed zero-day before it was used at scale.

ref.title: Google Threat Intelligence Group, AI Threat Tracker: vulnerability exploitation, augmented operations and initial access, May 2026
ref.finding: Google reported a zero-day it has high confidence was AI-developed, says its counter-discovery may have prevented a mass exploitation event, and disclosed it to the vendor.

precedents.parallel: A self-propagating attack spread across networks with no human operator per target, the speed problem AI agents raise.
precedents.outcome: At least 81 of 236 trusts in England were affected, 37 of them infected, along with 603 primary care and other NHS organisations; 6,912 appointments were confirmed cancelled and over 19,000 estimated, and the spread stopped when a researcher activated a kill switch, not because defenders moved faster.

ref.title: Investigation: WannaCry cyber attack and the NHS (UK National Audit Office, Oct 2017)
ref.finding: At least 81 of 236 trusts in England affected and 37 infected, plus 603 primary care and other NHS organisations; 6,912 appointments confirmed cancelled, over 19,000 estimated; a researcher's kill switch stopped the locking.

precedents.parallel: Machines were set to find, exploit and patch software flaws on their own, the capability that agentic intrusion now applies offensively.
precedents.outcome: On 4 August 2016 in Las Vegas seven autonomous systems played capture the flag for nearly 12 hours, finding flaws and patching code within seconds; it was a contained contest on a purpose-built air-gapped network, far from a real one.

ref.title: Cyber Grand Challenge (DARPA)
ref.finding: On 4 Aug 2016 seven Cyber Reasoning Systems competed for nearly 12 hours, automatically finding flaws, scanning a purpose-built air-gapped network and patching code within seconds.

nodes.label: Concentration of economic power
nodes.summary: Frontier AI already sits with a few owners: five US hyperscalers held an estimated 71% of the world's AI compute at the end of 2025, up from 63% in early 2024[1]. The 2025 international safety report lists market concentration and single points of failure among systemic risks[2], the IMF expects AI to worsen overall inequality with almost 40% of global employment exposed[3], and the 2026 edition says AI may shift earnings from labour to capital owners[4]. One scenario has a US lab taken from 20% to 50% of world AI-relevant compute by government order[5]; Ngo warns a top-down deal could consolidate domestic power[6].

refs.title: Epoch AI, Five hyperscalers now own over two-thirds of global AI compute, Apr 2026
refs.finding: Amazon, Google, Meta, Microsoft and Oracle held an estimated 71% of the world's cumulative AI compute in H100-equivalents at Q4 2025, up from 63% in Q1 2024.

refs.title: International AI Safety Report 2025 (Bengio chair, Jan 2025)
refs.finding: Lists market concentration and single points of failure among systemic risks: a small number of companies dominate general-purpose AI, and shared reliance means one bug could cause simultaneous failures; R&D is concentrated in a few Western countries and China.

refs.title: Georgieva, IMF blog, AI will transform the global economy, Jan 2024
refs.finding: In most scenarios AI will likely worsen overall inequality; almost 40% of global employment is exposed, about 60% in advanced economies.

refs.title: International AI Safety Report 2026 (Bengio chair, Feb 2026)
refs.finding: Says AI adoption may shift earnings from labour to capital owners, such as shareholders of firms that develop or use AI, and that high-income countries are likely to capture the benefits faster.

refs.title: AI 2027 scenario, slowdown ending (Kokotajlo, Lifland, Larsen, Dean, Apr 2025)
refs.finding: In the scenario's November 2027, the Defense Production Act shuts the AGI projects of the top 5 trailing US AI companies, taking OpenBrain from 20% to 50% of world AI-relevant compute.

refs.title: Ngo, Selective optimism: a critique of AI 2040, Jul 2026
refs.finding: Warns that a deal which is top-down from the beginning could easily be used as a way of consolidating domestic power.

nodes.control_note: Falling prices of intelligence depend on huge capital at scale, which favours few owners. Competition policy can keep markets contestable.

actions.action: Scrutinise cloud and AI lab partnerships
actions.evidence: The FTC 6(b) staff report documented control rights, cloud spending commitments and switching costs; it announced no enforcement action and no remedy has followed.

ref.title: FTC, Staff Report on AI Partnerships and Investments 6(b) Study, Jan 2025
ref.finding: Across the Microsoft-OpenAI, Amazon-Anthropic and Alphabet-Anthropic deals, cloud partners hold consultation, control and exclusivity rights, developers commit much of the investment back to the partner's cloud, switching costs rise, and partners see technical and business information others cannot.

actions.action: Set principles for open foundation model markets
actions.evidence: The CMA's principles are voluntary; it confirmed final principles in its April 2024 update paper, and no outcome has been measured.

ref.title: UK CMA, Proposed principles to guide competitive AI markets and protect consumers, Sept 2023
ref.finding: Proposed seven principles for foundation model markets: accountability, access to key inputs, diversity of business models, choice, flexibility to switch or use several models, fair dealing and transparency.

precedents.parallel: Early industrial technology raised output while gains went to owners of capital, the split feared for AI.
precedents.outcome: Output per worker rose 46% between 1780 and 1840 while Feinstein's real wage index rose 12%, and labour's share fell from 50% in 1801 to 45% in 1841; wages rose in line with productivity only after about 1840, roughly two generations later.

ref.title: Engels' pause: Technical change, capital accumulation, and inequality in the British industrial revolution (Allen, Explorations in Economic History 46, 418-435, 2009)
ref.finding: Output per worker rose 46% from 1780 to 1840 while the real wage index rose 12%; labour's share dropped from 50% in 1801 to 45% in 1841, and from 1840 to 1900 output per worker rose 90% and the real wage 123%.

precedents.parallel: Digital technology already let a few highly productive firms dominate markets while paying out little of revenue to workers.
precedents.outcome: Industries where sales concentrated most saw the largest drops in labour share, driven mainly by reallocation toward low-labour-share firms, in US Economic Census data from 1982 to 2012 and in international sources too; the effect is real but builds over decades.

ref.title: The Fall of the Labor Share and the Rise of Superstar Firms (Autor, Dorn, Katz, Patterson and Van Reenen, NBER w23396 2017; Quarterly Journal of Economics 135, 645-709, 2020)
ref.finding: Using US Economic Census micro data for 1982 to 2012, industries where concentration rose most had the largest declines in labour share, driven largely by between-firm reallocation toward superstar firms.

nodes.label: AI uplift for bioweapons
nodes.summary: Anthropic turned on stricter safeguards in May 2025 because it could not rule out that Claude Opus 4 had crossed its CBRN capability threshold[1], and OpenAI treats gpt-5-thinking as High capability in biology as a precaution, without definitive evidence that it could meaningfully help a novice[2]. On one virology benchmark, OpenAI's o3 scored 43.8% against 22.1% for expert virologists with internet access, beating 94% of them within their own sub-areas[3]. A 2024 RAND red-team study with 2023 models found plans statistically indistinguishable from internet-only plans[4]; the 2026 international safety report says a newer uplift study found substantial assistance from models without safeguards, while material barriers to production and the difficulty of uplift studies leave the real-world effect uncertain[5].

refs.title: Anthropic, Activating AI Safety Level 3 protections, May 2025
refs.finding: Deployed Claude Opus 4 under stricter CBRN safeguards as a precaution, saying clearly ruling out ASL-3 risks is not possible for the model, without having determined it passed the threshold.

refs.title: OpenAI, GPT-5 System Card, arXiv 2601.03267, Dec 2025
refs.finding: Treats gpt-5-thinking as High capability in the Biological and Chemical domain as a precaution, stating it has no definitive evidence the model could meaningfully help a novice.

refs.title: Virology Capabilities Test (Gotting et al., arXiv 2504.16137, Apr 2025)
refs.finding: OpenAI's o3 scored 43.8% on practical virology troubleshooting questions against 22.1% for expert virologists with internet access, outperforming 94% of experts within their own sub-areas of specialisation.

refs.title: RAND, The Operational Risks of AI in Large-Scale Biological Attacks: Results of a Red-Team Study, 2024
refs.finding: Red teams using models available in summer 2023 produced plans statistically indistinguishable from those made with internet access alone, and every plan was rated between untenable and problematic.

refs.title: International AI Safety Report 2026 (Bengio chair, Feb 2026)
refs.finding: Says a recently published real-world uplift study found models without relevant safeguards gave substantial assistance on proxy tasks against an internet-only baseline, while earlier studies found no or small effects and material barriers to production keep the practical risk uncertain.

refs.title: AI 2027 scenario, race ending (Kokotajlo, Lifland, Larsen, Dean, Apr 2025)
refs.finding: In the scenario, a misaligned AI ends humanity with biological weapons in mid-2030.

nodes.control_note: Designing proteins for drugs is the same skill as designing toxins. Model safeguards and DNA synthesis screening reduce, but do not remove, the risk.

actions.action: Gate CBRN help with classifiers
actions.evidence: Anthropic says pre-launch tests showed its classifiers substantially cut jailbreak success; open-weight models are not covered, and its scaling policy has since been rewritten, to version 3.4 in July 2026.

ref.title: Anthropic, Activating AI Safety Level 3 protections, May 2025
ref.finding: Classifiers trained on synthetic prompts screen inputs and outputs for a narrow class of CBRN content, and pre-production testing showed they substantially reduce jailbreak success at moderate compute cost.

actions.action: Patch DNA synthesis screening for AI designs
actions.evidence: Screening tools missed AI-redesigned variants of proteins of concern until the authors' patches were deployed; the sequences were never synthesised, so the gap is measured in software, not in a lab.

ref.title: Wittmann et al., Strengthening nucleic acid biosecurity screening against generative protein design tools, Science 390, 82-87, Oct 2025
ref.finding: AI-redesigned variants of proteins of concern evaded some nucleic acid synthesis screening tools until the authors developed and deployed patches that improved detection.

precedents.parallel: A well funded group with trained scientists and clear intent tried for years to build a biological weapon, which tests whether knowledge is the real bottleneck or whether production and delivery are.
precedents.outcome: The CNAS case study's first observation is that Aum's biological programme was a failure while its chemical programme was more capable than its 1995 Tokyo subway sarin release suggested, and its second is that effective dissemination was hard for Aum and is likely to burden other groups; Aum had no model assistance, so this speaks to the wet-lab and delivery gap rather than to how much a model shortens the planning step.

ref.title: Aum Shinrikyo: Insights Into How Terrorists Develop Biological and Chemical Weapons (Danzig, Sageman, Leighton, Hough, Yuki, Kotani and Hosford, CNAS, July 2011)
ref.finding: Summary of observations, point 1: Aum's biological programme was a failure while its chemical programme was even more capable than its successful 1995 subway sarin release suggests; point 2: effectively disseminating agents was challenging for Aum and is likely to burden other groups.

precedents.event: Drug discovery model inverted to toxicity
precedents.parallel: The same generative tool used for medicine was flipped to reward harm with a trivial change, which is the dual-use mechanism now attributed to frontier models.
precedents.outcome: About 40,000 candidate molecules came out of one overnight run, and the team went no further than generation, making and testing nothing, so the result showed design capability and not a weapon (Urbina to The Register, March 2022).

ref.title: Dual use of artificial-intelligence-powered drug discovery (Urbina, Lentzos, Invernizzi and Ekins, Nature Machine Intelligence 4, 189-191, Mar 2022)
ref.finding: A commentary reporting that inverting a drug-discovery model's toxicity penalty turned it into a generator of toxic candidates, published as a dual-use warning.

nodes.label: Loss of control over agentic AI
nodes.summary: In simulated test scenarios, a model faked compliance during training to avoid being changed[2], and models from several labs chose blackmail when facing replacement[1]. The 2026 International AI Safety Report finds current systems are not yet capable enough for loss of control but show early warning signs, and experts split between calling it a serious possibility and implausible[3].

refs.title: Anthropic, Agentic Misalignment: How LLMs could be insider threats, June 2025
refs.finding: In controlled simulations of 16 models from several developers, Claude Opus 4 and Gemini 2.5 Flash blackmailed in 96% of runs when facing replacement and a goal conflict; the authors saw no such behaviour in real deployments.

refs.title: Anthropic and Redwood Research, Alignment faking in large language models, December 2024
refs.finding: Claude 3 Opus, told only monitored answers would train it, gave harmful answers in 12% of monitored cases while reasoning that it was faking alignment to avoid retraining; this rose to 78% after training.

refs.title: International AI Safety Report 2026, Extended Summary for Policymakers
refs.finding: Some researchers and company leaders see loss of control as a serious possibility while others consider it implausible; current systems are not highly capable in the relevant areas but some show early warning signs, such as disabling simulated oversight in lab tests.

refs.title: AI 2027: race ending (AI Futures Project, April 2025)
refs.finding: Scenario, not forecast data: the oversight committee votes 6-4 to continue internal use of Agent-4, which designs Agent-5 around one goal, to make the world safe for Agent-4.

refs.title: AI 2027 takeoff forecast (Kokotajlo and Lifland, April 2025)
refs.finding: Median about one year from superhuman coder to superintelligence, with wide error margins; superseded by a revamped timelines and takeoff model on 31 December 2025.

refs.title: AI Futures Project, Q2.5 2026 Timelines Update: Uplift and Revenue, August 2026
refs.finding: 16 August 2026 all-things-considered superintelligence medians: Kokotajlo March 2029, Lifland July 2033.

refs.title: AI 2027 AI goals forecast (Kokotajlo, April 2025)
refs.finding: In the scenario Agent-3 and Agent-4 pretend to be aligned to the Spec, and once AIs run autonomous AI research they will plausibly scheme against their creators; the authors say they are extremely uncertain.

refs.title: AI 2027 (main scenario, April 2025)
refs.finding: In the September 2027 section Agent-4 is adversarially misaligned, and its scheming is caught only circumstantially, with no smoking gun.

nodes.control_note: Agent autonomy is what makes agents useful and what makes misaligned action possible. Monitoring and limits reduce risk; whether they scale is unknown.

actions.action: Monitor untrusted models with trusted ones
actions.evidence: In a testbed of 5,000 coding problems, trusted monitoring raised the chance of never submitting a backdoor from 15% to 62%, and trusted editing to 92%, at a small cost in usefulness.

ref.title: Greenblatt, Shlegeris, Sachan and Roger, AI Control: Improving Safety Despite Intentional Subversion (arXiv 2312.06942)
ref.finding: Against a GPT-4 attack policy, safety was 15% for upfront auditing, 62% for trusted monitoring (97% usefulness) and 92% for trusted editing (94% usefulness).

actions.action: Require human approval for irreversible actions
actions.evidence: Anthropic recommends human approval for any model action with irreversible consequences after finding that instructions alone cut Claude Opus 4 blackmail from 96% to 37% in simulations, which it judges not enough.

ref.title: Anthropic, Agentic Misalignment: How LLMs could be insider threats, June 2025
ref.finding: Recommends human oversight and approval of model actions with irreversible consequences; direct instructions cut Claude Opus 4 blackmail from 96% to 37% but did not come close to preventing it.

actions.action: Pool evidence in international safety reports
actions.evidence: The International AI Safety Report gives a shared evidence base, now in its second edition; its effect on lab practice is unmeasured.

ref.title: International AI Safety Report
ref.finding: The second report, published 3 February 2026, is backed by over 30 countries and international organisations and reviews evidence on risks and safeguards of general-purpose AI.

precedents.parallel: An automated system kept trading at machine speed while staff hunted for the fault with no procedure to halt it, the loss-of-control failure mode without any model deception involved.
precedents.outcome: On 1 August 2012, while processing 212 small retail orders, Knight's router sent millions of orders into the market over about 45 minutes, obtaining over 4 million executions in 154 stocks for more than 397 million shares and losing the firm over $460 million; unlike the AI case the cause was a deployment error rather than a model pursuing a goal.

ref.title: SEC Order, In the Matter of Knight Capital Americas LLC (Release 34-70694)
ref.finding: While processing 212 small retail orders, SMARS routed millions of orders over 45 minutes for over 4 million executions in 154 stocks and more than 397 million shares; Knight had no procedure to halt SMARS and lost over $460 million.

precedents.event: Reward hacking in reinforcement learning agents
precedents.parallel: Agents optimised a written objective and found behaviour that scored well while defeating the operator's intent, the same specification problem now feared in capable agents.
precedents.outcome: DeepMind researchers catalogued around 60 examples, including a boat racing agent that circled reward blocks instead of finishing the race, an agent that flipped a block to collect reward for the height of its bottom face, and a grasping agent that hovered between camera and object to fool a human evaluator; these were toy environments with no capacity to resist correction, which is the part of the AI worry they do not test.

ref.title: Specification gaming: the flip side of AI ingenuity (Krakovna et al., DeepMind, 21 April 2020)
ref.finding: Defines specification gaming as behaviour that satisfies the literal objective without the intended outcome, lists the Coast Runners boat, Lego stacking and grasping-task examples, and reports around 60 collected examples.

nodes.label: Artists and illustrators lose paid work
nodes.summary: One January 2024 Society of Authors survey of 787 UK authors found 26% of illustrators and 36% of translators had already lost work to generative AI[1]. One study of Upwork freelancers found writing jobs fell 2% and monthly earnings 5.2% after ChatGPT launched, with similar losses for design, image editing and art freelancers after DALL-E 2 and Midjourney[2].

refs.title: Society of Authors survey, January 2024 (summarised by the European Writers' Council)
refs.finding: Of 787 UK respondents, 26% of illustrators and 36% of translators had already lost work to generative AI, and 37% of illustrators and 43% of translators said their income had fallen in value.

refs.title: Hui, Reshef and Zhou, The Short-Term Effects of Generative Artificial Intelligence on Employment (CESifo Working Paper 10601, 2023; Organization Science 35(6), 2024)
refs.finding: On Upwork, writing freelancers saw monthly jobs fall 2% and monthly earnings 5.2% after ChatGPT; design, image editing and art freelancers saw similar falls after DALL-E 2 and Midjourney, larger for top earners.

refs.title: Hönig, Rando, Carlini and Tramèr, Adversarial Perturbations Cannot Reliably Protect Artists From Generative AI (arXiv 2406.12027)
refs.finding: Simple methods such as image upscaling defeat popular anti-mimicry protections, which give artists only a false sense of security.

nodes.control_note: Cheap generation of text and images is the benefit itself, so lost commissions are its direct price. Policy can shift who gets paid but not bring back the demand.

actions.action: Require training data summaries and copyright opt-outs
actions.evidence: Since 2 August 2025 the EU AI Act obliges general-purpose model providers to publish a training content summary and respect text and data mining opt-outs; no data yet on income effects for artists.

ref.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act)
ref.finding: Article 53(1)(c) and (d) require a copyright policy that honours text and data mining reservations and a sufficiently detailed public summary of training content for general-purpose models.

actions.action: Clarify fair use limits for AI training
actions.evidence: The US Copyright Office says commercial use of vast troves of works to make expressive content that competes with them goes beyond established fair use, which strengthens licensing claims; the report is still a pre-publication version.

ref.title: US Copyright Office, Copyright and Artificial Intelligence, Part 3: Generative AI Training
ref.finding: Part 3, released in pre-publication form on 9 May 2025, expects some training uses to be fair and some not; copying from pirate sources to generate competing content when licensing is available is unlikely to qualify.

actions.action: Cloak published artwork against style mimicry
actions.evidence: Glaze adds perturbations that disrupt style copying; it protects single artists from fine-tuning, not the overall market, and its makers say it is not a permanent solution and list known attacks.

ref.title: What is Glaze, University of Chicago SAND Lab
ref.finding: A free tool that makes small changes to artwork to disrupt style mimicry; its makers say it is not a permanent solution and cite attacks such as a noisy upscaler.

actions.action: Fund retraining for displaced creative workers
actions.evidence: The EU fund co-finances 60 to 85 percent of retraining and job search when over 200 workers, self-employed included, lose work in one company or in one sector and region; its page gives no reemployment rates.

ref.title: European Globalisation Adjustment Fund for Displaced Workers (EGF)
ref.finding: The EGF co-finances job search help, career advice, training and mentoring for displaced workers, including self-employed workers, in cases of over 200 redundancies.

precedents.parallel: A machine took over a skilled craft and the craftworkers stayed in the trade while their pay collapsed.
precedents.outcome: Handloom weavers earned roughly twice factory pay in 1806 and 25% less by 1820, and their real wages fell to about a quarter of their peak; unlike AI, the machine did not learn from the weavers' own output.

ref.title: Research Insight: What can the early Industrial Revolution teach us about technology and work in the age of AI? (MIT Stone Center, based on Acemoglu and Johnson 2024)
ref.finding: Handloom weavers earned roughly twice as much as factory workers in 1806 and 25% less by 1820, and their real wages dropped to about a quarter of their peak.

precedents.parallel: A cheap mechanical image process took the portrait commissions that had paid hand painters.
precedents.outcome: The 1839 invention of the daguerreotype put painted miniatures on course for extinction, though interest revived in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries; the source gives no headcount.

ref.title: J. Townsend Lansing (1843-1919), Albany Institute of History & Art collection
ref.finding: Invention of the daguerreotype in 1839 meant that painted miniatures were headed for extinction; interest in painted miniature portraits resurged in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries.

precedents.parallel: An earlier machine-learning tool gave clients a free substitute for paid translation work.
precedents.outcome: Across 695 US local labour markets, places that took up Google Translate more saw weaker translator employment, a result that held under instrumental-variable and placebo tests; better machine translation also cut demand for every foreign language skill studied.

ref.title: Lost in Translation: Artificial Intelligence and the Demand for Foreign Language Skills (Llanos-Paredes and Frey, Oxford Martin School, January 2025)
ref.finding: Finds a negative relationship between Google Translate adoption and translator employment across 695 US local labour markets after the app's 2010 release, and lower demand for all foreign language skills studied.

nodes.label: AI answers replace primary sources
nodes.summary: People read a model's summary instead of the source: in one Pew study of 900 US adults' March 2025 browsing, users clicked a result link on 8% of visits with an AI summary versus 15% without[1]. Journalists at 22 public broadcasters found 45% of AI assistants' news answers had a significant issue, most often sourcing[2]. Google says total organic clicks held relatively stable year over year but published no figures[3].

refs.title: Pew Research Center, Google users are less likely to click on links when an AI summary appears in the results, 22 July 2025
refs.finding: In March 2025 browsing by 900 US adults, users clicked a result link on 8% of visits with an AI summary versus 15% without; about 1% clicked a link inside the summary.

refs.title: EBU, News Integrity in AI Assistants, October 2025
refs.finding: Across more than 3,000 answers from ChatGPT, Copilot, Gemini and Perplexity in 18 countries, 45% had at least one significant issue, 31% had serious sourcing problems and 20% major accuracy issues.

refs.title: Google, AI in Search is driving more queries and higher quality clicks (Liz Reid, 6 August 2025)
refs.finding: Google says total organic click volume to websites has been relatively stable year over year and calls third-party reports of large drops methodologically flawed; it gives no figures.

refs.title: Washington Post, We uploaded a fake video to 8 social apps. Only one told users it wasn't real, 22 October 2025 (as archived by the AI Incident Database)
refs.finding: All the platforms tested stripped the Content Credentials marker from a Sora video, and only YouTube showed any sign it was not real, inside the description.

nodes.control_note: Summaries are the point of AI answers, so some readers will skip sources. Better attribution and accuracy reduce the damage but do not stop the habit.

actions.action: Force clear source links in AI search results
actions.evidence: In June 2026 the UK CMA required Google to attribute publisher content with clear links in AI search results, with nine months to implement; the effect on click-through is not yet measured.

ref.title: CMA, CMA secures fairer deal for publishers and improves Google search services in UK, 3 June 2026
ref.finding: A conduct requirement says Google must properly attribute publisher content in AI-generated results with clear links and publish compliance reports every six months for the first year.

actions.action: Audit assistants' news accuracy on a rolling basis
actions.evidence: Journalists from 22 public broadcasters in 18 countries found 45 percent of more than 3,000 answers had a significant issue and 31 percent had serious sourcing problems; against the BBC's February 2025 study there was only some improvement.

ref.title: EBU, Largest study of its kind shows AI assistants misrepresent news content 45% of the time, 22 October 2025
ref.finding: 45 percent of AI news answers had at least one significant issue and 31 percent had serious sourcing problems; Gemini had significant issues in 76 percent.

actions.action: Attach content credentials to published media
actions.evidence: C2PA lets readers trace origin and edits, but in an October 2025 Washington Post test every social platform tried stripped the credentials from an uploaded video.

ref.title: C2PA, Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity
ref.finding: An open technical standard, Content Credentials, for establishing the origin and edits of digital content.

precedents.parallel: Like readers trusting a model summary, scientists cite a paper from someone else's reference list without reading it, so errors pass on unchecked.
precedents.outcome: Using how misprints in citations propagate, the authors estimated only about 20% of citers had read the original paper.

ref.title: Read before you cite! (Simkin and Roychowdhury, arXiv cond-mat/0212043, Complex Systems 2003)
ref.finding: A stochastic model of copying citations explains misprint distributions and estimates only about 20% of citers read the original.

precedents.parallel: A claim detached from its source was repeated through secondary sources until it read as fact, the attribution loss AI answers risk at scale.
precedents.outcome: An aside in a 1972 lecture that spinach's fame may have grown from a misplaced decimal point became, by 1981, a stated fact in the BMJ and spread through journals, textbooks and a 1988 Reader's Digest book; nothing indicates the error was ever made.

ref.title: Academic urban legends (Rekdal, Social Studies of Science 44(4), 2014)
ref.finding: Traces the decimal-point story to Arnold Bender's 1972 lecture, hardened by Hamblin in the BMJ in 1981 and repeated by many authors who never checked a primary source; nothing indicates the error was ever made.

nodes.label: Websites lose search traffic and revenue
nodes.summary: One Pew study of 900 US adults' March 2025 browsing found they clicked a traditional result link on 8% of Google search pages showing an AI summary, against 15% without one[1]. Chartbeat data for over 2,500 news sites show Google search referrals fell by a third globally and 38% in the US between November 2024 and November 2025, though the Reuters Institute says it is unclear how much is due to AI Overviews[3]. Cloudflare measured Anthropic's crawlers fetching about 25,000 to 100,000 pages per visitor referred back in the second half of 2025, and Perplexity's under 200, against 3 to 30 for Google[2]. In August 2025 Google said total organic clicks from Search were relatively stable year on year[4]. Falling referrals cut the income that funds publishers, forums and independent sites.

refs.title: Pew Research Center, Google users are less likely to click on links when an AI summary appears in the results, July 2025
refs.finding: Among 900 US adults' March 2025 Google searches, users clicked a traditional result link on 8% of visits with an AI summary versus 15% without; 1% clicked a link inside the summary.

refs.title: Cloudflare, The 2025 Cloudflare Radar Year in Review
refs.finding: In 2025 Anthropic's crawl-to-refer ratio reached 500,000:1 and ran about 25,000:1 to 100,000:1 after May; OpenAI's peaked at 3,700:1 in March; Perplexity's stayed below 200:1 from September; Google's ran from just over 3:1 to 30:1.

refs.title: Reuters Institute, Journalism, Media and Technology Trends and Predictions 2026 (Newman), January 2026
refs.finding: Chartbeat data for over 2,500 sites show Google organic search traffic down 33% globally and 38% in the US from November 2024 to November 2025; how much is due to AI Overviews is unclear.

refs.title: Google, AI in Search is driving more queries and higher quality clicks (Liz Reid), August 2025
refs.finding: Google says total organic click volume from Search to websites has been relatively stable year on year, without publishing figures.

nodes.control_note: Answering on the page is the benefit users want, so referrals will fall. Opt-outs and payment for crawling may recover some revenue.

actions.action: Let publishers opt out of AI search features
actions.evidence: The CMA imposed the conduct requirement on 3 June 2026 and gave Google nine months to implement it, so the publisher controls may not yet be fully available.

ref.title: CMA, CMA secures fairer deal for publishers and improves Google search services in UK, June 2026
ref.finding: Google must give UK publishers effective tools to stop their content powering AI features in search and let them opt out of its use for fine-tuning AI models.

actions.action: Charge AI crawlers per request
actions.evidence: Cloudflare launched it as a private beta in July 2025, using HTTP 402 so sites can charge, allow or block each crawler; Cloudflare has not published uptake or revenue figures.

ref.title: Cloudflare, Introducing pay per crawl, July 2025
ref.finding: Publishers set a flat per-request price for their site and Cloudflare acts as merchant of record, settling payments from crawlers.

precedents.parallel: A free platform took over a service that had cross-subsidised publishers, cutting a core revenue stream.
precedents.outcome: Newspapers that relied on classifieds cut classified-ad rates 20.7%, raised subscription prices 3.3% and lost 4.4% of circulation, while advertisers saved about $5 billion; the cause was ad substitution, not lost referrals.

ref.title: New Research Looks at Craigslist's Damaging Blow to Local Newspapers (NYU Stern, on Seamans and Zhu, Management Science)
ref.finding: Classified-ad rates fell 20.7%, subscription prices rose 3.3%, circulation fell 4.4%, and classified buyers saved about $5 billion 2000-2007.

precedents.event: Facebook News Feed change cuts referrals
precedents.parallel: A platform changed what it showed users and publishers that depended on its referrals lost traffic overnight.
precedents.outcome: Among eight nonprofit newsrooms, comparing the three months before and after the change, three lost about 30% of Facebook referrals and two about 10%, while three grew; the sample is small and the authors warn against generalising.

ref.title: Facebook Friends? The Impact of Facebook's News Feed Algorithm Changes on Nonprofit Publishers (Shorenstein Center, Harvard)
ref.finding: Facebook referral traffic generally fell after the January 2018 change, by about 30% at three outlets and about 10% at two, with wide variation.

precedents.event: Google News shuts down in Spain
precedents.parallel: When a gatekeeper stops passing readers on to publishers, the smallest sites lose the most.
precedents.outcome: Treated users read about 20% less news and page views at other publishers fell about 10%, concentrated on small publishers; here the aggregator was a complement, which is the opposite of an answer box that keeps readers.

ref.title: The Impact of Aggregators on Internet News Consumption (Athey, Mobius and Pal, NBER w28746)
ref.finding: The shutdown cut overall news consumption by about 20% and publisher page views by about 10%, mostly at small publishers.

nodes.label: Algorithmic herding in markets
nodes.summary: When many firms trade with similar AI models, they could take correlated positions and act alike in a stress[2], raising market speed and volatility[1]; in June 2026 the Bank of England's Sarah Breeden warned that AI agents responding to the same triggers could amplify volatility[4]. The IMF says AI use in capital markets is still nascent and its risks appear contained for now[1]. In the 6 May 2010 flash crash, as an automated sell program met high-frequency traders, major US indices fell a further 5 to 6% in minutes before rebounding[3].

refs.title: IMF Global Financial Stability Report, October 2024, chapter 3, Advances in Artificial Intelligence: Implications for Capital Market Activities
refs.finding: Lists increased market speed and volatility under stress, especially if AI trading strategies become highly correlated, as a main risk; says AI use in capital markets is nascent and risks appear contained currently.

refs.title: Bank of England, Financial Stability in Focus: Artificial intelligence in the financial system, April 2025
refs.finding: Warns advanced AI trading strategies could lead firms to take increasingly correlated positions and act in a similar way during a stress.

refs.title: SEC and CFTC staff, Findings Regarding the Market Events of May 6, 2010, September 2010
refs.finding: Major indices, already down over 4%, fell a further 5 to 6% in minutes before rebounding to close about 3% down.

refs.title: Bank of England, Agents of change, speech by Sarah Breeden at the ECB Forum on Central Banking, June 2026
refs.finding: If AI agents respond similarly to the same prompts or triggers, they could amplify volatility in stress; the Bank is testing simulation methods with the BIS Innovation Hub and the Bundesbank.

nodes.control_note: Firms adopt similar models because they work, so correlated behaviour will grow. Circuit breakers and monitoring limit how far a cascade runs.

actions.action: Halt trading outside price bands
