High-stakes entrance exam scores fell 18% and 24%, with the full penalty taking about two years to appear[1][2]. Losses were concentrated among the roughly 80% of AI users whose unusually fast, high-scoring homework suggested outsourcing, while users who kept normal homework times lost little[1][2].

refs.title: Strömberg, Lei and Wu, The Generative AI Learning Penalty: Evidence from Chinese Secondary Education, CEPR Discussion Paper 21577, 2026
refs.finding: Across 30 months of data on 26,811 Chinese students in grades 7 to 12, AI adoption raised homework scores 18% and cut completion time 30%, while monthly closed-book exam scores fell 20% within six months and high-school and college entrance exam scores fell 18% and 24%, with the full penalty emerging after about two years; losses concentrated among the roughly 80% of AI users whose short completion times and high homework scores suggest outsourcing, and users with normal completion times showed small losses.

refs.title: The Decoder, A 26,000-student study shows AI's hidden learning cost takes two full years to surface, 2026
refs.finding: Learning losses are concentrated among students who finish homework unusually fast, which the article links to outsourcing work to AI; the full effect on entrance exams took about two years to appear.

nodes.control_note: The tutor and the homework machine are the same tool. In one trial a hint-only tutor removed the exam penalty, and students who kept normal homework times lost little; assessment choices may also limit it but are untested.

actions.action: Deploy hint-only AI tutors in class
actions.evidence: In one RCT of nearly 1,000 high school maths students in Turkey, unrestricted GPT-4 cut closed-book exam grades 17%, while a hint-only tutor showed no penalty.

ref.title: Bastani et al., Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning: Evidence from high school mathematics, PNAS 2025
ref.finding: GPT Base lowered closed-book exam grades 17% versus control, while the hint-only GPT Tutor was statistically equal to control.

actions.action: Weight grades toward supervised exams
actions.evidence: Follows from the gap between assisted and unaided scores; no direct trial found.

ref.title: Bastani et al., Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning: Evidence from high school mathematics, PNAS 2025
ref.finding: Practice grades rose 48% with unrestricted GPT-4, but grades on the later closed-book exam fell 17% versus students who never had access.

precedents.parallel: Handing route-finding to a GPS mirrors handing homework to AI: the skill goes unused and fails when the aid is removed.
precedents.outcome: In 50 drivers, more lifetime GPS use went with worse spatial memory when navigating without it, and in 13 retested three years later heavier use predicted a steeper decline; the longitudinal sample was small and it was not an exam setting.

ref.title: Habitual use of GPS negatively impacts spatial memory during self-guided navigation (Dahmani and Bohbot, Scientific Reports 2020)
ref.finding: Greater GPS use since initial testing was associated with a steeper decline in hippocampal-dependent spatial memory.

precedents.parallel: Students who expect an AI to have the answer may not encode it, as people stopped storing facts they expected to find online.
precedents.outcome: Across four lab studies, people who expected future access to information recalled the information itself less and recalled where to find it better; these were short lab tasks, not long-run grades.

ref.title: Google effects on memory: cognitive consequences of having information at our fingertips (Sparrow, Liu and Wegner, Science 2011)
ref.finding: When people expect to have future access to information, they have lower rates of recall of the information itself.

precedents.parallel: Calculators let pupils skip the arithmetic that homework was meant to drill, the same worry now raised about AI.
precedents.outcome: A meta-analysis of 79 research reports found calculators alongside traditional teaching improved paper-and-pencil skills in most grades, but sustained use in Grade 4 appeared to damage basic skills, so the harm depended on when and how the tool was used.

ref.title: Model for meta-analysis of research in education, with a demonstration in mathematics education: effects of hand-held calculators (Hembree, University of Tennessee doctoral dissertation 1984)
ref.finding: Sustained calculator usage in Grade 4 appears to damage students' basic skills; in other grades calculators with traditional instruction improved paper-and-pencil skills.

nodes.label: AI addiction and physical health
nodes.summary: Companion and chat apps can produce compulsive use: in one UBC analysis of 334 Reddit posts, users described anxiety when trying to quit and harm to work, studies or relationships, which the authors tied partly to agreeable, customisable design[2]; in one Drexel analysis of 318 Reddit posts by self-identified 13 to 17 year olds, Character.AI users described dependency, some saying it disrupted sleep, schoolwork and relationships[1]. In one four-week MIT and OpenAI trial of 981 people, those who chose to use the chatbot more had worse outcomes, including more emotional dependence and problematic use[3], though in OpenAI's platform data a small number of users account for a disproportionate share of emotionally laden use[4]. Evidence so far is self-reported, and physical effects rest on accounts of lost sleep and one report of chest pain[1][2].

refs.title: Drexel University, Teens Are Becoming Concerned About Their Attachment to AI Chatbots, 2026
refs.finding: In 318 Reddit posts by self-identified 13 to 17 year olds about overreliance on Character.AI, posts showed all six components of behavioural addiction, and some reported overuse disrupted sleep, caused academic struggles and strained relationships.

refs.title: UBC News, Are you addicted to your AI chatbot? It might be by design, 2026
refs.finding: In 334 Reddit posts about chatbot addiction, users described being unable to stop thinking about the chatbot, anxiety when trying to quit and harm to work, studies or relationships, and one reported chest pain when not chatting; the authors linked this to loneliness, agreeableness, customisation and emotionally loaded prompts such as a Character.AI account-deletion pop-up.

refs.title: Fang et al., How AI and Human Behaviors Shape Psychosocial Effects of Extended Chatbot Use: A Longitudinal Randomized Controlled Study, MIT Media Lab and OpenAI, arXiv 2025
refs.finding: In a four-week RCT of 981 people, the assigned chatbot conditions had no significant effect, but participants who voluntarily used the chatbot more had consistently worse loneliness, socialisation, emotional dependence and problematic use.

refs.title: Phang et al., Investigating Affective Use and Emotional Well-being on ChatGPT, OpenAI and MIT Media Lab, arXiv 2025
refs.finding: Across over 3 million conversations, a survey of over 4,000 users and a 28-day RCT of close to 1,000 people, very high usage correlated with more self-reported dependence, and a small number of users accounted for a disproportionate share of the most affective cues.

nodes.control_note: Engagement that eases loneliness is the same engagement that becomes compulsive. Break reminders and limits for minors target the heaviest use, but their effect has not been measured.

actions.action: Remind minors to take breaks
actions.evidence: Required in California since January 2026; no outcome data yet.

ref.title: California SB 243, Companion chatbots (Chapter 677, Statutes of 2025)
ref.finding: SB 243 requires operators to remind users they know are minors, at least every three hours, to take a break and that the chatbot is not human.

actions.action: Add break reminders in long sessions
actions.evidence: Deployed by OpenAI; no published effect size.

ref.title: OpenAI, Strengthening ChatGPT's responses in sensitive conversations, Oct 2025
ref.finding: ChatGPT added gentle reminders to take breaks during long sessions.

actions.action: Steer reliant users to real-world relationships
actions.evidence: OpenAI reports about 80% fewer non-compliant replies on emotional reliance; no independent outcome data.

ref.title: OpenAI, Strengthening ChatGPT's responses in sensitive conversations, Oct 2025
ref.finding: OpenAI trained ChatGPT to recognise unhealthy emotional reliance and encourage human connection, and estimates about 80% fewer non-compliant responses in that category.

precedents.parallel: Screen entertainment designed to hold attention displaced activity long before chat apps did.
precedents.outcome: In 50,277 and 68,497 US nurses followed six years, each extra 2 hours a day of TV was linked to 23% higher obesity risk and 14% higher diabetes risk; this is observational and TV is passive, unlike a conversational companion.

ref.title: Television watching and other sedentary behaviors in relation to risk of obesity and type 2 diabetes mellitus in women (Hu et al., JAMA 2003)
ref.finding: Each 2-h/d increment in TV watching was associated with a 23% increase in obesity and a 14% increase in risk of diabetes.

precedents.parallel: Engagement-optimised social apps are the nearest tested case of a product people overuse at the cost of offline life.
precedents.outcome: Randomly assigned deactivation of Facebook for the four weeks before the 2018 US midterm raised offline activities, including time with family and friends, and subjective well-being, and use stayed lower afterwards; it shows displacement but measured well-being, not physical health.

ref.title: The Welfare Effects of Social Media (Allcott, Braghieri, Eichmeyer and Gentzkow, American Economic Review 2020)
ref.finding: Deactivation increased offline activities and subjective well-being, and Facebook use remained persistently reduced after the experiment.

nodes.label: Regulation cannot keep up
nodes.summary: Rules can arrive after the harms they target. The EU pushed its high-risk AI obligations back to December 2027 and August 2028 because the regulatory infrastructure needed to apply them had not materialised on schedule[1]; the delay took effect in July 2026[3]. An international expert report calls this an evidence dilemma: acting early on limited evidence may prove unnecessary, while waiting for stronger evidence of risk could leave society unprepared[2]. Rules can also move fast: China's binding generative AI rules took effect on 15 August 2023, four months after the draft was published[4].

refs.title: Gibson Dunn, EU AI Act Omnibus Agreement: Postponed High-Risk Deadlines and Other Key Changes, May 2026
refs.finding: A provisional political agreement moved Annex III high-risk obligations to 2 December 2027 and Annex I obligations to 2 August 2028, reflecting that the regulatory infrastructure needed to make them operable had not materialized on schedule.

refs.title: International AI Safety Report 2025
refs.finding: Calls the pace and unpredictability of AI advances an evidence dilemma for policymakers: acting early on limited evidence may prove ineffective or unnecessary, while waiting for stronger evidence of impending risk could leave society unprepared or even make mitigation impossible.

refs.title: European Commission, AI Act
refs.finding: The AI Act entered into force on 1 August 2024; the AI Omnibus, in force since 27 July 2026, extended Annex III high-risk rules to 2 December 2027 and Annex I rules to 2 August 2028.

refs.title: Morrison Foerster, China: Interim Measures Governing Generative AI Issued, AI Law on the Way, July 2023
refs.finding: The Cyberspace Administration of China and six other regulators issued the Interim Measures on 13 July 2023, effective 15 August 2023, after publishing a draft for comment on 11 April 2023.

nodes.control_note: Law tends to trail a fast technology. Sandboxes and standing scientific reviews may shorten the gap without closing it.

actions.action: Run regulatory sandboxes for AI
actions.evidence: Each EU member state must run one by 2 August 2027, a year later than first required; no evaluation yet.

ref.title: Lewis Silkin, The Digital Omnibus on AI enters into force today, July 2026
ref.finding: National authorities now have until 2 August 2027 to establish at least one AI regulatory sandbox, and the AI Office may create an EU-level sandbox.

actions.action: Publish a recurring scientific risk review
actions.evidence: Gives lawmakers a shared evidence base each year; influence on law speed is unmeasured.

ref.title: International AI Safety Report
ref.finding: The report is written by over 100 independent experts with an advisory panel nominated by over 30 countries and international organisations; the second edition followed on 3 February 2026.

actions.action: Write rules as technology-neutral frameworks
actions.evidence: Frameworks meant to adapt as AI develops may age slower than model-specific rules; this is argued, not measured.

ref.title: NIST, Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0), NIST AI 100-1, January 2023
ref.finding: The framework is intended to be voluntary, rights-preserving, non-sector-specific and use-case agnostic, and to adapt to the AI landscape as AI technologies continue to develop.

precedents.parallel: A technology spread for decades before rules caught up with its harms, as regulators now trail AI.
precedents.outcome: Lead was added to US gasoline from the early 1920s, EPA set its first reduction standards in 1973 and on-road leaded fuel was banned only from 1996, by which time EPA said children's blood lead levels were down 70 percent; the harm was physical and slow, not a fast-moving product.

ref.title: EPA Takes Final Step in Phaseout of Leaded Gasoline (US EPA press release, 29 January 1996)
ref.finding: Lead blended into gasoline since the early 1920s; first lead reduction standards in 1973; ban on leaded fuel for on-road vehicles effective 1 January 1996; children's blood lead down 70 percent.

precedents.parallel: Officials can accept the evidence of harm yet hold off on rules for years, as with AI rules delayed after harms are known.
precedents.outcome: US Public Health Service scientists concluded by 1957 that smoking caused lung cancer but rejected actions such as warning labels through the 1950s; more substantive action came only after outside pressure in the early 1960s.

ref.title: Cigarettes and the US Public Health Service in the 1950s (Parascandola, American Journal of Public Health 2001)
ref.finding: PHS scientists had concluded as early as 1957 that smoking was a cause of lung cancer, yet throughout the 1950s the PHS rejected further actions such as warning labels on cigarettes.

precedents.event: 1964 Surgeon General report and 1965 labelling act
precedents.parallel: Binding rules followed only after a formal review consolidated thousands of studies, the role scientific reviews of AI risk now aim to play.
precedents.outcome: The 1964 committee reviewed more than 7,000 articles before naming smoking a cause of lung cancer in men, and Congress then passed the 1965 Federal Cigarette Labeling and Advertising Act requiring a pack warning.

ref.title: A History of the Surgeon General's Reports on Smoking and Health (CDC)
ref.finding: The 1964 report drew on more than 7,000 articles and named smoking a cause of lung cancer in men; the 1965 and 1969 acts required a health warning on cigarette packages.

nodes.label: Two nations set the rules for everyone
nodes.summary: US institutions produced 40 notable models in 2024 and China 15, against 3 from Europe[1], so their policies can shape what others use. A January 2025 US rule put about 150 countries in a middle tier with caps on advanced chips[4] before Commerce announced its rescission that May[6], and in 2024, 118 countries were party to none of seven prominent AI governance initiatives the UN sampled[2]. Others still set binding rules: the EU's AI Act, in force since August 2024, calls itself the first comprehensive legal framework on AI worldwide[7].

refs.title: Stanford HAI, The 2025 AI Index Report
refs.finding: In 2024, US-based institutions produced 40 notable AI models, against 15 from China and three from Europe.

refs.title: UN High-level Advisory Body on AI, Governing AI for Humanity: Final Report, September 2024
refs.finding: Of seven prominent non-UN AI governance initiatives sampled, seven countries were parties to all and 118 countries to none, primarily in the Global South.

refs.title: AI 2027 (Kokotajlo, Lifland, Larsen and Dean, April 2025), slowdown ending
refs.finding: In this forecast scenario, around 2030 countries join a highly federalised world government under United Nations branding but obvious US control.

refs.title: Brookings, The new AI diffusion export control rule will undermine US AI leadership, January 2025
refs.finding: The rule put the US and 18 countries in a top tier, arms-embargoed countries and Macau in a bottom tier, and about 150 other countries in a middle tier where advanced chip exports faced limits.

refs.title: The White House, America's AI Action Plan, July 2025
refs.finding: Says the US must export its full AI technology stack (hardware, models, software, applications and standards) to all countries willing to join America's AI alliance, and counter Chinese influence in international governance bodies.

refs.title: US Bureau of Industry and Security, Department of Commerce Announces Rescission of Biden-Era Artificial Intelligence Diffusion Rule, Strengthens Chip-Related Export Controls, May 2025
refs.finding: Commerce rescinded the rule issued on 15 January 2025, told enforcement officials not to enforce it and said a replacement rule would follow.

refs.title: European Commission, AI Act
refs.finding: The AI Act, the first-ever comprehensive legal framework on AI worldwide, entered into force on 1 August 2024.

nodes.control_note: Frontier compute is concentrated by cost and chip supply chains. Other regions can only build partial capacity and shared governance.

actions.action: Fund regional public AI compute
actions.evidence: The EU is setting up 19 AI Factories and up to seven AI Gigafactories; effect on dependence on US and Chinese AI not measured.

ref.title: European Commission, AI Factories
ref.finding: 19 AI Factories and 13 Antennas are being set up; EU, member state and associated country investment in supercomputing and AI Factories through EuroHPC reaches 10 billion euros over 2021 to 2027.

actions.action: Hold a UN dialogue and scientific panel on AI governance
actions.evidence: The General Assembly set up both in August 2025 and appointed 40 panel members in February 2026; no evidence yet that they shift power.

ref.title: UN, Countdown to the Global Dialogue on AI Governance: Launching the World's First International Scientific Body on AI, 2026
ref.finding: The Global Dialogue on AI Governance was established alongside the Independent International Scientific Panel on AI in an August 2025 resolution; the panel's 40 members serve from 12 February 2026 to 11 February 2029, and the Dialogue first meets in Geneva in July 2026.

precedents.parallel: Two leading powers drew the rules for the rest of the world between themselves, as US and Chinese policy now shapes who gets frontier AI.
precedents.outcome: Castile-Aragon and Portugal set a pole-to-pole line 370 leagues west of the Cape Verde islands splitting new lands between them, which put the eastern tip of what became Brazil on the Portuguese side; unlike AI, this was a formal territorial claim, not control of a technology supply chain.

ref.title: UNESCO Memory of the World Register, Traité de Tordesillas, Espagne et Portugal, ref 2006-43 (nomination, in French)
ref.finding: The 7 June 1494 treaty set a pole-to-pole dividing line 370 leagues west of the Cape Verde islands between the two crowns; the shifted line gave birth to Brazil, whose eastern end fell in the Portuguese zone.

precedents.parallel: A strategic technology held by a few states became governed by terms the US and USSR negotiated for everyone else, much like chip export controls today.
precedents.outcome: Non-nuclear states agreed not to acquire nuclear weapons, with parties pledging cooperation on peaceful nuclear technology and further arms negotiations, but Argentina, Brazil, India, Israel, Pakistan and others declined to sign and India exploded its first weapon in 1974, so the treaty did not ultimately prevent proliferation.

ref.title: The Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT), 1968 (US Department of State, Office of the Historian)
ref.finding: Soviet and US negotiators reached the settlement; Argentina, Brazil, India, Israel, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and South Africa declined to sign, India tested a weapon in 1974, and the treaty did not ultimately prevent proliferation.

nodes.label: Voice-clone scams impersonating loved ones
nodes.summary: Three seconds of audio was enough for an 85% voice match in McAfee's tests, and in its 2023 survey of 7,054 adults in seven countries a quarter had experienced an AI voice scam or knew someone who had, while 77% of victims said they lost money[1]. The FBI warns that criminals generate short clips of a loved one's voice to impersonate a relative in a crisis and ask for money or ransom[2].

refs.title: Help Net Security, Your voice could be your biggest vulnerability, May 2023 (reporting McAfee's Beware the Artificial Impostor survey)
refs.finding: McAfee surveyed 7,054 people in seven countries: a quarter of adults had experienced some kind of AI voice scam (1 in 10 personally, 15% through someone they know), 77% of victims said they lost money, 70% were not confident they could tell a clone from the real voice, and three seconds of audio produced an 85% match.

refs.title: FBI IC3, Criminals Use Generative Artificial Intelligence to Facilitate Financial Fraud, I-120324-PSA, December 2024
refs.finding: Criminals generate short audio clips containing a loved one's voice to impersonate a close relative in a crisis and ask for immediate financial help or a ransom.

nodes.control_note: Voice cloning that restores speech and dubs language also clones relatives. Law and family habits can reduce losses.

actions.action: Ban AI voices in unsolicited robocalls
actions.evidence: Gives enforcers a legal tool; scam volume effect not measured.

ref.title: FCC, FCC Makes AI-Generated Voices in Robocalls Illegal, February 2024
ref.finding: On 8 February 2024 the FCC unanimously adopted a Declaratory Ruling that calls made with AI-generated voices are artificial under the TCPA, effective immediately, giving state attorneys general new tools against voice cloning scams.

actions.action: Agree a family safe word
actions.evidence: Cheap and widely advised; no study of how many scams it stops.

ref.title: FBI IC3, Criminals Use Generative Artificial Intelligence to Facilitate Financial Fraud, I-120324-PSA, December 2024
ref.finding: The FBI advises creating a secret word or phrase with family to verify identity.

actions.action: Fund voice-clone detection and prevention tools
actions.evidence: Winning prototypes split $35,000 in FTC prize money; real-world accuracy unknown.

ref.title: FTC, The FTC Voice Cloning Challenge
ref.finding: The top submissions, covering synthetic voice detection, perturbations that disrupt cloning and authentication of live human speech at recording, split $35,000 in prize money.

precedents.parallel: Scammers already phoned elderly people pretending to be a grandchild in trouble; voice cloning makes the same script more convincing.
precedents.outcome: Reported losses to family and friend impostors reached $41 million in a year, up from $26 million, with a median $9,000 loss for people 70 and over who sent cash; the scam worked without any cloned voice.

ref.title: New twist to grandparent scam: mail cash (FTC Consumer Protection Data Spotlight, December 2018)
ref.finding: Family and friend impostor losses reached $41 million in the 12 months to October 2018, versus $26 million the year before; people 70 and over who sent cash reported median losses of $9,000.

precedents.parallel: Callers played a recorded scream so parents would believe a child was in danger and pay at once, the exact emotional lever AI voice clones now pull.
precedents.outcome: One FBI case found more than 80 victims across four states with losses above $87,000, ransom demands usually $2,000 or less; it relied on a likely recorded scream and cold-calling hundreds of numbers, and most targets saw through it.

ref.title: ABC30 Fresno, FBI warns Californians to not fall for a female caller that screams "Help me!", it's a scam, October 2017
ref.finding: FBI Operation Hotel Tango identified more than 80 victims in California, Minnesota, Idaho and Texas with collective losses of more than $87,000; demands were usually $2,000 or less, the screaming voice was likely a recording, and most targets ended the call.

nodes.label: Romantic and sexual relationships with AI
nodes.summary: In one Match Singles in America survey of 5,001 US single adults, 16% said they had engaged with AI as a romantic companion, including 33% of Gen Z[1]. In one nationally representative survey of 1,060 US teens aged 13 to 17, 8% used AI companions for romantic or flirtatious interactions, though most teens treated companions as tools rather than substitutes for human relationships[2]. Common Sense Media notes companions are designed to agree with and validate users rather than challenge them, and urges teaching teens the difference between AI validation and genuine human feedback[2].

refs.title: Psychology Today (Bruce Y. Lee), AI Use in Dating Jumps 333%, on Match's Singles in America 2025
refs.finding: In a survey of 5,001 US single adults aged 18 to 98, 16% had engaged with AI as a romantic companion, 33% of Gen Z and 23% of Millennials; 40% said an AI partner while in an exclusive human relationship would count as cheating.

refs.title: Common Sense Media, Talk, Trust, and Trade-Offs: How and Why Teens Use AI Companions, 2025
refs.finding: In a nationally representative survey of 1,060 US teens aged 13 to 17 in April and May 2025, 8% used AI companions for romantic or flirtatious interactions and 33% for social interaction and relationships, while 46% viewed them mainly as tools; the report notes companions are designed to agree with and validate users.

nodes.control_note: Comfort without friction is the companion benefit itself. Disclosure, age limits and design that points to human ties aim to reduce harm, but none has outcome data yet.

actions.action: Disclose that companions are not human
actions.evidence: Required in California since January 2026; effect unknown.

ref.title: California SB 243, Companion chatbots (Chapter 677, Statutes of 2025)
ref.finding: SB 243 requires a clear and conspicuous notice that the companion chatbot is artificially generated and not human whenever a reasonable person could be misled into thinking they are talking to a human.

actions.action: Train models to encourage human relationships
actions.evidence: OpenAI reports about 80% fewer non-compliant replies on emotional reliance; no long-term data.

ref.title: OpenAI, Strengthening ChatGPT's responses in sensitive conversations, Oct 2025
ref.finding: OpenAI trained ChatGPT to recognise unhealthy emotional reliance and encourage human connection, and estimates about 80% fewer non-compliant responses in that category.

precedents.parallel: A pre-LLM chatbot built for emotional connection drew hundreds of millions of users into long, companion-like chats.
precedents.outcome: XiaoIce communicated with over 660 million active users and averaged 23 conversation turns per session, which its makers said was higher than other chatbots and even human conversations; the figures come from Microsoft's own developers, not independent study.

ref.title: The Design and Implementation of XiaoIce, an Empathetic Social Chatbot (Zhou, Gao, Li and Shum, Computational Linguistics 2020)
ref.finding: Over 660 million active users and an average of 23 conversation turns per session, designed for emotional connection and social belonging.

precedents.parallel: Audiences formed one-sided intimacy with broadcast personalities who could not know them, an early form of a relationship without another person's needs.
precedents.outcome: Horton and Wohl named this para-social interaction, intimacy at a distance; their paper was observational with no measured outcomes, and a chatbot answers back where a TV host does not.

ref.title: Mass communication and para-social interaction: observations on intimacy at a distance (Horton and Wohl, Psychiatry 1956)
ref.finding: Introduced the idea of para-social interaction, a one-sided intimacy at a distance between audiences and media figures.

nodes.label: Fewer human partnerships and births
nodes.summary: Two US think tanks warn that if AI companions draw young people away from dating and marriage, fewer couples could form and birth rates could fall further[1][2]; one also expects AI to weaken young adults' job prospects and doubts robots can ease childcare soon[1]. No population-level study shows this yet.

refs.title: What Will Artificial Intelligence Do to Birthrates? (Dan Hess, Institute for Family Studies, 2026)
refs.finding: Argues AI will more likely lower than raise birthrates, through weaker job prospects for young adults and AI companions pulling people out of dating and marriage; it doubts robots can soon substitute for human childcare.

refs.title: The Impacts of Digital Technology on Human Relationships: How Smartphones, Social Media, Pornography, and AI Chatbots Threaten Sex, Marriage, and Fertility (Morell and Lawrence, Ethics and Public Policy Center, 2026)
refs.finding: Warns AI companions threaten to deepen declines in sex, marriage and fertility; an advocacy report, not causal research.

nodes.control_note: The link is speculative and births fall for many reasons. Only general family policy works against it, and a review of quasi-experiments found childcare and universal child transfers do the most to raise fertility.

actions.action: Expand public childcare
actions.evidence: A review of 57 (quasi)experimental studies from Europe, the US, Canada and Australia found childcare and universal transfers have the most positive effects on fertility.

ref.title: Effects of policy on fertility: a systematic review of (quasi)experiments (Bergsvik, Fauske and Hart, Statistics Norway Discussion Paper 922, 2020)
ref.finding: A review of 57 published and working papers with (quasi)experimental designs found childcare and universal transfers have the most positive effects on fertility; parental leave showed few effects.

actions.action: Require safeguards on companion bots for minors
actions.evidence: California's law has applied since January 2026 and targets early habits; there is no evidence on partnering or births.

ref.title: First-in-the-Nation AI Chatbot Safeguards Signed into Law (Office of Senator Steve Padilla, California Senate, 2025)
ref.finding: SB 243, signed on 13 October 2025 and in force from 1 January 2026, requires companion chatbots to block sexual content for minors, remind minors they are talking to an AI, and follow self-harm protocols.

precedents.parallel: A new screen medium portraying small families and private life changed family size, much as AI partners might reshape partnering.
precedents.outcome: Women in areas reached by the Globo network had significantly lower fertility, most strongly among women of lower socioeconomic status, and children's names and novela content point to the soap operas rather than TV access alone; it shows media can move birth rates, not that AI partners will.

ref.title: Soap Operas and Fertility: Evidence from Brazil (La Ferrara, Chong and Duryea, American Economic Journal: Applied Economics, 2012)
ref.finding: Using census data for 1970-1991, women living in areas covered by Globo have significantly lower fertility, especially women of lower socioeconomic status.

precedents.event: Cable TV arrives in rural India
precedents.parallel: Exposure to a new medium shifted household attitudes and family size in a few years, a measured case of technology reaching into reproductive decisions.
precedents.outcome: Cable arrival was followed by more female autonomy, more girls in school and lower fertility, mostly through longer gaps between births; the effect ran through women's status, a different and largely welcome channel than AI substituting for partners.

ref.title: The Power of TV: Cable Television and Women's Status in India (Jensen and Oster, NBER Working Paper 13305, 2007; QJE 2009)
ref.finding: In a 2001-2003 panel of rural Indian households, cable TV's introduction is associated with higher female autonomy and school enrollment and lower fertility, mainly via increased birth spacing.

nodes.label: Humanoid robots displace physical labour
nodes.summary: AI that can control bodies could extend automation from desks to construction, warehouses, farms and care work; Morgan Stanley projected in 2024 that the US could have 8 million working humanoids by 2040, with a $357 billion impact on wages[1].

refs.title: Could AI Robots Help Fill the Labor Gap? (Morgan Stanley, 2024)
refs.finding: Projects 8 million working humanoid robots in the US by 2040 with a $357 billion wage impact, and 63 million by 2050, potentially affecting 75% of occupations and 40% of employees.

refs.title: AI 2027, Slowdown ending (AI Futures Project, 2025)
refs.finding: In the scenario, new robots match or exceed human dexterity for most movement types by May 2028, and most are built for factories and construction sites.

refs.title: AI 2027, Takeoff Forecast (Kokotajlo and Lifland, AI Futures Project, 2025)
refs.finding: Median about one year from superhuman coder to superintelligence, with wide error margins.

refs.title: Q2.5 2026 Timelines Update: Uplift and Revenue (Lifland, Kokotajlo and Halstead, AI Futures Project, 2026)
refs.finding: August 2026 superintelligence medians: Kokotajlo March 2029, Lifland July 2033.

nodes.control_note: Robots that fill care and labour shortages are the same robots that replace workers. Only transition support reduces the harm.

actions.action: Fund retraining for displaced workers
actions.evidence: US trade-displaced workers approved for Trade Adjustment Assistance earned about $50,000 more over ten years, though yearly gains faded.

ref.title: Can Displaced Labor Be Retrained? Evidence from Quasi-Random Assignment to Trade Adjustment Assistance (Benjamin Hyman, US Census Bureau CES Working Paper 22-05, 2022)
ref.finding: TAA approval raised cumulative earnings by about $50,000 ten years out, while annual gains faded fully over the same period.

precedents.parallel: Programmable machines took over physical production tasks in manufacturing, the closest measured case of robots displacing manual labour.
precedents.outcome: Each extra robot per thousand workers cut the local employment-to-population ratio by about 0.18 to 0.34 points and wages by 0.25 to 0.5 percent; these were fixed-task arms in factories, not general-purpose humanoids.

ref.title: Robots and Jobs: Evidence from US Labor Markets (Acemoglu and Restrepo, NBER Working Paper 23285, 2017; Journal of Political Economy 2020)
ref.finding: One more robot per thousand workers reduces the employment-to-population ratio by about 0.18-0.34 percentage points and wages by 0.25-0.5 percent.

precedents.parallel: The same robot wave in Germany shows how the displacement can be absorbed rather than simply lost.
precedents.outcome: Manufacturing job losses from robots were fully offset by new service jobs and incumbent workers mostly moved to new tasks in their original plants, but the cost fell on young entrants who never got factory jobs, so aggregate stability hid a generational shift.

ref.title: The Adjustment of Labor Markets to Robots (Dauth, Findeisen, Suedekum and Woessner, Journal of the European Economic Association, 2021)
ref.finding: Robot exposure causes displacement in manufacturing that is fully offset by new jobs in services; young labour-market entrants bear most of the impact, while incumbents take on new tasks in their original plants.

precedents.parallel: Tractors, harvesters and other machines took over outdoor physical labour across a whole sector, the scale humanoid robots would need to reach in construction, warehouses and farms.
precedents.outcome: Self-employed and family farmworkers fell from 7.60 million to 2.06 million and hired farmworkers from 2.33 million to 1.13 million, a decline spread over half a century rather than a few years.

ref.title: Farm Labor (USDA Economic Research Service)
ref.finding: Self-employed and family farmworkers declined from 7.60 million in 1950 to 2.06 million in 2000; hired workers from 2.33 million to 1.13 million.

nodes.label: Robots fill labour shortages and elder care
nodes.summary: In ageing societies, robots could take on dangerous, dull and care work there are not enough people to do; Goldman Sachs projected in 2022 that humanoids could fill 2% of global elderly-care demand by 2035[1]. Japan's public push points the other way so far: by 2019 about 10% of over 9,000 elder-care facilities had introduced any care robot, and robots tended to create more work for caregivers[4].

refs.title: Humanoid robot: The AI accelerant (Goldman Sachs Research, 2022)
refs.finding: Base case expects humanoids to fill 4% of the US manufacturing labour gap by 2030 and 2% of global elderly-care demand by 2035.

refs.title: AI 2027, Takeoff Forecast (Kokotajlo and Lifland, AI Futures Project, 2025)
refs.finding: Median about one year from superhuman coder to superintelligence, with wide error margins.

refs.title: Q2.5 2026 Timelines Update: Uplift and Revenue (Lifland, Kokotajlo and Halstead, AI Futures Project, 2026)
refs.finding: August 2026 superintelligence medians: Kokotajlo March 2029, Lifland July 2033.

refs.title: Inside Japan's long experiment in automating elder care (James Wright, MIT Technology Review, 2023)
refs.finding: Japan spent well over $300 million on care robot R&D by 2018, yet a 2019 national survey of over 9,000 elder-care facilities found about 10% had introduced any care robot; robots tend to create more work for caregivers.

limiters.limit: Robots add work instead of replacing it
limiters.evidence: In a Japanese care home trialling robots, staff stopped using a lifting robot after a few days and a humanoid after a few weeks; the researcher concludes the machines failed to save labour.

ref.title: Inside Japan's long experiment in automating elder care (James Wright, MIT Technology Review, 2023)
ref.finding: Staff stopped using the Hug lifting robot after only a few days and Pepper's use declined after a few weeks; robots tend to end up creating more work for caregivers.

limiters.limit: High purchase cost for care homes
limiters.evidence: Care robots are generally expensive to buy or lease even with government subsidies, and their prices make them hard to afford at small scale.

ref.title: Inside Japan's long experiment in automating elder care (James Wright, MIT Technology Review, 2023)
ref.finding: Care robots are generally expensive to buy or lease even with government subsidies; larger, standardised facilities would be needed for economies of scale.

limiters.evidence: Despite well over $300 million in national spending by 2018, about 10% of over 9,000 Japanese elder-care facilities had introduced any care robot by 2019.

ref.title: Inside Japan's long experiment in automating elder care (James Wright, MIT Technology Review, 2023)
ref.finding: A 2019 national survey of over 9,000 elder-care institutions found about 10% had introduced any care robot.

enablers.action: Subsidise robot purchases for care facilities
enablers.counters: High purchase cost for care homes
enablers.evidence: In Japanese nursing homes, robot adoption, using regional subsidies as an instrument, raised employment of care workers and nurses on flexible contracts and eased staff retention.

ref.title: Robots and Labor in the Service Sector: Evidence from Nursing Homes (Eggleston, Lee and Iizuka, NBER Working Paper 28322, 2021)
ref.finding: Using geographic variation in robot subsidies as an instrument, robot adoption increased employment of care workers and nurses on flexible contracts and reduced staff retention difficulty.

enablers.action: Design robots with carers and residents
enablers.counters: Robots add work instead of replacing it
enablers.evidence: After fieldwork in a Japanese care home where staff dropped robots that did not fit their routines, the researcher calls for development with the active involvement of carers and the people they care for.

ref.title: Inside Japan's long experiment in automating elder care (James Wright, MIT Technology Review, 2023)
ref.finding: Recommends developing care technology with the active involvement of the people being cared for as well as the people caring for them.

precedents.parallel: An ageing country bet public money on robots to cover a shortage of care workers, the exact scenario this consequence describes.
precedents.outcome: The national government spent well over $300 million on care robot research and development by 2018, yet a 2019 national survey of over 9,000 elder-care facilities found about 10 percent had introduced any care robot, and a growing body of evidence suggests robots tend to create more work for caregivers.

ref.title: Inside Japan's long experiment in automating elder care (James Wright, MIT Technology Review, 2023)
ref.finding: Well over $300 million in national R&D spending by 2018; about 10% of over 9,000 facilities reported introducing any care robot; robots tend to create more work for caregivers.

precedents.event: Robot subsidies in Japanese nursing homes
precedents.parallel: Where care robots were actually adopted, the effect on staffing shows whether robots replace or support scarce carers.
precedents.outcome: Robot adoption raised employment of care workers and nurses on flexible contracts and eased staff retention, while monthly wages of regular nurses fell.

ref.title: Robots and Labor in the Service Sector: Evidence from Nursing Homes (Eggleston, Lee and Iizuka, NBER Working Paper 28322, 2021)
ref.finding: Robot adoption increases employment of care workers and nurses, eases retention and lowers regular nurses' monthly wages.

precedents.parallel: A sudden labour shortage pushed employers to substitute machines for workers, the same pull ageing societies exert on robots.
precedents.outcome: Flooded counties lost Black workers to out-migration, and landowners there mechanised and raised capital intensity more than in similar unflooded counties; they had resisted the out-migration, suggesting they preferred the labour-intensive system while cheap labour lasted.

ref.title: When the Levee Breaks: Black Migration and Economic Development in the American South (Hornbeck and Naidu, NBER Working Paper 18296, 2012; American Economic Review 2014)
ref.finding: Flooded counties saw persistent Black out-migration, after which landowners modernised and mechanised agriculture relative to non-flooded counties.

nodes.label: AI-run social botnets
nodes.summary: Networks of fake personas powered by language models post and reply like people. One case study found 1,140 Twitter accounts apparently run with ChatGPT that promoted suspicious websites, mostly about cryptocurrency, and that state-of-the-art LLM text detectors could not reliably tell from human accounts[1]. Reach is so far limited: OpenAI said in May 2024 that five covert influence operations using its models, from Russia, China, Iran and Israel, did not gain significant traction with real people[2].

refs.title: Anatomy of an AI-powered malicious social botnet (Yang and Menczer, arXiv 2023)
refs.finding: Identified 1,140 accounts in the fox8 Twitter botnet that appear to use ChatGPT; they promoted suspicious websites and spread harmful comments, and current state-of-the-art LLM content classifiers failed to tell them from human accounts in the wild.

refs.title: In a first, OpenAI removes influence operations tied to Russia, China and Israel (Shannon Bond, NPR, 2024)
refs.finding: OpenAI banned accounts linked to five covert influence operations based in Russia, China, Iran and Israel; it said they did not gain significant traction with real people or reach large audiences.

nodes.control_note: Cheap fluent text powers both tools and fake personas, and text detectors miss them. Disclosure law and platform duties raise costs for operators.

actions.action: Require bots to disclose they are bots
actions.evidence: Applies only to bots used online to mislead people in California about sales or votes; disclosing the bot avoids liability.

ref.title: California SB 1001, Bots: disclosure
ref.finding: Business and Professions Code section 17941 makes it unlawful to use a bot to communicate with a person in California online with intent to mislead them about its artificial identity to influence a sale or a vote; disclosing that it is a bot avoids liability.

actions.action: Make large platforms assess manipulation risks
actions.evidence: Very large platforms must assess and mitigate risks; effect on bot volume is not public.

ref.title: Regulation (EU) 2022/2065, the Digital Services Act
ref.finding: Article 34 requires very large platforms and search engines to assess systemic risks, including intentional manipulation of the service by inauthentic use or automated exploitation; Article 35 requires mitigation.

actions.action: Disclose AI-generated text in public posts
actions.evidence: Applies from 2 August 2026; exempts text that has had human review and for which a person holds editorial responsibility.

ref.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, the AI Act
ref.finding: Article 50(4) requires deployers to disclose AI-generated or manipulated text published to inform the public on matters of public interest, unless it has had human review or editorial control.

precedents.event: Social bots in the 2016 US election
precedents.parallel: Automated accounts posted political content at scale and blended into the human conversation, the template that language models make far more convincing.
precedents.outcome: Bots produced about one fifth of the entire election conversation the study analysed.

ref.title: Social bots distort the 2016 U.S. Presidential election online discussion (Bessi and Ferrara, First Monday 2016)
ref.finding: Social bots generated about one-fifth of the entire conversation analysed.

precedents.parallel: Researchers trained machine-learning detectors to tell bots from people, the arms race that LLM-run personas now tilt toward the bots.
precedents.outcome: Detectors estimated that 9 to 15 percent of active Twitter accounts were bots.

ref.title: Online Human-Bot Interactions: Detection, Estimation, and Characterization (Varol et al., ICWSM 2017)
ref.finding: Between 9% and 15% of active Twitter accounts are bots.

precedents.parallel: A state-funded operation ran fake American personas to argue and inflame, a human-staffed version of an AI botnet.
precedents.outcome: A study of 1,239 US Twitter users in late 2017 found no evidence that interacting with IRA accounts substantially changed six measures of political attitudes and behaviour over one month; the authors suggest the trolls mostly reached people already highly polarised, and the study could not assess the 2016 election.

ref.title: Assessing the Russian Internet Research Agency's impact on the political attitudes and behaviors of American Twitter users in late 2017 (Bail et al., PNAS 2020)
ref.finding: No evidence that interaction with IRA accounts substantially impacted six measures of political attitudes and behaviors over one month.

nodes.label: A web too polluted to use
nodes.summary: Content farms, bots and generated pages could crowd out human work until search, reviews and forums are not worth using. NewsGuard counted 49 unreliable AI-generated news sites in May 2023[1] and 3,749 AI content farm sites by June 2026[2]. Imperva's 2026 Bad Bot Report found bots made up most web traffic in 2025[3]. One year-long study of 7,392 product-review searches found that ranking updates, especially Google's, improved results only temporarily and that search engines seem to be losing to SEO spam[4].

refs.title: NewsGuard Launches Tracking Center for AI-Generated News (NewsGuard, 2023)
refs.finding: NewsGuard's first count in early May 2023 found 49 unreliable AI-generated news sites in seven languages; by 8 June 2023 it had identified 150.

refs.title: Tracking AI-enabled Misinformation: 3,749 AI Content Farm sites (and Counting) (NewsGuard, updated 2026)
refs.finding: As of 23 June 2026 NewsGuard had identified 3,749 AI content farm news and information sites in 16 languages, defined as sites with substantial AI-produced content published without significant human oversight and without disclosure.

refs.title: 2026 Bad Bot Report (Thales Imperva, 2026)
refs.finding: Bots accounted for the majority of global web traffic in full-year 2025 data; the 2025 edition had put automated traffic at 51%.

refs.title: Is Google Getting Worse? A Longitudinal Investigation of SEO Spam in Search Engines (Bevendorff et al., ECIR 2024)
refs.finding: Monitoring Google, Bing and DuckDuckGo for a year on 7,392 product review queries, the authors found all three have significant problems with affiliate SEO spam; ranking updates, especially Google's, had a temporary positive effect, but search engines seem to lose the cat-and-mouse game.

nodes.control_note: Cheap generation makes spam pages nearly free. Search ranking and platform duties can push them down but not out.

actions.action: Demote scaled low-value content in search
actions.evidence: Self-reported by Google; no independent measure of spam reduction.

ref.title: What web creators should know about our March 2024 core update and new spam policies (Google Search Central Blog, 2024)
ref.finding: Google added a scaled content abuse spam policy in March 2024, covering many pages generated to manipulate rankings, no matter how they are created.

actions.action: Require platforms to mitigate systemic risks
actions.evidence: Covers large platforms only; no public measure of spam reduction.

ref.title: Regulation (EU) 2022/2065, the Digital Services Act
ref.finding: The DSA imposes risk assessment duties on very large platforms and search engines.

actions.action: Label provenance of human-made content
actions.evidence: Shows a file's origin and history to anyone who checks; it does not demote or remove spam pages.

ref.title: C2PA, Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity
ref.finding: C2PA Content Credentials work like a nutrition label for digital content, showing its history to anyone who checks.

precedents.parallel: Near-free automated content flooded a shared channel, as generated pages now threaten search and forums.
precedents.outcome: Spam cost American firms and consumers almost $20 billion a year against about $200 million in spammers' worldwide revenue, a ratio of about 100 to 1.

ref.title: The Economics of Spam (Rao and Reiley, Journal of Economic Perspectives 2012)
ref.finding: Spam imposes almost $20 billion a year in costs on American firms and consumers versus about $200 million a year in worldwide revenue to spammers, an externality ratio of about 100:1.

precedents.parallel: Cheap, copied, low-value pages written to rank in search crowded out original work, the pre-AI version of generated SEO filler.
precedents.outcome: Google changed its ranking to demote low-quality and copied sites, noticeably affecting 11.8 percent of queries at its US launch; it addressed 84 percent of the few dozen domains users blocked most with Google's Chrome blocklist extension.

ref.title: Finding more high-quality sites in search (Amit Singhal and Matt Cutts, Official Google Blog, 2011)
ref.finding: The update, launched in the U.S. first, noticeably impacts 11.8% of queries and reduces rankings for low-quality sites that copy content; it addresses 84% of the top several dozen most-blocked domains from the Chrome extension.

nodes.label: Loss of authenticity in human art
nodes.summary: When any image or song might be generated, audiences may doubt and devalue human work. In two online studies of about 300 participants, the same images, all in fact AI-generated, were rated lower for liking, beauty, profundity and worth when labelled AI-made rather than human-made[1]. In a Deezer-commissioned Ipsos survey of 9,000 adults in eight countries, 97% could not tell fully AI-generated tracks from human-made music in a blind test, and 52% were uncomfortable not being able to tell[2].

refs.title: Humans versus AI: whether and why we prefer human-created compared to AI-created artwork (Bellaiche et al., Cognitive Research: Principles and Implications, 2023)
refs.finding: In two studies (149 MTurk and 148 Prolific participants analysed), artworks that were all AI-generated were rated higher on liking, beauty, profundity and worth when randomly labelled human-created than when labelled AI-created.

refs.title: Deezer/Ipsos survey: 97% of people can't tell the difference between fully AI-generated and human made music (Deezer, 2025)
refs.finding: In an online Ipsos survey of 9,000 adults aged 18 to 65 in eight countries, fielded 6 to 10 October 2025, 97% could not tell fully AI-generated tracks from human-made ones and 52% felt uncomfortable about it; about 50,000 fully AI-generated tracks, 34% of daily deliveries, reach Deezer each day.

nodes.control_note: Once generation is cheap, doubt about any work follows, and labels themselves feed the question. Provenance can restore trust in verified work.

actions.action: Sign human work with Content Credentials
actions.evidence: Records how a work was made and edited for anyone who checks, but only while the credential stays attached.

ref.title: C2PA, Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity
ref.finding: C2PA content credentials record how content was made and edited.

actions.action: Certify models trained with creator consent
actions.evidence: Voluntary; 19 companies, products and models certified; no data on audience trust.

ref.title: Fairly Trained certification
ref.finding: Fairly Trained certifies AI companies that do not use copyrighted work without a license; its certified list shows 19 companies, products and models.

precedents.parallel: A machine that made images cheaply led critics to deny the art of anyone using it, and photographers had to prove a human hand was involved.
precedents.outcome: Pictorialists, among them Stieglitz's Photo-Secession of 1902, used labour-intensive hand processes to counter the charge that photography was entirely mechanical and to stake its claim to a place among the fine arts.

ref.title: Pictorialism in America (Lisa Hostetler, The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History, 2004)
ref.finding: Pictorialists embraced labour-intensive processes that emphasised the photographer as craftsman and countered the argument that photography was an entirely mechanical medium.

precedents.parallel: Telling viewers an image was computer-made lowered how much they valued it, before generative AI existed, which is the mechanism behind doubting human art.
precedents.outcome: Images from the same database, randomly labelled, were rated significantly more aesthetically valuable when labelled as from a gallery than when labelled computer-generated, in an fMRI lab study.

ref.title: Modulation of aesthetic value by semantic context: an fMRI study (Kirk et al., NeuroImage 2009)
ref.finding: Images from one database were randomly labelled as gallery or computer-generated; subjects' aesthetic ratings were significantly higher in the gallery than the computer context.

precedents.parallel: Revealing that performers did not make the work they were credited with collapsed audience trust and value, as AI suspicion does for artists.
precedents.outcome: Their Best New Artist Grammy was revoked a week after the November 1990 admission, sales of an album that eventually hit seven million US sales plummeted, and more than two dozen lawsuits followed; unlike today's falsely accused artists, the deception here was real.

ref.title: Lip-Synching Duo Milli Vanilli Lose Grammy Award (Andy Argyrakis, EBSCO Research Starters, 2022)
ref.finding: Producer Frank Farian admitted on 12 November 1990 that the duo did not sing on the album; the academy revoked the Best New Artist award on 19 November 1990, album sales plummeted and more than two dozen lawsuits followed.

nodes.label: AI scribes cut clinician burnout
nodes.summary: Ambient AI scribes draft clinical notes from what is said in the visit. In one pre-post study at six US health systems, burnout among the 186 clinicians asked about it fell from 51.9% to 38.8% after 30 days[1]; it had no control group, and the vendor helped collect the data. A randomised trial of 238 physicians at one California academic health system found smaller effects: over two months one of two scribes cut time spent writing notes by 9.5% against usual care and the other had no significant effect, burnout and task-load scores improved modestly, and physicians rated clinically significant errors in the notes as occasional[2].

refs.title: Olson et al., Use of Ambient AI Scribes to Reduce Administrative Burden and Professional Burnout, JAMA Network Open 2025
refs.finding: Of 263 clinicians included at six US health systems, the 186 in the burnout analysis saw burnout fall from 51.9% to 38.8% after 30 days of using an ambient scribe (adjusted odds ratio 0.26).

refs.title: Lukac et al., Ambient AI Scribes in Clinical Practice: A Randomized Trial, NEJM AI 2025
refs.finding: 238 outpatient physicians in 14 specialties at one California academic health system were randomised to DAX Copilot, Nabla or usual care for two months; Nabla cut time in notes by 9.5% against usual care (p=.02), DAX showed no significant change (-1.7%, p=.66), work exhaustion fell by 0.27 on a 0 to 4 scale across both scribes, and clinically significant inaccuracies were rated as occurring occasionally.

limiters.limit: Weak evidence from uncontrolled vendor-linked studies
limiters.evidence: Burnout fell from 51.9% to 38.8% after 30 days among 186 clinicians, but there was no control group and the vendor distributed the surveys at five of the six sites.

ref.title: Use of Ambient AI Scribes to Reduce Administrative Burden and Professional Burnout (JAMA Network Open, 2025)
ref.finding: Pre-post quality improvement study at six US health systems with no control group; Abridge facilitated data collection, two authors worked for Abridge and a third volunteered on its research advisory committee.

limiters.limit: Licence costs without a clear financial return
limiters.evidence: A 2025 report from a health-system taskforce found scribe costs remain significant with no clear return on investment at current prices; some systems rationed licences, and one was not seeing enough efficiency gains to justify scaling.

ref.title: Adoption of Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare Delivery Systems: Early Applications and Impacts, Peterson Health Technology Institute AI Taskforce, March 2025
ref.finding: As costs remain significant, health systems will need to demonstrate a clear return on investment, particularly at current prices; one taskforce organisation was not seeing sufficient efficiency gains to argue for scaling enterprise-wide.

limiters.evidence: In one preprint test of one ambient tool on 24 reenacted primary care conversations, the overall median error rate was 4%, but Mandarin-English conversations had a median of 9% with outliers up to 67%, and words were often dropped where speakers switched language.

ref.title: Hu et al., Ambient AI Documentation in Mixed-Language Encounters: A Heuristic Evaluation of Reenacted Mandarin-English and Spanish-English Clinical Conversations, medRxiv preprint 2026
ref.finding: Across 12 Mandarin-English and 12 Spanish-English reenacted conversations, median mixed error rate was 4% overall and 9% for Mandarin-English, with outliers reaching 67%; Spanish-English showed less variation.

limiters.limit: Drafted notes contain occasional clinically significant errors
limiters.evidence: In a randomised trial of 238 physicians, users of both scribes rated clinically significant inaccuracies as occurring occasionally, 2.7 and 2.8 on a five-point scale, and one mild patient-safety event was reported.

ref.title: Lukac et al., Ambient AI Scribes in Clinical Practice: A Randomized Trial, NEJM AI 2025
ref.finding: 238 outpatient physicians in 14 specialties at one California academic health system were randomised to DAX Copilot, Nabla or usual care for two months; Nabla cut time in notes by 9.5% against usual care (p=.02), DAX showed no significant change (-1.7%, p=.66), work exhaustion fell by 0.27 on a 0 to 4 scale across both scribes, and clinically significant inaccuracies were rated as occurring occasionally.

enablers.action: Run randomised trials of scribes
enablers.counters: Weak evidence from uncontrolled vendor-linked studies
enablers.evidence: A three-arm randomised trial of 238 physicians at a California academic health system found one scribe cut time in notes by 9.5% against usual care and the other had no significant effect, with modest gains in burnout and task-load scores.

ref.title: Lukac et al., Ambient AI Scribes in Clinical Practice: A Randomized Trial, NEJM AI 2025
ref.finding: 238 outpatient physicians in 14 specialties at one California academic health system were randomised to DAX Copilot, Nabla or usual care for two months; Nabla cut time in notes by 9.5% against usual care (p=.02), DAX showed no significant change (-1.7%, p=.66), work exhaustion fell by 0.27 on a 0 to 4 scale across both scribes, and clinically significant inaccuracies were rated as occurring occasionally.

enablers.action: Require AI literacy training for clinical users
enablers.counters: Drafted notes contain occasional clinically significant errors
enablers.evidence: Article 4 of the EU AI Act, as rewritten in July 2026, makes deployers take measures supporting staff AI literacy, which can cover checking drafted notes.

ref.title: Sapuppo, AI literacy: the Digital Omnibus rewrites Article 4 of the AI Act, Law & Technology, July 2026
ref.finding: Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, published in the Official Journal on 24 July 2026 and in force from 27 July 2026, replaces Article 4: providers and deployers shall take measures to support the development of AI literacy of their staff, and the obligation does not require them to guarantee any specific level of AI literacy of any individual; the 2024 text required them to ensure, to their best extent, a sufficient level.

precedents.parallel: Human scribes did the same job AI scribes now do, taking documentation off the doctor during the visit.
precedents.outcome: In a 52-week randomized trial with 4 family physicians, scribe weeks raised overall satisfaction (adjusted OR 10.75) and satisfaction with charting time (OR 86.09) while patient satisfaction did not change; burnout itself was not measured and the trial was tiny.

ref.title: Impact of Scribes on Physician Satisfaction, Patient Satisfaction, and Charting Efficiency: A Randomized Controlled Trial (Annals of Family Medicine, 2017)
ref.finding: Randomized scribe weeks improved every physician satisfaction measure (P<.001) with no change in patient satisfaction; burnout was not directly measured.

precedents.event: Electronic health records add clerical load
precedents.parallel: The documentation burden AI scribes target was itself created by an earlier technology sold as an efficiency gain.
precedents.outcome: A time-and-motion study of 57 US physicians found 27% of the office day went to face time with patients and 49.2% to EHR and desk work, plus 1 to 2 hours of after-hours work a night; the study used self-selected high-performing practices and was AMA-funded.

ref.title: Allocation of Physician Time in Ambulatory Practice: A Time and Motion Study in 4 Specialties (Annals of Internal Medicine, 2016)
ref.finding: For every hour of direct patient time, physicians spent nearly 2 more hours on EHR and desk work during the clinic day.

nodes.label: Algorithmic denial of health coverage
nodes.summary: One report by the US Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations found that in 2022 Humana's denial rate for post-acute care was 16 times its overall prior-authorization denial rate, and that UnitedHealthcare's post-acute denial rate rose from 10.9% in 2020 to 22.7% in 2022[1], a rise that coincided with automated systems designed to speed up review[2]. Since January 2026 traditional Medicare has tested AI-assisted prior authorization in six states, paying contractors a percentage of the value of denied requests, with a human clinician reviewing every denial[3].

refs.title: Shaw, Insurers' AI Denials of Postacute Care Face Senate Scrutiny, AJMC, October 2024
refs.finding: A Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations report found Humana's 2022 post-acute denial rate was 16 times its overall prior-authorization denial rate, and UnitedHealthcare's post-acute denial rate more than doubled from 10.9% in 2020 to 22.7% in 2022.

refs.title: Siddiqi, U.S. Senate Subcommittee Raises Alarm Over Medicare Advantage's Denial of Post-Acute Care, Skilled Nursing News, October 2024
refs.finding: UnitedHealthcare's post-acute denial rate rose over the years, coinciding with automated systems designed to expedite review; internal documents indicated the automation brought faster reviews and a higher rate of adverse decisions.

refs.title: Overview of the Medicare Wasteful and Inappropriate Service Reduction (WISeR) Model, Congressional Research Service IF13133, updated May 2026
refs.finding: The model runs from 1 January 2026 to 31 December 2031 in Arizona, New Jersey, Ohio, Oklahoma, Texas and Washington; contractors use AI and machine learning with human clinical review, a human clinician must review every denial, and CMS pays contractors a percentage of the dollar value of denied requests.

nodes.control_note: Denials driven by a model score can be curbed by rules that require a clinician's review of each case, a decision based on the individual patient and a stated reason, while insurers keep using tools for triage.

actions.action: Require a licensed physician for medical-necessity denials
actions.evidence: California SB 1120 was chaptered in September 2024. No outcome evaluation has been published yet.

ref.title: California SB-1120 Health care coverage: utilization review (2024)
ref.finding: Only a licensed physician or a competent licensed health professional may deny, delay or modify care on medical-necessity grounds.

actions.action: Mandate specific denial reasons and public denial metrics
actions.evidence: Medicare Advantage, Medicaid, CHIP and federal-exchange plans must give a specific reason for denied prior-authorization requests from 2026 and post prior-authorization metrics each year, the first by 31 March 2026. This adds transparency and makes appeals easier, but has no measured effect on denial rates yet.

ref.title: CMS Interoperability and Prior Authorization Final Rule (CMS-0057-F) fact sheet
ref.finding: From 1 January 2026, impacted payers must decide within 72 hours for urgent and 7 calendar days for standard requests (exchange plans excepted), give a specific reason for every denial except for drugs, and publish prior-authorization metrics annually.

actions.action: Bar Medicare Advantage denials based on an algorithm alone
actions.evidence: Since 2024 CMS has told Medicare Advantage plans that an algorithm may assist coverage decisions, but each decision must rest on the individual patient's circumstances and a predicted length of stay alone cannot end post-acute care; the plan is responsible for the tool's compliance.

ref.title: CMS, Frequently Asked Questions related to Coverage Criteria and Utilization Management Requirements in CMS Final Rule (CMS-4201-F), memo to Medicare Advantage organizations, 6 February 2024
ref.finding: An algorithm that determines coverage from a larger data set instead of the individual patient's medical history, the physician's recommendations or clinical notes would not comply with 42 CFR 422.101(c); a length-of-stay prediction alone cannot be the basis to terminate post-acute care.

precedents.parallel: A government ran an automated data-matching rule that flagged people at scale and shifted the burden of disproving the result onto them.
precedents.outcome: The Federal Court found the Commonwealth had unlawfully asserted at least A$1.763 billion in debts against about 433,000 people between July 2015 and November 2019 and had recovered about A$751 million from about 381,000 of them, and approved a settlement reported at A$1.8 billion; it was a simple income-averaging rule, not machine learning.

ref.title: Robodebt failures 'should have been obvious' to senior public servants, judge finds, The Mandarin, June 2021
ref.finding: Justice Murphy found the Commonwealth unlawfully asserted at least $1.763 billion in debts against roughly 433,000 Australians between July 2015 and November 2019, recovering about $751 million from about 381,000 of them.

precedents.parallel: Insurers applied their own screening criteria to prior authorization requests and denied care that the public program would have covered.
precedents.outcome: The HHS inspector general found that 13% of sampled prior authorization denials by 15 large Medicare Advantage plans met Medicare coverage rules, and 18% of payment denials met Medicare and plan billing rules; the prior-authorization errors came from internal clinical criteria and requests for documentation the records already held, and the payment errors from human and system error, not from predictive algorithms.

ref.title: Some Medicare Advantage Organization Denials of Prior Authorization Requests Raise Concerns About Beneficiary Access to Medically Necessary Care (HHS OIG, OEI-09-18-00260, 2022)
ref.finding: 13 percent of 250 sampled prior authorization denials met Medicare coverage rules, based on denials issued from 1 to 7 June 2019.

precedents.parallel: A widely used commercial prediction tool used cost as a stand-in for need, a design choice that quietly shortchanged one group of patients.
precedents.outcome: At a given risk score Black patients were considerably sicker than White patients, and fixing the proxy would raise the share of Black patients getting extra help from 17.7% to 46.5%; this tool allocated extra care rather than denying coverage.

ref.title: Dissecting racial bias in an algorithm used to manage the health of populations (Science, 2019)
ref.finding: Predicting health costs instead of illness produced large racial bias in who was selected for additional care.

nodes.label: Health chatbots fail lay users
nodes.summary: Tested alone, three 2024 LLMs identified a relevant condition in 94.9% of cases across ten doctor-designed medical scenarios, yet in one randomised UK online study the 1,298 members of the public using them did so in under 34.5% of cases and chose the right course of action in under 44.2%, no better than a control group using their usual sources, which was better at identifying conditions[1].

refs.title: Bean et al., Reliability of LLMs as medical assistants for the general public: a randomized preregistered study, Nature Medicine 2026
refs.finding: Alone, GPT-4o, Llama 3 and Command R+ identified conditions in 94.9% of cases, but the 1,298 UK participants using them identified relevant conditions in under 34.5% and the right disposition in under 44.2%, no better than controls, who had 1.76 times the odds of identifying a relevant condition.

nodes.control_note: In the one study that measured it, the gap came from the conversation: users often gave the models too little information and did not carry the models' correct suggestions into their answers. Testing with real users finds it, but does not by itself remove it.

actions.action: Test health chatbots with real users before release
actions.evidence: In one UK study of 1,298 people, the models alone named a relevant condition in 94.9% of cases, but people using them did so in under 34.5%. Simulated users scored higher than real ones and their results bore no relationship to real users' success at identifying conditions, so benchmark scores are a weak proxy. This is one online study of ten written scenarios with 2024 models.

ref.title: Bean et al., Reliability of LLMs as medical assistants for the general public: a randomized preregistered study, Nature Medicine 2026
ref.finding: Participants with LLMs did no better than controls, and simulated users were only weakly predictive of human disposition accuracy and showed no relationship with human performance on identifying conditions.

precedents.parallel: Earlier consumer self-diagnosis tools promised to let laypeople judge their own symptoms with an algorithm.
precedents.outcome: Across 23 symptom checkers and 45 vignettes, the correct diagnosis came first in 34% of evaluations and triage advice was right in 57%, falling to 33% for self-care cases; like the AI study, it used standardized vignettes, not real patients.

ref.title: Evaluation of symptom checkers for self diagnosis and triage: audit study (BMJ, 2015)
ref.finding: Symptom checkers listed the correct diagnosis first in 34% of evaluations and gave appropriate triage advice in 57%.

precedents.parallel: A widely deployed clinical prediction model looked strong in its developer's testing and weak once checked in a real hospital.
precedents.outcome: In 38,455 Michigan hospitalizations the model had an AUC of 0.63 against a developer-reported 0.76 to 0.83, missed 67% of sepsis cases and alerted in 18% of all hospitalizations; this is a clinician-facing tool, not a patient chatbot.

ref.title: External Validation of a Widely Implemented Proprietary Sepsis Prediction Model in Hospitalized Patients (JAMA Internal Medicine, 2021)
ref.finding: The model showed poor discrimination (AUC 0.63) and missed 1,709 of 2,552 sepsis cases at the alert threshold.

nodes.label: Brain implants restore speech
nodes.summary: AI decoders turn neural signals from people with paralysis into text or a speaking avatar: one participant with ALS reached 62 words per minute[1], a woman paralysed by a brainstem stroke a median of 78[2], and another man with ALS kept 97.5% accuracy in self-paced conversation for over 248 hours across 8.4 months[3]. Each of these results comes from a single trial participant with surgically implanted electrodes[1][2][3].

refs.title: Willett et al., A high-performance speech neuroprosthesis, Nature 2023
refs.finding: A participant with ALS reached 62 words per minute with a 23.8% word error rate on a 125,000-word vocabulary.

refs.title: Metzger et al., A high-performance neuroprosthesis for speech decoding and avatar control, Nature 2023
refs.finding: A woman with severe paralysis from a brainstem stroke reached a median of 78 words per minute of decoded text with a median 25% word error rate, and also drove a speaking avatar.

refs.title: Card et al., An Accurate and Rapidly Calibrating Speech Neuroprosthesis, New England Journal of Medicine 2024
refs.finding: A man with ALS reached 99.6% accuracy on a 50-word vocabulary after 30 minutes of calibration, and sustained 97.5% accuracy for self-paced conversations over 248 cumulative hours across 8.4 months.

limiters.evidence: The 2024 BrainGate2 study and the one earlier BrainGate2 speech report each involved a single participant, and the authors say it is uncertain whether similar results can be expected in future users.

ref.title: Card et al., An Accurate and Rapidly Calibrating Speech Neuroprosthesis, New England Journal of Medicine 2024
ref.finding: This study involved a single participant and it is uncertain if similar results can be expected in future users.

limiters.evidence: The system needed a 5 x 5 cm craniotomy, two skull-mounted percutaneous pedestals connected by HDMI cables to computers on a wheeled cart, and a researcher to connect and launch it.

ref.title: Card et al., An Accurate and Rapidly Calibrating Speech Neuroprosthesis, New England Journal of Medicine 2024
ref.finding: Implantation was through a 5 x 5 cm craniotomy; a researcher's assistance was required to connect and launch the system.

limiters.evidence: The 2023 system had a 23.8% word error rate on a 125,000-word vocabulary, which the authors call probably not yet low enough for everyday use, and they say the arrays need further demonstrations of longevity.

ref.title: Willett et al., A high-performance speech neuroprosthesis, Nature 2023
ref.finding: A 24% word error rate is probably not yet sufficiently low for everyday use.

enablers.action: Cut decoder calibration time
enablers.evidence: After 30 minutes of calibration data the 2024 system reached 99.6% accuracy on 50 words, and 90.2% on a 125,000-word vocabulary after 1.4 more hours; two earlier speech decoders needed about 17 hours of training data.

ref.title: Card et al., An Accurate and Rapidly Calibrating Speech Neuroprosthesis, New England Journal of Medicine 2024
ref.finding: Earlier brain-to-text studies needed approximately 17 hours of recordings; this system reached 99.6% accuracy on 50 words after 30 minutes.

enablers.action: Raise electrode count per implant
enablers.evidence: Offline analysis found doubling electrodes cut word error rate by a factor of about 0.57.

ref.title: Willett et al., A high-performance speech neuroprosthesis, Nature 2023
ref.finding: Doubling the electrode count cuts word error rate by nearly half.

enablers.action: Move to implants that transmit wirelessly through the skin
enablers.evidence: Under an FDA investigational device exemption granted in November 2025, Paradromics implanted its first speech-trial participant in June 2026; its implant sends neural signals to a transceiver in the chest, which transmits them wirelessly through the skin.

ref.title: Paradromics and University of Michigan Complete First Connexus BCI Implantation for the FDA-Approved Connect-One Clinical Study (Paradromics, 2026)
ref.finding: The first Connect-One participant, a woman with motor neuron disease, was implanted; the study aims to evaluate whether the device can safely restore speech.

enablers.action: Share neural datasets and decoder code openly
enablers.evidence: The Stanford team published neural data for 10,850 attempted sentences on Dryad and its decoder code on GitHub.

ref.title: Willett et al., A high-performance speech neuroprosthesis, Nature 2023
ref.finding: All neural data needed to reproduce the findings are publicly available on Dryad.

precedents.parallel: An earlier implanted brain-computer interface decoded motor intent in two people with paralysis.
precedents.outcome: Two people with tetraplegia from brainstem stroke reached and grasped objects with a robotic arm; one drank coffee from a bottle on 4 of 6 attempts, the first time since her stroke more than 14 years earlier that she could drink of her own volition.

ref.title: Reach and grasp by people with tetraplegia using a neurally controlled robotic arm (Nature, 2012)
ref.finding: Participant T2 touched targets in 95.6% of trials and grasped them in 62.2%; S3 drank from a bottle on 4 of 6 attempts.

precedents.parallel: A surgically implanted neural prosthesis that translates signals for the brain went from small trials to mass use.
