precedents.outcome: About 736,900 devices had been implanted worldwide by December 2019; they give useful but not normal hearing, results vary, and the path from FDA approval to scale took decades.

ref.title: Cochlear Implants (NIH National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders)
ref.finding: As of December 2019 approximately 736,900 registered devices had been implanted worldwide; an implant does not restore normal hearing.

nodes.label: AI detectors flag non-native writers
nodes.summary: Detectors used to police cheating can wrongly flag non-native English writing: in one 2023 study, seven detectors misclassified on average 61.22% of 91 TOEFL essays as AI-generated, against near-perfect accuracy on 88 US eighth-graders' essays, which puts students who write in a second language at risk of false accusations[1]. Later work is mixed: an ETS review reports that carefully built detectors tested on a large dataset did not necessarily disadvantage non-native English speakers[2], and a 2026 study of Czech texts found no systematic bias across three detector families[3].

refs.title: Liang et al., GPT detectors are biased against non-native English writers, Patterns/arXiv 2023
refs.finding: Seven detectors misclassified 91 TOEFL essays by non-native writers as AI-generated at an average false positive rate of 61.22%, while classifying 88 US eighth-grade essays near-perfectly; 97.8% of the TOEFL essays were flagged by at least one detector. The authors call their sample sizes relatively small.

refs.title: Hao, Detecting AI-Generated Essays in Writing Assessment: Responsible Use and Generalizability Across LLMs, ETS Research Institute/arXiv 2026
refs.finding: Liang et al. reported higher false positives for non-native writers on a small dataset; later ETS studies by Jiang et al. (2024) on a large dataset showed carefully developed detectors do not necessarily bias against non-native English speakers.

refs.title: Al Ali, Helcl and Libovicky, Different Time, Different Language: Revisiting the Bias Against Non-Native Speakers in GPT Detectors, EACL 2026 Student Research Workshop
refs.finding: The perplexity of texts by non-native speakers of Czech was not lower than that of native speakers, and detectors from three separate families showed no systematic bias against non-native speakers.

nodes.control_note: The harm comes from using detector scores to punish students. Schools can stop doing that at little cost, because detection is easy to evade and accuracy varies widely between detectors.

actions.action: Disable AI-text detectors in grading tools
actions.evidence: Vanderbilt turned off Turnitin's detector in August 2023. It noted that Turnitin's claimed 1% false-positive rate, applied to the 75,000 papers it submitted in 2022, would have mislabelled around 750 student papers.

ref.title: Vanderbilt University, Guidance on AI Detection and Why We're Disabling Turnitin's AI Detector (2023)
ref.finding: Vanderbilt disabled the detector for the foreseeable future, citing its opacity, research showing detectors more often label non-native English writing as AI-written, and doubts that AI detection is effective.

actions.action: Never use a detector score as sole evidence
actions.evidence: OpenAI's own classifier caught only 26% of AI-written text and flagged 9% of human text. OpenAI said it should not be used as a primary decision-making tool and withdrew it on 20 July 2023 for low accuracy.

ref.title: OpenAI, New AI classifier for indicating AI-written text (2023)
ref.finding: The classifier was withdrawn on 20 July 2023 for low accuracy, at a 26% true-positive and 9% false-positive rate.

actions.action: Audit detectors on non-native writing samples
actions.evidence: Turnitin tested its detector on writing by English language learners and reported no statistically significant difference in false positives for documents of 300 words or more, but a larger gap for shorter texts; the test was the vendor's own.

ref.title: Turnitin, New research: Turnitin's AI detector shows no statistically significant bias against English Language Learners (2023)
ref.finding: For documents of at least 300 words, the false-positive gap between English learners and native writers was small and not statistically significant; below 300 words the gap was greater.

precedents.parallel: An automated detector run by a test provider flagged non-native English speakers as cheats, and authorities acted on the flags.
precedents.outcome: ETS used voice recognition, checked by human listeners, to label 97% of 58,458 UK tests invalid or questionable; 25,115 people with a flag faced some form of Home Office action, at least 11,356 left the UK, and individuals won 3,714 First-tier appeals. The NAO said the degree of error was difficult to determine accurately without piloting or a control group.

ref.title: Investigation into the response to cheating in English language tests (National Audit Office, 2019)
ref.finding: ETS identified 97% of all UK tests as invalid or questionable using voice recognition it had not used before for TOEIC.

precedents.parallel: A detector with modest accuracy, applied to a population where real cheats are rare, produces far more false accusations than true catches.
precedents.outcome: The National Research Council calculated that screening 10,000 employees including 10 spies, at a setting that catches 8 of them, would also flag 1,598 loyal employees, and judged polygraph accuracy insufficient to justify reliance on it for employee security screening in federal agencies.

ref.title: The Polygraph and Lie Detection (National Research Council, 2003)
ref.finding: Polygraph accuracy is insufficient to justify reliance on its use in employee security screening in federal agencies.

nodes.label: AI gives teachers time back
nodes.summary: In one Gallup poll of 2,232 US public school teachers, those using AI weekly estimated they save 5.9 hours a week, about six weeks per school year, and 57% to 74% of AI users said it improved the quality of their work, depending on the task[1]. The savings are self-reported, and only about three in ten teachers use AI weekly[1]. In one school-randomised trial of 259 Year 7 and 8 science teachers in 68 schools, ChatGPT with a guide cut lesson and resource planning from 81.5 to about 56.2 minutes a week, with no evidence of a difference in resource quality[2].

refs.title: Gallup / Walton Family Foundation, Three in 10 Teachers Use AI Weekly, Saving Six Weeks a Year, 2025
refs.finding: Of 2,232 US public K-12 teachers surveyed in March and April 2025, weekly AI users estimated they save 5.9 hours a week, about six weeks per school year; 32% used AI at least weekly.

refs.title: NFER, ChatGPT in lesson preparation - A Teacher Choices Trial (2024)
refs.finding: In a ten-week school-randomised trial of 259 Year 7 and 8 science teachers from 68 schools, the ChatGPT group spent about 56.2 minutes a week on lesson and resource planning against 81.5 minutes for teachers barred from generative AI, and an expert panel found no evidence that resource quality differed.

limiters.evidence: In 2024-25, 68% of US public school teachers had not taken any school or district training on AI, and more taught themselves to use it (52%) than were trained by their school or district (31%).

ref.title: Gallup / Walton Family Foundation, Teaching for Tomorrow: Unlocking Six Weeks a Year With AI (2025)
ref.finding: Most teachers (68%) have not engaged in any training provided by their school or district on how to use AI or AI tools.

limiters.evidence: Only 19% of US public school teachers said their school had a policy on how to use AI.

ref.title: Gallup / Walton Family Foundation, Teaching for Tomorrow: Unlocking Six Weeks a Year With AI (2025)
ref.finding: Only about one in five teachers (19%) are employed at schools with an AI policy.

limiters.limit: Only a minority use AI weekly
limiters.evidence: About 32% of US teachers use AI weekly, and the 5.9 hours saved is self-reported by those users.

ref.title: Gallup / Walton Family Foundation, Three in 10 Teachers Use AI Weekly, Saving Six Weeks a Year, 2025
ref.finding: Teachers who use AI tools at least weekly estimate they save 5.9 hours per week, on average; 32% of teachers use AI tools at least weekly.

enablers.action: Train teachers on effective AI use
enablers.evidence: Gallup and the Walton Family Foundation warn that schools unable to support teachers with training and schoolwide AI policies risk widening the gap between teachers with and without AI skills.

ref.title: Gallup / Walton Family Foundation, Teaching for Tomorrow: Unlocking Six Weeks a Year With AI (2025)
ref.finding: Schools that are unable to support their teachers with training and schoolwide policies on AI may risk widening the gaps between teachers with and without AI skills.

enablers.action: Adopt a school AI policy
enablers.evidence: Teachers at schools with an AI policy were more likely to have used AI in the past year (70% vs. 60%), and those schools reported 2.3 rather than 1.7 hours saved per teacher per week; the survey shows a correlation, not a cause.

ref.title: Gallup / Walton Family Foundation, Teaching for Tomorrow: Unlocking Six Weeks a Year With AI (2025)
ref.finding: Schools with an AI policy are earning an AI dividend that is 26% greater than schools without an AI policy (2.3 vs. 1.7 hours saved per week per teacher).

enablers.action: Measure time savings beyond self-report
enablers.counters: Only a minority use AI weekly
enablers.evidence: One school-randomised trial measured planning time directly and found a saving of about 25 minutes a week on Year 7 and 8 science lesson and resource planning, a narrower task than the six in the Gallup estimate.

ref.title: NFER, ChatGPT in lesson preparation - A Teacher Choices Trial (2024)
ref.finding: Teachers using ChatGPT spent around 56.2 minutes per week on lesson and resource planning, against 81.5 minutes in the group not using generative AI.

precedents.parallel: Technologies sold as time-savers for routine work often fail to shrink the hours spent on that work once rising standards absorb the gain.
precedents.outcome: Using the 1997 Australian Time Use Survey with appliance inventories, the authors found domestic technology rarely reduced women's unpaid working time and may even have increased some domestic labour; housework differs from paid teaching, which has fixed contract hours.

ref.title: Bittman, Rice and Wajcman, Appliances and their impact: the ownership of domestic technology and time spent on household work (British Journal of Sociology, 2004)
ref.finding: Domestic technology rarely reduces women's unpaid working time and may even increase some domestic labour.

precedents.parallel: Time savings that teachers report about themselves are estimates, and time estimates drift from what diaries record.
precedents.outcome: In US and Belgian data, employed respondents overestimated their work hours by 5 to 10% compared with their time diaries, mostly among those estimating long hours; a 2014 BLS article disputed this analysis and found any bias in the main US hours survey to be small, so the size of the bias is contested.

ref.title: Robinson, Martin, Glorieux and Minnen, The overestimated workweek revisited (Monthly Labor Review, US Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2011)
ref.finding: Respondents overestimated work hours by 5 to 10 percent relative to their time diaries, mostly those estimating longer hours.

nodes.label: Vision AI cuts herbicide use
nodes.summary: Camera sprayers recognise individual weeds and spray only those[2]. John Deere says farmers using See & Spray on more than five million acres in 2025 cut non-residual herbicide use by almost 50% on average, saving nearly 31 million gallons of herbicide mix[1]. A three-year University of Arkansas soybean trial found 43 to 59% less herbicide than broadcast spraying at the lowest sensitivity setting, but that setting let Palmer amaranth populations grow 280% a year, and the researchers advise the high setting[2].

refs.title: John Deere See and Spray saves millions (Farms.com, 2025)
refs.finding: Deere-reported 2025 results: See & Spray was used on more than five million acres, cutting non-residual herbicide use by almost 50 percent and saving nearly 31 million gallons of herbicide mix.

refs.title: Precision agriculture research measures effectiveness of See & Spray technology (University of Arkansas System Division of Agriculture, 2025)
refs.finding: A three-year Arkansas soybean field trial found the system allows a 43-59 percent reduction in herbicide use compared to broadcast applications at the lowest sensitivity setting; the low setting increased the Palmer amaranth population by 280 percent each year, and the lead researcher found the high-sensitivity setting best in most scenarios.

limiters.evidence: Arkansas researchers estimate a $25,000 upgrade pays back after about 819 acres and a $75,000 upgrade after about 2,460 acres, assuming early and mid post-emergence spraying in one season.

ref.title: Precision agriculture research measures effectiveness of See & Spray technology (University of Arkansas System Division of Agriculture, 2025)
ref.finding: The sprayer would pay for itself after treating 819 acres for a $25,000 upgrade and 2,460 acres for a $75,000 upgrade.

limiters.limit: Wrong settings grow weed seed banks
limiters.evidence: At the low sensitivity setting, Palmer amaranth populations grew 280% a year; misuse could speed herbicide resistance or force extra sprays, costing Arkansas growers upwards of $60 million a year.

ref.title: Precision agriculture research measures effectiveness of See & Spray technology (University of Arkansas System Division of Agriculture, 2025)
ref.finding: Operating at a low sensitivity setting increased the Palmer amaranth population by 280 percent each year; improper use could cost Arkansas producers upwards of $60 million per year.

limiters.evidence: Arkansas researchers note a learning curve to using the technology correctly, and residual herbicides ideally need to be broadcast at planting, which on the single-tank Premium model means extra passes.

ref.title: Precision agriculture research measures effectiveness of See & Spray technology (University of Arkansas System Division of Agriculture, 2025)
ref.finding: Like any new technology, there is a learning curve to using it correctly; if a Premium is used, growers need to make multiple passes.

enablers.action: Default to high sensitivity settings
enablers.counters: Wrong settings grow weed seed banks
enablers.evidence: Assuming a $25,000 upgrade, the high sensitivity setting saved $30.49 per acre over the season and posed no increased risk relative to broadcast spraying.

ref.title: Precision agriculture research measures effectiveness of See & Spray technology (University of Arkansas System Division of Agriculture, 2025)
ref.finding: Assuming a $25,000 upgrade cost, the high sensitivity setting saved $30.49 per acre over the entire season with no increased risk relative to the broadcast method.

enablers.action: Publish independent university field trials
enablers.evidence: A three-year Arkansas soybean trial found 43% to 59% less herbicide than broadcast spraying at the lowest sensitivity setting.

ref.title: Precision agriculture research measures effectiveness of See & Spray technology (University of Arkansas System Division of Agriculture, 2025)
ref.finding: Targeted spraying at the lowest sensitivity setting allowed a 43-59 percent reduction in herbicide use compared to broadcast applications.

enablers.action: Offer cheaper entry-level models
enablers.evidence: The cheaper Premium model is more widely adopted in Arkansas than the Ultimate model.

ref.title: Precision agriculture research measures effectiveness of See & Spray technology (University of Arkansas System Division of Agriculture, 2025)
ref.finding: The Premium model is the more affordable and more widely adopted option in Arkansas.

precedents.parallel: Herbicide-tolerant and Bt crops were sold partly on the promise that targeted technology would cut chemical use, as vision sprayers are now.
precedents.outcome: Bt crops cut insecticide use by about 56 million kg, but herbicide-tolerant crops added about 239 million kg of herbicide as glyphosate-resistant weeds spread, a net rise of about 7 percent; this is one modelled estimate by an author critical of GE crops.

ref.title: Impacts of genetically engineered crops on pesticide use in the U.S. -- the first sixteen years (Benbrook, Environmental Sciences Europe, 2012)
ref.finding: Herbicide-resistant crops raised US herbicide use by 239 million kg in 1996-2011 while Bt crops cut insecticide applications by 56 million kg; overall pesticide use rose an estimated 183 million kg, about 7 percent.

nodes.label: AI's freshwater footprint
nodes.summary: Data centres use freshwater on site for cooling and, indirectly, at the power plants that supply them, which may strain water-stressed regions. One modelled study projects global AI demand at 4.2 to 6.6 billion cubic metres of water withdrawal in 2027, more than half the UK's annual total, though most of that is withdrawn for power generation and only 0.38 to 0.60 billion cubic metres would be consumed[1]. Google reports that a median Gemini text prompt used about 0.26 millilitres of water in May 2025, estimated from its data-centre water efficiency and not independently verified[2].

refs.title: Making AI Less 'Thirsty': Uncovering and Addressing the Secret Water Footprint of AI Models (Li, Yang, Islam and Ren, arXiv 2023, revised 2025; published in Communications of the ACM, 2025)
refs.finding: The combined scope-1 and scope-2 water withdrawal of global AI is projected to reach 4.2 to 6.6 billion cubic metres in 2027, more than half of the UK's annual withdrawal; scope-2 (power generation) accounts for 4.10 to 6.46 billion, and total consumption is 0.38 to 0.60 billion cubic metres.

refs.title: How much energy does Google's AI use? We did the math (Google Cloud Blog, 2025)
refs.finding: The median Gemini Apps text prompt in May 2025 used 0.24 Wh and consumed 0.26 millilitres of water, estimated from Google's 2024 fleetwide water usage effectiveness; the data have not been verified by an independent third party.

nodes.control_note: Any growth in compute uses water for cooling and power. Siting, timing and cooling choices can reduce the strain, since dry and direct-liquid cooling use little or no water on site, but water used to generate the power remains.

actions.action: Require data centres to meter and report water
actions.evidence: EU data centres with at least 500 kW of IT power must report water input every year, from which WUE is calculated. In the first round 770 data centres reported, about 36% of those covered, with an average WUE of 0.58 cubic metres per MWh. Data is published only anonymised and sets no limits; a rating label was adopted in 2026 and minimum standards that could include WUE are at consultation stage.

ref.title: Report from the Commission to the European Parliament and the Council on the energy efficiency of data centres in the EU, COM(2026) 500 final (European Commission, 2026)
ref.finding: Data centres of at least 500 kW must report KPIs including water consumption to the European database, first by 15 September 2024, then by 15 May 2025 and every year after; 770 reported in the first period, about 36% of those covered; reported data are anonymised; average 2024 WUE was 0.58 m3/MWh; a rating scheme regulation has been adopted and minimum performance standards are at consultation.

actions.action: Schedule workloads where and when water efficiency is high
actions.evidence: Modelled only. One study finds water efficiency varies by site and hour and argues that choosing when and where to train models can cut the water footprint, but it reports no measured gains from scheduling.

ref.title: Making AI Less 'Thirsty': Uncovering and Addressing the Secret Water Footprint of AI Models (Li, Yang, Islam and Ren, arXiv 2023, revised 2025; published in Communications of the ACM, 2025)
ref.finding: Water efficiency exhibits a spatial-temporal diversity; judiciously deciding when and where to train a large AI model can significantly affect the water footprint, and the authors argue water should be addressed together with carbon.

precedents.parallel: Power plants, like data centres, draw large volumes of water for cooling, and the gap between water withdrawn and water actually consumed drives very different headline numbers.
precedents.outcome: In 2020 thermoelectric plants in the lower 48 US states withdrew about 59,889 million gallons of freshwater a day, yet only about 3.9 percent of withdrawals were consumed; power cooling is a far larger and older load than data centres, and the 2020 USGS figures are modelled estimates.

ref.title: Thermoelectric Power Water Use (U.S. Geological Survey)
ref.finding: Thermoelectric power is one of the top two US water use categories; in 2020 about 59,889 million gallons per day of freshwater was withdrawn across the lower 48 states and about 3.9 percent (2,359 million gallons per day) was consumptive use; 2020 values are modelled estimates.

nodes.label: Generative AI e-waste
nodes.summary: By one modelled estimate, generative AI could add 1.2 to 5.0 million tonnes of cumulative e-waste between 2020 and 2030, with rapid server turnover and limits on chip imports making it worse[1]. Circular-economy measures could cut that by 16 to 86%[1]. For scale, the world produced 62 million tonnes of e-waste in 2022 alone[2].

refs.title: E-waste challenges of generative artificial intelligence (Wang, Zhang, Tzachor and Chen, Nature Computational Science, 2024)
refs.finding: Under different scenarios, generative AI e-waste could accumulate to 1.2 to 5.0 million tonnes during 2020 to 2030, aggravated by rapid server turnover and restrictions on semiconductor imports; circular economy strategies along the value chain could reduce it by 16 to 86%.

refs.title: The Global E-waste Monitor 2024: Electronic Waste Rising Five Times Faster than Documented E-waste Recycling (ITU and UNITAR, 2024)
refs.finding: A record 62 million tonnes of e-waste was produced in 2022, up 82 percent from 2010, and 22.3 percent was documented as properly collected and recycled.

nodes.control_note: More AI compute means more servers, and operators replace them quickly to cut running costs. Longer use, reuse and recycling reduce the volume but do not remove it.

actions.action: Extend server lifetimes and reuse components
actions.evidence: Modelled only. One study estimates 1.2 to 5.0 million tonnes of accumulated e-waste over 2020 to 2030 and finds circular-economy strategies along the generative-AI value chain could cut it by 16 to 86%.

ref.title: E-waste challenges of generative artificial intelligence (Wang, Zhang, Tzachor and Chen, Nature Computational Science, 2024)
ref.finding: Circular economy strategies along the generative-AI value chain could reduce e-waste generation by 16 to 86%.

precedents.parallel: Bitcoin miners, like AI data centres, cycle through short-lived specialised hardware as faster generations arrive.
precedents.outcome: Researchers estimated bitcoin mining produced about 30.7 thousand tonnes of e-waste a year as of May 2021, possibly above 64.4 thousand tonnes in the midterm at the peak prices of early 2021; mining hardware differs from AI servers, so the figure does not transfer directly.

ref.title: Bitcoin's growing e-waste problem (Technical University of Munich, 2021, summarising de Vries and Stoll, Resources, Conservation and Recycling)
ref.finding: Bitcoin's e-waste adds up to 30.7 metric kilotons annually as of May 2021, and at peak Bitcoin price levels seen early in 2021 may grow beyond 64.4 metric kilotons in the midterm.

precedents.parallel: Fast replacement of phones, laptops and screens created a waste stream that grew much faster than recycling, which is the path GPU refresh cycles could follow.
precedents.outcome: Global e-waste reached 62 million tonnes in 2022, up 82 percent since 2010, and only 22.3 percent was documented as properly collected and recycled.

ref.title: The Global E-waste Monitor 2024: Electronic Waste Rising Five Times Faster than Documented E-waste Recycling (ITU and UNITAR, 2024)
ref.finding: A record 62 million tonnes of e-waste was produced in 2022, up 82 percent from 2010, with 22.3 percent documented as properly collected and recycled; e-waste is rising five times faster than documented recycling.

nodes.label: Decoding animal communication
nodes.summary: Analysis of animal call recordings is revealing hidden structure: one study of 8,719 sperm whale codas from a single Caribbean clan found combinable features that form a repertoire of nearly an order of magnitude more distinguishable codas than the 21 known coda types[1], and a 2025 study of codas recorded off Dominica found vowel-like spectral patterns[2]. In one study of wild African elephants in Kenya, machine learning predicted who a call was addressed to from its acoustic structure, and in playbacks elephants responded differently to calls originally addressed to them[3]. Structure is not yet meaning: no referential meaning has been established for sperm whale codas[2], and critics warn that machine learning is prone to spurious correlations, so any inferred meaning has to be checked in experiments with the animals[4].

refs.title: Sharma et al., Contextual and combinatorial structure in sperm whale vocalisations, Nature Communications 2024
refs.finding: Analysis of 8,719 codas from the Eastern Caribbean 1 clan found two context-sensitive features, rubato and ornamentation, that combine with rhythm and tempo into a repertoire of nearly an order of magnitude more distinguishable codas than the 21 previously defined coda types; the analysis used statistical tests, not machine learning.

refs.title: Beguš, Sprouse, Leban, Silva and Gero, Vowel- and Diphthong-Like Spectral Patterns in Sperm Whale Codas, Open Mind 2025
refs.finding: Analysis of 1,214 codas recorded off Dominica between 2005 and 2018 found two recurring vowel-like spectral patterns and diphthong-like formant changes; the authors write that no referential meaning has yet been established for sperm whale codas.

refs.title: Pardo et al., African elephants address one another with individually specific name-like calls, Nature Ecology & Evolution 2024
refs.finding: Machine learning predicted the receiver of wild elephant calls in Kenya from their acoustic structure, and elephants responded differently to playbacks of calls originally addressed to them; a 2025 author correction fixed playback data errors and said none of the results changed qualitatively.

refs.title: Yovel and Rechavi, AI and the Doctor Dolittle challenge, Current Biology 2023
refs.finding: AI can generate animal signals, but their context is very difficult to determine, AI is prone to finding spurious correlations, so inferred context must be validated with controlled experiments on animal responses, and animal communication covers only a narrow set of contexts such as alarm and courtship.

limiters.evidence: The sperm whale study describes structure only, with no semantics and no playback experiments.

ref.title: Sharma et al., Contextual and combinatorial structure in sperm whale vocalisations, Nature Communications 2024
ref.finding: Our study investigates the basic structural elements, and not the semantics, of the sperm whale communication system; the study features no playback experiments.

limiters.evidence: The analysis rests on 8,719 codas from one clan recorded from 2005 to 2018, including recordings from 42 tags deployed on 25 whales.

ref.title: Sharma et al., Contextual and combinatorial structure in sperm whale vocalisations, Nature Communications 2024
ref.finding: The Eastern Caribbean 1 clan dataset comprises 8,719 codas making up 21 previously defined coda types, recorded between 2005 and 2018; 42 tags were deployed on 25 individuals.

limiters.evidence: The authors warn that whale-in-the-loop experiments could have long-term effects on an extremely vulnerable population.

ref.title: Sharma et al., Contextual and combinatorial structure in sperm whale vocalisations, Nature Communications 2024
ref.finding: Whale-in-the-loop experiments with potentially long-term effects on the population, which in this case is extremely vulnerable, require a deep understanding of the communication system first.

enablers.action: Release annotated data and code openly
enablers.evidence: The coda dataset and analysis code are public on GitHub.

ref.title: Sharma et al., Contextual and combinatorial structure in sperm whale vocalisations, Nature Communications 2024
ref.finding: All data generated in this study has been deposited on GitHub, and the custom scripts used are available at github.com/pratyushasharma/sw-combinatoriality.

enablers.action: Run careful playback studies with wild whales
enablers.evidence: The authors say interactive playback experiments with wild whales are needed to ground hypotheses about meaning, once the communication system is well understood.

ref.title: Sharma et al., Contextual and combinatorial structure in sperm whale vocalisations, Nature Communications 2024
ref.finding: Future research requires interactive playback experiments with whales in the wild to ground hypotheses about the meaning and function of codas.

enablers.action: Fund long-term field recording programs
enablers.evidence: The Dominica Sperm Whale Project collected the multi-year recordings with fieldwork grants, and Project CETI funded the analysis through philanthropic grants.

ref.title: Sharma et al., Contextual and combinatorial structure in sperm whale vocalisations, Nature Communications 2024
ref.finding: The Dominica Sperm Whale Project team collected the data; this analysis was funded by Project CETI via grants from Dalio Philanthropies and Ocean X, with further support named in the acknowledgements.

precedents.event: Von Frisch decodes the bee dance
precedents.parallel: Patient analysis of a structured animal signal led to a claim about what it means, the step machine learning on whale and bird calls has not yet reached.
precedents.outcome: Von Frisch showed that the angle and speed of the dance encode the direction and distance of food and shared the 1973 Nobel Prize with Tinbergen and Lorenz; the theory in his 1923 book, that the round dance meant nectar and the waggle dance pollen, later proved incorrect and was revised during the Second World War.

ref.title: Karl von Frisch, Scientist of the Day (Tania Munz, Linda Hall Library, 2017)
ref.finding: Von Frisch published his first theory of the bee dances in a 1923 book, a theory that later proved incorrect; he worked out the second version during the Second World War, showing that dance speed and angle encode distance and direction, and won a share of the 1973 Nobel Prize with Niko Tinbergen and Konrad Lorenz.

precedents.parallel: Ape sign-language projects found apparent structure in animal output and read meaning and grammar into it, a warning for claims that detected patterns are language.
precedents.outcome: Analysis of more than 19,000 multisign utterances first suggested structural constraints, but videotape analyses showed most were prompted by the teacher's prior utterance, and the authors concluded the videotapes invalidated the structure claim.

ref.title: Terrace, Petitto, Sanders and Bever, Can an ape create a sentence?, Science 1979
ref.finding: Regularities in more than 19,000 of Nim's multisign utterances suggested structural constraint, a conclusion invalidated by videotape analyses showing most utterances were prompted by the teacher's prior utterance.

nodes.label: Facial recognition wrongful arrests
nodes.summary: Police have arrested people on erroneous face-recognition matches: an April 2026 ACLU count lists 14 publicly known wrongful arrests in the US, most of them of Black people[1]. A 2025 Washington Post investigation found at least 15 police departments in 12 states had arrested people identified through AI matches without independent evidence, often against their own policies, and that authorities routinely failed to tell defendants facial recognition was used, which limits their ability to challenge a match[2].

refs.title: ACLU of Georgia, More than a Dozen Wrongful Arrests Due to Police Reliance on Facial Recognition Technology, 2026
refs.finding: Kimberlee Williams, an Oklahoma grandmother jailed for six months on Maryland warrants after a facial recognition lead, is the fourteenth person publicly known to have been wrongfully arrested in the US after a facial recognition match; most known cases were Black people, and some were white.

refs.title: Arrested by AI (The Washington Post, 2025), Online Journalism Awards entry, Online News Association
refs.finding: At least 15 police departments in 12 states arrested suspects identified through AI matches without any independent evidence connecting them to the crime, often against their own policies; at least eight people were wrongfully arrested in the US, and authorities routinely failed to inform defendants about their use of facial recognition.

nodes.control_note: An arrest on a face match alone is a policy choice, and rules that demand independent evidence target it directly. Written rules are not enough on their own: departments have arrested on uncorroborated matches against their own policies, and the matching itself will still err.

actions.action: Bar arrests based only on face matches
actions.evidence: Detroit adopted this rule in a June 2024 court settlement that the court enforces for four years; no published audit results or outcome data were found.

ref.title: ACLU, Civil Rights Advocates Achieve the Nation's Strongest Police Department Policy on Facial Recognition Technology, 2024
ref.finding: The Detroit settlement bars arrests based solely on facial recognition results, bars lineups from a facial recognition lead without independent and reliable evidence, requires training, and orders an audit of all cases since 2017 in which facial recognition was used to obtain an arrest warrant; the court retains jurisdiction for four years.

actions.action: Test and pick algorithms with low demographic error
actions.evidence: NIST found false positive rates often differ by factors of 10 to over 100 across demographic groups, but some highly accurate identification algorithms showed no detectable false positive differentials, so the choice of algorithm matters.

ref.title: NIST, NISTIR 8280 Face Recognition Vendor Test (FRVT) Part 3: Demographic Effects (Grother, Ngan and Hanaoka), 2019
ref.finding: Across demographics, false positive rates often vary by factors of 10 to beyond 100 times, across many but not all algorithms; some developers supplied highly accurate identification algorithms for which false positive differentials are undetectable.

actions.action: Disclose face recognition use to the defense
actions.evidence: Advocates argue disclosure lets defendants challenge a bad match early; no evaluation of effect exists.

ref.title: Christina Swarns, When Artificial Intelligence Gets It Wrong (Innocence Project, 2023)
ref.finding: Calls for any AI use in a criminal case to be immediately disclosed to the defense, and notes that, as of September 2023, all six people known to have been falsely accused after a facial recognition match were Black.

precedents.parallel: A computer database search put a close but wrong candidate in front of examiners, and their trust in the match led to the detention of an innocent man, as with uncorroborated face-recognition hits.
precedents.outcome: The FBI wrongly matched Mayfield, a Muslim lawyer in Oregon, to a print from the 2004 Madrid train bombings; he was arrested as a material witness on May 6 and released on May 20 after Spanish police identified an Algerian national as the source. The Inspector General blamed the unusual similarity of the prints, bias from Mayfield's known prints and examiner errors, and found that excessive faith in the IAFIS database did not contribute to the error.

ref.title: A Review of the FBI's Handling of the Brandon Mayfield Case (US DOJ Office of the Inspector General, March 2006)
ref.finding: Primary causes of the misidentification were the unusual similarity of the prints, bias from Mayfield's known prints and reliance on tiny Level 3 details; excessive faith in IAFIS technology is listed among explanations found not to have contributed. Mayfield was released on May 20, 2004, after the Spanish National Police identified Ouhnane Daoud, an Algerian national.

precedents.parallel: Human identification of strangers, especially across races, was trusted as evidence long before face recognition and produced wrongful convictions that came to light only later.
precedents.outcome: Eyewitness misidentification was involved in 69% of the 375 US DNA exonerations from 1989 to 2020, and 42% of those misidentifications were cross-racial; unlike face recognition, the error source is human memory.

ref.title: DNA Exonerations in the United States (1989 - 2020) (Innocence Project)
ref.finding: The first DNA exoneration took place in 1989; of 375 DNA exonerations, 69% involved eyewitness misidentification, and 42% of those involved a cross-racial misidentification.

nodes.label: Liar's dividend: real evidence dismissed as fake
nodes.summary: Across five US survey experiments with over 15,000 adults, politicians who falsely claimed that text reports of their scandals were misinformation or fake news gained support across partisan groups[1]. Claiming that a scandal video was a deepfake was largely ineffective, and in one study a fact-check removed the gain[1]. The move is already being tried in US courts: Tesla's lawyers suggested a recorded Elon Musk statement could be a deepfake, and two January 6 defendants claimed Capitol video could have been manipulated by AI; the judge rejected Tesla's argument and both defendants were found guilty[2].

refs.title: Schiff, Schiff and Bueno, The Liar's Dividend: Can Politicians Claim Misinformation to Evade Accountability?, American Political Science Review 2025 (online 2024)
refs.finding: Across 5 survey experiments with over 15,000 American adults, false claims of misinformation raised support for politicians across partisan subgroups when scandals were reported in text, were largely ineffective against video evidence, and did not reduce general trust in media.

refs.title: Shannon Bond, People are trying to claim real videos are deepfakes. The courts are not amused (NPR, 2023)
refs.finding: Tesla's lawyers argued Musk is the subject of many deepfake videos when a family cited his 2016 self-driving remarks; Judge Evette Pennypacker called this deeply troubling and ordered him to testify. Two January 6 defendants who claimed video could have been manipulated by AI were found guilty.

nodes.control_note: Once realistic fakes exist, anyone can claim real evidence is fake, so the claim can only be blunted, not prevented. Fast fact-checks and provenance labels help in experiments, but neither has been tested against the liar's dividend in real scandals.

actions.action: Attach signed provenance credentials to authentic media
actions.evidence: One online experiment with 6,114 people in the US, UK and Norway found C2PA labels on news images raised perceived transparency, credibility and trust in the source; it did not test the liar's dividend directly.

ref.title: Trattner, Forstner, Starke and Knudsen, C2PA Provenance Labels Increase Trust in Digital News Platforms Across Western Countries, ICWSM 2026
ref.finding: In an online experiment with 6,114 participants reflecting the audiences of six news sources in the US, UK and Norway, provenance labels on news images improved perceived transparency and credibility of the image and trust in the news source.

actions.action: Fact-check false 'it is fake' claims quickly
actions.evidence: In one survey experiment a fact-check removed the support gain from a misinformation claim about a text scandal, but the rebuttal came almost at once, which the authors call a best case.

ref.title: Schiff, Schiff and Bueno, The Liar's Dividend: Can Politicians Claim Misinformation to Evade Accountability?, American Political Science Review 2025 (online 2024)
ref.finding: In Study 2, a fact-check of the politician's misinformation claim about a text scandal eliminated the support gain; the design used near-simultaneous scandals and rebuttals, a best-case scenario.

actions.action: Require labelling of deepfakes by law
actions.evidence: The EU duty applies from 2 August 2026, with until 2 December 2026 for generative systems already on the market; there is no evidence yet on whether it changes public trust.

ref.title: EU AI Act, Article 50: Transparency obligations
ref.finding: Providers must mark synthetic output in a machine-readable format detectable as artificially generated or manipulated, and deployers must disclose deepfakes; applies from 2 August 2026.

precedents.parallel: Eisenhower expected that real evidence of atrocities would later be waved away as fabrication, the same move the liar's dividend describes.
precedents.outcome: He toured Ohrdruf on April 12, 1945 so he could give first-hand evidence, ordered troops to photograph the camp and urged that reporters and members of Congress see the camps, and Marshall organised trips for congressional leaders and eighteen newspaper editors; the source does not measure whether this later blunted claims that the atrocities were propaganda.

ref.title: Documenting History: Eisenhower and the Holocaust (U.S. National Park Service)
ref.finding: Eisenhower toured Ohrdruf on April 12, 1945 and wrote to Marshall on April 15 that he made the visit to be able to give firsthand evidence if the atrocities were ever dismissed as propaganda; he ordered troops to photograph the camp and urged more press and Congressional visits, which Marshall organised.

nodes.label: AI mediators for citizen deliberation
nodes.summary: In experiments with 5,734 UK participants, people preferred group statements written by an AI mediator, the Habermas Machine, over those written by human mediators 56% of the time[1], and AI-mediated deliberation reduced division within groups on issues such as Brexit and immigration[2][3]. Outside judges also rated the AI statements higher for quality, clarity, informativeness and perceived fairness[3]. The results come from these UK experiments only; participants were not explicitly told an AI wrote the statements, and a DeepMind author said the model cannot fact-check, keep discussion on topic or moderate it[1].

refs.title: MIT Technology Review (Rhiannon Williams), AI could help people find common ground during deliberations, 2024
refs.finding: Across experiments with 5,734 UK participants, people chose the AI-generated statement over the human mediator's 56% of the time; participants were not explicitly told an AI would write the statements, and the lead author said the model lacks fact-checking, staying on topic and moderating discourse.

refs.title: Complexity Digest, AI can help humans find common ground in democratic deliberation (summary of Tessler et al., Science), 2024
refs.finding: An LLM mediator helped small UK groups find common ground on issues including Brexit, immigration, the minimum wage, climate change and universal childcare, producing statements that won wide agreement and left groups less divided.

refs.title: Tessler et al., AI can help humans find common ground in democratic deliberation (Science, 2024)
refs.finding: Participants (N = 5734) preferred AI-generated statements to those written by human mediators, rating them more informative, clear and unbiased; external judges also rated them higher, AI-mediated deliberation reduced division within groups, and results replicated in a virtual citizens' assembly with a demographically representative UK sample.

limiters.evidence: All experiments used 5,734 UK participants, including one virtual citizens' assembly.

ref.title: Tessler et al., AI can help humans find common ground in democratic deliberation (Science, 2024)
ref.finding: Participants (N = 5734) preferred AI-generated statements to those written by human mediators.

limiters.evidence: The authors say fair debate requires representative users who contribute in good faith.

ref.title: Tessler et al., AI can help humans find common ground in democratic deliberation (Science, 2024)
ref.finding: Steps must be taken to ensure users are representative of the target population and prepared to contribute in good faith.

limiters.evidence: All experiments were run with UK residents; no other country or language was tested.

ref.title: Tessler et al., AI can help humans find common ground in democratic deliberation (Science, 2024)
ref.finding: Experiments with over 5000 participants from the United Kingdom.

limiters.evidence: The lead author said the model lacks mediation capacities such as fact-checking, staying on topic and moderating discourse.

ref.title: MIT Technology Review (Rhiannon Williams), AI could help people find common ground during deliberations, 2024
ref.finding: Tessler said the model does not have the mediation-relevant capacities of fact-checking, staying on topic or moderating the discourse.

enablers.action: Pair AI mediation with citizens' assemblies
enablers.evidence: Results replicated in a virtual citizens' assembly drawn from a representative UK sample.

ref.title: Tessler et al., AI can help humans find common ground in democratic deliberation (Science, 2024)
ref.finding: Findings were replicated in a virtual citizens' assembly with a demographically representative UK sample.

enablers.action: Open-source mediator data for audit
enablers.evidence: DeepMind published the dataset used to train and evaluate the Habermas Machine on GitHub, with code for a prompted version.

ref.title: Google DeepMind, habermas_machine repository (GitHub)
ref.finding: Contains the Habermas Machine dataset used in the Science paper (candidate comparisons, preference rankings, statement ratings and survey responses); software under Apache 2.0, other materials under CC-BY 4.0.

enablers.action: Replicate in other countries and languages
enablers.evidence: No trial outside the UK has been reported in the paper.

ref.title: Tessler et al., AI can help humans find common ground in democratic deliberation (Science, 2024)
ref.finding: Experiments with over 5000 participants from the United Kingdom; replication used a representative UK sample.

precedents.parallel: A randomly selected citizen body produced recommendations on a divisive issue, the role AI mediators aim to support.
precedents.outcome: 99 randomly chosen citizens met over five weekends between November 2016 and April 2017 and heard medical, legal and ethical specialists; their recommendations went to a parliamentary committee, a referendum bill followed, and 66.4% voted for repeal in 2018. The process relied on a secretariat, expert testimony and five months of meetings, and the source notes only that the Assembly and referendum results were similar, not that one caused the other.

ref.title: Government Communications (UK Cabinet Office), Ireland's Citizens' Assembly on abortion rights, 2026
ref.finding: 99 members chosen at random met over five weekends between November 2016 and April 2017; the Joint Committee on the Eighth Amendment reported to the Oireachtas, and 66.4% voted to repeal the Eighth Amendment.

nodes.label: Grief bots and digital resurrection
nodes.summary: Chatbots that imitate dead people from their digital traces are already sold, including Project December and HereAfter, and similar services have appeared in China[2]. Cambridge researchers used three speculative design scenarios to warn of psychological harm, advertising delivered in the manner of a dead loved one and distress to children[1][2]. Direct evidence on users is small and qualitative: interviews with 10 mourners found chatbots helped them cope with grief[3], and interviews with 26 deadbot users found the bots gave a private space to grieve but raised concerns about memory distortion and dependency[4].

refs.title: Hollanek and Nowaczyk-Basinska, Griefbots, Deadbots, Postmortem Avatars: on Responsible Applications of Generative AI in the Digital Afterlife Industry (Philosophy and Technology), 2024
refs.finding: Three speculative design scenarios map ethical concerns about re-creation services and recommend procedures for retiring deadbots, meaningful transparency, limiting access to adults and mutual consent between data donors and interactants.

refs.title: University of Cambridge, Call for safeguards to prevent unwanted 'hauntings' by AI chatbots of dead loved ones, 2024
refs.finding: Some companies already offer deadbots, such as Project December and HereAfter, and similar services have begun to emerge in China; researchers warn of psychological harm, an overwhelming emotional weight, advertising in the manner of a departed loved one, and distress to children.

refs.title: Xygkou et al., The 'Conversation' about Loss: Understanding How Chatbot Technology was Used in Supporting People in Grief (CHI 2023)
refs.finding: Semi-structured interviews with 10 mourners who used chatbots found seven ways of coping, with chatbots acting as a listener, a simulation of the deceased, a romantic partner, a friend or an emotion coach.

refs.title: Li and Lan, Remember You: Understanding How Users Use Deadbots to Reconstruct Memories of the Deceased (arXiv preprint), 2026
refs.finding: In-depth interviews with 26 deadbot users found the bots gave mourners a private space to grieve, but AI-generated memories came to blur with real ones; the authors raise concerns about memory distortion and dependency and call for clinical research.

nodes.control_note: Chatbots can be set up to imitate a dead person from their messages, and the Cambridge authors argue that banning bots built without the dead person's consent would be unfeasible. Consent, age limits, transparency and ways to retire a bot are proposed to reduce the harm, but their effect has not been tested.

actions.action: Require consent from the person before death
actions.evidence: Recommended by ethicists from scenario analysis; untested, and the authors judge a ban on bots built without the dead person's consent unfeasible.

ref.title: University of Cambridge, Call for safeguards to prevent unwanted 'hauntings' by AI chatbots of dead loved ones, 2024
ref.finding: Hollanek and Nowaczyk-Basinska (Philosophy and Technology) urge seeking consent before death, age restrictions, no use for advertising and meaningful transparency that users are talking to an AI.

actions.action: Offer opt-out and a dignified retirement of the bot
actions.evidence: Proposed to give users emotional closure; no outcome data.

ref.title: University of Cambridge, Call for safeguards to prevent unwanted 'hauntings' by AI chatbots of dead loved ones, 2024
ref.finding: Recommends dignified ways to retire deadbots, such as a digital funeral, opt-out protocols that let users end the relationship with closure, and safeguarding the rights of those who interact with the bot.

precedents.event: Seance boom after the First World War
precedents.parallel: Mass bereavement created a market for contact with the dead through mediums, the same need grief bots now sell to.
precedents.outcome: Spiritualist mediums were in high demand after nearly 9 million soldiers died, Oliver Lodge's 1916 book Raymond, based on seances with the medium Mrs Leonard, ran to many editions and spawned dozens of copycat publications, and the history of seances is rife with fraud; the author argues seances also eased the suffering of many, so harm and solace coexisted.

ref.title: Alice Vernon, After the first world war, seances boomed - and dead soldiers 'wrote' home (The Conversation, republished by Aberystwyth University), 2025
ref.finding: Spiritualism was reinvigorated after the war and mediums were in high demand as grieving families sought contact with loved ones; the author notes it is easy to dismiss mediums as charlatans exploiting grief and that the history is rife with fraud, but says it eased the suffering of many.

precedents.parallel: Even a trivially simple chatbot drew people into private emotional conversations, the attachment that grief bots build on.
precedents.outcome: Weizenbaum's secretary asked him to leave the room after a few exchanges with ELIZA, and he went on criticising AI until his death in 2008; ELIZA imitated a psychotherapist, not a dead relative.

ref.title: 99% Invisible, episode 382: The ELIZA Effect, 2019
ref.finding: After a few exchanges with ELIZA, Weizenbaum's secretary asked him to leave the room; the ELIZA effect names our tendency to anthropomorphise computers and believe programs understand when they do not.

nodes.label: AI-generated kill lists compress targeting decisions
nodes.summary: Israeli intelligence officers told +972 Magazine and Local Call that an AI system called Lavender, fed by mass surveillance of Gaza's residents, marked suspected militants; four of the six interviewed said it marked as many as 37,000 Palestinians, and a senior officer said he spent about 20 seconds on each target before a strike was approved[1]. The IDF denied using an AI system that identifies terrorist operatives and called Lavender a database for cross-referencing intelligence sources[2]. In the 2026 US-Iran war, Defense News, citing The Washington Post, reported that the US Maven targeting system generated hundreds of strike coordinates in the first 24 hours, enabling more than 1,000 targets to be hit; lawmakers asked whether AI helped identify a school in Minab where UN and Iranian officials said at least 168 people were killed, the Pentagon had given no explanation, and former officials blamed outdated human-curated data[3]. NATO bought an AI system that supports targeting in 2025[4], and the US, Israel and Russia voted against the 2025 UN General Assembly resolution on autonomous weapons, which passed 164 to 6[5].

refs.title: +972 Magazine and Local Call (Yuval Abraham), 'Lavender': The AI machine directing Israel's bombing spree in Gaza, 2024
refs.finding: Six Israeli intelligence officers described the system; four said it marked some 37,000 Palestinians as suspected militants, one said he spent about 20 seconds per target, and sources said it erred in about 10 percent of cases; the IDF denied the existence of a kill list.

refs.title: Fortune (David Meyer), Israel's reported use of AI in its Gaza war may explain thousands of civilian deaths, 2024
refs.finding: In a statement to the Guardian, the IDF said Lavender is a database whose purpose is to cross-reference intelligence sources and denied using an AI system that identifies terrorist operatives or tries to predict whether a person is a terrorist.

refs.title: Defense News (Katie Livingstone), Deadly Iran school strike casts shadow over Pentagon's AI targeting push, 2026
refs.finding: The Washington Post reported that Maven generated hundreds of strike coordinates in the first 24 hours, enabling more than 1,000 targets to be hit; a strike on a school in Minab killed at least 168 people per UN and Iranian officials; lawmakers asked whether AI was used to identify it, the Pentagon had not explained, and former officials blamed stale human-curated data.

refs.title: The Defense Post, NATO Finalizes Rapid Procurement of AI Warfighting Platform, 2025
refs.finding: NATO finalised acquisition of the Maven Smart System NATO on 25 March 2025; it supports intelligence fusion, targeting, situational awareness, planning and faster decision-making.

refs.title: UN Project, Lethal autonomous weapons systems (A/RES/80/57) vote record, 2025
refs.finding: Adopted 1 December 2025 by 164 votes to 6 with 7 abstentions; Belarus, Burundi, North Korea, Israel, Russia and the United States voted against, and China abstained.

nodes.control_note: States are adopting AI for intelligence and targeting, and no treaty limits it, so only agreed limits and real human review can reduce errors. Agreement is slow: the US, Israel and Russia voted against the 2025 UN resolution on autonomous weapons, and treaty talks have not started.

actions.action: Negotiate binding limits on autonomous weapons
actions.evidence: A CCW expert group adopted a report in September 2026 that recognises the need for human judgement and control but lacks specific prohibitions, including on anti-personnel autonomous weapons, according to the Stop Killer Robots campaign; states decide at the November 2026 Review Conference whether to open negotiations.

ref.title: Stop Killer Robots, Nothing less than negotiations, 2026
ref.finding: The 31 August to 4 September 2026 GGE session adopted its final report by consensus; it characterises autonomous weapons and recognises the need for human control, but proposed prohibitions were not strengthened; negotiations have not begun.

actions.action: Mandate human control and limits on target types
actions.evidence: The ICRC set out these limits in 2021 for autonomous weapon systems; no treaty has adopted them.

ref.title: ICRC position on autonomous weapon systems, 2021
ref.finding: Calls to ban unpredictable and anti-personnel autonomous weapons and, for the rest, to limit target types, duration, area and situations of use and require effective human supervision with timely intervention and deactivation.

precedents.parallel: Patriot batteries ran a largely automatic engagement protocol with operators trained to trust the software, compressing human review as AI targeting is said to.
precedents.outcome: Patriot was involved in three fratricide incidents; two were firings at coalition aircraft in which three aircrew were lost, amid a 4,000-to-1 ratio of friendly sorties to enemy missiles, and the review called for more operator involvement and control.

ref.title: Report of the Defense Science Board Task Force on Patriot System Performance, Report Summary (January 2005)
ref.finding: Patriot was involved in three fratricide incidents and three aircrew were lost in two of them; the operating protocol was largely automatic and operators were trained to trust the system's software; the solution is more operator involvement and control.

precedents.parallel: Crew on an Aegis cruiser acted on a fast, system-mediated threat picture and misread a civilian airliner as an attacking fighter.
precedents.outcome: All 290 people aboard were killed; the official investigation found the plane was squawking a civilian code yet judged the crew's actions appropriate, and the US paid Iran $131.8 million in 1996 without accepting liability.

ref.title: USS Vincennes Shoots Down Iran Air Flight 655 (Association for Diplomatic Studies and Training)
ref.finding: Operators believed the airliner was an F-14 preparing to attack; 290 died; the Fogarty report found it was squawking the civilian channel; a 1996 settlement paid $131.8 million.

nodes.label: AI revitalises endangered languages
nodes.summary: Some Indigenous communities are building their own speech models while keeping control of their data; in New Zealand, Te Hiku Media reports 92% accuracy for its te reo Maori speech recognition, and 82% on mixed English and Maori speech[1]. These figures are self-reported, not independently evaluated. Large multilingual speech models still perform poorly on most languages, because accuracy tracks the amount of training data per language and most languages have under 1,000 hours[2].

refs.title: NVIDIA Blog, Maori Speech AI Model Helps Preserve and Promote New Zealand Indigenous Language, 2024
refs.finding: Te Hiku Media's speech recognition transcribes te reo Maori with 92% accuracy and bilingual English and te reo speech with 82% accuracy; the organisation uses its Kaitiakitanga license to maintain data sovereignty.

refs.title: Radford et al., Robust Speech Recognition via Large-Scale Weak Supervision (arXiv), 2022
refs.finding: Of Whisper's 680,000 training hours, 117,000 cover 96 languages other than English; most languages have less than 1,000 hours, performance on a language is very well predicted by its amount of training data (squared correlation 0.83 between log error rate and log hours), and recognition is still quite poor on many languages.

limiters.evidence: Whisper's 680,000 training hours are English-heavy and most languages get under 1,000 hours; error rates track training data per language, so languages with tiny corpora fare worst.

ref.title: Radford et al., Robust Speech Recognition via Large-Scale Weak Supervision (arXiv), 2022
ref.finding: 117,000 of 680,000 hours cover 96 non-English languages; most languages have less than 1,000 hours; performance on a language is very well predicted by its amount of training data.

limiters.evidence: Te Hiku licenses all content on its site under its own Kaitiakitanga License and points to concerns about Big Tech, digital colonisation and the appropriation of culture by AI.

ref.title: Data Sovereignty and the Kaitiakitanga License (Te Hiku Media), 2022
ref.finding: All content hosted on tehiku.nz is protected under the Kaitiakitanga License; the page links to writing on the threat of Big Tech to Indigenous data and the dangers of digital colonisation.

limiters.evidence: About 2.6 billion people, 32% of the world, were offline in 2024, 1.8 billion of them in rural areas.

ref.title: ITU, Global Internet use continues to rise but disparities remain, especially in low-income regions, 2024
ref.finding: An estimated 2.6 billion people, 32% of the world population, were offline in 2024; 1.8 billion of them live in rural areas, where 48% of people are online versus 83% in cities.

enablers.action: License community data under Indigenous stewardship terms
enablers.evidence: Te Hiku applies the Kaitiakitanga licence to its content and prioritises Indigenous requesters.

ref.title: Data Sovereignty and the Kaitiakitanga License (Te Hiku Media), 2022
ref.finding: Te Hiku prioritises licence requests from Indigenous communities and from people and organisations committed to helping Indigenous communities revitalise their language and culture.

enablers.action: Crowdsource open speech data in minority languages
enablers.evidence: Common Voice's December 2025 release covers 289 languages and 38,932 hours of volunteer recordings, including a Dholuo dataset under a community licence; no independent accuracy evaluation for small languages is cited here.

ref.title: Release live: MCV Scripted Speech 24.0 and Spontaneous Speech 2.0 (Mozilla Discourse), 2025
ref.finding: Scripted Speech 24.0 covers 289 languages with 38,932 total hours (25,886 validated), released on Mozilla Data Collective; the Dholuo set is CC-0 and a separate DhoNam Dholuo set uses the Nwulite Obodo Open Data License.

precedents.parallel: Archive recordings made with new technology were later restored and returned to the community for language revival, the same pipeline speech models now extend.
precedents.outcome: Fewkes's 31 Passamaquoddy recordings are the oldest ethnographic field recordings known to survive anywhere; the Library has digitised and restored early Native field recordings since 2015 and works with the Passamaquoddy to recover language and culture from them, releasing recordings selectively because communities do not want all of them public. The source gives no measure of speakers gained.

ref.title: "Language is Life" and Native American Historical Voices (Library of Congress blog), 2024
ref.finding: Fewkes recorded Passamaquoddy folktales, origin stories and vocabulary on wax cylinders in 1890; the 31 recordings are the oldest ethnographic field recordings known to survive; the Library collaborates with the Passamaquoddy to recover language and cultural practices from them; NAVCC has digitised and restored early Native field recordings since 2015 and releases them selectively because communities do not want all materials public; linguists predict only 20 Native languages will be spoken in North America by 2050, down from more than 300 in 1492.

nodes.label: AI classifiers find unseen child abuse material
nodes.summary: Thorn reports that its detection work with tech platforms flagged 4.16 million suspected abuse files in 2024, 2.24 million of them classified as suspected abuse material and 1.98 million matched to known files[1]. Classifiers can find new material that hash matching misses, but at higher error rates; the only public precision figure, cited in the EU impact assessment from vendor tests, is 99.9% precision while finding 80% of the material in a test set, and EU data protection authorities say such figures cannot be verified[2]. In the EU, rules allowing voluntary scanning lapsed on 3 April 2026 and were reinstated until 3 April 2028, excluding end-to-end encrypted chats[3]. More flagged files also add to US tipline volume, which already overwhelms law enforcement according to AP reporting on a 2024 Stanford study[4].

refs.title: Thorn, 2024 Impact Report
refs.finding: In 2024: 4,162,256 total suspected CSAM files detected, 2,237,225 files classified as suspected CSAM and 1,979,406 known CSAM files matched; 60+ companies use Thorn's CSAM detection products. No precision or accuracy figures are given.

refs.title: EDPB-EDPS Joint Opinion 04/2022 on the Proposal for a Regulation to prevent and combat child sexual abuse, 2022
refs.finding: Hash matching has an estimated false positive rate of no more than 1 in 50 billion; classifiers for new CSAM have generally significantly higher error rates, with one able to be set at 99.9% precision while identifying only 80% of the CSAM in the data set; there is no information on the tests or benchmarks vendors used, so the figures cannot be replicated or validated.

refs.title: eucrim, Interim Rules on Voluntary CSAM Detection Reinstated Until 2028, 2026
refs.finding: The interim regime expired on 3 April 2026 after Parliament rejected an extension; Regulation (EU) 2026/1881 reinstates it until 3 April 2028 and does not apply to end-to-end encrypted interpersonal communications; the permanent CSA Regulation is still in trilogue.

refs.title: Associated Press, Report urges fixes to online child exploitation CyberTipline before AI makes it worse (Bangor Daily News), 2024
refs.finding: A Stanford Internet Observatory report found the sheer amount of CyberTipline reports is overwhelming law enforcement and makes it hard to know which to prioritise; a single detective may be responsible for 2,000 reports a year; the tipline received more than 36 million reports in 2023.

limiters.evidence: The only public figure, from vendor tests cited in the EU impact assessment, is a classifier that at 99.9% precision finds 80% of the abuse material in a test set; EU data protection authorities say no test details exist to verify it.

ref.title: EDPB-EDPS Joint Opinion 04/2022 on the Proposal for a Regulation to prevent and combat child sexual abuse, 2022
ref.finding: New-CSAM classifiers have generally significantly higher error rates than hash matching; one can be set at 99.9% precision but then identifies only 80% of the CSAM in the data set; there is no information on the tests or benchmarks vendors used to measure performance.

limiters.evidence: NCMEC received 21.3 million CyberTipline reports in 2025 and referred more than 18.8 million to law enforcement; more than 10% of industry reports lacked the information needed to determine where the offence occurred.

ref.title: NCMEC, CyberTipline Data (2025 CyberTipline Report)
ref.finding: 21,351,493 reports in 2025 covering 61.8 million files; more than 18.8 million referred to law enforcement and more than 4.5 million designated informational; more than 10% of tech industry reports contained inadequate information to determine where the offence occurred.

limiters.evidence: EU data protection authorities found that orders to detect unknown abuse material and grooming in private messages, given their intrusiveness, probabilistic nature and error rates, go beyond what is necessary and proportionate.

ref.title: EDPB-EDPS Joint Opinion 04/2022 on the Proposal for a Regulation to prevent and combat child sexual abuse, 2022
ref.finding: Adopted 28 July 2022; detection of unknown CSAM and grooming in interpersonal communications goes beyond what is necessary and proportionate due to intrusiveness, probabilistic nature and error rates; grooming provisions should be removed.

enablers.action: Fund hotlines that confirm and triage reports
enablers.evidence: IWF received 424,047 reports suspected to contain child sexual abuse imagery in 2024 and confirmed that 291,273 did.

ref.title: IWF Annual Data & Insights Report 2024
ref.finding: 424,047 reports suspected to contain child sexual abuse imagery in 2024; 291,273 reports confirmed to contain child sexual abuse imagery.

enablers.action: Offer self-hosted detection that shares minimal data
enablers.evidence: Safer offers self-hosted deployment that limits data shared with the vendor.

ref.title: CSAM Detection from Experts in Child Safety Technology | Safer by Thorn
ref.finding: With the self-hosted option customers share limited data; a secure API-based deployment is also available.

enablers.action: Give platforms a time-limited legal basis for voluntary scanning
enablers.evidence: Regulation (EU) 2026/1881 reinstated voluntary detection until 3 April 2028 after the earlier rules lapsed on 3 April 2026, but it does not cover end-to-end encrypted communications.

ref.title: eucrim, Interim Rules on Voluntary CSAM Detection Reinstated Until 2028, 2026
ref.finding: Regulation (EU) 2026/1881 of 24 July 2026 applies until 3 April 2028 and does not apply to interpersonal communications to which end-to-end encryption is applied.

precedents.parallel: Microsoft and NCMEC deployed automated matching to find abuse images at platform scale, the step before classifiers that flag unseen images.
precedents.outcome: PhotoDNA was designed to match resized or similarly altered copies of known images, and Microsoft donated it to NCMEC to share with online service providers; NCMEC had reviewed almost 30 million images and videos since 2003, but the release gives no measured accuracy and the method only finds images already identified.

ref.title: Microsoft and National Center for Missing & Exploited Children Push for Action to Fight Child Pornography (Microsoft press release), 2009
ref.finding: PhotoDNA creates a signature for an image that still matches when the image is resized or similarly altered; NCMEC can make it available to online service providers; NCMEC had reviewed almost 30 million photos and videos since 2003 and its victim identification programme reviews 250,000 a week.

nodes.label: AI flood warnings for data-poor regions
nodes.summary: In one Nature study across 5,680 river gauges, an AI model's flood forecasts for ungauged basins were as reliable five days ahead as same-day nowcasts from the leading global system[1]. Google says its forecasts now cover 100 countries where 700 million people live, with an updated model as accurate at seven days as the old one was at five[2]; whether warnings change behaviour is less proven, and Google's account of use is anecdotal.

refs.title: Nearing et al., Global prediction of extreme floods in ungauged watersheds (Nature), 2024
refs.finding: Across 5,680 gauges, AI forecasts of extreme riverine events in ungauged watersheds were as reliable at up to five days lead time as same-day nowcasts from the Copernicus Global Flood Awareness System, and accuracy on five-year return period events matched or beat current accuracy on one-year events; the model runs in a free public warning system in over 80 countries.

refs.title: Google, How we're helping partners with improved and expanded AI-based flood forecasting, 2024
refs.finding: Coverage expanded to 100 countries (up from 80) in areas where 700 million people live (up from 460 million); the improved model has the same accuracy at seven days lead time as the previous model had at five; examples of use in Brazil are anecdotal.

limiters.evidence: 2.6 billion people, 32% of the world, were offline in 2024, 1.8 billion of them in rural areas, so online flood maps cannot reach them directly.

ref.title: ITU, Global Internet use continues to rise but disparities remain, especially in low-income regions, 2024
ref.finding: An estimated 2.6 billion people, 32% of the world population, were offline in 2024; 1.8 billion of them live in rural areas.

limiters.evidence: In 2025, 119 countries (60%) reported having a multi-hazard early warning system, only 43% of small island developing states did, and fewer than a third of countries reported risk-knowledge capabilities.

ref.title: WMO, Early warning systems reach new heights, but critical gaps jeopardize global progress, 2025
ref.finding: 119 countries, or 60% of all countries, report a multi-hazard early warning system; 43% of small island developing states do; fewer than a third of countries report risk-knowledge capabilities; funding is not always sustained for operation and maintenance.

limiters.evidence: Across 5,680 gauges, the AI model matched the benchmark's same-day reliability at up to five days of lead time, giving days rather than weeks of warning.

ref.title: Nearing et al., Global prediction of extreme floods in ungauged watersheds (Nature, PMC copy), 2024
ref.finding: Forecasts cover 0 to 7 days; reliability similar to or better than same-day benchmark nowcasts at up to five days lead time; trained and tested across 5,680 streamflow gauges.

enablers.action: Link forecasts to national warning and response systems
enablers.evidence: The UN Early Warnings for All initiative aims to protect everyone on Earth with early warning systems by the end of 2027.

ref.title: WMO, Early Warnings for All
ref.finding: UN initiative to protect everyone from hazardous weather, water or climate events through early warning systems by the end of 2027.

enablers.action: Publish free forecasts for ungauged basins
enablers.evidence: Flood Hub publishes public river flood forecasts, labelled approximate and for informational purposes only, and tells users to check official sources.

ref.title: Google, Flood Hub
ref.finding: Public flood forecast map; flood conditions are approximate and for informational purposes only; check official sources.

precedents.parallel: An early-warning system built for a poor, exposed coastline paired warnings with shelters, evacuation plans and volunteers spreading alerts, so that forecasts reached people.
precedents.outcome: Cyclone deaths in Bangladesh fell from more than 500,000 in 1970 and almost 140,000 in 1991 to 4,234 in 2007, a 100-fold drop the authors credit to early warning, shelters, evacuation plans, embankments, reforestation and awareness; illiteracy and poor communication still hampered evacuation, so better forecasts were only one part of this.

ref.title: Haque et al., Reduced death rates from cyclones in Bangladesh: what more needs to be done? (Bulletin of the World Health Organization), 2012
ref.finding: Cyclone mortality fell more than 100-fold, from 500,000 deaths in 1970 to 4,234 in 2007, with almost 140,000 deaths in 1991; credited to early warning systems, shelters, evacuation plans, embankments, reforestation and awareness; evacuation remains a challenge due to illiteracy, lack of awareness and poor communication; preparedness improved after the Bangladesh Red Crescent Society's Cyclone Preparedness Programme.

precedents.parallel: Famine early-warning systems flagged the crisis in time, but warnings did not turn into action, the gap the AI flood summary flags.
precedents.outcome: Warnings clearly identified famine risk in South Central Somalia, yet timely action was not taken and the famine is thought to have killed 258,000 people; the authors blame the war and the tactics of the warring parties, along with problems of access, funding and the aid coordination system, not the warnings.

ref.title: Seal and Bailey, The 2011 Famine in Somalia: lessons learnt from a failed response? (Conflict and Health), 2013
ref.finding: Famine early warning systems clearly identified the risk of famine in 2010-2011 but timely action was not taken; the famine is thought to have cost 258,000 lives; the main factor turning drought into famine was the war and the tactics of the belligerents; the coordination and funding system contributed to the failed response.

nodes.label: Faces scraped into police search engines
nodes.summary: Clearview AI scrapes face photos from the internet into an identity-matching search it sells to customers including law enforcement[1]. In 2024 the Dutch regulator fined it 30.5 million euros over a database of about 30 billion images that it said should never have been built, after 2022 fines by regulators in France, Italy, Greece and the UK[1]. Clearview says it has no place of business in the EU and calls the decision unenforceable[1]; in 2025 the privacy group noyb said it ignores about 100 million euros in fines from four EU regulators and filed a criminal complaint against its managers in Austria[2].

refs.title: TechCrunch, Clearview AI hit with its largest GDPR fine yet as Dutch regulator considers holding execs personally liable, 2024
refs.finding: The Dutch data protection authority fined Clearview 30.5 million euros, plus up to 5.1 million euros for continued non-compliance, over a database of 30 billion scraped images; Clearview said it has no place of business in the Netherlands or the EU and the decision is unenforceable.

refs.title: noyb, Criminal complaint against facial recognition company Clearview AI, 2025
refs.finding: French, Greek, Italian and Dutch authorities fined Clearview about 100 million euros combined, which noyb says the company ignores given the lack of enforcement; noyb filed a criminal complaint against Clearview and its managers with Austrian prosecutors on 28 October 2025.

nodes.control_note: Scraping faces into a search engine is not needed for any listed benefit, and law can ban it. Enforcement against firms based abroad is the weak point.

actions.action: Ban untargeted scraping of facial images
actions.evidence: The EU ban applies from 2 February 2025; its effect on firms outside the EU is untested.

ref.title: EU AI Act, Article 5: Prohibited AI practices
ref.finding: Prohibits AI systems that build facial recognition databases through untargeted scraping from the internet or CCTV.

actions.action: Enforce biometric privacy law through lawsuits
actions.evidence: Under Illinois BIPA, a 2022 settlement permanently barred Clearview from selling to most private businesses nationwide and to Illinois government and police for five years; it can still serve federal agencies and police outside Illinois.

ref.title: AP via Insurance Journal, Face-Scanner Clearview Agrees to Limits in Court Settlement, 2022
ref.finding: Clearview agreed to permanently stop selling access to its face database to private businesses or individuals around the US and to stop serving Illinois state government and local police for five years, while continuing to serve federal agencies and other law enforcement outside Illinois.

actions.action: Restrict police real-time biometric identification
actions.evidence: EU law has allowed it since 2 February 2025 only for listed serious cases with prior authorisation; it covers live identification, not later searches of scraped photos, and no data on its effect have been published.
