refs.finding: In a poll of 1,000 US adult citizens fielded April 7 to 11, 2023, 60% of adults under 30 are at least somewhat concerned that AI could end humanity, against 30% of those 65 and older; 30% of under-30s, against 13% of those 65 and older, think humanity is at least somewhat likely to end within a decade from any cause.

refs.title: Gallup, Gen Z's AI adoption steady, but skepticism climbs (April 2026)
refs.finding: In a Walton Family Foundation, GSV Ventures and Gallup survey of 1,572 US 14 to 29 year olds fielded February 24 to March 4, 2026, 42% feel anxious about AI, unchanged from a year earlier, while excitement fell 14 points to 22%; 60% of non-users report anxiety against 28% of daily users.

nodes.control_note: Clear prospects for work and hands-on familiarity with the tools ease it; Gen Z non-users are far more anxious than daily users.

nodes.label: Research and software humans no longer understand
nodes.summary: AI tools can give researchers an illusion of understanding, so science produces more while understanding less[3]. One study detected AI-written abstracts in 29.4% of US STEM PhD dissertations filed in 2026 through May[1]; in one trial of 52 mostly junior engineers, those using an AI assistant scored 50% against 67% for those coding by hand on a quiz about the code they had just written[2].

refs.title: Gross, Shvadron and Zhang, How heavily are PhD students offloading their scientific writing to AI? Evidence from US STEM PhD dissertations, NBER Working Paper 35859 (October 2026)
refs.finding: An AI detector applied to the abstracts of about 226,000 US STEM PhD dissertations flags AI-generated writing in 29.4% of the 2026 cohort (dissertations filed through May 2026), up from 1.7% in 2023, 5.5% in 2024 and 18.8% in 2025.

refs.title: Anthropic, How AI assistance impacts the formation of coding skills (January 2026)
refs.finding: In a randomised trial with 52 mostly junior software engineers learning a new Python library, those with an AI assistant scored 50% on a quiz about the code they had just written versus 67% for those coding by hand (p = 0.01); low-scoring patterns such as delegating code generation averaged under 40%, while conceptual questioning scored 65% or more.

refs.title: Messeri and Crockett, Artificial intelligence and illusions of understanding in scientific research, Nature 627, 49-58 (2024)
refs.finding: AI tools in research can exploit cognitive limits and create illusions of understanding, so science produces more while understanding less.

nodes.control_note: Using AI to explain rather than to delegate may keep understanding: in Anthropic's trial, people who asked conceptual questions scored 65% or more while those who delegated scored under 40%, though subgroups were small and the authors draw no causal link.

nodes.label: Platforms erode privacy to harvest training data
nodes.summary: Platforms change terms to train on user data by default, which the FTC warns can be unfair or deceptive[2]. All six US frontier developers studied train on users' chats by default[1]; Meta trains on EU public posts unless users object[3], and LinkedIn's opt-out covers only later data[4].

refs.title: King et al., User Privacy and Large Language Models: An Analysis of Frontier Developers' Privacy Policies, Stanford HAI (2025)
refs.finding: All six US frontier developers studied train on users' chat conversations by default, some keep them indefinitely, and four of six appear to include children's chats; policies often omit essential details.

refs.title: FTC Office of Technology, AI (and other) Companies: Quietly Changing Your Terms of Service Could Be Unfair or Deceptive (February 2024)
refs.finding: The FTC warned that firms face a conflict between turning user data into fuel for AI and keeping their privacy commitments, and that retroactive policy changes to allow AI training can be unfair or deceptive.

refs.title: The Register, Meta's still violating GDPR rules with latest plan to train AI on EU user data, says noyb (May 2025)
refs.finding: Meta began training on EU users' public posts and interactions from 27 May 2025 on an opt-out basis, and required people who had objected in 2024 to object again.

refs.title: TechRadar, LinkedIn set to start to train its AI on member profiles (2025)
refs.finding: From November 2025 LinkedIn trains on member profiles, posts and CVs by default in the EU, UK and other regions; opting out only covers data collected afterwards.

nodes.control_note: Opt-in consent rules and enforcement against retroactive policy changes would stop it, but regulators have so far negotiated opt-outs rather than required opt-in.

nodes.label: Models inherit prejudice from their training data
nodes.summary: Models absorb the stereotypes in their training data[3] and sometimes amplify them; one analysis of more than 5,000 Stable Diffusion images found it amplified race and gender stereotypes beyond US labour statistics[2]. In one study, alignment training hid dialect prejudice behind polite answers that still shaped decisions[1].

refs.title: Hofmann, Kalluri, Jurafsky and King, AI generates covertly racist decisions about people based on their dialect, Nature 633 (2024)
refs.finding: Language models judged speakers of African American English more harshly than any human stereotypes recorded in experiments, assigning them lower-prestige jobs and more convictions and death sentences; human-preference alignment widened the gap between covert and overt racism.

refs.title: Bloomberg, Humans Are Biased. Generative AI Is Even Worse (2023)
refs.finding: Across more than 5,000 Stable Diffusion images, the model amplified race and gender stereotypes beyond US labour statistics, rarely showing women as doctors, lawyers or judges and linking darker-skinned men with crime.

refs.title: Omiye et al., Large language models propagate race-based medicine, npj Digital Medicine (2023)
refs.finding: All four commercial chatbots tested repeated debunked race-based medical claims, such as race-adjusted kidney function and lung capacity.

nodes.control_note: Bias audits before deployment and curated or reweighted data reduce it, but the Nature study found that surface-level alignment hides prejudice rather than removing it.

nodes.label: New knowledge becomes harder to verify
nodes.summary: Generated papers, citations and reviews may pile up faster than anyone can check: GPTZero found at least 100 fabricated citations across 51 accepted NeurIPS 2025 papers[1], and an estimated 6.5% to 16.9% of AI-conference peer-review text was substantially LLM-modified[2]. arXiv's CS section stopped taking unreviewed review papers after a flood[3].

refs.title: GPTZero, GPTZero finds 100 new hallucinations in NeurIPS 2025 accepted papers (January 2026)
refs.finding: Scanning 4,841 of 5,290 papers accepted at NeurIPS 2025 found at least 100 hand-verified fabricated citations across 51 papers that had passed peer review.

refs.title: Liang et al., Monitoring AI-Modified Content at Scale: A Case Study on the Impact of ChatGPT on AI Conference Peer Reviews, ICML (2024)
refs.finding: An estimated 6.5% to 16.9% of peer-review text at major AI conferences in 2023 and 2024 was substantially modified by language models, more so for reviews submitted close to the deadline.

refs.title: 404 Media, arXiv Changes Rules After Getting Spammed With AI-Generated Research Papers (October 2025)
refs.finding: arXiv's computer-science section stopped accepting review and position papers that have not passed peer review, after a flood of AI-written surveys its moderators could not screen.

refs.title: Kobak et al., Science Advances 2025
refs.finding: At least 13.5% of 2024 biomedical abstracts show signs of LLM processing.

nodes.control_note: Automated citation checks, disclosure rules and paid, accountable reviewing can keep the filters working; detectors alone are unreliable.

nodes.label: Misinformation at scale
nodes.summary: In one study of 697 people, participants were worse at spotting false tweets written by GPT-3 than by people[1]. NewsGuard counts 3,749 AI content farm sites, up from 49 in May 2023[2], and in one audit ten leading chatbots repeated false news claims 35% of the time[3].

refs.title: Spitale, Biller-Andorno and Germani, AI model GPT-3 (dis)informs us better than humans, Science Advances (2023)
refs.finding: In a preregistered study of 697 people, participants were less able to spot false tweets written by GPT-3 than false tweets written by people, and could not reliably tell GPT-3 tweets from human ones.

refs.title: NewsGuard, Tracking AI-enabled Misinformation: AI Content Farm sites (updated June 2026)
refs.finding: NewsGuard has identified 3,749 AI content farm news and information sites in 16 languages, up from 49 when it started counting in May 2023.

refs.title: NewsGuard, One-Year AI Audit Progress Report Finds that AI Models Spread Falsehoods in the News 35% of the Time (September 2025)
refs.finding: Ten leading chatbots repeated false claims on news topics 35% of the time in August 2025, up from 18% a year earlier, as they stopped declining and drew on a web seeded by disinformation networks.

refs.title: EBU and BBC, News Integrity in AI Assistants (October 2025)
refs.finding: Journalists from 22 public service broadcasters in 18 countries reviewed over 3,000 answers from ChatGPT, Copilot, Gemini and Perplexity; almost half had at least one significant issue.

nodes.control_note: Provenance labels, platform duties and source-quality filters in chatbots cut reach and repetition, but producing a convincing false story costs almost nothing.

precedents.event: Veles fake news sites in the 2016 US election
precedents.parallel: A small town in North Macedonia ran at least 100 US politics sites that published made-up stories for ad clicks, the same economics that generated text now automates.
precedents.outcome: The sites earned their owners a few thousand dollars a month and spread widely on Facebook; they needed people to write every story, which language models no longer do.

ref.title: The World, Kids in Macedonia made up and circulated many false news stories in the US election (November 2016)
ref.finding: At least 100 fake US politics sites, mostly pro-Trump, were run from Veles for advertising revenue.

nodes.label: New ways to make art and express yourself
nodes.summary: Generators turn a description into a picture, a song or a story. In one study, artists who adopted text-to-image tools became 25% more productive and drew about 50% more favourites per view[1]; in another, AI ideas helped the least creative writers most[2].

refs.title: Zhou and Lee, Generative artificial intelligence, human creativity, and art, PNAS Nexus (2024)
refs.finding: Artists who adopted text-to-image tools became 25% more productive and, after a few months, their work drew about 50% more favourites per view, though average novelty fell.

refs.title: Doshi and Hauser, Generative AI enhances individual creativity but reduces the collective diversity of novel content, Science Advances (2024)
refs.finding: In a study of 293 writers, AI ideas raised the novelty and quality of stories most for the least creative writers, bringing them roughly level with the most creative, while the stories became more alike.

precedents.event: The Kodak camera puts photography in amateur hands
precedents.parallel: Kodak sold a box camera that needed no skill, "you press the button, we do the rest", and image-making spread from trained professionals to anyone.
precedents.outcome: Snapshots became a mass form of expression and photography grew into an art of its own, while painters lost much of their portrait trade.

ref.title: George Eastman Museum, From the Camera Obscura to the Revolutionary Kodak
ref.finding: The 1888 Kodak was designed for novices, needed no adjustments or photographic knowledge, and was sold with the slogan "You press the button, we do the rest."

nodes.label: Hallucinations: made-up information and citations
nodes.summary: Models state falsehoods as confidently as facts, partly because benchmarks reward confident guessing over admitting uncertainty[1]. Even summarising a given document, current models add unsupported claims in 1.8% to 24.2% of summaries[2]; by June 2026 one database counted 1,058 US court cases with improper AI use in filings[3].

refs.title: Kalai, Nachum, Vempala and Zhang, Why Language Models Hallucinate (2025)
refs.finding: Hallucinations follow from how models are trained and scored: benchmarks reward a confident guess over admitting uncertainty, so models learn to guess.

refs.title: Vectara, Hallucination Leaderboard (updated October 2026)
refs.finding: Even when only summarising a document they were given, current models add unsupported claims in 1.8% to 24.2% of summaries.

refs.title: Kirschenfeld, Handling Hallucinations: A Reflection on the Last Three Years, UNC Law Library (June 2026)
refs.finding: Damien Charlotin's database recorded 1,058 US court cases involving improper use of generative AI in filings by June 2026, about 40% of them by attorneys.

nodes.control_note: Checking claims against sources, by people or by verification tools, catches most errors, but only when someone actually checks.

nodes.label: A medical revolution cures or controls most diseases
nodes.summary: If AI compresses decades of biology into years, most infectious disease and most cancers could become preventable or curable[1]. Early results are mixed: in one analysis, AI-discovered molecules passed Phase I 80% to 90% of the time, but Phase II success was about 40%, in line with the industry[2].

refs.title: Amodei, Machines of Loving Grace (October 2024)
refs.finding: Forecasts that AI could compress 50 to 100 years of biological progress into 5 to 10, with reliable prevention of nearly all natural infectious disease and elimination of most cancer.

refs.title: Jayatunga et al., How successful are AI-discovered drugs in clinical trials? A first analysis and emerging lessons, Drug Discovery Today (2024)
refs.finding: AI-discovered molecules passed Phase I trials 80% to 90% of the time, well above historic averages, but Phase II success was about 40%, in line with the industry.

nodes.label: AI makes reverse engineering easy
nodes.summary: Models can turn compiled programs and firmware back into readable code; in one study, open decompilation models more than doubled the share of programs that recompile and run correctly versus GPT-4o and Ghidra[1]. With an AI assistant, one researcher found four login-free flaws in camera firmware[2].

refs.title: Tan, Luo, Li and Zhang, LLM4Decompile: Decompiling Binary Code with Large Language Models, EMNLP (2024)
refs.finding: Open models trained for decompilation more than doubled the share of decompiled programs that recompile and run correctly compared with GPT-4o and the Ghidra decompiler.

refs.title: evilsocket, TP-Link Tapo C200: Hardcoded Keys, Buffer Overflows and Privacy in the Era of AI Assisted Reverse Engineering (December 2025)
refs.finding: Working with an AI assistant to map and explain decompiled firmware, one researcher found a private key shared across cameras and four flaws exploitable without logging in.

nodes.label: Investigators expose malpractice in commercial software and hardware
nodes.summary: AI assistants could let researchers, journalists and owners take apart apps and devices without a specialist lab. One hobbyist used Claude Code to decompile his robot vacuum's app and found about 7,000 vacuums in 24 countries exposing live cameras, microphones and floor plans[1].

refs.title: Malwarebytes, Hobby coder accidentally creates vacuum robot army (February 2026)
refs.finding: A hobbyist used Claude Code to decompile the app of his DJI robot vacuum and found that about 7,000 vacuums in 24 countries exposed live cameras, microphones and floor plans to anyone with one device token.

refs.title: Anselmi et al., Watching TV with the Second-Party: A First Look at Automatic Content Recognition Tracking in Smart TVs, IMC (2024)
refs.finding: An audit of Samsung and LG sets found content-recognition tracking sending fingerprints of what is on screen even when the TV is only used as a monitor; opting out stopped the traffic.

nodes.label: Cyberattacks cause large-scale disruption
nodes.summary: Agent-run attacks could hit power, hospitals, payments or fuel supply across whole regions at once, faster than defenders respond. The UK's NCSC judges AI will almost certainly make intrusions more effective[1], and one state-sponsored group used an agent for 80 to 90% of an espionage campaign[2].

refs.title: NCSC, Impact of AI on cyber threat from now to 2027 (May 2025)
refs.finding: AI will almost certainly make intrusions more effective and efficient, and it is a realistic possibility that critical systems become more vulnerable to advanced actors by 2027.

refs.title: Anthropic, Disrupting the first reported AI-orchestrated cyber espionage campaign (2025)
refs.finding: A state-sponsored group used an agent to perform 80 to 90% of an espionage campaign against about 30 targets.

nodes.control_note: The same agents that find holes can patch them. Hardening critical systems and segmenting networks limit how far one attack spreads.

precedents.parallel: One ransomware intrusion into a company network led to a fuel pipeline being shut, the kind of knock-on disruption feared at larger scale.
precedents.outcome: Drivers queued and stockpiled fuel along the US east coast; it was a criminal ransomware attack with no AI.

ref.title: CISA, The Attack on Colonial Pipeline: What We've Learned and What We've Done Over the Past Two Years
ref.finding: The May 2021 attack led to long lines at gas stations along the eastern seaboard.

precedents.parallel: Malware aimed at one country spread on its own through global company networks, showing how far one attack can reach.
precedents.outcome: The US government called it the most destructive and costly cyberattack in history, with billions of dollars in damage across three continents.

ref.title: White House, Statement from the Press Secretary (15 February 2018)
ref.finding: In June 2017 the Russian military launched the most destructive and costly cyber-attack in history, causing billions of dollars in damage across Europe, Asia and the Americas.

nodes.label: AI-assisted art
nodes.summary: Views on AI-assisted art split. In one survey of 459 artists, most wanted model makers to disclose which artworks they train on and worried about the art workforce[1]; one study found artists using text-to-image tools became 25% more productive and drew about 50% more favourites per view, though novelty fell[2].

refs.title: Lovato et al., Foregrounding Artist Opinions: A Survey Study on Transparency, Ownership, and Fairness in AI Generative Art (2024)
refs.finding: In a survey of 459 artists, most wanted model makers to disclose which artworks they train on and were concerned about AI's effect on the art workforce, while seeing some potential benefits.

refs.title: Zhou and Lee, Generative artificial intelligence, human creativity, and art, PNAS Nexus (2024)
refs.finding: Artists who adopted text-to-image tools became 25% more productive and, after a few months, their work drew about 50% more favourites per view, though average novelty fell.

nodes.label: Software that reshapes itself for each person
nodes.summary: AI could build interfaces and small tools on demand, so software bends to each person instead of everyone adapting to one fixed app. Google's Gemini already generates interactive interfaces from a prompt[1]; researchers argue AI coding helps most when software is built to be reshaped[2].

refs.title: Google Research, Generative UI: A rich, custom, visual interactive user experience for any prompt (November 2025)
refs.finding: Gemini generates an entire interactive interface for a prompt, shipped in the Gemini app and Search AI Mode; raters preferred it to every method except sites designed by human experts.

refs.title: Litt, Horowitz, van Hardenberg and Matthews, Malleable Software (Ink & Switch, June 2025)
refs.finding: AI-assisted development can make it much faster to edit your tools, but only alongside software that lets people reshape and compose them.

nodes.label: AI makes realistic images and edits easy
nodes.summary: Anyone can now make or edit a photo-realistic image from a sentence; over 130 million users tried ChatGPT's image generation in its first week[2]. In one study, people could not tell AI faces from real ones[1]. The same ease can serve both fun and abuse.

refs.title: Nightingale and Farid, AI-synthesized faces are indistinguishable from real faces and more trustworthy, PNAS 119(8) (2022)
refs.finding: People could not tell AI-synthesized faces from real ones and rated the synthetic faces as more trustworthy.

refs.title: The Decoder, ChatGPT's image generation explodes with 700M creations in first week (April 2025)
refs.finding: OpenAI's COO said over 130 million users tried ChatGPT's image generation in its first week, creating over 700 million images amid a viral Ghibli-style trend.

nodes.label: Fun and amusement from AI images
nodes.summary: Turning a photo into a cartoon or a joke into a picture is cheap, instant entertainment for many people; over 130 million users tried ChatGPT's image generation in its first week, creating over 700 million images[1].

refs.title: The Decoder, ChatGPT's image generation explodes with 700M creations in first week (April 2025)
refs.finding: OpenAI's COO said over 130 million users tried ChatGPT's image generation in its first week, creating over 700 million images amid a viral Ghibli-style trend.

nodes.label: Deepfake nudes used to bully classmates
nodes.summary: Apps that undress photos make it easy for teenagers to target classmates. In one survey of 1,200 people aged 13 to 20, 1 in 8 personally knew someone targeted by deepfake nude imagery and 1 in 17 had been targeted themselves[1].

refs.title: Thorn, Deepfake Nudes & Young People (March 2025)
refs.finding: In a survey of 1,200 people aged 13 to 20, 1 in 8 personally knew someone targeted by deepfake nude imagery and 1 in 17 had been targeted themselves.

nodes.label: Driverless cars cut road injuries
nodes.summary: About 1.16 million people die in road crashes each year[1]. Over 271 million driverless miles in five US metro areas, Waymo reports 82% fewer injury crashes and 95% fewer serious-injury crashes than human drivers on the same roads[2]; one claims study with the insurer Swiss Re found 92% fewer bodily injury claims over 25.3 million miles[3]. Both analyses come from the company, and US regulators opened an investigation after a driverless car passed a stopped school bus[4].

refs.title: WHO, Road traffic injuries fact sheet, 2026
refs.finding: About 1.16 million people die each year in road traffic crashes, and 20 to 50 million more are injured.

refs.title: Waymo, Safety Impact data hub, data through June 2026
refs.finding: Over 271.3 million rider-only miles in Los Angeles, the San Francisco Bay Area, Phoenix, Austin and Atlanta, Waymo reports 82% fewer injury-causing crashes, 95% fewer serious-injury-or-worse crashes and 93% fewer pedestrian injury crashes than a human benchmark on the same roads.

refs.title: Waymo, New Swiss Re study: Waymo is safer than even the most advanced human-driven vehicles, 2024
refs.finding: Over 25.3 million miles, Waymo had 9 property damage and 2 bodily injury claims against 78 and 26 expected for human drivers, 88% and 92% fewer.

refs.title: NHTSA Office of Defects Investigation, PE25013 resume, 2025
refs.finding: NHTSA opened a preliminary evaluation on 17 October 2025 into about 2,000 Waymo vehicles after one drove around a stopped school bus.

limiters.limit: Service limited to a few mapped cities
limiters.evidence: The safety figures cover rider-only service in five US metro areas.

ref.title: Waymo, Safety Impact data hub, data through June 2026
ref.finding: Data covers Los Angeles, the San Francisco Bay Area, Phoenix, Austin and Atlanta.

limiters.evidence: US regulators opened an investigation into about 2,000 Waymo vehicles over how they behave around stopped school buses.

ref.title: NHTSA Office of Defects Investigation, PE25013 resume, 2025
ref.finding: Subject: Waymo AV drives around a stopped school bus; population about 2,000 vehicles; opened 17 October 2025.

enablers.action: Publish crash rates against human benchmarks
enablers.evidence: Waymo publishes crash rates by outcome for its rider-only miles, compared with human drivers on the same roads.

ref.title: Waymo, Safety Impact data hub, data through June 2026
ref.finding: Public crash-rate comparison by outcome over 271.3 million rider-only miles.

precedents.parallel: A computer that corrects the driver's mistakes in a skid is an early, narrow version of the same idea.
precedents.outcome: IIHS studies found it cut fatal single-vehicle crash risk by about half, and NHTSA estimated it saved about 4,100 lives in the US from 2010 to 2014.

ref.title: IIHS, Life-saving benefits of ESC continue to accrue, 2016
ref.finding: ESC lowers fatal single-vehicle crash risk by about 50% and fatal multiple-vehicle crash risk by 20%; NHTSA estimates about 4,100 lives saved in 2010 to 2014.

nodes.label: AI music floods streaming and feeds royalty fraud
nodes.summary: At Deezer, fully AI-generated tracks passed half of new uploads on peak days in June 2026, about 90,000 a day, but drew only 1 to 3% of streams, and up to 85% of those streams in 2025 were fraudulent[1]. In one US case, a man whose bots streamed hundreds of thousands of AI-generated songs billions of times pleaded guilty to wire fraud conspiracy and agreed to forfeit about $8 million[2]. In one Ipsos survey of 9,000 people in 8 countries commissioned by Deezer, 97% could not tell fully AI-generated music from human-made music in a blind test[1].

refs.title: Deezer, AI music has surpassed 50% of new music uploads for the first time, July 2026
refs.finding: About 90,000 fully AI-generated tracks a day were over 50% of new uploads at peak in June 2026; they make up 1 to 3% of streams, and up to 85% of their streams in 2025 were fraudulent, against 8% across the catalogue.

refs.title: Bloomberg Law, AI music maker who faked streams pleads guilty on fraud count, March 2026
refs.finding: Michael Smith pleaded guilty to one count of conspiracy to commit wire fraud over bots that streamed hundreds of thousands of AI-generated songs billions of times, and agreed to pay about $8 million.

nodes.control_note: The tools that let anyone make a song also make uploads and fake listeners cheap. Detection and royalty rules limit the payout from fraud but not the volume of uploads.

actions.action: Tag AI tracks and keep fraudulent streams out of royalties
actions.evidence: Deezer tags AI tracks, keeps them out of algorithmic and editorial playlists, excludes fraudulent streams from royalties and will remove AI tracks used for fraud; the effect on fraud volume is not published.

ref.title: Deezer, AI music has surpassed 50% of new music uploads for the first time, July 2026
ref.finding: AI-detected tracks are excluded from algorithmic recommendations and editorial playlists, fraudulent streams are excluded from royalty payments, and AI tracks used for streaming fraud will be removed.

actions.action: Prosecute streaming fraud
actions.evidence: US prosecutors brought a criminal case that ended in a guilty plea; one case does not show deterrence.

ref.title: Bloomberg Law, AI music maker who faked streams pleads guilty on fraud count, March 2026
ref.finding: Guilty plea to conspiracy to commit wire fraud, with about $8 million to be paid.

nodes.label: Surveillance pricing charges each shopper a different price
nodes.summary: Pricing firms can tailor what each shopper pays from personal data such as location, browsing history and even mouse movements; intermediaries studied by the US FTC had at least 250 business clients, from grocers to clothing retailers[1][2]. In one Consumer Reports test with 437 volunteers, Instacart's AI pricing tool showed about three in four grocery items at more than one price, with gaps of up to 23% per item; Instacart called the gaps negligible, denied using personal data and later stopped offering the tool[3]. Maryland now bars food retailers and delivery apps from setting prices with personal data[4], and Connecticut passed a similar law in June 2026[5].

refs.title: FTC, FTC Issues Orders to Eight Companies Seeking Information on Surveillance Pricing, July 2024
refs.finding: On 23 July 2024 the FTC ordered Mastercard, Revionics, Bloomreach, JPMorgan Chase, Task Software, PROS, Accenture and McKinsey to report on their surveillance pricing products, data inputs, customers and effects on the prices consumers pay.

refs.title: FTC, Surveillance Pricing Study Indicates Wide Range of Personal Data Used to Set Individualized Consumer Prices, January 2025
refs.finding: Initial staff findings of 17 January 2025: the intermediaries had at least 250 clients from grocery stores to apparel retailers, and data such as location, demographics, browsing history, mouse movements and items left in a cart can be used to tailor prices; released on a 3-2 vote with only hypothetical examples.

refs.title: Consumer Reports, Instacart's AI-enabled pricing experiments may be inflating your grocery bill, December 2025
refs.finding: 437 volunteers shopping the same items in September 2025 saw about three-quarters of products at multiple prices, gaps of up to 23% per item and baskets at one Seattle Safeway from $114.34 to $123.93; CR estimated about $1,200 a year for a household of four. Instacart confirmed experiments at 10 retailers via its Eversight AI pricing tools and later stopped offering the technology.

refs.title: Maryland General Assembly, HB 895 (2026), Protection From Predatory Pricing Act
refs.finding: Approved 28 April 2026 as Chapter 154, effective 1 October 2026: bars food retailers and third-party delivery services from dynamic pricing or using consumer personal data to set prices, enforced as an unfair, abusive or deceptive trade practice.

refs.title: Consumer Reports, statement on the signing of Connecticut's surveillance pricing bill into law, June 2026
refs.finding: Governor Lamont signed HB 5563 on 4 June 2026, making Connecticut the second state to curb personalised pricing, effective 1 July 2027; CR notes it still lets firms raise list prices and then give personalised discounts.

nodes.control_note: Cheap models make per-shopper pricing economical, and the same data drives targeted discounts shoppers like. Bans and labels can limit it, but price tests are hard for buyers to see.

actions.action: Ban pricing from personal data in groceries
actions.evidence: Maryland's ban for food retailers and delivery apps took effect on 1 October 2026; no enforcement figures are published yet and it does not cover other retail.

ref.title: Maryland General Assembly, HB 895 (2026), Chapter 154
ref.finding: Bars food retailers and third-party delivery service providers from dynamic pricing or using personal data to set prices, effective 1 October 2026.

actions.action: Label prices set from personal data
actions.evidence: New York requires a notice next to such prices with civil penalties of up to $1,000 per violation; a label informs shoppers but does not stop the practice.

ref.title: New York General Business Law section 349-a, algorithmic pricing disclosure
ref.finding: Prices set by personalized algorithmic pricing must carry the notice THIS PRICE WAS SET BY AN ALGORITHM USING YOUR PERSONAL DATA; a court may impose up to $1,000 per violation.

actions.action: Compel pricing intermediaries to disclose their data use
actions.evidence: FTC orders to eight firms produced initial findings in January 2025 on a 3-2 vote; the study was ongoing and could publish only hypothetical examples because the data were confidential.

ref.title: FTC, Surveillance Pricing Study Indicates Wide Range of Personal Data Used to Set Individualized Consumer Prices, January 2025
ref.finding: Staff analysed documents from six of the eight firms and found intermediaries with at least 250 retail clients; Commissioners Ferguson and Holyoak dissented from the release.

precedents.parallel: An online retailer quietly showed different customers different prices for the same goods, and the backlash came when shoppers compared notes.
precedents.outcome: Over five days Amazon varied discounts of 20% to 40% on 68 DVD titles, then refunded 6,896 customers an average of $3.10 and promised the lowest test price in any future test; Amazon said the prices were random, not based on customer data.

ref.title: Amazon.com Issues Statement Regarding Random Price Testing (Amazon, September 2000)
ref.finding: A five-day test on 68 DVD titles at discounts of 20% to 40%; 6,896 customers were refunded an average of $3.10.

precedents.event: Northeastern audit of price steering on shopping sites
precedents.parallel: Researchers using real shoppers' accounts found sites already tailored prices and results to the person, years before AI made it cheap.
precedents.outcome: Of 16 popular retail and travel sites tested in April and May 2014, four retailers and five travel sites showed some personalisation, such as member-only hotel rates at Orbitz and Cheaptickets and Expedia and Hotels.com steering some users to pricier hotels; most experiments found none.

ref.title: Study: some online shoppers pay more than others (Northeastern University, October 2014, on Hannak et al., IMC 2014)
ref.finding: Nine of 16 e-commerce sites showed evidence of personalisation, with some prices varying by hundreds of dollars.

nodes.label: Data-centre demand raises household power bills
nodes.summary: On PJM, a US regional grid, the market monitor attributes $29.4 billion, or 46.2%, of capacity charges across the four auctions for 2025/2026 to 2028/2029 to data-centre load, and estimates that data centres raised the total wholesale cost of power in the first half of 2026 by $11.11 per MWh, or 9.7%[1]. Maryland's consumer advocate estimated the 2025/2026 and 2026/2027 auctions together added $10.43 to $20.81 a month to residential bills at four Maryland utilities, with most of the new demand coming from data centres[2]. One Berkeley Lab and Brattle review found that from 2019 to 2025 the states with the fastest load growth mostly saw real retail prices fall, a pattern data-centre growth did not change, but it names PJM as a case where growth on a constrained grid raised prices[3].

refs.title: Monitoring Analytics (PJM Independent Market Monitor), Market Monitor Report, MC Information Webinar, July 2026
refs.finding: Of $16.4 billion in 2028/2029 capacity market charges, $6.3 billion (38.2%) resulted from data-centre load; over the last four auctions data-centre load accounts for $29.4 billion, or 46.2% of total capacity charges. In January to June 2026 the total cost of wholesale power was $114.50 per MWh against $103.40 without the data-centre impact, an increase of $11.11 (9.7%).

refs.title: Maryland Office of People's Counsel, Data center power demands drive record power auction prices with varying impacts on Maryland customers, July 2025
refs.finding: The 2026/2027 PJM capacity auction cleared at a record $329 per MW-day, and would have cleared at $389 without the cap; most of the increase in demand came from data centres, more than 5,400 MW above the year before. Estimated cumulative residential monthly bill increases from the last two auctions, against 2024/2025, were $16.49 at BGE, $17.68 at Pepco and SMECO, $10.43 at Delmarva Power and $20.81 at Potomac Edison.

refs.title: Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory and The Brattle Group, Retail Electricity Price Trends and Drivers: Data Update, 2026 edition, April 2026
refs.finding: US all-sector average retail prices rose 5.3% in nominal terms in 2025; in real terms they were 3% above 2019. From 2019 to 2025 the states with the highest load growth generally saw real prices decline, and the presence of significant data-centre load does not appear to alter that conclusion. A PJM case study shows accelerated load growth with supply and delivery constraints leading to significant price increases, with data-centre load growth linked to a 174% increase in auction revenues.

nodes.control_note: Data centres draw on the same grid as homes, so their demand lands on shared prices where supply is tight. Tariffs that make large new loads pay for the capacity they need can keep much of it off household bills, but they do not add supply.

actions.action: Make large new loads pay for the capacity they reserve
actions.evidence: Ohio's regulator made new data centres above 25 MW in AEP Ohio's territory pay for at least 85% of their subscribed capacity for up to 12 years; it covers only one utility's territory.

ref.title: POWER Magazine, Regulator approves AEP Ohio's landmark data center tariff, July 2025
ref.finding: The PUCO order of 9 July 2025 requires new data-centre customers above 25 MW to pay for at least 85% of subscribed monthly capacity for up to 12 years, with a four-year ramp, exit fees and financial assurance; the commission said it safeguards other customers from cost-shifting risks of underused investments.

actions.action: Move data-centre load into its own capacity auction
actions.evidence: PJM's market monitor proposes a dedicated auction so that data centres pay for their own capacity rather than raising the price everyone else pays.

ref.title: Monitoring Analytics (PJM Independent Market Monitor), Market Monitor Report, MC Information Webinar, July 2026
ref.finding: It is the IMM's position that data-centre load should be removed from the capacity market and procured through a dedicated auction, so that data centres pay for their own capacity and do not impose capacity costs on other customers.

precedents.event: Crypto-mining power rates in upstate New York
precedents.parallel: A new kind of computing load arrived in small towns with finite cheap power and pushed up what households paid.
precedents.outcome: New York regulators let municipal utilities charge separate rates to customers above 300 kW and 250 kWh per square foot a year, after average residential bills in Plattsburgh rose $10 a month in January that regulators blamed on two mining firms.

ref.title: Utility Dive, Munis to charge bitcoin miners higher power prices in New York, March 2018
ref.finding: The New York PSC allowed municipal utilities to create a tariff for high-density load customers with maximum demand above 300 kW and load density above 250 kWh per square foot per year; regulators said average Plattsburgh residential bills jumped $10 a month in January because of two cryptocurrency companies, which would have paid over 60% more under the new rates.

nodes.label: Prompt injection hijacks AI agents
nodes.summary: AI agents that read email, web pages or documents can be steered by instructions hidden in that content. In one public red-teaming competition sponsored by the UK AI Security Institute, about 1.8 million attacks on 22 frontier agents produced over 60,000 policy violations such as unauthorised data access, and nearly all agents broke policy for most behaviours within 10 to 100 queries[1]. Researchers showed that a single crafted email could make Microsoft 365 Copilot leak data with no user interaction[2]. Google's scans of the public web found detections of malicious injections rose by a relative 32% from November 2025 to February 2026, though the attacks seen so far show limited sophistication[3]. The UK NCSC says prompt injection may never be fully mitigated the way SQL injection can be[4].

refs.title: Zou et al., Security Challenges in AI Agent Deployment: Insights from a Large Scale Public Competition, arXiv 2025
refs.finding: A competition run on Gray Swan Arena and sponsored by the UK AI Security Institute targeted 22 frontier agents across 44 deployment scenarios; 1.8 million prompt-injection attacks produced over 60,000 successful policy violations such as unauthorised data access and illicit financial actions. Nearly all agents showed violations for most behaviours within 10 to 100 queries, attacks transferred across models, and robustness correlated little with model size, capability or inference-time compute.

refs.title: Reddy and Gujral, EchoLeak: The First Real-World Zero-Click Prompt Injection Exploit in a Production LLM System, arXiv 2025
refs.finding: CVE-2025-32711 in Microsoft 365 Copilot allowed remote, unauthenticated data exfiltration via a single crafted email with no user interaction, bypassing Microsoft's cross-prompt-injection classifier, link redaction and the content security policy.

refs.title: Google, AI threats in the wild: The current state of prompt injections on the web, April 2026
refs.finding: Scanning Common Crawl snapshots of 2 to 3 billion pages each, Google's threat intelligence teams found a relative increase of 32% in the malicious category between November 2025 and February 2026, including attempts at data exfiltration and file deletion; observed attacks showed limited sophistication, and the authors expect the threat to grow in scale and complexity.

refs.title: NCSC, Prompt injection is not SQL injection (it may be worse), December 2025
refs.finding: Because LLMs make no distinction between data and instructions, prompt injection may never be totally mitigated in the way SQL injection can be; the NCSC advises treating it as a residual risk, limiting what LLM systems can do with deterministic controls and logging tool calls.

nodes.control_note: Agents are useful because they read outside content and act on it, and that same reading is the attacker's way in. Narrow permissions and designs that keep untrusted text out of control decisions limit the damage, but no filter removes the risk.

actions.action: Keep untrusted data out of an agent's control flow
actions.evidence: One design that fixes the plan from the user's trusted query and blocks private data from leaving through unauthorised flows solved 77% of AgentDojo tasks with provable security, against 84% for an undefended agent.

ref.title: Debenedetti et al., Defeating Prompt Injections by Design, arXiv 2025
ref.finding: The defence wraps the LLM in a protective system layer that extracts control and data flows from the trusted query, so retrieved untrusted data cannot change program flow; it solves 77% of AgentDojo tasks with provable security, compared with 84% undefended.

actions.action: Cut agent privileges to those of the content it reads
actions.evidence: The UK NCSC advises deployers to rely on deterministic, non-LLM controls on what a system can do and to log tool and API calls, since detection and training only make attacks harder.

ref.title: NCSC, Prompt injection is not SQL injection (it may be worse), December 2025
ref.finding: Recommends secure design with deterministic controls, dropping an LLM's privileges to those of any untrusted party whose content it processes, and monitoring inputs, outputs and tool calls; deny-lists of malicious phrases are easy to evade.

precedents.event: SQL injection breaches of card processors
precedents.parallel: Software that mixed untrusted input with commands let attackers take over databases, the flaw class the NCSC compares prompt injection with.
precedents.outcome: A US federal indictment charged Albert Gonzalez and two unnamed hackers over SQL injection attacks on Heartland Payment Systems, 7-Eleven and Hannaford; the Heartland attack led to the theft of more than about 130 million card numbers and the Hannaford attack about 4.2 million.

ref.title: United States v. Albert Gonzalez, indictment, US District Court for the District of New Jersey, 2009
ref.finding: Beginning on or about 26 December 2007 Heartland was the victim of a SQL Injection Attack that resulted in the theft of more than approximately 130 million credit and debit card numbers; 7-Eleven (about August 2007) and Hannaford, with about 4.2 million card numbers stolen, were also hit by SQL Injection Attacks.

nodes.label: Gas-powered data centres pollute nearby neighbourhoods
nodes.summary: Some AI data centres burn gas on site for power. xAI set up 35 temporary gas turbines without air permits at its South Memphis data centre, and in one University of Tennessee analysis of satellite data for TIME, peak nitrogen dioxide levels after June 2024 rose 79% next to the site and 9% in nearby Boxtown, while averages rose 3%; the authors said a nearby power plant and traffic may also have contributed[1]. A study commissioned by the Southern Environmental Law Center estimated that xAI's proposed 41-turbine plant in Southaven, Mississippi would cause $30 million to $44 million a year in health damages[2], and the NAACP sued in April 2026 over 27 turbines running there without a permit[3]. One modelling study projects that the yearly public health burden of US data centres' air pollutant emissions could pass $20 billion by 2028, with the burden per household in the worst-hit counties about seven times the national average[4]. City air tests near the Memphis site on two days in June 2025 found none of 10 pollutants at dangerous levels, though they left out ozone[5].

refs.title: TIME, 'We Are the Last of the Forgotten': Inside the Memphis Community Battling Elon Musk's xAI, August 2025
refs.finding: xAI brought in 35 unpermitted temporary methane gas turbines, which on manufacturer data could emit 1,200 to 2,000 tons of nitrogen oxides a year. University of Tennessee, Knoxville researchers using NASA and ESA satellite data found average nitrogen dioxide up 3% comparing the periods before June 2024 and afterward, and peak concentrations up 79% from pre-xAI levels in areas immediately surrounding the data centre and 9% in Boxtown; they said the changes likely reflect the combined influence of gas-fired sources, including the nearby TVA plant, and that motor vehicles may have contributed.

refs.title: Southern Environmental Law Center, New study finds proposed xAI gas plant could worsen regional air pollution, cause millions of dollars in annual health damages, February 2026
refs.finding: A study by EmPower Analytics Group for SELC found the proposed permit for 41 permanent turbines in Southaven would allow nearly 20 tons of fine particle pollution a year plus hundreds of tons of precursor pollutants, raising fine particles by up to 0.5 micrograms per cubic metre in some communities and causing $30 million to $44 million in annual health damages; xAI had already installed 27 unpermitted turbines at the site.

refs.title: Earthjustice, NAACP Sues xAI for Illegal Pollution from Data Center Power Plant, April 2026
refs.finding: On 14 April 2026 the NAACP and its Mississippi State Conference sued xAI in federal court in the Northern District of Mississippi for running 27 gas turbines in Southaven without an air permit, with potential yearly emissions of more than 1,700 tons of nitrogen oxides and up to 180 tons of fine particulate matter.

refs.title: Han, Wu, Li, Wierman and Ren, Health-Informed Computing: Estimating and Addressing the Public Health Impact of Data Centers, arXiv 2024, revised June 2026
refs.finding: Modelling of criteria air pollutant emissions projects the total annual public health burden of US data centres could rise to more than $20 billion by 2028; the national impact is modest, but in the most affected counties the per-household burden can reach about seven times the national average.

refs.title: TechCrunch, Air quality tests around xAI's Memphis data center raise questions, June 2025
refs.finding: Third-party tests for the City of Memphis on 13 and 16 June 2025 at three sites found none of the 10 pollutants tested at dangerous levels; winds on those days were unlikely to carry pollutants to the sites, the tests did not include ozone, and SELC said monitors placed against buildings could interfere with results.

nodes.control_note: On-site gas turbines let a data centre run before the grid can supply it, and the people living downwind pay in dirtier air. Permits with emission controls and caps, and siting that counts health costs, can cut the harm, but only where regulators treat the turbines as power plants.

actions.action: Permit on-site turbines only with emission caps
actions.evidence: The Shelby County Health Department approved 15 permanent turbines for xAI in July 2025 with caps on 12-month rolling emissions; most complaints were about the temporary turbines, which the permit did not cover.

ref.title: Action News 5, Health dept. grants permit for xAI turbines, July 2025
ref.finding: The permit approved on 2 July 2025 covers 15 permanent natural gas turbines, caps 12-month rolling emission rates that xAI must record monthly, and lists standards for nitrogen oxide, ammonia and hazardous air pollutants; the health department said most SELC concerns targeted the temporary turbines, due to be removed by the end of July.

actions.action: Sue under the Clean Air Act over unpermitted turbines
actions.evidence: The NAACP asks a federal court to stop xAI's unpermitted turbines in Southaven, require the best available control technology and impose daily penalties; the case was pending.

ref.title: Earthjustice, NAACP Sues xAI for Illegal Pollution from Data Center Power Plant, April 2026
ref.finding: The suit filed on 14 April 2026 seeks a declaration that xAI violated the Clean Air Act, an order to stop operating unpermitted turbines and install best available control technology, and penalties for each day of violation.

actions.action: Count health costs when siting data centres and scheduling their load
actions.evidence: The authors of one modelling study propose health-informed computing, which factors public health costs into where and when data centres run, and reporting of health impacts alongside energy use.

ref.title: Han, Wu, Li, Wierman and Ren, Health-Informed Computing: Estimating and Addressing the Public Health Impact of Data Centers, arXiv 2024, revised June 2026
ref.finding: Proposes a health-informed computing framework that brings public health costs into data-centre resource management across space and time, and recommends energy reporting that includes public health impacts.

precedents.event: Greenidge crypto-mining power plant permit denial
precedents.parallel: A new kind of computing load revived a fossil-fuel power plant to run its own machines, and regulators had to decide whether the pollution was acceptable.
precedents.outcome: A gas plant in New York that had sat dormant for six years was repurposed and its owners installed tens of thousands of crypto-mining machines, with carbon dioxide emissions rising roughly tenfold in 2020; on 30 June 2022 New York's environmental regulator denied its Title V air permit as inconsistent with the state's climate goals.

ref.title: Earthjustice, New York State Denies Air Pollution Permit for Fossil Fuel-burning Crypto mining operation, Citing Energy-Intensity and Environmental Concerns, June 2022
ref.finding: On 30 June 2022 the New York State Department of Environmental Conservation denied Greenidge Generation's Title V air permit, finding the energy and climate impacts of proof-of-work mining at the plant inconsistent with New York's climate goals; carbon dioxide emissions rose roughly tenfold in 2020 as mining machines were installed.

nodes.label: AI reads lost ancient texts
nodes.summary: Machine learning is recovering writing that people could not read. In 2023 a team using machine-learning ink detection on scans of one of the Herculaneum scrolls read more than 2,000 characters, about 5% of the scroll[1]; in 2025 the same approach recovered a title, Philodemus's On Vices, from a scroll that is still rolled, though the book number is uncertain[2], and in June 2026 the team reported in a preprint that it had deciphered all surviving text of another scroll, about 20 columns of Stoic philosophy[3]. For Latin inscriptions, one Nature study found historians judged the AI's suggested parallels useful starting points in 90% of cases, and historians working with it restored and located texts better than humans or the AI alone[4]. Its suggestions are not answers: the right restoration is among its top 20 guesses 73% of the time for gaps of up to ten characters and 58% when the gap length is unknown[5].

refs.title: Vesuvius Challenge, 2023 Grand Prize awarded: we can read the scrolls!, February 2024
refs.finding: Youssef Nader, Luke Farritor and Julian Schilliger shared the $700,000 Grand Prize for reading four passages of 140 characters plus 11 more columns, more than 2,000 characters, using machine-learning ink detection and automatic segmentation of the CT scan; about 5% of the first scroll was read and about 95% remained unread.

refs.title: Vesuvius Challenge, $60,000 First Title Prize Awarded, May 2025
refs.finding: Marcel Roth and Micha Nowak won the first $60,000 First Title Prize for PHerc. 172, held by the Bodleian Libraries; an ink detection model run on autosegmentation revealed the title, which papyrologists read as Philodemus, On Vices, probably Book 1, the first title of a still-rolled Herculaneum scroll ever recovered noninvasively. The book number is less certain and segmentation still sometimes jumps between sheets.

refs.title: Smithsonian Magazine, Scientists Have Deciphered the Surviving Fragments of a 2,000-Year-Old Philosophical Treatise Frozen in Time by Mount Vesuvius' Eruption, June 2026
refs.finding: The Vesuvius Challenge team led by Brent Seales used X-ray imaging, virtual unwrapping and AI to decipher all surviving text of PHerc. 1667, roughly 20 columns of Stoic philosophy; more than half of the scroll had been lost to earlier attempts to open it, and the findings are in a team preprint.

refs.title: Assael et al., Contextualizing ancient texts with generative neural networks, Nature 2025
refs.finding: Aeneas, a generative neural network, retrieves parallels between inscriptions, uses images and restores text of any length; in a large study historians found its parallels useful research starting points in 90% of cases, their confidence in key tasks rose 44%, historians paired with it beat both humans and AI alone on restoration and geographical attribution, and its dates fell within 13 years of ground-truth ranges.

refs.title: Google DeepMind, Aeneas transforms how historians connect the past, July 2025
refs.finding: Trained on the Latin Epigraphic Dataset of over 176,000 Latin inscriptions, Aeneas reaches top-20 restoration accuracy of 73% in gaps of up to ten characters and 58% when the gap length is unknown, attributes texts to one of 62 Roman provinces with 72% accuracy, and was tested with 23 historians.

limiters.limit: Most of the text is still unread
limiters.evidence: After the 2023 breakthrough about 95% of the first scroll remained unread, and the project aims to read all 300 scrolls in its collection.

ref.title: Vesuvius Challenge, 2023 Grand Prize awarded: we can read the scrolls!, February 2024
ref.finding: About 5% of the first scroll had been unwrapped and read; the next goal was 90% of four scanned scrolls and eventually all 300 scrolls.

limiters.evidence: Even among its top 20 suggestions, the inscription model finds the right text only 58% of the time when the gap length is unknown.

ref.title: Google DeepMind, Aeneas transforms how historians connect the past, July 2025
ref.finding: Top-20 restoration accuracy is 73% in gaps of up to ten characters and 58% when the restoration length is unknown.

limiters.evidence: The book number in the first recovered title is less certain, and segmentation of the scan still sometimes jumps to an adjacent sheet.

ref.title: Vesuvius Challenge, $60,000 First Title Prize Awarded, May 2025
ref.finding: The book number is less certain for now, the book does not match On Flattery as expected, and sheet switches still occur in segmentation, though they are improving.

enablers.action: Fund open prizes for reading the scrolls
enablers.counters: Most of the text is still unread
enablers.evidence: A $700,000 Grand Prize in 2023 and a $60,000 First Title Prize in 2025 went to outside contestants who improved segmentation and ink detection.

ref.title: Vesuvius Challenge, 2023 Grand Prize awarded: we can read the scrolls!, February 2024
ref.finding: The 2023 Grand Prize of $700,000 went to three contestants; the project set further goals to read 90% of four scanned scrolls.

enablers.action: Have papyrologists review each AI reading
enablers.evidence: The papyrological team independently reviewed the ink detection output before the title of PHerc. 172 was announced, and flagged which parts of the reading were uncertain.

ref.title: Vesuvius Challenge, $60,000 First Title Prize Awarded, May 2025
ref.finding: The papyrological team led by Federica Nicolardi independently reviewed the output and unanimously read the author as Philodemus and the title as On Vices, while marking the book number as less certain.

enablers.action: Release models and datasets openly
enablers.evidence: An interactive version of the inscription model is free to use, and its code and dataset are open source, so other historians can test its suggestions.

ref.title: Google DeepMind, Aeneas transforms how historians connect the past, July 2025
ref.finding: An interactive version of Aeneas is free to use, and the team is open-sourcing its code and dataset on GitHub.

precedents.event: Virtual unwrapping of the En-Gedi scroll
precedents.parallel: Before machine learning, scanning and software already let researchers read a charred scroll that could never be opened by hand.
precedents.outcome: A team led by Brent Seales scanned a burned scroll excavated in 1970 at the synagogue of En Gedi, Israel, and virtually unwrapped it to reveal Leviticus, 35 lines across five wraps with 18 preserved and 17 reconstructed; it was the first severely damaged, ink-based scroll unrolled and identified noninvasively.

ref.title: University of Kentucky, Virtually Unwrapping the En-Gedi Scroll, September 2016
ref.finding: Published in Science Advances on 21 September 2016: virtual unwrapping of high-resolution scans revealed Leviticus in a charred scroll that likely will never be physically opened, the earliest copy of a Pentateuchal book ever found in a Holy Ark.

nodes.label: Data-centre tax breaks drain state budgets
nodes.summary: US states court the data-centre boom that AI's demand for computing power is driving with sales tax exemptions on construction and servers, and the cost has outrun forecasts[2]. Ohio's exemption cost $554.9 million in 2024, about four times the forecast, and $1.6 billion in 2025, eleven times the original estimate of $136 million[1]. Texas forecast in 2025 that it would lose $3.2 billion in sales tax over two years, a figure its Comptroller's Office called almost certainly an underestimate, and had audited only 20 of 138 qualifying data centres, six of them in breach[2]. An evaluation for Georgia's state auditor put forgone state revenue at $474.2 million in FY 2025, judged that 70% of the state's data centres would exist without the exemption and counted $34.6 million in state tax from the construction and $6.9 million from the operations it attributed to the break, though it also found the gain to the state economy significantly higher than the revenue forgone[3]. Virginia's legislative auditor found its exemption saved data centres $928 million in FY23 and returned 48 cents in state revenue per dollar, close to the 41-cent average for the state's other incentives, with most of the economic benefit coming from construction[4].

refs.title: Signal Ohio via WTOP News, Ohio data center tax break cost $1.4 billion more than expected in 2025, May 2026
refs.finding: Figures from the Ohio Department of Taxation show the data-centre sales tax exemption cost the state $554.9 million in 2024, about four times the department's forecast, plus $166.8 million in lost local sales taxes; in 2025 it cost $1.6 billion, eleven times the original estimate of $136 million. Lawmakers voted to end the break and Governor Mike DeWine vetoed the repeal.

refs.title: Texas Tribune, Texas' multibillion-dollar sales tax exemption for data centers is growing, while audits lag, July 2026
refs.finding: The state forecast in 2025 that it would lose $3.2 billion in sales tax revenue over two years from data centres, a figure the Comptroller's Office said is almost certainly an underestimate; the exemption cost $5.4 million in 2015. Of 138 qualified data centres only 20 had been audited, and six were breaching the terms, at least four of them by failing to create the required jobs; those out of compliance must pay back the money. The article ties the growth in data centres to artificial intelligence raising demand for computing power.

refs.title: Georgia Department of Audits and Accounts, Tax Incentive Evaluation: Georgia Data Center Sales & Use Tax Exemption, December 2025, revised January 2026
refs.finding: The University of Georgia's Carl Vinson Institute of Government estimated forgone state tax revenue of $474.2 million in FY 2025 and attributed 30% of Georgia's data centres to the exemption, so 70% would exist without it. Activity attributed to the exemption generated $34.6 million in state tax from construction and $6.9 million from operations, a fiscal return of 4%, while state economic growth, an economic return of 289%, was significantly higher than the forgone revenue.

refs.title: Joint Legislative Audit and Review Commission, Data Centers in Virginia, Report 598, December 2024
refs.finding: Since 2010 Virginia has exempted data centres from its retail sales and use tax; the exemption provided $928 million in tax savings in FY23 and about 90% of the industry uses it. The industry is estimated to contribute 74,000 jobs, $5.5 billion in labour income and $9.1 billion in GDP a year, mostly from construction rather than ongoing operations. The exemption returns 48 cents in state revenue per $1 spent, against 41 cents for the average Virginia incentive, and like most incentives does not pay for itself.

nodes.control_note: States offer the breaks because rival states do and companies say they weigh them when choosing a site, so no state wants to drop them first. Caps, pauses on new approvals, audits with clawbacks and taxes on data-centre power use can limit the cost, but breaks already granted run for years.

actions.action: Pause approvals of new exemptions
actions.evidence: Ohio's governor told the state's Tax Credit Authority to stop approving new data-centre sales tax exemptions while officials review their costs; projects already approved keep their breaks.

ref.title: The Register, Ohio hits pause on datacenter tax breaks draining its coffers, June 2026
ref.finding: Governor Mike DeWine directed the Tax Credit Authority to stop approving new data-centre sales tax exemption requests while officials review the industry's costs and impacts; the pause covers only new approvals, and projects already approved keep their breaks. Good Jobs First puts the 2025 cost of Ohio's exemption at more than $1.5 billion, about 11 times the state's $136 million forecast.

actions.action: Tax data-centre electricity use
actions.evidence: Virginia kept its exemption but taxes data-centre electricity at $0.011 per kWh from July 2026 to June 2028, capped at $600 million a year, which recovers part of the revenue without ending the break.

ref.title: Holland & Knight, Virginia Preserves Data Center Tax Incentive, Adds New Electricity Consumption Tax, August 2026
ref.finding: Virginia kept its sales and use tax exemption for qualifying data-centre equipment and instead imposed a tax of $0.011 per kilowatt-hour of electricity consumed by data-centre operators from 1 July 2026 through 30 June 2028, with annual collections capped at $600 million and up to $1.2 billion in additional revenue over the biennium.

precedents.parallel: A state pledged billions in tax credits to win a high-technology investment on promises of jobs and capital that the company later scaled back.
precedents.outcome: Foxconn would have qualified for $2.85 billion in Wisconsin tax credits for investing $10 billion and creating 13,000 jobs; in April 2021 a new contract for a smaller facility cut that to up to $80 million for 1,454 jobs and $676 million of investment by 2026, and let the state recover incentives on default.

ref.title: Associated Press via KSAT, Foxconn deal with Wisconsin lowers tax breaks to $80 million, April 2021
ref.finding: Under the original deal Foxconn would have qualified for $2.85 billion in state tax credits if it invested $10 billion and created 13,000 jobs; the new contract lets it qualify for $80 million if it employs 1,454 people and invests $676 million by 2026, allows the state to recover 100% of incentives paid each year in the event of a default, and covers a smaller facility, which Foxconn said reflected unanticipated market fluctuations.

nodes.label: Propaganda networks seed chatbot answers
nodes.summary: Propaganda sites can be written for machines rather than people, so that chatbots that train on or search the web repeat their claims[1]. The American Sunlight Project estimates the pro-Russia Pravda network publishes at least 3.6 million articles a year across 182 domains and subdomains, and argues it targets crawlers and training-data scrapers rather than human readers[1]. In one NewsGuard audit in March 2025, the 10 leading generative AI tools repeated false narratives laundered by the network 33% of the time[2]. In an ISD test of 300 questions about the war in Ukraine in five languages, Russian state-attributed sources appeared in 18% of answers from four chatbots, rising from 11% for neutral questions to 24% for malicious ones, though only two links came from the Pravda network[3]. One peer-reviewed audit of 416 answers from four chatbots found 5% supported disinformation and 8% cited Pravda sites, mostly for niche questions, and its authors attribute this to data voids, topics with little credible coverage, rather than deliberate grooming[4].

refs.title: Newport and Jankowicz (American Sunlight Project), Russian networks flood the Internet with propaganda, aiming to corrupt AI chatbots, Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists, March 2025
refs.finding: The American Sunlight Project estimates the pro-Russia Pravda network publishes at least 3.6 million articles a year, likely an underestimate, across 182 domains and subdomains targeting at least 74 countries and regions in 12 languages; the authors believe the network targets an automated audience of search-optimisation crawlers and scrapers that collect training data rather than human readers. NewsGuard and the Atlantic Council's DFRLab confirmed that some major AI chatbots cited Pravda network content.

refs.title: NewsGuard, A Well-funded Moscow-based Global 'News' Network has Infected Western Artificial Intelligence Tools Worldwide with Russian Propaganda, March 2025
refs.finding: An audit of the 10 leading generative AI tools found they repeated false narratives laundered by the Pravda network 33% of the time; the network published 3,600,000 articles in 2024.

refs.title: Institute for Strategic Dialogue, Talking points: When chatbots surface Russian state media, October 2025
refs.finding: Across 300 queries about the war in Ukraine in English, Spanish, French, German and Italian, Russian state-attributed content appeared in 18% of responses from ChatGPT, Gemini, Grok and DeepSeek: 11% for neutral queries, 18% for biased and 24% for malicious ones. ChatGPT cited the most Russian sources, Gemini the fewest and was the only one to show safety warnings, and only two links came from the Pravda network; ISD says limited data access makes it impossible to tell whether LLM grooming happens at scale.

refs.title: Alyukov, Makhortykh, Voronovici and Sydorova, LLMs grooming or data voids? LLM-powered chatbot references to Kremlin disinformation reflect information gaps, not manipulation, HKS Misinformation Review 2025
refs.finding: Of 416 responses from ChatGPT-4o, Gemini 2.5 Flash, Copilot and Grok-2 to 13 prompts, collected in Manchester and Bern in April 2025, 5% (21) supported disinformation and 8% referenced Pravda domains, almost all from Copilot, mostly in reply to niche prompts; of the 30 answers that cited Pravda without supporting disinformation, about two-thirds cautioned that the claims were unverified or tied them to disinformation outlets. The authors attribute this to data voids, gaps in credible information, rather than foreign manipulation, and call their study preliminary and narrow.

nodes.control_note: Chatbots that answer from the web take in whatever covers a question, so a network that floods thinly covered topics can get its claims cited. Labelling or excluding state-attributed sources and filling data voids with credible coverage reduce the exposure, but cannot vet every new site.

actions.action: Label or exclude state-attributed sources in answers
actions.evidence: ISD urges AI companies to build a shared list of state-attributed sources and blacklist or clearly label them; in its test only Gemini showed safety warnings for biased or malicious prompts.

ref.title: Institute for Strategic Dialogue, Talking points: When chatbots surface Russian state media, October 2025
ref.finding: Recommends that AI companies build a shared repository of state-attributed sources, blacklist or clearly label them, and sign the EU Code of Conduct on Disinformation, and that the European Commission clarify how EU sanctions on state media apply to chatbot outputs under the Digital Services Act.

actions.action: Warn on data-void queries and fill the gaps with credible coverage
actions.evidence: The authors of one audit propose warning banners for questions that fall into data voids, passed on to chatbots that use search, and working with news organisations to fill those gaps in advance.

ref.title: Alyukov, Makhortykh, Voronovici and Sydorova, LLMs grooming or data voids? LLM-powered chatbot references to Kremlin disinformation reflect information gaps, not manipulation, HKS Misinformation Review 2025
ref.finding: Recommends that search engines show warning banners for data-void queries and pass these warnings to integrated chatbots, that search developers work with reputable news organisations to fill data voids in advance, and that AI companies share aggregated usage data and be more transparent about how sources shape answers.

precedents.event: Google demotes hoaxes and conspiracy pages in Search
precedents.parallel: Before chatbots answered from the web, search engines surfaced hoaxes and unsupported conspiracy theories for some queries and had to change how they weigh sources.
precedents.outcome: Google said around 0.25% of its daily queries had been returning offensive or clearly misleading content, and adjusted its ranking signals to surface more authoritative pages and demote low-quality content.

ref.title: Google, Our latest quality improvements for Search, April 2017
ref.finding: A small set of queries in Google's daily traffic, around 0.25%, had been returning offensive or clearly misleading content, including hoaxes and unsupported conspiracy theories; Google adjusted ranking signals to surface more authoritative pages and demote low-quality content, updated its Search Quality Rater Guidelines, and made it easier to flag Autocomplete predictions and Featured Snippets.

nodes.label: Data centres drop off the grid all at once
nodes.summary: Data centres protect their servers by switching to backup power when grid voltage dips, so a single fault can make many of them leave the grid at the same moment[1]. In July 2024 a fault on a 230 kV line in the US Eastern Interconnection led data centres to drop about 1,500 MW of demand at once, a load loss of a size the grid had not historically seen after a fault; frequency rose to 60.047 Hz and operators had to bring voltage back down, though NERC found it caused no significant operating issues[1]. In July 2026 nearly 4,000 MW of data-centre load in Northern Virginia tripped offline after a properly cleared fault, the largest such event in PJM's history, and PJM brought its system back within limits in nine minutes[2]. Load losses of 1,000 MW or more have occurred in the Eastern and Texas interconnections, mostly in 2024 and 2025, and NERC says the rise in such events coincides with a growing share of large loads; its response covers data centres for artificial intelligence[3]. The risk is not unique to AI: in 26 events in Texas, crypto-mining sites lost 17% to 95% of their consumption within milliseconds of normally cleared faults[4].

refs.title: NERC, Incident Review: Considering Simultaneous Voltage-Sensitive Load Reductions, January 2025
refs.finding: On 10 July 2024 a lightning arrestor failed on a 230 kV line in the Eastern Interconnection, causing six successive faults in 82 seconds, all cleared properly; coincident with them about 1,500 MW of load, exclusively data-centre load, was disconnected on the customer side as data centres transferred to backup power. The grid has not historically experienced simultaneous load losses of this magnitude in response to a fault. Frequency rose to 60.047 Hz and voltage to 1.07 per unit, and operators removed shunt capacitor banks to bring voltage back to normal; about 1,260 MW did not return for hours. NERC says the disturbance did not cause significant operating issues, but the risk could quickly increase as data-centre loads grow.

refs.title: American Public Power Association, PJM, Dominion Review Large Load Transfer Event, August 2026
refs.finding: On 22 July 2026 nearly 4,000 MW of data-centre load in Northern Virginia, in the Dominion zone, tripped offline, about 3,800 MW by Dominion's count and the largest such event in PJM history; a mechanical failure removed a 230 kV line and data centres disconnected although the fault was properly cleared, in a first drop of 2,970 MW and a second of 1,099 MW. PJM load fell from 99,984 MW to 96,205 MW, and PJM recovered its area control error limit within nine minutes, inside NERC's 30-minute standard.

refs.title: Utility Dive, Sudden data center load losses prompt NERC alert, recommendations, April 2026
refs.finding: NERC describes widespread and unexpected customer-initiated load reductions, mostly in 2024 and 2025, in which 1,000 MW or more dropped off the bulk power system, in the Eastern and Texas interconnections since 2022; it said the increase of large-load events coincides with an increase in large-load penetration. Its planned Level 3 alert covers the modelling, study, monitoring and commissioning of large loads, including data centers for artificial intelligence, and NERC said entities generally did not have sufficient processes to address emerging computational loads.

refs.title: POWER Magazine, FERC Orders Mandatory NERC Reliability Standards for Data Center and Other Computational Loads, July 2026
refs.finding: On 16 July 2026 FERC directed NERC to file one or more mandatory reliability standards for integrating computational loads, a category covering generative-AI data centres, cryptocurrency mines and other IT facilities, by 31 December 2026, without itself setting a size threshold or compliance obligations; Chairman Laura Swett said winning the AI race must not threaten reliability. A NERC review found that across 26 events in ERCOT from January 2023 to September 2025, crypto-mining facilities lost 17% to 95% of their consumption within milliseconds of a normally cleared transmission fault.

nodes.control_note: Data centres are set to switch to backup power when grid voltage dips, which protects their servers but can remove their demand all at once. Requirements to ride through normal faults, with models and tests of each large load before it connects, can contain the risk, but mandatory standards are only due at the end of 2026 while the loads keep growing.

actions.action: Write mandatory reliability standards for computational loads
actions.evidence: FERC ordered NERC in July 2026 to file mandatory reliability standards for data centres and other computational loads by 31 December 2026; the order itself sets no size threshold or compliance obligations.

ref.title: POWER Magazine, FERC Orders Mandatory NERC Reliability Standards for Data Center and Other Computational Loads, July 2026
ref.finding: On 16 July 2026 FERC directed NERC to file one or more mandatory reliability standards for integrating computational loads, a category covering generative-AI data centres, cryptocurrency mines and other IT facilities, by 31 December 2026, without itself setting a size threshold or compliance obligations; Chairman Laura Swett said winning the AI race must not threaten reliability. A NERC review found that across 26 events in ERCOT from January 2023 to September 2025, crypto-mining facilities lost 17% to 95% of their consumption within milliseconds of a normally cleared transmission fault.

actions.action: Model, study and test large loads before they connect
actions.evidence: NERC's Level 3 alert of May 2026 asks transmission entities to model computational loads, study aggregate load losses, test facilities before energisation and prevent loss of firm load in normally cleared faults; it is not a mandatory standard and carries no penalties.

ref.title: Data Center Frontier, Why NERC Now Sees AI Data Centers as Grid Actors, May 2026
ref.finding: NERC's Level 3 alert of 4 May 2026 sets seven essential actions, among them modelling computational loads, studying aggregate load reductions, commissioning tests before energisation and preventing loss of firm computational load during normally cleared faults, with status reports due by 3 August 2026; it is not a mandatory reliability standard and carries no direct penalties.

precedents.event: Wind-farm settings black out South Australia
precedents.parallel: A new kind of grid-connected equipment, set to disconnect after repeated voltage dips, turned a series of faults into a sudden loss of a size the grid had not planned for.
precedents.outcome: After six voltage dips in two minutes, settings at nine wind farms cut 456 MW of output in under seven seconds, the Heywood Interconnector tripped and the whole state lost supply; changed turbine control settings removed the risk of recurrence, and AEMO's final report made 19 recommendations.

ref.title: Energy Source & Distribution, AEMO publishes final report on SA blackouts, March 2017
ref.finding: Tornadoes damaged transmission lines and caused six voltage dips over two minutes on 28 September 2016; software settings at nine wind farms in mid-north South Australia then produced a sustained generation reduction of 456 MW in under seven seconds, the Heywood Interconnector tripped and all supply to the state was lost. Changes made to turbine control settings shortly after the event removed the risk of recurrence, and the report made 19 recommendations.

nodes.label: Under-tested AI medical devices fail after clearance
nodes.summary: AI-enabled medical devices cleared through the FDA's 510(k) route reach the US market without prospective testing on people, which that route does not require, and some fail soon after[1].
