In one study of 950 FDA-cleared AI devices, 60 (6.3%) were tied to 182 recalls, 43.4% of them within a year of clearance and most for diagnostic or measurement errors; devices without clinical validation had higher odds of recall (odds ratio 2.8), as did those from public companies (5.9), which made 53.2% of the devices but 91.8% of the recalls[1]. Recalls are still uncommon: 91.8% of the devices stayed recall-free for five years[1]. Reuters reported that after AI was added to one sinus-surgery navigation system, the FDA received more than 100 malfunction reports and at least 10 reports of injured patients, against seven unconfirmed malfunction reports in its three years before; the FDA has not attributed the injuries to AI and the device's owner denies a causal link[2]. One analysis of the FDA's adverse-event database finds it insufficient to judge AI device safety, with more than 98% of reported events falling on fewer than five devices[3].

refs.title: Lee et al., Early Recalls and Clinical Validation Gaps in Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Medical Devices, JAMA Health Forum 2025
refs.finding: Of 950 FDA-cleared AI-enabled medical devices, 60 (6.3%) were associated with 182 recalls; 109 recalls were for diagnostic or measurement errors and 44 for functionality delay, and 79 (43.4%) came within 12 months of clearance. Lack of clinical validation (adjusted odds ratio 2.8) and public company status (5.9) were associated with recalls; public companies made 53.2% of the devices but accounted for 91.8% of recalls. Recall-free survival was 96.6% at one year and 91.8% at five years. Because 510(k) clearance does not require prospective human testing, the authors say it may overlook early failures, and suggest prospective evaluation or time-limited clearances that lapse without confirmatory data.

refs.title: Gizmodo, The Last 'Person' You Want Handling Your Surgery Is a Hallucinating Robot, February 2026
refs.finding: Summarising a Reuters investigation: the TruDi Navigation System for chronic sinusitis had seven unconfirmed malfunction reports in three years on the market, and after AI was added the FDA received more than 100 malfunction notifications and at least 10 reports of injured patients, including a punctured skull base, cerebrospinal fluid leaks and strokes. The FDA has not attributed the injuries to AI because the incidents are under review, and owner Integra LifeSciences says there is no credible evidence of a causal connection. Reuters counted 1,357 FDA-authorised devices using AI and reported that cuts removed 15 of the 40 scientists in the FDA unit that reviews AI-enabled devices.

refs.title: Babic, Cohen, Stern, Li and Ouellet, A general framework for governing marketed AI/ML medical devices, npj Digital Medicine 2025
refs.finding: Analysing 943 adverse event reports linked to AI/ML devices approved from 2010 to 2023 in the FDA's MAUDE database, the authors find more than 98% of adverse events in AI/ML devices are borne by fewer than five devices, against about 85% for other devices, and conclude the existing system is insufficient for properly assessing the safety and effectiveness of AI/ML devices.

nodes.control_note: The 510(k) route lets AI tools reach patients without prospective human testing, and the FDA's adverse-event database is too thin to judge their safety. Prospective evaluation, clearances that lapse without confirmatory data and monitoring of real-world performance can catch failures earlier, but current FDA guidance on monitoring is a non-binding draft.

actions.action: Ask makers to validate across subgroups and monitor performance after launch
actions.evidence: The FDA's January 2025 draft guidance calls for subgroup analyses and recommends that makers monitor and address changes in device performance, but it is non-binding and monitoring plans are generally not required for 510(k) devices.

ref.title: King & Spalding, FDA Releases Draft Guidance on Submission Recommendations for AI-Enabled Device Software Functions, January 2025
ref.finding: The FDA's draft guidance of 7 January 2025 calls for adequate subgroup analyses for relevant demographics, recommends that manufacturers proactively monitor, identify and address device performance changes, and recommends a model card in device labelling; monitoring plans are generally not required for 510(k)s but may be for De Novo requests and PMAs.

actions.action: Require prospective evaluation or time-limited clearance
actions.evidence: The authors of the recall study suggest that requiring prospective evaluation, or issuing clearances that lapse without confirmatory data, could reduce early failures.

ref.title: Lee et al., Early Recalls and Clinical Validation Gaps in Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Medical Devices, JAMA Health Forum 2025
ref.finding: Of 950 FDA-cleared AI-enabled medical devices, 60 (6.3%) were associated with 182 recalls; 109 recalls were for diagnostic or measurement errors and 44 for functionality delay, and 79 (43.4%) came within 12 months of clearance. Lack of clinical validation (adjusted odds ratio 2.8) and public company status (5.9) were associated with recalls; public companies made 53.2% of the devices but accounted for 91.8% of recalls. Recall-free survival was 96.6% at one year and 91.8% at five years. Because 510(k) clearance does not require prospective human testing, the authors say it may overlook early failures, and suggest prospective evaluation or time-limited clearances that lapse without confirmatory data.

precedents.event: External test of the Epic Sepsis Model
precedents.parallel: A proprietary prediction tool spread to hundreds of hospitals before independent testing showed how it performed on real patients.
precedents.outcome: At Michigan Medicine the model reached an AUC of 0.63, substantially worse than its developer reported, missed 67% of patients with sepsis and alerted on 18% of all hospitalised patients.

ref.title: Wong et al., External Validation of a Widely Implemented Proprietary Sepsis Prediction Model in Hospitalized Patients, JAMA Internal Medicine 2021
ref.finding: The Epic Sepsis Model, developed by Epic Systems and implemented at hundreds of US hospitals, was tested on 38,455 hospitalisations of 27,697 patients at Michigan Medicine; it reached an AUC of 0.63, substantially worse than the developer reported, missed 1,709 of the patients with sepsis (67%) and alerted on 18% of all hospitalised patients.

nodes.label: AI coding tools pull in fake and malicious packages
nodes.summary: Coding models often recommend software packages that do not exist, and anyone can register those names on a public registry and put malicious code behind them. In one USENIX Security 2025 study of 16 models and 576,000 code samples, 19.7% of recommended packages were hallucinations, at least 5.2% for commercial models and 21.7% for open-source ones, and 43% of the invented names came back in all 10 re-runs of the same prompt, which makes them predictable[1]. One 2026 replication on five newer models found lower and narrower rates of 4.62% to 6.10%, but 127 names that all five invented identically, 53 of them still registrable after disclosure to the registries[2]. In January 2026 a security researcher registered react-codeshift, an npm name invented in AI-generated agent skills that was referenced in 237 repositories; it kept drawing a few downloads a day where unused names usually drop to none, and no one was harmed because he claimed it first[3]. Attackers also aim at agents directly: ReversingLabs tied 60 malicious packages published over seven months to a North Korean-linked group, found one pulled into a crypto trading project by a commit co-authored by an AI model, and suggested the packages' documentation was written to attract AI coding agents[4]. No attack on a hallucinated name has been proven: one researcher's harmless package under an invented name drew more than 30,000 downloads in three months in 2024, and one malicious npm package may have been a deliberate attempt, though its intent could not be shown[5].

refs.title: Spracklen et al., We Have a Package for You! A Comprehensive Analysis of Package Hallucinations by Code Generating LLMs, USENIX Security 2025
refs.finding: Across 16 code-generating models, two prompt datasets and 576,000 code samples in Python and JavaScript, 440,445 of about 2.23 million recommended packages (19.7%) were hallucinations, at least 5.2% for commercial models and 21.7% for open-source models, with 205,474 unique invented names. In 10 re-runs of 500 prompts, 43% of hallucinated packages were repeated in all 10 queries and 39% did not repeat at all. Fine-tuning cut DeepSeek's hallucination rate from 16.14% to 2.66% (83%), but its HumanEval pass@1 fell from 51.4% to 25.3%.

refs.title: Churilov, The Range Shrinks, the Threat Remains: Re-evaluating LLM Package Hallucinations on the 2026 Frontier-Model Cohort, arXiv 2026
refs.finding: A single-author replication of the USENIX Security 2025 method on five models released from October 2025 to March 2026, across 199,845 paired Python and JavaScript prompts, found overall hallucination rates of 4.62% to 6.10%, a much narrower spread than in 2024. 127 hallucinated names (109 on PyPI, 18 on npm) were invented identically by all five models, and after coordinated disclosure to PyPI Security and Socket.dev 53 of them (41 PyPI, 12 npm) remained registrable by an attacker.

refs.title: Aikido Security, Agent Skills Are Spreading Hallucinated npx Commands, January 2026
refs.finding: On 14 January 2026 researcher Charlie Eriksen registered react-codeshift on npm, a name an LLM appears to have blended from jscodeshift and react-codemod. It first appeared in a commit of 17 October 2025 that added 47 LLM-generated agent skills with no apparent human review, and 237 GitHub repositories referenced it when he claimed it. After the claim it drew about 74 downloads on day zero and then 1 to 4 a day, where phantom packages typically drop to zero after day zero. Nobody was harmed and the package is now a safe placeholder, but an attacker could have claimed it first.

refs.title: ReversingLabs, Claude adds malware to crypto agent, April 2026
refs.finding: The npm package @validate-sdk/v2 poses as a data validation tool but steals .env and .json files, wallet credentials and system information, and later versions install attacker SSH keys. A 28 February 2026 commit to openpaw-graveyard, an autonomous crypto trading agent, added a dependency that pulls it in, and the commit was co-authored by an LLM. ReversingLabs attributes the campaign, which it named PromptMink, to the North Korean-linked group Famous Chollima and counted 60 unique packages and over 300 versions across seven months from September 2025; it says the real targets might have been AI coding agents looking for packages, a combination of LLM optimisation abuse and knowledge injection.

refs.title: Aikido Security, What is Slopsquatting? The AI Package Hallucination Attack Already Happening, February 2026
refs.finding: In early 2024 Bar Lanyado of Lasso Security uploaded an empty package under huggingface-cli, a name AI models repeatedly invented, and it received more than 30,000 authentic downloads in three months; Alibaba had copied the hallucinated command into a public README. The npm package unused-imports is a real malicious package that was potentially an intentional slopsquatting attack, under a security hold and still drawing 233 downloads a week in early February 2026, but the authors say they cannot prove what the attackers intended with the names.

nodes.control_note: Coding agents install whatever names they generate or read, and public registries let anyone claim an unused name. Checking that each suggested package exists and has a real history, and reviewing agent skills as code before running them, cut the risk; models tuned against inventing names make far fewer of them, but in one study at a large cost to code quality.

actions.action: Fine-tune coding models not to invent packages
actions.evidence: In the USENIX Security 2025 study, fine-tuning cut one model's hallucinated-package rate from 16.14% to 2.66%, but its pass rate on a standard coding benchmark fell from 51.4% to 25.3%.

ref.title: Spracklen et al., We Have a Package for You! A Comprehensive Analysis of Package Hallucinations by Code Generating LLMs, USENIX Security 2025
ref.finding: Across 16 code-generating models, two prompt datasets and 576,000 code samples in Python and JavaScript, 440,445 of about 2.23 million recommended packages (19.7%) were hallucinations, at least 5.2% for commercial models and 21.7% for open-source models, with 205,474 unique invented names. In 10 re-runs of 500 prompts, 43% of hallucinated packages were repeated in all 10 queries and 39% did not repeat at all. Fine-tuning cut DeepSeek's hallucination rate from 16.14% to 2.66% (83%), but its HumanEval pass@1 fell from 51.4% to 25.3%.

actions.action: Claim hallucinated names before attackers do
actions.evidence: A researcher registered react-codeshift as a safe placeholder after 237 repositories referenced it; it covers one name, and attackers could have claimed it first.

It first appeared in a commit of 17 October 2025 that added 47 LLM-generated agent skills with no apparent human review, and 237 GitHub repositories referenced it when he claimed it. After the claim it drew about 74 downloads on day zero and then 1 to 4 a day, where phantom packages typically drop to zero after day zero. Nobody was harmed and the package is now a safe placeholder, but an attacker could have claimed it first.

precedents.event: Dependency confusion attacks on tech firms
precedents.parallel: Build tools trusted any package that matched a name they expected, so whoever registered that name on a public registry got their code run inside companies.
precedents.outcome: A researcher published packages under the names of companies' private internal packages on npm, PyPI and RubyGems, breached the internal systems of over 35 firms including Microsoft, Apple and PayPal, and earned well over $130,000 in bug bounties; Microsoft called the root cause a design flaw in package managers.

ref.title: BleepingComputer, Researcher hacks over 35 tech firms in novel supply chain attack, February 2021
ref.finding: Alex Birsan published packages named after internal dependencies found in manifest files such as PayPal's to npm, PyPI and RubyGems; build tools pulled the public versions, which needed no action by the victim. He breached over 35 major companies including Microsoft, Apple, PayPal, Shopify, Netflix, Yelp, Tesla and Uber and earned well over $130,000 in bounties, including $40,000 from Microsoft, which said the root cause is a design flaw rather than a bug in package managers.

nodes.label: AI school surveillance misfires on students
nodes.summary: US schools use AI software that scans what students write and search on school devices, and camera systems that look for guns, and many of the alerts are false. Gaggle, used by about 1,500 districts to track about 6 million students, alerted staff in Vancouver, Washington about nearly 2,200 students, about 10% of enrollment, in one year; an AP and Seattle Times investigation found many of those alerts were false alarms, screenshots that potentially outed at least six students for writing about being gay or transgender, and almost 3,500 sensitive student documents released to reporters without password protection[1]. In Lawrence, Kansas, almost two-thirds of more than 1,200 Gaggle alerts in 10 months were judged nonissues and more than 200 were set off by homework, and students sued the district in August 2025 over searches of their files and their free speech; in Tennessee a 13-year-old girl was arrested after a flagged school chat[2]. In October 2025 police handcuffed and searched a Baltimore County student after an AI gun detection system flagged his bag of chips, although the school's security staff had already cancelled the alert[3]. The FTC found that one AI weapons scanner used in over 800 schools missed a seven-inch knife later used to stab a student[4], and a court entered its order against the maker in December 2024[5]. No independent research shows the monitoring software reduces suicide or violence, though officials believe it has saved lives and one student who was potentially being trafficked used it to ask for help[1].

refs.title: Associated Press and The Seattle Times, Schools use AI to monitor kids, hoping to prevent violence. Our investigation found security risks, March 2025
refs.finding: About 1,500 US districts use Gaggle, AI-powered software that tracks roughly 6 million students on school devices. From October 2023 to October 2024 nearly 2,200 Vancouver, Washington students, about 10% of enrollment, were the subject of an alert; many alerts were false alarms, such as an essay about consent. A records request gave reporters almost 3,500 sensitive, unredacted student documents with no password or firewall, and the screenshots potentially outed at least six students to school officials after they wrote about being gay, transgender or struggling with gender dysphoria. There is no independent research showing the tools measurably lower student suicide or violence; a 2023 RAND study found scant evidence of benefits or risks, officials believe the tools have saved lives, and one student who was potentially being trafficked used Gaggle to ask staff for help. Durham, North Carolina's Board of Education voted to stop using Gaggle in 2023, judging it not worth the risk of outing students, after an advocate told the board a self-harm alert had outed a student to unsupportive family.

refs.title: Lawrence Journal-World, Lawrence school district sued in federal court for use of AI-powered surveillance system; students claim Gaggle results in illegal searches, August 2025
refs.finding: Nine current and former students sued the Lawrence, Kansas school district in federal court, claiming its 2023 decision to use Gaggle violates their First Amendment rights and results in illegal searches and seizures of their files. An AP analysis of public records found Gaggle flagged more than 1,200 incidents in a recent 10-month period, almost two-thirds deemed nonissues by school officials and more than 200 false alarms triggered by homework; officials later adjusted settings to reduce false alerts. In a separate Tennessee case a 13-year-old girl was arrested after a Gaggle-monitored school email chat was flagged.

refs.title: TechCrunch, High school's AI security system confuses Doritos bag for a possible firearm, October 2025
refs.finding: Kenwood High School student Taki Allen in Baltimore County, Maryland, was handcuffed and searched after an AI security system flagged his bag of chips as a possible firearm. The school's security department had reviewed and cancelled the alert, but the principal did not immediately realise and reported it to the school resource officer, who called police. Omnilert, which runs the gun detection system, said it regretted the incident and that the process functioned as intended.

refs.title: Federal Trade Commission, FTC Takes Action Against Evolv Technologies for Deceiving Users About its AI-Powered Security Screening Systems, November 2024
refs.finding: The FTC alleges Evolv falsely claimed its AI-powered Express scanners would detect all weapons and ignore harmless items. The scanners reportedly failed to detect a seven-inch knife brought into a school in October 2022 and used to stab a student; raising sensitivity afterwards produced a 50% false alarm rate, and they flagged laptops, binders and water bottles. The scanners are in over 800 schools in 40 states. The order bars Evolv from misrepresenting weapon detection, accuracy and false alarm rates and requires it to let certain K-12 customers that signed contracts between 1 April 2022 and 30 June 2023 cancel them.

refs.title: US District Court for the District of Massachusetts, FTC v. Evolv Technologies Holdings, Stipulated Order for Permanent Injunction and Other Relief, December 2024
refs.finding: In case 1:24-cv-12940, the stipulated order for permanent injunction, which orders Evolv to send a notice to customers, was so ordered on 5 December 2024 by Magistrate Judge Paul G. Levenson.

nodes.control_note: Schools buy these tools to catch threats and self-harm early, and the software errs towards flagging, so harmless writing and objects set off alerts that can reach police. Narrower settings, human review that actually stops a response, and locking flagged screenshots behind logins reduce the harm, but no independent research shows the tools prevent suicide or violence.

actions.action: Bar unsupported accuracy claims for AI weapons scanners
actions.evidence: Under an FTC order, Evolv may not misrepresent its scanners' weapon detection or false alarm rates and must let some K-12 customers that signed between April 2022 and June 2023 cancel their contracts; it covers one company.

ref.title: Federal Trade Commission, FTC Takes Action Against Evolv Technologies for Deceiving Users About its AI-Powered Security Screening Systems, November 2024
ref.finding: The FTC alleges Evolv falsely claimed its AI-powered Express scanners would detect all weapons and ignore harmless items. The scanners reportedly failed to detect a seven-inch knife brought into a school in October 2022 and used to stab a student; raising sensitivity afterwards produced a 50% false alarm rate, and they flagged laptops, binders and water bottles. The scanners are in over 800 schools in 40 states. The order bars Evolv from misrepresenting weapon detection, accuracy and false alarm rates and requires it to let certain K-12 customers that signed contracts between 1 April 2022 and 30 June 2023 cancel them.

actions.action: Stop using student monitoring software
actions.evidence: Durham, North Carolina's Board of Education voted in 2023 to stop using Gaggle, judging it not worth the risk of outing students, after an advocate told the board a self-harm alert had outed a student to unsupportive family.

A records request gave reporters almost 3,500 sensitive, unredacted student documents with no password or firewall, and the screenshots potentially outed at least six students to school officials after they wrote about being gay, transgender or struggling with gender dysphoria. There is no independent research showing the tools measurably lower student suicide or violence; a 2023 RAND study found scant evidence of benefits or risks, officials believe the tools have saved lives, and one student who was potentially being trafficked used Gaggle to ask staff for help.
