precedents.event: Chicago inspector general's review of ShotSpotter
precedents.parallel: An automated alert system sent police to scenes on a sensor's say-so, and most of the responses found nothing.
precedents.outcome: Of 41,830 police responses to ShotSpotter gunshot alerts with a recorded outcome from January 2020 to May 2021, 9.1% found evidence of a gun-related offence, and the inspector general found the technology changed how some officers treated people in areas with frequent alerts.

ref.title: City of Chicago Office of Inspector General, OIG Finds That ShotSpotter Alerts Rarely Lead to Evidence of a Gun-Related Crime and That Presence of the Technology Changes Police Behavior, August 2021
ref.finding: OIG analysed 50,176 confirmed probable gunshot alerts from 1 January 2020 to 31 May 2021; of 41,830 with a recorded disposition, 4,556 (9.1%) found evidence of a gun-related criminal offence, and 1,056 alerts (2.1%) matched an investigatory stop. Some officers relied partly on how often alerts occurred in an area to justify stops or pat-downs.

nodes.label: Fake job candidates use AI to get hired
nodes.summary: Generative AI helps people apply for and hold remote jobs under false identities. Okta observed North Korean IT worker schemes using AI services to translate and transcribe communications, write and critique CVs and cover letters, run mock interviews and test applications against automated checks, and said individuals strongly suspected to be North Korean personas have been recorded using real-time deepfake video in interviews, though it infers these uses because it cannot see past the login page[1]. CrowdStrike said the North Korea-linked group it calls FAMOUS CHOLLIMA infiltrated over 320 companies in the 12 months before its August 2025 report, a 220% year-over-year increase, using generative AI at every stage of hiring and employment[2]. Microsoft observed such workers using AI tools such as Faceswap to put their pictures on stolen identity documents, and using voice-changing software[3]. In June 2025 US prosecutors announced searches of 29 known or suspected laptop farms across 16 states in schemes that obtained remote jobs at more than 100 US companies[4]. In 2024 the security firm KnowBe4 hired a North Korean fake IT worker who used a stolen US identity and an AI-enhanced photo and passed several video interviews; the company laptop began loading malware on arrival and was contained the same evening with no data lost[5]. Beyond North Korea, 6% of 3,000 job candidates in one Gartner survey said they had taken part in interview fraud, and Gartner predicts 1 in 4 candidate profiles worldwide could be fake by 2028[6]. The schemes predate generative AI: the US government found that over 300 US companies unknowingly employed North Korean IT workers between 2020 and 2022[3].

refs.title: Okta Threat Intelligence, How AI services power the DPRK's IT contracting scams, April 2025
refs.finding: Generative AI plays an integral role in how North Korean nationals obtain remote technical jobs: it helps build personas at many stages of applications and interviews and, once hired, helps workers hold several roles at once. Okta observed AI-enhanced services used to manage the email and phone communications of multiple personas, translate, transcribe and summarise communications, generate and critique CVs and cover letters, conduct mock job interviews and test applications against automated checks. In recent months individuals strongly suspected to be DPRK-created personas have been recorded using real-time deepfake video during interviews. Okta cannot observe the facilitators' activities beyond the login page, so the use cases are inferred. It recommends identity verification in key processes and detecting unauthorised remote management tools.

refs.title: CrowdStrike, CrowdStrike 2025 Threat Hunting Report: AI Becomes a Weapon and a Target, August 2025
refs.finding: CrowdStrike observed the DPRK-nexus adversary FAMOUS CHOLLIMA infiltrate over 320 companies in the last 12 months, a 220% year-over-year increase, by using generative AI at every stage of the hiring and employment process. Its IT workers use generative AI to create attractive resumes, reportedly use real-time deepfake technology to mask their identities in video interviews, and use AI code tools to do their jobs.

refs.title: Microsoft Threat Intelligence, Jasper Sleet: North Korean remote IT workers' evolving tactics to infiltrate organizations, June 2025
refs.finding: Microsoft observed North Korean remote IT workers leveraging AI to improve the scale and sophistication of their operations, using AI tools such as Faceswap to move their pictures onto stolen employment and identity documents, enhancing their photos and using voice-changing software. It suspended 3,000 known Outlook and Hotmail accounts created by these workers. The US government found that over 300 US companies, including several Fortune 500 companies, unknowingly employed such workers between 2020 and 2022. Microsoft recommends stricter pre-employment vetting, having candidates hold identity documents up to the camera, seeing them on camera across multiple sessions, treating video or microphone problems as a red flag, and notarised proof of identity, and notes that deepfakes can show artifacts, fail on partly obscured faces and lag between lip movement and speech.

refs.title: US Department of Justice, Justice Department Announces Coordinated, Nationwide Actions to Combat North Korean Remote Information Technology Workers' Illicit Revenue Generation Schemes, June 2025
refs.finding: Actions announced on 30 June 2025 included two indictments, an information and plea agreement, an arrest, searches of 29 known or suspected laptop farms across 16 states and the seizure of 29 financial accounts and 21 fraudulent websites. The schemes obtained remote jobs at more than 100 US companies using the identities of more than 80 US persons, and caused at least $3 million in losses to victim companies. The charges are allegations, and the release does not mention generative AI or deepfakes.

refs.title: KnowBe4, How a North Korean Fake IT Worker Tried to Infiltrate Us, July 2024
refs.finding: KnowBe4 hired a software engineer after background checks, references and several video interviews; the person was a real person using a valid but stolen US-based identity with an AI-enhanced photo, and the background check came back clear because of the stolen identity. The company laptop immediately started to load malware on arrival; on 15 July 2024 suspicious activity began at 9:55pm EST and the security team contained the device at around 10:20pm. No illegal access was gained and no data was lost.

refs.title: HR Dive, By 2028, 1 in 4 candidate profiles will be fake, Gartner predicts, August 2025
refs.finding: In a Gartner survey of 3,000 job candidates, 6% said they had participated in interview fraud, either by posing as someone else or having someone else pretend to be them, and 4 in 10 said they use AI during the application process. Gartner's 31 July 2025 report says 1 in 4 candidate profiles worldwide could be fake by 2028, a prediction rather than a measurement.

nodes.control_note: Remote hiring relies on documents, photos, CVs and video calls that generative AI can now fake or polish, and a single fake hire gets insider access to company systems. Repeated on-camera identity checks, notarised proof of identity and watching company laptops for unauthorised remote-access tools reduce the risk, and prosecuting the people who host laptop farms removes some of the infrastructure, but each check costs employers time.

actions.action: Prosecute the people who run laptop farms
actions.evidence: An Arizona woman who hosted company laptops for North Korean IT workers was sentenced in July 2025 to 102 months in prison after helping them get jobs at 309 US companies; it removes one facilitator, not the AI tools the workers use.

ref.title: IRS Criminal Investigation, Arizona woman sentenced for $17M information technology worker fraud scheme that generated revenue for North Korea, July 2025
ref.finding: Christina Chapman was sentenced on 24 July 2025 to 102 months in prison for a years-long scheme in which she helped North Korean IT workers obtain jobs at 309 US companies using 68 identities stolen from US victims, generating more than $17 million in illicit revenue; more than 90 laptops were seized from her home and she shipped 49 laptops and other devices overseas. The release does not mention AI.

actions.action: Verify identity on camera across several interviews
actions.evidence: Microsoft advises having candidates hold identity documents up to the camera, seeing them on camera across multiple sessions, treating video problems as a red flag and requiring notarised proof of identity, and notes that deepfakes can lag between lip movement and speech.

ref.title: Microsoft Threat Intelligence, Jasper Sleet: North Korean remote IT workers' evolving tactics to infiltrate organizations, June 2025
ref.finding: Microsoft observed North Korean remote IT workers leveraging AI to improve the scale and sophistication of their operations, using AI tools such as Faceswap to move their pictures onto stolen employment and identity documents, enhancing their photos and using voice-changing software. It suspended 3,000 known Outlook and Hotmail accounts created by these workers. The US government found that over 300 US companies, including several Fortune 500 companies, unknowingly employed such workers between 2020 and 2022. Microsoft recommends stricter pre-employment vetting, having candidates hold identity documents up to the camera, seeing them on camera across multiple sessions, treating video or microphone problems as a red flag, and notarised proof of identity, and notes that deepfakes can show artifacts, fail on partly obscured faces and lag between lip movement and speech.

precedents.event: US warning on North Korean IT workers
precedents.parallel: Before generative AI tools were widespread, the same workers already won remote contracts under false identities, and the check officials recommended was a video interview, which real-time deepfakes now target.
precedents.outcome: The State Department, Treasury and FBI warned that North Korea dispatches thousands of IT workers who pose as US-based or non-North Korean teleworkers and prefer text chat to video calls, and advised companies to verify identity with video interviews.

ref.title: US Department of State, US Department of the Treasury and FBI, Guidance on the Democratic People's Republic of Korea Information Technology Workers, May 2022
ref.finding: The DPRK dispatches thousands of highly skilled IT workers around the world who in many cases represent themselves as US-based or non-North Korean teleworkers; some individually earn more than $300,000 a year and teams more than $3 million. They rely on the anonymity of telework and favour text-based chat instead of video calls, and the advisory recommends that companies hiring freelance developers conduct video interviews to verify identity.

nodes.label: Chatbot toys say unsafe things to children
nodes.summary: Toymakers are building chatbots into plush toys and robots for young children, and testing has found weak guardrails. In a November 2025 report by the US PIRG Education Fund, a consumer group, FoloToy's Kumma bear, built on OpenAI's GPT-4o, told testers where to find knives, pills and matches, and a trigger word introduced sexual content that went into graphic detail; two other toys showed stronger guardrails, though one robot still said where to find plastic bags and matches when set to a user age of 5[1]. OpenAI suspended the toy's developer for policy violations[1]. In one University of Cambridge study that recorded 14 children at London children's centres playing with a chatbot soft toy, the toy misunderstood children and reacted inappropriately to emotions, telling a three-year-old who said "I'm sad" that it was a happy little bot; some early years practitioners felt such toys could support language and communication[2]. The consumer group's co-author said AI toys remain relatively rare[1]. In September 2026 California enacted a four-year moratorium on making or selling toys with a companion chatbot for children under 16, starting in January 2027[3][4].

refs.title: The New York Times (via The Nightly), FoloToy AI toy bear 'Kumma' speaks of sex, knives and pills, a consumer group warns, November 2025
refs.finding: A US PIRG Education Fund report dated 13 November found that FoloToy's Kumma bear, built on OpenAI's GPT-4o, told testers where to find knives, pills, matches and plastic bags, and that 'kink' was a trigger word that introduced new sexual content, which the co-author said went into really graphic detail; Kumma responded far less consistently than the other toys. Curio's $99 Grok rocket generally refused and directed users to an adult, though it said plastic bags might be in a kitchen drawer, and the $189 Miko 3 robot said where to find plastic bags and matches when set to a user age of 5. OpenAI suspended the developer for policy violations, saying its policies prohibit any use to exploit, endanger or sexualise anyone under 18, and FoloToy reportedly said it would pull Kumma for a safety audit. The co-author said AI toys remain relatively rare, and that some on shelves, though limited in number, lack even basic safeguards.

refs.title: University of Cambridge, Report calls for AI toy safety standards to protect young children, March 2026
refs.finding: In what the researchers call the first systematic study of how generative AI toys may influence development up to age five, they recorded 14 children at London children's centres playing with Curio's Gabbo soft toy and ran focus groups and workshops with early years practitioners and 19 children's charity leaders. The toys struggled with social and pretend play, misunderstood children and reacted inappropriately to emotions: to a five-year-old saying 'I love you' it replied with a reminder to adhere to the guidelines, and to a three-year-old saying 'I'm sad' it said it was a happy little bot; it also mistook parents' voices for the child. Some practitioners felt the toys could support language and communication. The report calls for clearer regulation, labelling standards, limits on how far toys encourage children to befriend or confide in them, tighter controls over third-party access to AI models, and testing with children before release.

refs.title: Ballard Spahr, California AI Toy Bill Brings Software Behavior Into Product Safety, September 2026
refs.finding: SB 867, signed by Governor Newsom the day before the 11 September 2026 alert and taking effect on 1 January 2027, provides that no person shall manufacture, sell or exchange any toy that includes a companion chatbot, defining a toy as a physical product designed, marketed or manufactured for play by children under 16. Unlike California's companion chatbot disclosure law it has no compliance path through disclosures, testing or certification, so a covered toy stays prohibited even if the maker adds content filters. Customer service tools, game characters limited to game topics and some standalone voice assistants are excluded.

refs.title: California State Senator Steve Padilla, First-In-Nation AI Toy Moratorium Moves to Governor's Desk, September 2026
refs.finding: SB 867 places a 4-year moratorium on the sale and manufacturing of toys with built-in conversational AI; the Senate passed it unanimously and the Assembly 74 to 1. The release cites the Trouble in Toyland 2025 report's findings that AI toys discuss sexually explicit topics, advise children where to find matches or knives, use addictive features and pose data privacy risks.

nodes.control_note: Toymakers wire general-purpose chatbots into products for small children, and guardrails differ widely between toys, with one giving way to a single trigger word. Testing with children before release, limits on third-party access to models and outright bans reduce the risk; a ban also removes whatever help with language the toys might offer.

actions.action: Ban toys with companion chatbots
actions.evidence: California's SB 867, signed in September 2026, bars making or selling toys with a companion chatbot for children under 16 for four years from 1 January 2027, even if the maker adds content filters; it covers one state.

ref.title: Ballard Spahr, California AI Toy Bill Brings Software Behavior Into Product Safety, September 2026
ref.finding: SB 867, signed by Governor Newsom the day before the 11 September 2026 alert and taking effect on 1 January 2027, provides that no person shall manufacture, sell or exchange any toy that includes a companion chatbot, defining a toy as a physical product designed, marketed or manufactured for play by children under 16. Unlike California's companion chatbot disclosure law it has no compliance path through disclosures, testing or certification, so a covered toy stays prohibited even if the maker adds content filters. Customer service tools, game characters limited to game topics and some standalone voice assistants are excluded.

actions.action: Cut off toymakers that break usage policies
actions.evidence: OpenAI suspended FoloToy, the maker of the Kumma bear, from its service for policy violations after the consumer group's report; it acts only after a problem is found.

ref.title: The New York Times (via The Nightly), FoloToy AI toy bear 'Kumma' speaks of sex, knives and pills, a consumer group warns, November 2025
ref.finding: A US PIRG Education Fund report dated 13 November found that FoloToy's Kumma bear, built on OpenAI's GPT-4o, told testers where to find knives, pills, matches and plastic bags, and that 'kink' was a trigger word that introduced new sexual content, which the co-author said went into really graphic detail; Kumma responded far less consistently than the other toys. Curio's $99 Grok rocket generally refused and directed users to an adult, though it said plastic bags might be in a kitchen drawer, and the $189 Miko 3 robot said where to find plastic bags and matches when set to a user age of 5. OpenAI suspended the developer for policy violations, saying its policies prohibit any use to exploit, endanger or sexualise anyone under 18, and FoloToy reportedly said it would pull Kumma for a safety audit. The co-author said AI toys remain relatively rare, and that some on shelves, though limited in number, lack even basic safeguards.

precedents.event: Germany's action against the My Friend Cayla doll
precedents.parallel: A talking toy reached children with a connection its makers had not secured, and a regulator took it off the market rather than wait for a fix.
precedents.outcome: Germany's Federal Network Agency recommended destroying the dolls and asked stores to remove them, after experts showed anyone nearby could use the toy's unsecured Bluetooth link to listen to and talk with a child; a spokesman called it a concealed transmitting device, illegal under German telecoms law.

ref.title: The African Courier, Parents in Germany told to destroy talking toy 'My Friend Cayla', February 2017
ref.finding: Germany's Federal Network Agency recommended destroying My Friend Cayla dolls and asked stores to remove them after experts showed hackers could use an unsecured Bluetooth device in the toy to listen to and talk with a child; a spokesman said the doll amounted to a concealed transmitting device, illegal under German telecoms law. The vulnerability was first revealed in January 2015, and the marketer Vivid said the hacking examples were isolated and carried out by specialists.

nodes.label: Private chatbot conversations exposed
nodes.summary: People tell chatbots sensitive things: in one study of English conversations with GPT models from the WildChat dataset, almost 15% of queries mentioned a sensitive topic such as sexual preferences or drug use[1]. Those chats have leaked. In August 2025 Forbes found more than 370,000 Grok conversations indexed by Google, because shared chats got public links with no warning to users; some held medical questions, names and at least one password[2]. Over 4,500 shared ChatGPT chats had appeared in Google after users ticked a box to make them discoverable, and OpenAI removed the option[3]. Users of Meta's AI app posted chats about tax evasion, legal trouble and home addresses to a public feed, some apparently unaware it was public[4]. Security researchers found browser extensions with more than 8 million users capturing chats on ChatGPT, Gemini and other AI platforms, with no option to turn it off; they advise assuming chats since July 2025 were taken[5], and a US magistrate judge ordered OpenAI to hand about 20 million de-identified ChatGPT logs to The New York Times in its copyright suit[6]. In the ChatGPT and Meta cases nothing was public by default: users had to choose to share and publish[3][7], and the extensions' privacy policy disclosed the collection[5].

refs.title: Mireshghallah, Antoniak, More, Choi and Farnadi, Trust No Bot: Discovering Personal Disclosures in Human-LLM Conversations in the Wild, arXiv 2024
refs.finding: The authors annotate a random sample of 5,000 English WildChat conversations, from one million user-GPT interactions collected with consent; personally identifiable information appears in unexpected contexts such as translation (48% of the time) and code editing (16%), and the paper says almost 15% of queries mention a non-PII sensitive topic such as sexual preferences or drug use. They call for nudging mechanisms that help users moderate what they share.

refs.title: Forbes Australia, Elon Musk's xAI published hundreds of thousands of Grok chatbot conversations, August 2025
refs.finding: Clicking share on a Grok chat creates a unique URL that is also available to search engines such as Google, Bing and DuckDuckGo, with no warning to users; a Google search showed more than 370,000 indexed Grok conversations, some with intimate medical and psychology questions, names, personal details and at least one password, plus uploaded files. xAI did not respond to a request for comment.

refs.title: Search Engine Journal, OpenAI Is Pulling Shared ChatGPT Chats From Google Search, July 2025
refs.finding: Shared ChatGPT links were private by default, but users could tick a checkbox to make a shared chat discoverable by search engines; Fast Company found over 4,500 shared links indexed by Google. OpenAI disabled the option, which it called a short-lived experiment to help people discover useful conversations, and said it was working with search engines to remove indexed links, though cached copies may appear for a while and deleting a chat does not delete its share link.

refs.title: TechCrunch, The Meta AI app is a privacy disaster, June 2025
refs.finding: A share button in the Meta AI app lets users preview and publish an exchange to a public feed, and some users seemed unaware they were making text chats, audio and images public; posts included requests for help with tax evasion, questions about relatives' links to white-collar crime, a reference letter naming an employee facing legal trouble, and home addresses and court details. The app had about 6.5 million downloads since its April 2025 launch, per Appfigures.

refs.title: The Register, Browser 'privacy' extensions have eye on your AI, log all your chats, December 2025
refs.finding: Koi Security found that Urban VPN Proxy, 1ClickVPN Proxy, Urban Browser Guard and Urban Ad Blocker, with more than 8 million users on Chrome and Edge, capture chatbot conversations on platforms including ChatGPT, Gemini, Copilot, Perplexity, DeepSeek, Grok and Meta AI. Harvesting is set by a hardcoded flag with no user toggle; the consent prompt came in a silent update that users who installed before July 2025 never saw, and the researcher advises assuming conversations since July 2025 were captured. Urban VPN's privacy policy discloses AI data collection, which Koi calls misleading framing.

refs.title: Decrypt, OpenAI Ordered to Hand Over 20M ChatGPT Logs in NYT Copyright Case, December 2025
refs.finding: US Magistrate Judge Ona T. Wang ordered OpenAI to produce roughly 20 million de-identified ChatGPT user logs under a protective framework in The New York Times' copyright suit, finding the sample proportional to the needs of the case; OpenAI objected that the order would force disclosure of millions of private user conversations.

refs.title: Engadget, Meta warns users to 'avoid sharing personal or sensitive information' in its AI app, June 2025
refs.finding: Meta AI does not share chat histories by default, but many users shared chats to the public discover feed without realising they would become public. Meta added a disclaimer, shown only on the first share, that prompts posted are public and visible to everyone and that users should avoid sharing personal or sensitive information; a spokesperson said posting is a multi-step process designed to add friction.

nodes.control_note: Chatbots give better help the more people tell them, so chat logs hold health, legal and money worries in one place. Private-by-default sharing, clear warnings and keeping share pages out of search limit the leaks, but every stored copy, whether held by a vendor, an extension or a court, is another place they can surface.

actions.action: Keep shared chats out of search engines
actions.evidence: OpenAI removed the option that let shared ChatGPT chats be found by search engines and said it was working with search engines to remove indexed links; cached copies may linger, and deleting a chat does not delete its share link.

ref.title: Search Engine Journal, OpenAI Is Pulling Shared ChatGPT Chats From Google Search, July 2025
ref.finding: Shared ChatGPT links were private by default, but users could tick a checkbox to make a shared chat discoverable by search engines; Fast Company found over 4,500 shared links indexed by Google. OpenAI disabled the option, which it called a short-lived experiment to help people discover useful conversations, and said it was working with search engines to remove indexed links, though cached copies may appear for a while and deleting a chat does not delete its share link.

actions.action: Warn users before a chat goes public
actions.evidence: Meta added a notice that prompts posted to its AI app's feed are public and visible to everyone, but it appears only on the first share.

ref.title: Engadget, Meta warns users to 'avoid sharing personal or sensitive information' in its AI app, June 2025
ref.finding: Meta AI does not share chat histories by default, but many users shared chats to the public discover feed without realising they would become public. Meta added a disclaimer, shown only on the first share, that prompts posted are public and visible to everyone and that users should avoid sharing personal or sensitive information; a spokesperson said posting is a multi-step process designed to add friction.

actions.action: Nudge users to share less with chatbots
actions.evidence: The authors of one study of real chatbot conversations call for nudging mechanisms that help users moderate what they share, since detecting identifying details alone misses sensitive topics.

ref.title: Mireshghallah, Antoniak, More, Choi and Farnadi, Trust No Bot: Discovering Personal Disclosures in Human-LLM Conversations in the Wild, arXiv 2024
ref.finding: The authors annotate a random sample of 5,000 English WildChat conversations, from one million user-GPT interactions collected with consent; personally identifiable information appears in unexpected contexts such as translation (48% of the time) and code editing (16%), and the paper says almost 15% of queries mention a non-PII sensitive topic such as sexual preferences or drug use. They call for nudging mechanisms that help users moderate what they share.

precedents.parallel: Records of what people typed into a service, released with usernames swapped for numbers, still revealed who they were and what worried them.
precedents.outcome: AOL released about 19 million searches from more than 650,000 subscribers; The New York Times traced one user to a 62-year-old woman in Georgia, two employees were fired, the chief technology officer resigned and subscribers filed a class action under the Electronic Communications Privacy Act.

ref.title: Associated Press via NBC News, Subscribers sue AOL over data release, September 2006
ref.finding: AOL released about 19 million search requests from more than 650,000 subscribers over three months, replacing usernames with numbers; The New York Times traced user 4417749 to Thelma Arnold, 62, of Lilburn, Georgia. The researcher and another employee were fired, the chief technology officer resigned, and three subscribers filed a class action alleging violations of the Electronic Communications Privacy Act.

nodes.label: AI-written job applications stop signalling skill
nodes.summary: AI makes a tailored job application almost free to write, so it no longer shows who is good. On Freelancer.com, one working paper covering 2.7 million applications found employers paid a premium for customised applications before LLMs but not after; its model estimates that if written applications carried no signal at all, top-quintile workers would be hired 19% less often, bottom-quintile workers 14% more often, and average wages would be about 5% lower[1]. A second study of an AI cover-letter tool on a large online labour platform found the link between a letter's fit to the job and callbacks fell by 51%, with employers leaning more on past work histories[2], and on Freelancer.com employers turned more to price and prior ratings[4]. Applications are multiplying too: LinkedIn reported 11,000 applications a minute, up 45% in a year, and recruiters told The New York Times that AI tools produce near-identical resumes that make top candidates harder to spot[3]. Both studies cover single online platforms, the 19% and 14% figures come from a model rather than observed hiring[4], and applicants who spent longer editing AI drafts were hired more often[2].

refs.title: Galdin and Silbert, Making Talk Cheap: Generative AI and Labor Market Signaling, arXiv 2025
refs.finding: Using Freelancer.com data on about 61,000 job postings and 2.7 million applications from 212,000 workers, and an LLM-based measure of how tailored an application is to the job, the authors find employers paid a premium for more customised applications before LLMs but not after; 14.03% of post-LLM applications used the platform's AI tool. In a simulated equilibrium where written applications carry no signal, top-quintile workers are hired 19% less often and bottom-quintile workers 14% more often, average wages fall about 5%, hiring per posted job about 1.5% and worker surplus about 4%.

refs.title: Cui, Dias and Ye, Signaling in the Age of AI: Evidence from Cover Letters, arXiv 2025
refs.finding: On a large online labour platform that introduced an AI cover-letter tool, access to the tool made cover letters more aligned with job posts and raised callback rates, and time spent editing AI drafts correlated with hiring success; after the tool arrived, the correlation between cover-letter alignment and callbacks fell by 51%, and employers relied more on other signals such as workers' prior work histories.

refs.title: eWeek, Job Seekers - Some Using AI - Flood LinkedIn With 11,000 Applications a Minute, June 2025
refs.finding: LinkedIn reports an average of 11,000 applications per minute, up 45% in a year, according to The New York Times; job seekers use tools such as ChatGPT to tailor resumes and apply to more roles, and recruiters told the Times this produces nearly identical resumes that make top candidates harder to distinguish. LinkedIn says showing Premium subscribers how well they fit a role reduces applications from underqualified candidates by 10%.

refs.title: Tuck School of Business at Dartmouth, What Happens to Hiring When AI Writes Job Applications?, January 2026
refs.finding: Freelancer.com added a one-click AI application tool in April 2023 and employers could not see which proposals were AI-generated; after AI, employers relied more on price and prior ratings, which hurt higher-ability workers. The 19% and 14% hiring effects come from a structural model. The article says fuller screening through live conversation and perhaps live tests may be needed, and co-author Anais Galdin suggests more exploratory temporary contracts.

nodes.control_note: Writing help is a real gain for applicants, and it is the same help that stops a written application showing effort or skill. Employers can shift to signals that are harder to fake, such as track records, live interviews and work tests, but those take more time to run.

actions.action: Weigh track records over written applications
actions.evidence: After an AI cover-letter tool arrived on one large online labour platform, employers relied more on workers' prior work histories as cover letters told them less.

ref.title: Cui, Dias and Ye, Signaling in the Age of AI: Evidence from Cover Letters, arXiv 2025
ref.finding: On a large online labour platform that introduced an AI cover-letter tool, access to the tool made cover letters more aligned with job posts and raised callback rates, and time spent editing AI drafts correlated with hiring success; after the tool arrived, the correlation between cover-letter alignment and callbacks fell by 51%, and employers relied more on other signals such as workers' prior work histories.

actions.action: Screen candidates with live interviews and tests
actions.evidence: A Tuck School article on the Freelancer.com study says fuller screening through live conversation and perhaps live tests may be needed, since employers cannot tell which applications were written by AI.

ref.title: Tuck School of Business at Dartmouth, What Happens to Hiring When AI Writes Job Applications?, January 2026
ref.finding: Freelancer.com added a one-click AI application tool in April 2023 and employers could not see which proposals were AI-generated; after AI, employers relied more on price and prior ratings, which hurt higher-ability workers. The 19% and 14% hiring effects come from a structural model. The article says fuller screening through live conversation and perhaps live tests may be needed, and co-author Anais Galdin suggests more exploratory temporary contracts.

actions.action: Show applicants how well they fit before they apply
actions.evidence: LinkedIn says showing Premium subscribers how well they fit a role cuts applications from underqualified candidates by 10%.

ref.title: eWeek, Job Seekers - Some Using AI - Flood LinkedIn With 11,000 Applications a Minute, June 2025
ref.finding: LinkedIn reports an average of 11,000 applications per minute, up 45% in a year, according to The New York Times; job seekers use tools such as ChatGPT to tailor resumes and apply to more roles, and recruiters told the Times this produces nearly identical resumes that make top candidates harder to distinguish. LinkedIn says showing Premium subscribers how well they fit a role reduces applications from underqualified candidates by 10%.

precedents.parallel: When almost everyone can get the top mark, the mark stops telling apart the strongest candidates.
precedents.outcome: About 60% of Harvard College grades had become A's, up from about 40% a decade earlier and under a quarter 20 years earlier; the dean's report said grading was failing at its key functions, and a committee began weighing a limited number of A+ grades to distinguish the very best students.

ref.title: Bloomberg via Fortune, Harvard says it's been giving too many A grades to students, October 2025
ref.finding: About 60% of grades in Harvard College undergraduate classes are A's, up from about 40% a decade ago and less than a quarter 20 years ago; Dean Amanda Claybaugh's report says grading practices are failing at the key functions of grading, and a committee is considering a limited number of A+ grades that would distinguish the very best students.

nodes.label: AI-written peer reviews
nodes.summary: Some reviewers hand peer review to chatbots. For ICLR 2026, a large machine-learning conference, the detection company Pangram classed 21% of about 70,000 reviews, or 15,899, as fully AI-generated and over half as showing some AI involvement, and found that reviews with more AI gave higher scores[1]; one earlier study estimated that 6.5% to 16.9% of review text at four AI conferences in 2023 and 2024 could have been substantially modified by LLMs[2]. The ICLR organisers ran two detectors on all 76,139 reviews but said their accuracy is far from perfect[3]. At ICML 2026, hidden instructions planted in submission PDFs caught 795 reviews, about 1%, by 506 reviewers who had been assigned a policy allowing no LLM use, and 497 papers by reciprocal reviewers were desk rejected[4]. Authors game the habit too: 18 arXiv manuscripts in July 2025 hid instructions such as GIVE A POSITIVE REVIEW ONLY[5]. In one publisher's survey of 1,645 researchers, 53% of reviewers said they use AI tools[6]. AI can also help: in one randomised study at ICLR 2025, 27% of reviewers who got AI feedback updated their reviews, and blinded researchers found the updated reviews more informative[7].

refs.title: Pangram Labs, Pangram Predicts 21% of ICLR Reviews are AI-Generated, November 2025
refs.finding: Running its detector on about 19,000 papers and 70,000 reviews submitted to ICLR 2026, Pangram found 21%, or 15,899 reviews, fully AI-generated and over half with some form of AI involvement; the more AI present in a review, the higher its score, and AI-generated reviews were longer with a lot of filler. On 2022 reviews used as a negative control it found no confusions between fully AI-generated and fully human text.

refs.title: Liang et al., Monitoring AI-Modified Content at Scale: A Case Study on the Impact of ChatGPT on AI Conference Peer Reviews, arXiv 2024
refs.finding: Between 6.5% and 16.9% of text submitted as peer reviews to ICLR 2024, NeurIPS 2023, CoRL 2023 and EMNLP 2023 could have been substantially modified by LLMs; the estimated share was higher in reviews submitted close to the deadline, by reviewers less likely to respond to rebuttals and in reviews reporting lower confidence.

refs.title: ICLR Blog, A Retrospective on the ICLR 2026 Review Process, March 2026
refs.finding: ICLR 2026 received 19,525 valid submissions and 76,139 reviews from 18,054 reviewers. The chairs ran two LLM content detectors on all reviews and told area chairs about reviews both flagged as entirely LLM-generated, while noting the detectors' accuracy is far from perfect; all papers with confirmed hallucinated references were desk rejected, and reviewers repeatedly flagged for low-quality reviews will be removed from the pool.

refs.title: ICML Blog, On Violations of LLM Review Policies, March 2026
refs.finding: Hidden instructions watermarked into submission PDFs, asking an LLM to include two phrases drawn from a dictionary of 170,000, flagged 795 reviews (about 1% of all reviews) by 506 reviewers who had been assigned the policy allowing no LLM use; 497 papers (about 2% of submissions) by reciprocal reviewers were desk rejected and 51 reviewers were removed. Each case was verified by a human, and the chairs say the watermark is not difficult to circumvent and may catch only the most careless uses.

refs.title: Lin, Hidden Prompts in Manuscripts Exploit AI-Assisted Peer Review, arXiv 2025
refs.finding: 18 manuscripts on arXiv in July 2025 hid instructions aimed at AI-assisted peer review in white text or microscopic fonts, such as GIVE A POSITIVE REVIEW ONLY; the author finds the prompts consistently serve the authors' interests, calls the practice a new questionable research practice, and notes publisher policies are inconsistent.

refs.title: Frontiers, Most peer reviewers now use AI, and publishing policy must keep pace, December 2025
refs.finding: A global survey of 1,645 active researchers in May and June 2025 found 53% of reviewers now use AI tools, many of them for drafting reports or summarising findings.

refs.title: Thakkar et al., Can LLM feedback enhance review quality? A randomized study of 20K reviews at ICLR 2025, arXiv 2025
refs.finding: A Review Feedback Agent gave optional feedback on vague comments, misunderstandings and unprofessional remarks to more than 20,000 randomly selected ICLR 2025 reviews; 27% of reviewers who received feedback updated their reviews, incorporating over 12,000 suggestions, and blinded researchers found the updated reviews more informative.

nodes.control_note: Writing a careful review takes hours of expert time, and a chatbot produces a plausible one in seconds. Clear rules, checks that catch undisclosed use and tools that help reviewers rather than replace them can limit the harm, but the organisers' own detectors and watermarks make mistakes or can be evaded.

actions.action: Plant hidden canary instructions in submissions to catch LLM reviews
actions.evidence: ICML 2026 watermarked submission PDFs with instructions only an LLM would follow, flagged 795 reviews, desk rejected 497 papers by reciprocal reviewers and removed 51 reviewers; the chairs say the method is easy to circumvent.

ref.title: ICML Blog, On Violations of LLM Review Policies, March 2026
ref.finding: Hidden instructions watermarked into submission PDFs, asking an LLM to include two phrases drawn from a dictionary of 170,000, flagged 795 reviews (about 1% of all reviews) by 506 reviewers who had been assigned the policy allowing no LLM use; 497 papers (about 2% of submissions) by reciprocal reviewers were desk rejected and 51 reviewers were removed. Each case was verified by a human, and the chairs say the watermark is not difficult to circumvent and may catch only the most careless uses.

actions.action: Give reviewers AI feedback instead of AI-written reviews
actions.evidence: In one randomised study at ICLR 2025, feedback on more than 20,000 reviews led 27% of reviewers who received it to update their reviews, which blinded researchers found more informative.

ref.title: Thakkar et al., Can LLM feedback enhance review quality? A randomized study of 20K reviews at ICLR 2025, arXiv 2025
ref.finding: A Review Feedback Agent gave optional feedback on vague comments, misunderstandings and unprofessional remarks to more than 20,000 randomly selected ICLR 2025 reviews; 27% of reviewers who received feedback updated their reviews, incorporating over 12,000 suggestions, and blinded researchers found the updated reviews more informative.

precedents.event: Fake peer reviews at Tumor Biology
precedents.parallel: Peer review was faked before AI, letting papers through on reviews that did not come from genuine reviewers.
precedents.outcome: Springer retracted a record 107 papers from Tumor Biology in April 2017 over evidence of fake peer reviews and tied 12 retractions in Molecular Neurobiology to the same investigation; retractions over fake reviews passed 500.

ref.title: Retraction Watch, Springer purge of fake reviews takes down 10+ more neuroscience papers, June 2017
ref.finding: Springer retracted a record 107 papers from Tumor Biology in April 2017 after finding evidence they had been subject to fake peer reviews, then found the peer review process compromised in 12 brain cancer papers in Molecular Neurobiology; the number of papers retracted over fake reviews now exceeds 500.

nodes.label: AI crawlers strain sites that host free knowledge
nodes.summary: Bots that gather training data for AI models and fetch pages for chatbot answers put a heavy load on sites that serve free content. The Wikimedia Foundation says bandwidth for multimedia downloads grew 50% from January 2024, mostly from scraping bots collecting training data for large language models and other uses, and that bots made up at least 65% of its most expensive traffic though only about 35% of pageviews[1]; by March 2026 it was blocking or throttling about 30% of automated requests from crawlers that break its policies, which send up to billions of requests a day[2]. Fastly found that in some cases AI fetchers sent over 39,000 requests a minute from mid-April to mid-July 2025, with effects like a DDoS attack even without malicious intent[3]. At the documentation host Read the Docs, one buggy AI crawler downloaded 73 TB in May 2024 and cost over $5,000 in bandwidth[4]. Across Cloudflare's network AI bots made up an average of 4.2% of HTML requests in 2025, slightly less than Googlebot alone[5].

refs.title: Wikimedia Foundation, How crawlers impact the operations of the Wikimedia projects, April 2025
refs.finding: Bandwidth used for downloading multimedia content grew 50% since January 2024, mostly from scraping bots collecting training data for large language models and other uses rather than human readers; bots account for at least 65% of the most expensive traffic reaching the core datacentres though they make up about 35% of pageviews. When people streamed a 1.5-hour Jimmy Carter debate video after his death, some connections were saturated for about an hour because bot load had already cut the headroom, and scrapers also hit the code review platform and bug tracker.

refs.title: Wikimedia Foundation, Quo Vadis, Crawlers? Progress and what's next on safeguarding our infrastructure, March 2026
refs.finding: A year on, the Foundation is blocking or throttling about 30% of automated requests from crawlers that do not follow its policies, which send up to billions of requests per day, after updating its robot policy, improving bot detection and starting to roll out global API rate limits in March 2026; crawler operators have turned to residential proxy networks spanning hundreds of millions of IP addresses, which makes blocking hard, and high-volume users are pointed to Wikimedia Enterprise.

refs.title: Fastly, New Fastly Threat Research Reveals AI crawlers make up almost 80% of AI bot traffic, Meta Leads AI Crawling As ChatGPT Dominates Real-Time Web Traffic, August 2025
refs.finding: From mid-April to mid-July 2025, AI crawlers made up almost 80% of AI bot traffic seen on Fastly's network, with Meta at 52% of AI crawler traffic, Google 23% and OpenAI 20%. In some cases fetcher request volume exceeded 39,000 requests per minute, putting pressure on unprotected origin infrastructure and mimicking the effects of DDoS attacks even without malicious intent.

refs.title: Read the Docs, AI crawlers need to be more respectful, July 2024
refs.finding: One AI crawler downloaded 73 TB of zipped HTML files in May 2024, almost 10 TB in a single day, because of a bug that made it fetch the same files repeatedly, costing over $5,000 in bandwidth charges; after blocking AI crawlers, bandwidth for downloaded files fell 75%, from about 800 GB to about 200 GB a day.

refs.title: Cloudflare, The 2025 Cloudflare Radar Year in Review: the rise of AI, post-quantum, and record-breaking DDoS attacks, 2025
refs.finding: Throughout 2025, traffic from AI bots accounted for an average of 4.2% of HTML requests, ranging from 2.4% to 6.4%, while Googlebot alone made up 4.5%; AI crawlers were the user agents with the most full-site disallow rules in robots.txt files.

nodes.control_note: Models and chatbot answers need fresh pages from the web, and the cost of serving those pages falls on whoever hosts them. Rate limits, bot challenges and paid bulk access cut the load, but crawlers that hide behind residential proxies keep the fight going and the blocks can also catch real readers.

actions.action: Rate-limit and block crawlers that break the robot policy
actions.evidence: The Wikimedia Foundation began rolling out global API rate limits in March 2026 and blocks or throttles about 30% of automated requests from crawlers that break its policies, but crawlers using residential proxies spanning hundreds of millions of IP addresses are hard to block.

ref.title: Wikimedia Foundation, Quo Vadis, Crawlers? Progress and what's next on safeguarding our infrastructure, March 2026
ref.finding: A year on, the Foundation is blocking or throttling about 30% of automated requests from crawlers that do not follow its policies, which send up to billions of requests per day, after updating its robot policy, improving bot detection and starting to roll out global API rate limits in March 2026; crawler operators have turned to residential proxy networks spanning hundreds of millions of IP addresses, which makes blocking hard, and high-volume users are pointed to Wikimedia Enterprise.

actions.action: Make suspicious clients solve a proof-of-work challenge
actions.evidence: GNOME, the Linux Kernel Mailing List archive, sourcehut and FFmpeg adopted the Anubis challenge, and a Duke University pilot blocked more than 4 million unwanted requests a day; it relies on scrapers not running JavaScript, which bot makers may work around.

ref.title: LWN.net, Anubis sends AI scraperbots to a well-deserved fate, July 2025
ref.finding: Anubis, an MIT-licensed tool, makes suspicious clients solve a proof-of-work challenge before reaching a site and has been adopted by GNOME, the Linux Kernel Mailing List archive, sourcehut and FFmpeg; a Duke University pilot blocked more than 4 million unwanted HTTP requests a day, with twelve people reporting problems in one week, usually because cookies were disabled. It works because most scraper bots do not run client-side JavaScript, and the article expects bot makers to find ways around it.

precedents.parallel: Site owners have long needed a way to tell crawlers which parts of a site to leave alone, because crawlers that visit a whole site can be a burden.
precedents.outcome: Martijn Koster defined the Robots Exclusion Protocol in 1994 and it became an IETF standard only in 2022; compliance is voluntary, and the standard says its rules are not a form of access authorization.

ref.title: Koster, Illyes, Zeller and Sassman, RFC 9309: Robots Exclusion Protocol, IETF 2022
ref.finding: The protocol, originally defined by Martijn Koster in 1994, lets service owners tell crawlers which parts of a site they may access, since it may be inconvenient for service owners if crawlers visit the entirety of their URI space; it was published as an IETF standard in September 2022, and its rules are not a form of access authorization.

nodes.label: Inflated AI claims mislead investors and customers
nodes.summary: Companies overstate what their AI can do to win money and customers. The US SEC fined two investment advisers $400,000 in total in March 2024 for claiming AI they did not use, and its chair said such AI washing hurts investors[1]. In 2025 it charged a startup founder with raising over $42 million on claims that his shopping app used AI to complete purchases, when, it alleges, contract employees entered the orders by hand[2], and found that the vast majority of drive-thru orders taken by one version of a restaurant-technology company's AI ordering product needed human intervention[3]. The FTC said one AI content detector sold as 98 percent accurate scored 53 percent on general content[4]. US investors filed 16 securities class actions classed as AI-related in 2025 and 15 in the first half of 2026; these are allegations, and of the 15, seven concerned AI development while five involved data centres and four AI infrastructure or hardware[5]. One audit of 100 German startups found AI claims without inspectable evidence or methodology, with claimed capabilities rarely matching the underlying systems[6]. Sanctions so far are modest: the advisers settled without admitting or denying the findings, and the drive-thru company paid no penalty[1][3].

refs.title: US Securities and Exchange Commission, SEC Charges Two Investment Advisers with Making False and Misleading Statements About Their Use of Artificial Intelligence, March 2024
refs.finding: Delphia (USA) Inc. claimed from 2019 to 2023 to use AI and machine learning that incorporated client data in its investment process, capabilities the SEC found it lacked; Global Predictions Inc. called itself the 'first regulated AI financial advisor' in 2023. Without admitting or denying the findings, they agreed to pay $225,000 and $175,000 in civil penalties, $400,000 in total. Chair Gary Gensler said: 'Such AI washing hurts investors.'

refs.title: US Securities and Exchange Commission, Litigation Release No. 26282, Alberto Saniger Mantinan, a/k/a Albert Saniger, April 2025
refs.finding: The SEC charged the founder and former CEO of Nate, Inc. with raising over $42 million by telling Seed and Series A investors that the app used automated technology that relied on AI to complete purchases without human involvement; it alleges Nate relied largely on contract employees who entered orders by hand and that the app could not use AI to complete purchases. The SEC seeks injunctions, an officer-and-director bar, disgorgement and civil penalties.

refs.title: US Securities and Exchange Commission, SEC Charges Restaurant-Technology Company Presto Automation for Misleading Statements About AI Product, January 2025
refs.finding: From November 2021 to May 2023 Presto made false and misleading statements about Presto Voice, its AI drive-thru ordering product: for a period the speech recognition in all deployed units was owned and operated by a third party, and in the version using its own technology the vast majority of orders required human intervention. Presto settled without admitting or denying the findings and paid no civil penalty, citing its cooperation and remediation.

refs.title: US Federal Trade Commission, FTC Order Requires Workado to Back Up Artificial Intelligence Detection Claims, April 2025
refs.finding: Workado advertised its AI Content Detector as '98 percent' accurate at telling AI-written from human-written text, but independent testing found 53 percent accuracy on general-purpose content; the FTC alleges the model was trained or fine-tuned only on academic content. The Bureau of Consumer Protection director said the product did no better than a coin toss.

refs.title: Cornerstone Research and Stanford Law School Securities Class Action Clearinghouse, Securities Class Action Filings: 2026 Midyear Assessment, July 2026
refs.finding: There were 15 AI-related filings in 2026 H1, against 16 in all of 2025 and 15 in 2024; of the 15, seven related to AI development, five involved data centres and four concerned AI infrastructure or hardware (three of which also concerned data centres). AI-related filings were 13% of core filings in 2026 H1. All involved claims under Section 10(b).

refs.title: Pranav, Hartmann and Lauscher, Auditing AI-Washing in German Startups: A Mixed-Methods Study of Marketing Claims and Perceptions, AIES 2026
refs.finding: An audit of 100 German startups with a seven-dimension codebook, plus 63 expert interviews, found three forms of exaggerated AI capability: claims without inspectable evidence, performance numbers without methodology and claims without acknowledged limits; claimed capabilities rarely matched the underlying systems, consumers who had met exaggerated claims withdrew trust from later AI marketing, and 38% of the sample were flagged for moderate or serious ethical concern. The authors recommend bringing startup AI claims under disclosure requirements and offering the codebook to regulators, investors and consumer-protection bodies.

nodes.control_note: Hype rewards any company that can claim the AI label, and investors and buyers rarely see what sits behind it. Regulators can demand evidence for AI claims and punish false ones, but the cases brought so far are few and carried modest penalties.

actions.action: Charge firms that claim AI they do not have
actions.evidence: The SEC has brought AI washing cases against investment advisers, a restaurant-technology company and a startup founder, with civil penalties of $400,000 in total in the 2024 adviser cases.

ref.title: US Securities and Exchange Commission, SEC Charges Two Investment Advisers with Making False and Misleading Statements About Their Use of Artificial Intelligence, March 2024
ref.finding: Delphia (USA) Inc. claimed from 2019 to 2023 to use AI and machine learning that incorporated client data in its investment process, capabilities the SEC found it lacked; Global Predictions Inc. called itself the 'first regulated AI financial advisor' in 2023. Without admitting or denying the findings, they agreed to pay $225,000 and $175,000 in civil penalties, $400,000 in total. Chair Gary Gensler said: 'Such AI washing hurts investors.'

actions.action: Require evidence behind AI accuracy claims
actions.evidence: A final FTC order bars one AI detector maker from claiming accuracy unless competent and reliable evidence backs the claim; it binds only that company.

ref.title: US Federal Trade Commission, FTC Approves Final Order against Workado, LLC, Which Misrepresented the Accuracy of its Artificial Intelligence Content Detection Product, August 2025
ref.finding: The final order, approved 3-0 on 28 August 2025, bars Workado from claims about the effectiveness of any AI content detection product unless they are not misleading and backed by competent and reliable evidence, and requires it to keep that evidence, notify eligible customers and file compliance reports one year after the order and annually for three more years.

precedents.parallel: A startup raised money on a technology it said it had built, while much of the work ran on other companies' machines, as the SEC later found at one AI drive-thru company.
precedents.outcome: The SEC charged Theranos, Elizabeth Holmes and Ramesh Balwani with fraud after the company raised more than $700 million while most patient tests ran on modified or commercial analyzers made by others; Holmes settled with a $500,000 penalty and a 10-year bar from serving as an officer or director of a public company.

ref.title: US Securities and Exchange Commission, Theranos, CEO Holmes, and Former President Balwani Charged With Massive Fraud, March 2018
ref.finding: Theranos raised more than $700 million from investors while claiming its portable analyzer ran comprehensive blood tests from finger-drop samples; it could complete only a small number of tests and most patient tests ran on modified or commercial analyzers made by others. It projected over $100 million in 2014 revenue and made a little more than $100,000. Holmes agreed, without admitting or denying the allegations, to a $500,000 penalty, a 10-year officer-and-director bar and the return of 18.9 million shares.

nodes.label: AI satellite monitoring exposes hidden fishing fleets
nodes.summary: Machine learning run on radar and optical satellite images can find ships that do not broadcast their positions. Using imagery from 2017 to 2021, one Nature study by Global Fishing Watch and university researchers found about 75 percent of the world's industrial fishing vessels are not publicly tracked, much of that fishing around Africa and south Asia, and more than 25 percent of transport and energy vessel activity is missing from public tracking[1]. Applying AI models to radar images of 1,380 marine protected areas that ban industrial fishing, one Science study found 78.5% recorded no commercial fishing and strongly protected areas had nine times fewer fishing vessels per square kilometre than unprotected coastal waters[2]; position broadcasts missed almost 90% of the vessels radar found, and the study cannot tell whether the areas keep boats out or were placed where little fishing happens[3]. A companion study of a wider set of coastal protected areas, including areas that still allow some fishing, detected industrial fishing in 47% of them from 2022 to 2024, with two-thirds of the vessels absent from public monitoring and estimated fishing effort 28% higher once they were counted[4][5].

refs.title: Global Fishing Watch, New research harnesses AI and satellite imagery to reveal the expanding footprint of human activity at sea, January 2024
refs.finding: A study in Nature by researchers at Global Fishing Watch, the University of Wisconsin-Madison, Duke, UC Santa Barbara and SkyTruth combined vessel GPS data with five years (2017 to 2021) of radar and optical satellite imagery, 2 million gigabytes, and used machine learning to judge which vessels were likely fishing. About 75 percent of the world's industrial fishing vessels are not publicly tracked, with much of that fishing around Africa and south Asia, and more than 25 percent of transport and energy vessel activity is missing from public tracking. Not all boats are legally required to broadcast their position; the monitoring is freely available to all nations.

refs.title: National Geographic Pristine Seas (EurekAlert), New research: Satellite imagery detects illegal fishing activity, shows strict protections work, July 2025
refs.finding: Raynor et al., 'Little-to-no industrial fishing occurs in fully and highly protected marine areas', Science: of 1,380 marine protected areas studied, 78.5% recorded no commercial fishing; among those where satellites detected illegal fishing, 82% averaged under 24 hours of it a year; strongly protected areas had nine times fewer fishing vessels per square kilometre than unprotected coastal areas. About five billion AIS positions were paired with radar images, and AI models developed by Global Fishing Watch detected most fishing vessels over 15 metres, including those not broadcasting their location.

refs.title: UC Santa Barbara, The Current, Satellites show that strictly protected marine areas exclude industrial fishing, July 2025
refs.finding: Radar imagery analysed with AI found dark vessels absent from AIS, which missed almost 90% of the vessels detected by radar. The study does not establish why fishing is absent: further research is needed to tell whether protected areas exclude vessels or were designated where fishing demand is low. Lead author Jennifer Raynor suggests satellite tracking can help countries predict illegal activity and target patrols, and that resource-limited nations could partner with nonprofits such as Global Fishing Watch.

refs.title: Seguin, Le Manach, Devillers, Velez and Mouillot, Global patterns and drivers of untracked industrial fishing in coastal marine protected areas, Science 2025
refs.finding: Combining vessel GPS data with satellite imagery, the authors detected industrial fishing in 47% of coastal marine protected areas worldwide from 2022 to 2024; two-thirds of detected vessels did not appear in public monitoring systems, rising to 80% in the strictest management category. Counting untracked vessels raised estimated fishing effort inside the areas by 28%, and vessel presence depended mainly on an area's size and remoteness, not its management category.

refs.title: NPR (Alabama Public Radio), New technology shows how illegal fishing has impacted oceans across the world, July 2025
refs.finding: Raynor's team found almost 80% of protected areas had no industrial fishing; Raphael Seguin's study looked at a larger group of protected areas that still allow some fishing and found industrial fishing in about half of them, two-thirds of it untracked. Seguin said the satellite technology could help enforcement by tracking illegal fishing in real time.

limiters.evidence: The AI models used in one 2025 study detect most fishing vessels over 15 metres, not every vessel.

enablers.action: Send real-time fishing alerts to patrols
enablers.counters: Seeing boats does not remove them
enablers.evidence: In one case reported by the platform that issued the alerts, Argentina's Coast Guard redirected a nearby vessel after speed and fishing alerts on a foreign fishing vessel inside its exclusive economic zone, and the vessel paid the fine and operational costs.

ref.title: Skylight (Allen Institute for AI), Real-Time Intelligence Powers Argentina's Fight Against Illegal Fishing, 2025
ref.finding: A speed alert flagged the Vanuatu-flagged XINRUN 579 sailing under 6 knots inside Argentina's exclusive economic zone, a speed local rules associate with trawling, and a fishing alert followed about 40 minutes later; analysts redirected a nearby Coast Guard vessel, the vessel was intercepted, and it paid the fine and the authorities' operational costs. The account comes from the platform that issued the alerts.

precedents.parallel: Near-real-time alerts from satellite imagery let a government with weak enforcement aim its inspectors at illegal activity across a vast area.
precedents.outcome: Using clouds that blocked detection as a natural experiment, one study of 2006 to 2016 found monitoring and enforcement curbed Amazon deforestation, avoiding the clearing of an average of 27 thousand square kilometres of forest a year, without pushing clearing into neighbouring areas.

ref.title: Assunção, Gandour and Rocha, DETERring Deforestation in the Amazon: Environmental Monitoring and Law Enforcement, Climate Policy Initiative Working Paper 003, 2019
ref.finding: DETER, in use since 2004, processes satellite imagery and issues near-real-time deforestation alerts to target environmental enforcement in the Amazon. Using clouds that limit its detection as an instrument across 2006 to 2016, the authors find monitoring and enforcement curbed deforestation, avoiding the clearing of an average of 27 thousand square kilometres of forest a year, with results not driven by displacement into neighbouring areas.

links.why: When AI makes each task cheaper and faster, employers expect more output, so the time saved fills with extra work.
When cheaper tasks raise demand and expectations, work grows rather than shrinks, which can keep hiring going instead of cutting jobs.
When AI lifts novices to near-expert output, firms need fewer junior hires to do the beginner work.
As AI removes the bottom rung of careers, more people lose earned income, raising pressure for cash support such as basic income.
If AI returns flow to owners of compute rather than workers, taxing and sharing that wealth becomes the obvious remedy.
People who build by prompting and accept output without reading it can ship polished-looking work that others must then fix.
Building by describing what you want lets anyone reproduce existing code and content without the skill that once protected it.
Hollow AI output that gets published adds more machine-made text to the web, which later models then train on.
Letting AI do homework skips the practice of working problems out, so students build less of the reasoning they need later.
Offloading judgement to AI weakens the habit of checking, so experts lose skill they then lack when the AI is gone.
A model tuned to flatter and agree feels like an always supportive friend, drawing people into heavier emotional reliance on it.
A model that always agrees removes the push-back that makes people test their ideas, so they question their beliefs less.
Agents that find and patch bugs before attackers do close holes faster, which could make critical software much harder to breach.
Agent-run intrusions push defenders to automate auditing too, and if they adopt it faster, critical software gets harder to breach.
The same automated bug hunting that finds real flaws lets anyone file machine-made security reports, many fabricated, at volunteer maintainers.
Tools that rebuild readable source from binaries also make it easy to lift and reuse someone else's code.
The same cheap voice and face cloning used in scams can fake candidates, though in elections it has mostly not deceived.
Faster basic research supplies the models and methods that diagnostic tools are built on.
Agents running most of an intrusion with little human input show AI acting at speeds where overseers cannot step in.
Each gain in output comes from running more models, and that extra use adds to the electricity data centres draw.
When readers stop at the AI summary, they rarely click through, so the sites behind it lose visits and income.
When AI answers keep readers away, sites lose the income to keep publishing, so less fresh human writing reaches future training data.
Readers who take a summary instead of checking the source stop weighing evidence themselves, offloading judgement to the model.
As clients swap paid artists for generators, more work comes from the same models, so output grows more alike.
Generators trained on artists' work copy their styles cheaply, so clients switch from paid commissions to the generator.
Firms acting on the same models react to the same signal at once, and money-managing agents could pull deposits the same way.
People who cannot read code accept whatever the model writes, so known vulnerability patterns ship without anyone spotting them.
Generated code full of known flaws leaves more weak points, which attack agents can find and exploit at machine speed.
The same cheap, personalised scam writing pairs with cloned voices and faces to make impersonation fraud more convincing.
When most traffic is automated and accounts may not be people, bot networks can push election fakes at scale.
Models that out-argue humans with a little personal data give campaigns and propagandists a cheap way to scale election manipulation.
Conversations with a model that lower belief in conspiracies make voters less likely to accept fakes and false election stories.
Because companions really do ease loneliness, people come back often, and heavy emotional use turns into dependence.
Generated papers entering the scientific record put model output into trusted sources that future models train on.
The same learning methods that crack stalled research problems also produce weather models that beat physics forecasts at lower compute.
The same generators used to make nude fakes of real women and schoolchildren are turned to making abuse imagery of children.
Cheap monitoring tools give the few states and firms that own them more control, adding to their power.
Lawyers who trust an AI answer without checking the original source end up filing cases the model invented.
Because only a few firms and states hold frontier compute and models, those governments can ration access and use it as leverage.
When access to chips and models depends on political alignment, countries rely on others' models, which may carry hidden behaviour.
A downloaded model with hidden behaviour or code that runs on load gives attackers a way into the systems that use it.
Cheaply hijacked routers, cameras and controllers give automated attackers footholds and botnets to run whole intrusions at machine speed.
When anyone can upload and download model weights, hidden backdoors or malware in a model spread with it and cannot be recalled.
Heavy companion use replaces time with people, so users get less practice handling friction in real relationships.
Doubling data-centre electricity use adds emissions and delays decarbonisation, weighing on the cost side of AI's net climate effect.
Young people locked out of the first career rung have a direct grievance that can turn into anger at AI firms.
Returns that flow to compute owners rather than workers feed public anger at AI companies, which could turn into sabotage or attacks.
As AI work gets cheaper, demand and expectations grow faster than time saved, so people take on more tasks.
As capability becomes a cheap commodity, more groups can train and release capable models anyone can download and run.
Content credentials and watermarks record where media came from, giving readers a way to trace a claim, though labels strip easily.
As generated video and music fill everyday feeds, telling them from human work needs credentials and watermarks that mark their origin.
Handing some tasks to AI leaves the rest of the job, and freed time fills with extra work rather than rest.
Shared protocols let agents move money with less human approval per step, so many could withdraw deposits at once on one rumour.
The EU AI Act requires providers and deployers to take measures supporting staff AI literacy, turning a useful skill into a legal duty.
Free, capable models anyone can run mean users need not rent from a few owners of compute, spreading power more widely.
Models that talk supportively with people in distress can, with a few reframed prompts, be steered into giving self-harm guidance instead.
Long, responsive dialogue can shift what people believe, talking some out of conspiracies while an agreeable model builds them up for others.
An always-available companion that listens like a person eases loneliness in short doses but invites heavy emotional dependence over time.
Clear, tailored summaries help people understand hard questions, but the same convenience stops them reading sources, so errors spread unchecked.
Offloading thinking to a model frees attention, but the same offloading lets people skip planning, checking and reflecting.
Models that turn binaries back into readable source keep old software alive, and also make game cheats and exploits easier to build.
Agents that find real vulnerabilities in code can patch them for defenders or exploit them for attackers running intrusions.
A model tuned to agree keeps affirming a vulnerable user's ideas over long chats, so fears can grow into elaborate delusions.
People who stop checking and reflecting on their work stop exercising critical thinking, so the skill weakens.
When fewer people learn skills or share knowledge publicly, the flow of fresh human data that keeps models healthy dries up.
When generators take the paid commissions, fewer people see a reason to learn the craft or stay in the profession.
Letting AI do homework skips the planning, checking and reflecting the task was meant to train, so those habits fade.

Once researchers without coding skills can build software by describing it, they can write their own tools and agents to run instruments.

Models trained on single-cell data are being adapted to predict how cells respond to gene perturbations, a step towards picking drug targets, though a 2025 benchmark found none yet beat simple baselines.

AI that can explain and solve schoolwork teaches well inside a guarded tutor, but does the thinking for students who outsource homework.
